find them at all). Now:

- the Profiler dock offers the same Start/Stop actions as buttons
  beside the filter (shared QActions, so menu and buttons stay in
  sync);
- the actions are always enabled and explain themselves in the console
  when the state is wrong, instead of being greyed with the reason
  buried in a tooltip;
- the empty dock teaches the choreography in its status line rather
  than showing a bare table;
- profileStop's 'setopt --disasm ext' is reverted once the save has
  run — it previously leaked, silently switching the Disassembly
  pane's rendering for the rest of the session.

events.title: editor: insert a call's assembler binding from the reference dock
events.message:
editor: insert a call's assembler binding from the reference dock

The reference dock's list now offers the reverse trip as well: pick a
GEMDOS/BIOS/XBIOS call and the 'Insert binding into editor' button (or
the row's context menu) drops its canonical binding into the source
above the cursor's line — argument pushes in reverse declaration order
with the prototype's parameter names as placeholders, the function word
with its name in a comment, the trap, and the caller-side cleanup.
Pexec's fixed three-long layout, Mshrink/Frename's reserved zero word
and Dbmsg's literal 5 keep their documented shapes. One undo step;
a no-op when the current tab is not a source editor.

OsCallBinding parses the table's prototypes to generate the text, and
two whole-table invariants pin the generator against the data rather
than against hand-written expectations: the emitted pushes total every
entry's stackBytes, and every emitted binding scans back through
OsCallScan to the call it came from. The round-trip surfaced that the
scanner's 8-line bound cut off Flopfmt's nine-argument sequence; the
bound is now a sanity cap (the non-push stop is the real guard) sized
for the widest documented call.

events.title: editor: name the OS call a trap line makes, in the instruction dock
events.message:
editor: name the OS call a trap line makes, in the instruction dock

The instruction reference dock now covers the OS layer too: a new
OsCallRef table (53 GEMDOS + 46 XBIOS + 12 BIOS calls of the TOS
1.x/2.x set, with C prototype, d0 result, availability floor and stack
layout per call) and an OsCallScan resolver that reads the idiom —
scan back from a trap #1/#13/#14 line for the function-number push
(numeric, hex, symbolic or clr.w), and collect the argument pushes
above it. Cursor on a trap line or any push feeding it shows the call
being made and what it is being called with ('Calling with: #msg'),
not the generic TRAP/MOVE entry; a register-pushed number still falls
back to TRAP. The OS entries join the same dock list after the CPU
families, so the filter searches both.

Facts verified against tos.hyp (GPLv2) and Atari's 1986 GEMDOS manual;
prose is our own. The table already carries the corrections the
research surfaced: 7 is Crawcin, not Cnecin (the demos are fixed);
Mshrink and Frename push a reserved zero word; Maddalt/Mxalloc are
GEMDOS 0.19 (TOS 2.01+); Blitmode is officially TOS 1.02+ and fails
safe via a dispatcher side-effect.

Tests: 20 unit tests (table shape + the scanner's idiom matrix,
including a label sharing its line with a push) and a GUI test driving
the dock through the demo's Cconws sequence.

events.title: control: per-session token on the remote-control socket
events.message:
control: per-session token on the remote-control socket

Localhost-only still means every local user on a shared machine, and the
discovery file told any of them the port. A listening IDE now generates a
per-session token and requires it as the first line on every connection
('auth <token>'; anything else is an error and a drop), and the discovery
file carries it — written owner-only (0600), in an owner-only directory
(0700), so the people who can read it are exactly the people who could
already drive the IDE from its own session.

The shim takes --token or PIST_CONTROL_TOKEN, falling back to the
discovery file's third field, so zero-configuration operation is
unchanged: with the IDE started locally, pist-mcp still needs no flags at
all. listen(0) no longer publishes, so test runs stop overwriting a real
IDE's file (the test side effect the file had since it was introduced).

Verified: the file lands 0600 with port and token, a raw connection
saying anything but the token gets 'error auth required' and a drop, and
a flagless pist-mcp finds and authenticates against the running IDE.
tst_remotecontrol gains the two gate tests (wrong token, command before
auth) and every existing session authenticates.

events.title: control: three correctness items, and label breakpoints that always resolve
events.message:
control: three correctness items, and label breakpoints that always resolve

- read returns the document as JSON {path, text}: the block protocol ends
  on a lone '.' line, which assembly source can contain — raw text could
  truncate there. Errors on block-framed verbs (read, readmem, disasm,
  cmd) go back as blocks too, so a block wait never sits out its timeout
  on a plain error line.
- open answers 'error could not open' when the path never opened, via a
  new openPathQuiet: the interactive open shows a modal on failure, and
  a modal nobody can dismiss (offscreen, or an agent at the other end)
  hung the verb forever.
- profile stop blocks until the save is parsed (new profileResultsReady
  signal), so results called right after are this run's data, never the
  previous run's; results now carry numeric counts with the same
  tie-break order as the profiler table and gutter.
- pist_problems gains severity: the resolved diagnostics live in a member
  (severity never reached the tree widget — it was only a text colour).
- breakpoint-by-label resolves through a base-independent nextCodeLine
  over the listing (LineMap/ProgramLineMap): a label on its own line has
  no code there, so the toggle lands on the first code line at or after
  the definition — before Run too, where the program map is unresolved.
  An equate finds nothing and is a clean error.
- The stop verb, lost to an edit slip in the previous round, is restored
  and pinned in tst_mcp alongside the other pre-existing mappings.

Verified live: open failure is a prompt error, read comes back as JSON,
'count' resolves to hello.s:22 (not the bare label at :21) and the
breakpoint fires there, and profile stop returns only with parsed
results in hand.

events.title: aga: a palette write rides with the next present — the outgoing big picture no longer wears the incoming colours
events.message:
aga: a palette write rides with the next present — the outgoing big picture no longer wears the incoming colours

A1200 on v0.9.28: "almost 100% there", except a big picture "takes a second
or so to unload, like it leaves some pixels behind" before the next one or
the 3D view. Filmed at 25 fps in amiberry (-DFRUA_AUTOPLAY into a generated
design whose entry event is a bigpic, x11grab across the dismissing Return):
four frames before the screen settles — 1.4 s of the OUTGOING picture in the
DUNGEON's palette (black with magenta/orange speckle), the walk screen, then
1.6 s with the 3D view blacked out, then the final frame.

On a hardware-palette backend a CLUT write recolours the screen at once; the
pixels that want those colours arrive at the next present, a second or more
later here. #20 (sky/floor flash) was one instance fixed for one caller;
this is the rule. The #8 event-tail hold does not help — it holds pixels,
the palette still landed, and it is armed only for walk steps anyway.

dsp_backend_t.palette_with_present (last field; AGA sets it, video.cfg
agapalsync=off opts out for a hardware A/B): qd_set_palette keeps the
logical palette current and remembers a pending window, forwarded right
after the backend present, after a rect present, on a clean present, from
the engine's event pump when no hold is outstanding, and from jt1067 after
a colour-cycle commit. The title blackout supersedes anything pending, and
qd_set_palette_deferred routes straight through on such a backend. Not the
Nova (its ~0.5 s present is a different trade, untestable off the card);
TT is eligible and left alone.

After: picture in its own colours -> walk -> final. Both the recoloured
picture and the black view hole are gone; the picture's own cycling runs
throughout. The first version FROZE the SSI title's star animation — its
wait loop cycles the palette without presenting or pumping events — and the
title capture caught it (one colour-count signature where the release shows
five); hence the flush in jt1067. Title roll signature-identical to v0.9.28
again. Host tests green; ST and ECS build.

events.title: debug: shift the stderr dispatch watermark as lines are consumed
events.message:
debug: shift the stderr dispatch watermark as lines are consumed

Handlers run by the stderr line loop (the entry banner arming queued
commands) can dispatch while the buffer still holds un-consumed lines;
m_stderrAtDispatch then pointed past bytes the loop was about to remove,
so the trailing "> " of every later stop compared smaller than the
watermark and onPrompt never fired. On stderr-prompt builds (macOS CI)
that left every MainWindow session stuck at the entry stop. Shift the
watermark down with each consumed line, and consume the prompt on fire
so later stderr noise cannot re-fire it once the watermark has moved.

events.title: debug: chop the stale stderr prompt at command dispatch
events.message:
debug: chop the stale stderr prompt at command dispatch

On macOS Hatari's readline writes the prompt to stderr, not stdout, so every
command leaves the stderr buffer ending in "> ". The completion gate compared
buffer size against size-at-dispatch — and once a stale trailing prompt sat
there, a later stop's identical tail was indistinguishable from it, so
post-resume stops (breakpoints, watchpoints) were never detected while
command completion survived via the output-quiet settle path. Chopping the
stale prompt at dispatch makes any later trailing prompt provably new.

events.title: Address review: keep the adapter check off a guest's placeholder machine
events.message:
Address review: keep the adapter check off a guest's placeholder machine

A guest waits on a bare local machine until the host's bundle builds the
real one, so requiring the four-player adapter before the transfer turned
away every documented guest of a three- or four-player session. Check the
ports on the machines that actually run the game instead: the host's, and a
guest's once it has staged the bundle. The four-player session test now
starts its guests from bare machines and a plain configuration, which is
what the documented guest command produces.

Refuse a host allow-list that can never fill the session. An unlisted source
is turned away and one source holds one port, so a short or repeated list
left the host waiting for guests that were categorically blocked; take a
complete list or none at all. An Internet guest also adopts the player count
from the invitation it pastes, since the row that sets it belongs to the
host.

Update the browser checks and the remaining help and documentation for
protocol version 3: the layout assertions, the record walk that now opens
with a controller port, the browser queue's packet size, and the
--netplay-bind help that still called the endpoint two-player.

events.title: emu: content-probe Hatari capabilities on Windows
events.message:
emu: content-probe Hatari capabilities on Windows

Windows Hatari answers --version and -h by allocating a NEW console and
printing there (options.c Opt_ShowVersion -> Win_ForceCon), then waits for
Enter in Main_ErrorExit — a process probe pops a console window, stalls for
the timeout, and returns nothing, leaving every capability false and the
HRDB fork undetected. On Windows, probe the binary's content instead: the
option-table strings and the Hatari vX.Y.Z banner are all in the file.
Toolchain skips process-probing hatari there for the same reason, and
--diagnose falls back to the content-probed version.

events.title: release: 0.6.1
events.message:
release: 0.6.1

A maintenance release: floppy images, Windows, and the debug loop.

- Floppy images: real MSA read/write, 64-bit geometry math, duplicate
  entry names survive update, and a foreign disk asks before PiST's
  canonical 720 KiB layout rewrites it.
- Windows: files are no longer CRLF-converted on save — a floppy entry
  used to grow a carriage return each time it was edited.
- Debugger: breakpoints arm on code lines only (never data/bss),
  clearing breakpoints re-arms watchpoints, and the HRDB backend gains
  a command watchdog with a late-reply guard.
- Remote control: a use-after-free on peer disconnect is fixed, and a
  second blocking command is refused while one is waiting.
- Sprite editor: undo addresses the phase it was made in, and the
  readers reject hostile .pim/PI1/NEO input instead of trusting it.
- Build: an unparseable vasm listing fails the build rather than
  reporting success with no line map.

events.title: Play netplay with three and four players through the adapter
events.message:
Play netplay with three and four players through the adapter

Give every netplay participant one controller port, so a session can drive
the two game ports and both sockets of the passive parallel-port four-player
adapter. The adapter is wiring with no host peripheral behind it, so it
crosses the setup bundle and joins the machine fingerprint while a printer
or sampler stays refused.

Player 1 hosts and every other player connects to it, which reuses the star
topology spectators already ride on: the host relays each port's input to
every other player, so only the host needs a reachable endpoint and guests
never address each other. A host's socket or iroh endpoint becomes a
listener that admits each guest and spectator and hands out a per-peer
transport, and the connection holds one link per peer. Every player is
seated before frame zero, since a latecomer could not reproduce the frames
already executed. A caller that cannot be seated is refused on its own link
without ending the game for the players.

Protocol version 3 names the port each input record belongs to, carries the
session's player count, and acknowledges every player separately; a record
grows to 32 bytes and the largest packet to 1160, still one ordinary
datagram. Prediction, confirmation and replay now run over one input per
port, and the spectator feed carries the port count so a spectator of a
four-player game replays it correctly. A guest releases its local history on
the host's acknowledgement alone, because the host is the only route to the
other players and keeps each port's inputs until the last link has them.

Direct UDP admits a guest by its first control packet: the host names the
guest addresses it will accept, or names none and admits any source that
presents the session ID, as spectators always could. Internet mode seats
each guest on the next free port and names it in the offer, while a
direct-IP guest asks for the port it was configured for.

The launcher gains a Players row, the command line --netplay-players and a
repeatable --netplay-peer, and the local smoke check a --players flag.
Browser sessions stay two-player: a page has no parallel port to plug the
adapter into.

events.title: ui: re-arm watchpoints when clearing breakpoints via the menu
events.message:
ui: re-arm watchpoints when clearing breakpoints via the menu

clearAllBreakpoints sent b all (EmulatorHost::clearBreakpoints) while keeping
m_watchpoints. Watchpoints are armed as b conditions (Hatari has no data
watchpoints), so b all disarmed them on the emulator too — the panel kept
listing watchpoints that were dead on the host until the next arm. Re-derive
the host through armBreakpoints() instead: it clears then re-arms from the
models, so the cleared breakpoints go and the retained watchpoints come back.

Pre-existing, not introduced by the dock/menu split; no new test because the
only observable is a live watchpoint firing after a clear (disproportionate to
manufacture) and the fix delegates to the already-exercised armBreakpoints
re-sync. Full gui suite 56/56.

events.title: emu: remove dead capability/socket code and fix stale docs
events.message:
emu: remove dead capability/socket code and fix stale docs

Four P3 cleanups (C7, C10, C11, C5) — dead code and comments that contradict
the code they describe.

C7: HatariCapabilities::hasParse was probed (help.contains("--parse")) but never
read, while SessionConfig::toArgv emits --parse unconditionally. Deleted the dead
field and its probe line. Gating --parse on it would need caps plumbed into
toArgv (which has none); supported Hatari always has --parse, so the field was
purely vestigial.

C10: EmbedSocket::setFloppyImage had no callers (the live path is the backend's
own setFloppyImage, which uses setopt + symlink staging, not this hatari-option +
backslash-escape variant the live path deliberately avoids). Deleted it.

C11: the disasmRe comment claimed the register dump's byte-less inline
instruction is "deliberately not matched," but the regex's byte group is *
(optional), so such a line would match. Corrected the comment: no-byte lines
never reach this parser (parseDisassembly runs on `d` output, where every line
carries bytes; the `r` inline instruction is parsed by pcLineRe).

C5: IDebugBackend::pause() documented the native path as `hatari-stop`, but the
implementation arms `hatari-debug b pc ! 0 :once` because hatari-stop only clears
the VBL loop's active flag and never enters the debugger — a fixed wedge the doc
invited re-breaking. Corrected to name the real command and say why.

Build clean; full suite 11/11 (behaviour unchanged — deletions had no callers,
doc fixes touch no logic).

events.title: emu: share the backend session env and fix native refresh's triple error
events.message:
emu: share the backend session env and fix native refresh's triple error

C3 (partial): three of the four transport-lifecycle drift points between the
native and HRDB backends, where the duplication was genuine and the behaviour
identical.

Session environment: EmulatorHost::start and HrdbBackend::start built the same
QProcessEnvironment (HOME/XDG_CONFIG_HOME config isolation + the embedded
display's X11 vars) verbatim. Extracted makeSessionEnvironment into
DebugBackend.h beside the existing shared isBreakpointCommand; both call it.
Pure move.

refresh() guard: HrdbBackend::refresh bails with one "No emulator session is
running." when not running; EmulatorHost::refresh had no guard and enqueued
three snapshot commands, each of which dispatches and emits that same error —
three identical errors from one refresh. Added the matching guard to native.
This is a behaviour change, so it is pinned by refreshWithoutSessionEmitsOneError
(construct both backends, refresh with no session, assert exactly one error
each) — fork-free, and mutation-proven (removing the native guard makes it three).

Memory char column: HrdbBackend::formatMemoryDump inlined the printable-range
test that the shared renderMemoryChars already owns (MemoryView uses it too).
Now renders the char column through the shared function so the range cannot
drift. Output identical.

Left with rationale (in the review record): HRDB's inline start-reset (naming it
resetTransport is cosmetic; the reset happens), the resume() filter (over
per-backend Pending types), and the setFloppyImage prologue (its shared helpers
are already extracted; the dispatch differs).

tst_debug 22/22, tst_emulatorhost 20/20, full suite 11/11. HrdbBackend's start
env-move and formatMemoryDump reuse are compile + construction verified only
(tst_hrdb skips without the hrdb-main fork); its refresh guard is exercised by
the parity test.

events.message:
ui: fix import choice, Clear all, and phase-removal index

Three correctness issues from the review, each with a mutation-proven test.

Finding 7 / D2: importFile did Q_UNUSED(append), so the import dialog's
Add-frame vs Replace choice did nothing — both added a sheet. Honour it:
Replace resets to a fresh-editor document (the previously-dead
replaceDocument) sized to the default 32x32 staged phase with the current
palette kind, before the shared sheet path adds the import; Add frame keeps
the document and adds another sheet. Sizing the replacement to the imported
sheet instead regressed two placement tests — caught by the full suite, not
the new test, which only checks sheet counts.

A6: the breakpoints dock's Clear-all button enables when either list is
non-empty but was wired to clearAllBreakpoints, which cleared only
breakpoints, and refreshBreakpointMarkers never touches the panel's
watchpoint rows — so a lone watchpoint survived. Added clearAllDebugTargets
(clears both models, updates both panel lists, and b-all's the host;
watchpoints are armed as b conditions so b all removes them). The Run-menu
Clear Breakpoints action keeps the breakpoint-only handler.

D3: removePhase only clamped m_currentPhase's upper bound, so removing a
phase before the current one silently retargeted the selection (removeFrame
does the shift). Added the else-if fix-up. refreshPhases re-selected the
widget's own stale row; it now re-derives from m_doc.currentPhase() like
refreshFrames.

events.title: image: reject hostile .pim input at load
events.message:
image: reject hostile .pim input at load

Four load-time paths trusted the file; all closed at the single parse-time
choke point so no downstream reader has to re-guard.

pixelsFromJson allocates cellW*cellH from the *declared* cell size, not from
the pixels present, so an empty pixels array still demands the full buffer.
Cell size was already capped but the counts of sheets/phases/frames/layers
were not, and per-array caps multiply into a huge worst case. Bound the total
pixel allocation against the input byte size instead: a real .pim spends at
least one JSON byte per pixel so it can never declare more pixels than it has
bytes, while a hostile file can. fromJson rejects the moment the budget would
go negative; pixelsFromJson also stops allocating once it is spent (bounding
the within-frame layer explosion before rejection). Modest count caps bound
the container arrays.

phase.sheet was read raw and currentSheetIndex() returns it verbatim when >=0,
so sheets().at(sheet) indexed past the end (assert-only QList::at, UB in
Release). Clamp it to -1 at load; qBound sheet width/height to the ST screen
(silently mis-sized composeSheet before). loadSheetPixels gated on
QFileInfo::exists, true for /dev/zero/FIFOs/dirs, then readAll()ed the JSON
path — require a regular file (which is what fixes the hang) and keep a
generous 64 MiB size backstop (PNG/IFF sheets are variable-size, so no tight
per-format cap).

A phase with an empty frames array fell back to blankFrame(), which sizes its
buffer from the *previous* document (still the 32x32 constructor default mid-
load, since m_phases is only reassigned at the end) — so a 320x200 phase got a
1024-int composite and ImageCanvas::rebuildImage indexed pixels.at(y*width()+x)
to 63999 on it: OOB in Release. Build the fallback through frameFromJson with
the phase's own cell size instead, so the composite matches width()*height().

tst_image gains pimRejectsPixelAmplification, pimClampsSheetReference and
pimEmptyFramesSizedToPhase; mutation-proven per mechanism (removing the budget
check, the frame cap, the sheet clamp, or reverting the empty-frame fallback
each fails its test). 36/36, full suite 11/11.

events.title: tests: run two sessions on one EmulatorHost
events.message:
tests: run two sessions on one EmulatorHost

resetTransport() exists solely so a second session on the same object does
not inherit the first one's queue, buffers, owed prompts or pending
timers, and every one of the suite's fifteen host.start() sites built a
fresh EmulatorHost, so the reset had never run in anger.

Session 1 is ended in the shape this actually broke once (arms queued,
Continue at the entry stop before they flushed, then Stop), which is the
only shape that leaves anything observable behind: stop() already clears
the queue, the in-flight flag, both timers and the embed socket, so a
session ending cleanly leaves nothing the reset owns, and the first two
drafts of this test passed with resetTransport() reduced to return.

The surviving m_continueWhenIdle fires when dispatchNext() next finds the
queue empty, which in session 2 is after its first command's reply — so
isStopped() is asserted there rather than at the entry stop, where it
holds either way. With the reset deleted the test now fails as intended:
'session 2 resumed itself after its first command'.

19/19 in the suite, 11/11 overall.

events.title: build: read floppy entries by cluster so duplicate names survive update
events.message:
build: read floppy entries by cluster so duplicate names survive update

B9 (P3): FAT allows two directory entries with the same 8.3 name (foreign
images; PiST's own uniqueName11 never makes them). updateImage re-read each
existing entry via readFileRaw(raw, entry.path, ...), a name lookup that always
returns the first match — so both same-named entries got the first's bytes and
the second's content was silently lost on every update.

Entry now carries the leaf cluster (listDir sets it from the parsed dir entry),
and updateImage reads each file via readChain(raw, geo, entry.cluster, ...) —
its own bytes, not the first name-match's. writeImage canonicalises the
duplicate to a numbered name on rewrite, so both contents survive as distinct
entries.

Test floppyUpdatePreservesDuplicateNames writes A.TXT/B.TXT, hand-edits B's
root-dir entry name to duplicate A (keeping its cluster and bytes), updates, and
asserts both "first" and "second" survive. Mutation-proven (name lookup collapses
the second to the first). The existing floppyUpdateAddsAndRemoves guards the
normal path. tst_parsers 36/36.
events.author: idontwantyourspamthanks

events.title: image: re-mesh the loaded composite from its layers
events.message:
image: re-mesh the loaded composite from its layers

E12 (P3): frameFromJson loaded the composite straight from the stored "pixels"
field and left it authoritative over the layers. For a well-formed file they
agree, but a crafted or corrupt .pim whose "pixels" disagree with its "layers"
displayed the stored composite and then jumped to the merged layers on the first
repaint (which remeshes) — one image on load, another after any edit.

Now fromJson recomputes each frame's composite as mergedPixel over its layers
after building them, so load and first-paint agree and the layers are the single
source of truth. A no-op for well-formed files. Done in fromJson (a member)
rather than the free frameFromJson because mergedPixel is private. Also fixed
the "v1 shape" comment: v1 files are rejected outright, so a composite-only
frame is just a frame with no "layers" array, not a legacy format.

Test pimReMeshesCompositeFromLayers loads a frame whose stored composite (9,9,9,9)
disagrees with its layer (1,2,3,4) and asserts the loaded composite is the merge.
Mutation-proven (dropping the re-mesh leaves the 9s). tst_image 41/41.

events.title: image: harden format and document readers against hostile input
events.message:
image: harden format and document readers against hostile input

Four P3s in the untrusted-input / OOB family (same as finding 13).

IFF nPlanes (E5): nPlanes is a raw BMHD byte and the decode does
`stIndices[...] |= 1 << plane` for plane < nPlanes, so a value >= 31 is an
undefined shift and 5..255 silently mis-decodes. Reject nPlanes < 1 || > 4
(ST ILBM is 1-4 planes) before the body is touched.

fillIndices (E6): the flood's neighbour index is bounded by the grid, but
visited/data are sized to the data; a grid larger than the data indexed past
both. Bound the neighbour by data.size(). Defensive — every caller derives grid
and data from the same document, so no current path mismatches; no test for the
same reason (the OOB read is heap-garbage-dependent).

clampActive (E10): a crafted "active":[5,5,5] burned three palette registers.
Collapse duplicates, order-preserving.

frame(index) (E11): the const composite accessor did an unchecked .at(); a
stale preview/ghost frame index after frames were removed read out of bounds
(UB in Release), and every single-frame exporter routes through it. Clamp to a
real composite. The clamp's precondition (frames non-empty) is asserted: every
phase is created with >=1 frame and removeFrame refuses to drop the last, so a
future path that empties one trips in debug rather than hitting qBound(0,i,-1).

Three tests (iffRejectsBadPlaneCount, activePaletteDeduped,
frameIndexClampsToRange), each mutation-proven by reverting its guard.
tst_image 40/40.

events.title: emu: bound and validate the embed-size report
events.message:
emu: bound and validate the embed-size report

C9 (P3): EmbedSocket::onData treated the whole buffer as one "<w>x<h>" video-size
report and only cleared it on a successful parse. Two failures followed:

- A report split across reads ("320x2" then "00") parsed "320x2" as a real
  320x2 (both parts positive ints), emitted the wrong size, and cleared the
  buffer — so the trailing "00" was lost.
- A coalesced pair ("320x200640x400") never parses (the height field contains
  an 'x'), so the buffer was never cleared and grew without bound, and every
  later report was lost behind it.

Fix: parseEmbedSize now requires each dimension in [16, 4096] — an ST video
mode is always in range, so an absurd partial like height 2 is held in the
buffer to be completed by the next read, and coalesce overflow is rejected. And
onData drops the buffer when it exceeds one report's length (64 bytes) without
parsing, bounding growth and recovering after garbage.

Test embedSocketCompletesSplitSizeReport drives a real local socket: feeds the
split report (asserts no bogus emit, then the completed 320x200) and a
200-byte non-report blob followed by a valid report (asserts the cap dropped the
blob so the report still parsed). Both guards mutation-proven independently.
tst_emulatorhost 21/21, full suite 11/11.

events.title: debug: arm breakpoints only on code lines, not data/bss
events.message:
debug: arm breakpoints only on code lines, not data/bss

B10 (P3): a gutter breakpoint on a `dc.b`/`ds` line resolved to a data or bss
address and armed `b pc = $<data>`, which the panel shows as "resolved" but can
never fire (no code executes there).

The code/data distinction belongs at the breakpoint consumer, not in the general
resolver: watchpoints legitimately resolve data lines (tst_emulatorhost turns
val/val2 lines into watch addresses through addressFor). So LineMap gains
codeAddressFor (resolves only text/code sections, via a shared addressForImpl
flag) and ProgramLineMap delegates it; planBreakpoints now calls codeAddressFor.
addressFor is unchanged and stays general.

Test breakpointOnDataLineIsUnresolved: a breakpoint on the fixture's data `dc.b`
line is reported unresolved (not armed), while the general addressFor still
resolves it to the data base — pinning both the fix and the layering.
Mutation-proven (reverting planBreakpoints to addressFor arms the data line).
tst_debug 23/23.
events.author: idontwantyourspamthanks

events.title: build: reject an unparseable listing instead of reporting success
events.message:
build: reject an unparseable listing instead of reporting success

B11 (P3): LineMap::parseListing returned true even when it mapped nothing — a
wrong-format, truncated, or empty listing produced an empty map that masqueraded
as a good one, so breakpoints silently never resolved and the failure was
invisible. Now returns false (with an error) when no entries were parsed; the
caller (ProgramLineMap::addModule) already propagates that false.

Test lineMapRejectsUnparseableListing feeds a real file that maps nothing and
asserts parseListing fails; mutation-proven (removing the check makes it pass).
tst_parsers 34/34.

Note: B10 (addressFor resolving data/bss lines) was attempted here then reverted.
addressFor is a general line->address resolver — the watchpoint path resolves
data symbols through it (tst_emulatorhost uses it to turn val/val2 lines into
watch addresses), so a code-only filter is a layering violation. The "breakpoint
on a dc.b line arms and never fires" issue belongs in the arming consumer
(planBreakpoints), which needs the code/data distinction, not here.

events.title: emu: add an HRDB command watchdog, drop recovery, and late-reply guard
events.message:
emu: add an HRDB command watchdog, drop recovery, and late-reply guard

Finding 11 (P2): the native backend bounds every command with a timeout; HRDB
had only a handshake watchdog (getting to m_ready) and nothing once a command
was in flight. A dead or wedged debug link left m_haveCurrent stuck true, so
dispatchNext refused to send more, the queue froze, and isRunning() (process
still up) kept the UI showing a live session with a dead debug channel.

Three fixes, the first two mirroring the handshake-watchdog pattern already in
this file:

- Per-command watchdog: m_commandWatchdog (single-shot, 10 s = native's
  kCommandTimeoutMs) armed in dispatchNext after the write, cancelled at the top
  of completeCurrent. On timeout it fails the in-flight command
  (commandFinished(text, {}) + errorOccurred), clears the slot, and dispatches
  the next so the queue advances instead of hanging the caller's 120 s wait.

- Socket-drop recovery: the disconnected handler previously only logged. It now
  fails the in-flight command (capturing its text before stop() clears it) and
  calls stop(), which resets m_ready/m_haveCurrent and emits
  runningChanged(false) — the UI stops showing a live session the instant the
  link dies.

- Late-reply guard: after the watchdog fails a command, m_owedReply swallows the
  next socket reply so a slow-but-alive fork that answers just after the timeout
  can't be mis-attributed to the command dispatchNext had already sent — the
  cascading mis-frame native prevents with owed-prompts. Reset in start()/stop().

Verification: compiles clean, full suite 11/11, native path untouched. NOT
runtime-verified against a live HRDB session — tst_hrdb skips without the
hrdb-main fork, and a fake-server test (QTcpServer on 56001) is feasible but
fragile (hardcoded port races other holders, dummy Hatari process, handshake
timing), so it is not shipped rather than risk a flaky test. The confidence
argument is structural: the watchdog/recovery/guard mirror the handshake
watchdog beside them and native's proven timeout. Next step for real proof: run
tst_hrdb with $PIST_HRDB_HATARI set and add drop/timeout/late-reply cases.

events.title: ui: fix the sprite paint path's two hot spots
events.message:
ui: fix the sprite paint path's two hot spots

Finding 14, the two algorithmic fixes (the third, coalescing the per-move view
refreshes, is recorded as remaining — unmeasured and behavioural).

paintIndices deduped painted cells with m_strokeIndices.contains() — a linear
scan of the growing list per brush visit, so a full-canvas stroke was O(n^2).
The dedup is undo-critical (m_strokeBefore must capture each cell's original
value once), so it can't just be dropped. Replaced with a QBitArray sized to
the frame at stroke start: O(1), identical semantics. Measured on a standalone
benchmark of a 320x200 stroke (64k cells, 100k visits): contains 530 ms,
QBitArray under 1 ms, and the old cost is quadratic.

SheetCanvas::paintEvent issued one fillRect per cell per frame per phase (~64k
QPainter calls per repaint). Now composes each frame once into a cell-sized
ARGB32 image and blits it scaled. Behaviour-preserving: sets
SmoothPixmapTransform=false explicitly (matching ImageCanvas and
PalettePickerDialog) so each cell is a hard-edged m_scale square exactly as the
block fillRect was; transparent cells (composite value < 0) leave the
underlay/background showing. Composite read moved from .at() to .value(...,-1)
so a residual size mismatch renders transparent instead of indexing OOB.

Two tests, both mutation-proven: strokeDedupMakesUndoRestoreOriginal (drag
crossing one cell twice, undo must restore the original) and
sheetCanvasBlitsPhaseComposite (render the sheet, assert the painted colour is
drawn). tst_gui 58/58, full suite 11/11.

events.title: build: flush a step's final unterminated output line
events.message:
build: flush a step's final unterminated output line

B12 (P3): the readyRead handlers only consumed lines up to '\n', leaving a
trailing line without a newline in the buffer. That buffer was then cleared at
the next step's start (and never processed), so a tool's final diagnostic line
— vlink's last message often has no trailing newline — was silently dropped from
the build output.

The finished handler now drains any last bytes (readAllStandardError/Output) and
flushes the buffer remainder through handleStderrLine/handleStdoutLine BEFORE
advancing m_nextStep — the handlers route by m_steps.at(m_nextStep).isLinker, so
flushing after the increment would parse a final linker line as vasm. No
double-processing: the readyRead loop removes each consumed line, so the flush
only sees the unprocessed remainder.

Test buildServiceFlushesFinalUnterminatedLine runs a fake assembler that prints
a diagnostic with no trailing newline and asserts it reaches outputLine;
mutation-proven (disabling the flush drops it). Guarded Q_OS_WIN QSKIP: the fake
assembler is a /bin/sh script and tst_parsers runs on the Windows CI leg; the
flush is platform-independent so POSIX coverage suffices. The existing floppy and
build tests cover the normal newline-terminated path unchanged. tst_parsers 35/35.

events.title: build: write and read real MSA images
events.message:
build: write and read real MSA images

F6 asked for foreign floppy fixtures, on the theory that a codec only
ever tested against its own output can encode a private convention. For
MSA that turned out to be total: compressTrack emitted
$E5 <run:8> <value> and decompressTrack read count then value, while the
documented format -- quoted in Hatari's src/floppies/msa.c and
implemented there as Data = *p++; RunLength = get_mem_word(p) -- is
$E5 <value> <length:BE16>: six $AA bytes are $E5 $AA $00 $06.

Both directions were broken for anyone but PiST. Every .msa written by
Export, by saveRaw, or by an in-place updateImage rewrite of a mounted
.msa was unreadable in Hatari and every other ST archiver; and any .msa
obtained from the wild failed here with 'MSA track 0 side 0 does not
decompress', so the disk could not be mounted at all. The 8-bit count
also capped runs at 255 bytes, which cannot express a zero-filled track
-- the normal case on a floppy -- as one run.

Now: value then a 16-bit big-endian length, 0xE5 always escaped as a run,
runs to 0xFFFF, and malformed truncations refused with an error.
Deliberately stricter than Hatari elsewhere: it clamps over-long runs and
stops when input is exhausted, leaving the rest of the track as-is, which
suits an emulator where a partly-zero disk still boots. Here loadRaw
success is the gate on updateImage staging a rewrite over the user's
file, so a damaged archive decoded into a partly-zero disk could be
silently re-encoded and written back without the rewrite warning firing
(the decoded image reads as canonical) -- the decoder therefore requires
the track to fill exactly, and says so in the comment.

Two committed fixtures make this verifiable from outside: one written by
mkfs.fat 4.2 plus mtools (volume label, empty file, subdirectory,
two-cluster file; Qt-compressed to 1.1 KiB) and one packed from that same
disk by a throwaway Python implementation of the quoted spec, not by
encodeMsa -- reusing our own encoder would have rebuilt the
self-consistency trap this closes. The .msa stores one track uncompressed
(a length equal to the track size is spec-legal) and 159 as RLE, and the
test scans the headers to require one of each, covering the decoder's raw
branch and, via an incompressible track, the encoder's raw fallback.
Reading the mkfs image already passed before any change, so the MSA
failure is specific rather than general.

Verified against Hatari 2.6.1 rather than only against a second
implementation: ours.msa from saveRaw is accepted ('Inserted disk'), the
independently packed fixture is accepted, and a control file in the old
transposed form is rejected with 'MSA_UnCompress: Illegal run length ->
corrupted disk image?' -- so both the bug and the fix are third-party
confirmed.

.gitattributes marks tests/data binary: the Windows leg is now the one
that runs these tests and core.autocrlf would rewrite 0x0A bytes inside
them. tst_parsers gains PIST_SOURCE_DIR for the fixtures, passed through
file(TO_CMAKE_PATH) so a native Windows path cannot embed escapes like \a
and \P in the literal.

events.title: Find the action dispatch table, and watch the cast move
events.message:
Find the action dispatch table, and watch the cast move

FIND_RECORD ($9DBD) is the game's general lookup: three-byte records, a
key and a two-byte value, ending at a key of $FF, walked in order and
returning NZ if found. Of the tables it searches, $C730 has values that are
code addresses -- it is the action dispatch table, keyed by the action
code in $B6E7.

Codes 1 to 10 all go to one routine, MOVE ($8D9D), so the first guess was
that they are the ten directions. Putting a breakpoint on MOVE and typing
each direction appeared to say otherwise -- INVENTORY triggered it too, and
north and east came out the same -- until it was clear the breakpoint was
catching other characters' moves. MOVE walks everybody, and The Hobbit's
characters wander on their own every turn: one INVENTORY ran it 21 times
for nine different characters. Filtering to the player, which $B6EA being
zero identifies, gives one clean code per direction: north 1, south 2, east
3, up 9, down 10. West was blocked where the test stood and the diagonals
were not watched, so those are left open rather than filled in by pattern.

The table also feeds the code map. The playthrough reached 29 of its 31
handlers as routine entries, which settles that the values are code, and a
dispatch is exactly what following branches cannot see through -- so the
other two, for codes 42 and 55, are now seeds. Worth noting that code 55's
handler is the one $9B3B selects by writing $37 to $B6E7.

events.title: Decode The Hobbit's picture table and every picture in it
events.message:
Decode The Hobbit's picture table and every picture in it

L9DBD is the game's generic lookup: a table of three-byte records, a key
and a two-byte value, ending at a key of $FF, searched in order and
returning NZ if found. Eleven routines use it. One of its tables is the
picture table at $CC00, whose values are the location pictures' streams.

Every one of the 22 streams parses cleanly to its $00 under RUN_PICTURE's
own grammar, with not a single opcode it would have to skip, which proves
the table format and the picture format together rather than one by
guessing at the other. Between them they are 10,864 bytes -- over a quarter
of the whole 40,000 -- as 979 moves, 3,549 lines, 181 fills and 20
attribute paints. So that quarter of the image is now 22 described blocks
instead of anonymous data, and it lies exactly where the code map says no
code is, which is an independent check on the descent's containment: that
region is where the unbounded version had been decoding the database.

Two pairs of pictures overlap, and not by accident. Location 13's stream
steps exactly onto location 31's first opcode and from there the two walk
the same opcodes to a shared $00; location 5 does the same with 28. The
outer picture draws a few extra things and then runs straight on into the
other's whole drawing, and the inner one's border and attribute header is,
from the outer one's point of view, the operands of its last private
opcode. Two pictures for the price of one and a bit, with no pointer to pay
for, because the grammar makes the overlap work.

events.title: review: a picker sheet's mute outlives the next audio synchronisation
events.message:
review: a picker sheet's mute outlives the next audio synchronisation

One finding from review, and it is real. pick_paths muted live audio with
a direct suspend_live_audio_for_host_io call and then, on macOS, returned
with the sheet up and the loop running on under it. Anything that
re-reads the run state in that time -- a control client or a GDB session
changing it, a pause toggled and untoggled -- calls
sync_live_audio_suspension, whose predicate knew nothing of the sheet: on
a running machine it came out as "not suspended" and brought the sink
back while the machine was still held behind the picker.

The sheet is now part of the predicate. sync_live_audio_suspension reads
machine_advances, the run state with a pending sheet counted in, so every
synchronisation while one is up keeps the mute, and finish_pick lifts it
as before. open_deferred_pick synchronises once as the sheet goes up
instead of suspending directly, which also leaves a netplay session --
the one machine that runs on behind a sheet -- with its sound. The
blocking pickers on Windows and Linux keep the direct call: nothing else
runs on that thread until they answer.

a_picker_sheet_keeps_live_audio_suspended_across_later_synchronisation
holds a sheet up over a running machine, synchronises and toggles pause
under it, and fails on the old predicate. cargo test --locked: 3,880
passed, 43 ignored. cargo fmt --check, clippy --all-targets
--all-features -D warnings and the reduced-feature checks are clean, as
is clippy with the non-macOS path forced.

events.title: tests: keep the GUI suites' settings off the developer's disk
events.message:
tests: keep the GUI suites' settings off the developer's disk

tst_gui and tst_remotecontrol build a MainWindow, which reads and writes
QSettings; the setup dialog also persists setup/promptDismissed and the
appearance test writes appearance/*. The test binaries never set an
application or organisation name, so all of it landed in
~/.config/Unknown Organization/tst_gui.conf — a store shared with every
previous run, which is how a stale dismissal flag or a leftover
last/project makes a suite order-dependent, and one setApplicationName
away from being the developer's real PiST settings.

A custom main() in each redirects QSettings to a throwaway directory for
the whole run. Both calls are needed: setPath only covers the format it
is registered for, and a default-constructed QSettings uses NativeFormat
— the registry on Windows, a plist on macOS — so without forcing
IniFormat the Windows leg would keep writing real user settings and the
new isolation assertion would fail there on a registry path. That leg
only started running tst_gui at all with the GITHUB_PATH fix.

QStandardPaths::setTestModeEnabled is deliberately not used suite-wide:
it also moves the data location that toolchain::suggestedInstallDir() and
paths::suggestedRomDir() derive from, so a vasm or TOS ROM installed
through PiST's own setup dialog would become invisible — and with the
emulator gate plus PIST_REQUIRE_EMULATOR that is a failure, not a skip.
The two setup-dialog tests that need test mode keep it, now through an
RAII scope so a failing assertion cannot leave it on for the rest of the
suite.

initTestCase in both suites asserts the resolved settings path is under
the temporary directory; pre-fix it reported the Unknown Organization
path. The old conf file's mtime is unchanged across a full suite run.

events.title: emu: stop the memory dump parser absorbing the character column
events.message:
emu: stop the memory dump parser absorbing the character column

The row pattern's data field ends in [0-9A-Fa-f]{2,8} and its \s+
crosses the two spaces Hatari writes before the character column, so a
column beginning with hex digits was tokenised as data: memory holding
0123456789ABCDEF — what a pane pointed at text shows — parsed as 20
bytes instead of 16, breaking the documented one-row-per-16-bytes
contract. MemoryView clamps its hex cells but not its ASCII column, so
the absorbed digits rendered as extra characters, and the HRDB backend
feeds its own generator's output back through the same parser.

Cut the captured data field at the first run of two or more spaces
before tokenising. Keyed on a run, not a single space, so the spaces
between hex groups survive and the 4- and 8-digit widths of word and
long dumps still normalise; the tighter lookahead alternative would
drop a truncated final row that Hatari separates with one space.

The new test asserts 16 bytes with the first and last intact — pre-fix
it reported 20 — and parsesWordDump/parsesLongDump still pass, which
are the ones a too-eager separator rule would break.

events.title: build: leave modules unplaced when a link map is missing
events.message:
build: leave modules unplaced when a link map is missing

setLiveBases keyed its 'no map means single module' shortcut off
m_linkMap.isEmpty() rather than off the module count, so a multi-module
build whose .map was missing or failed to parse gave every module the
live section base and marked it placed. Lines in modules past the first
then resolved into module 1's address range: planBreakpoints armed
b pc = $<wrong address> and the panel reported it armed, and lineFor
could attribute the PC to the wrong file. unplacedModules() stayed
empty, so the '[link map] no placement for' warning that
rebuildProgramMap already carries — and whose comment states exactly
this intent — never fired.

The shortcut now keys off m_modules.size() == 1, the case it was
written for: a single-module build really is the program, so it owns
the whole section. With more than one module and no map, nothing is
placed — all of them, not all but the first, since vlink's placement
order is not something to guess at — and the existing warning names
every module.

The new test builds two modules, never calls setLinkMap, and asserts
both are unplaced and neither resolves an address; pre-fix
unplacedModules() was empty. singleModuleNeedsNoLinkMap still pins the
legitimate shortcut.

rebuilds the image when a text file extracted from a disk is saved back.
Saving into a mounted game disk silently refitted it to canonical 720 KiB
there, destroying its boot sector and anything past 720 KiB: the finding
verbatim, through a path the first pass missed. confirmFloppyRewrite is
now public on FileBrowser and called from MainWindow, so the policy has
one home.

The confirmation also introduced a hole of its own: it runs an event
loop, and each site had captured the image path before asking and wrote
to that captured path afterwards. A resync during the dialog — MainWindow
defers openRecentSource() at construction, and that lands in the first
event loop it finds — leaves the operation writing to a disk the user is
no longer looking at, after which refreshFloppy displays a different one.
All three sites now re-check the slot against the captured path and
abandon the operation on a mismatch.

Also correct the scroller codegen comment that E4 made stale: there is
one mulu now, not two, and the moveq still matters because with a single
frame neither offset runs and that zero is the offset.

control: refuse a second blocking command while one is waiting

A blocking command's nested event loop services every other connection,
so a second client's build/run/cmd ran inside the first one's wait and
connected to the same completion signals: a second build was answered
'ok' for a build that never ran (BuildService returns at its isRunning
guard without emitting), and concurrent cmd responses could be
delivered to the wrong waiter — MainWindow routes every debugger
response through one signal that the hardware view's own info refresh
also uses.

An m_busy guard now answers a second blocking command with 'error busy'
immediately, and the cmd waiter compares the command text before
accepting a response. The help block documents both, since it is the
protocol's own reference.

This is the minimal shape, not request identity: MainWindow still has
one m_pendingDebugCommand slot and the completion signals carry no
correlation id, so the RemoteBridge extraction remains the structural
fix. Staleness of that slot after a timeout is now bounded by
resetSessionState() clearing it at both ends of a session.

The test writes the second command from a timer so it lands inside the
first client's nested wait — the test thread is blocked in that loop, so
a sequential write cannot interleave. Pre-fix the second client received
'(no response)' after 11 s, having waited on the first client's signals.

events.title: ui: ask before rewriting a floppy image that is not ours
events.message:
ui: ask before rewriting a floppy image that is not ours

Every write to a mounted disk goes through floppy::updateImage, which
rebuilds the image with PiST's canonical 720 KiB FAT12 layout and a
synthetic boot sector. That is documented in the writer, and a disk too
full to fit already fails loudly, but nothing told the user: copying one
file onto a 1.44 MB game disk rewrote it non-bootable and dropped
everything past 720 KiB, with no warning and no way back.

The writer is unchanged — the behaviour is honest, it was just silent.
floppy::looksLikeCanonical720k() is a pure predicate over the decoded
image (720 KiB plus the mkfs.fat OEM field that both PiST's writer and
mkfs.vfat produce), and FileBrowser wraps it in confirmFloppyRewrite(),
which asks once, defaults to No, names the disk, and says so explicitly
when the image is larger than what survives. It guards all three
rewriting operations — host to floppy, a floppy to host move, and floppy
to floppy — before any work is done, so declining never leaves a
half-finished operation.

The GUI test declines and asserts the boot code and entry count are
untouched, then accepts and asserts the file landed and the disk is now
canonical. Note the mount must happen after MainWindow's queued
openRecentSource() has run, or that deferred project load re-syncs the
disk slots from empty settings at the first event loop — which is the
confirmation dialog's.

events.title: Drive the walkthrough from the dictionary, and rein in the descent
events.message:
Drive the walkthrough from the dictionary, and rein in the descent

The walkthrough was typing 11 of the game's 53 verbs, so two thirds of the
command dispatcher was never entered -- and no amount of following branches
reaches it, because a dispatch table is exactly what recursive descent
cannot see through. verb_drill derives a command per verb from the decoded
dictionary instead, so the list comes out of the game and cannot go stale:
116 commands now, and 4763 addresses executed against 4406.

That wider drill promptly broke the code map, which is the useful part.

Three addresses the CPU executed turned up inside instructions the descent
had decoded, with nothing branching to them. The cause was not the length
table this time: a byte in the game's variables reads as CALL NZ,$7874, and
following that phantom call decoded everything after it one byte out. So
any decoded instruction that straddles an address the CPU executed is now
struck out and the walk done again without it -- those boundaries came from
a processor, these came from a table, and there is no contest.

Worse, the unbounded descent was claiming 60% of the region as code against
26% executed, with 8517 starts in pages the CPU never touched at all --
including $CCxx, the picture table, and $B6xx, the variables. It was
decoding the database. One wrong byte in data manufactures a whole
plausible routine, and the round-trip check cannot tell the difference,
which is the whole reason this has to be argued rather than measured.

So speculation is bounded twice. Branches are followed only out of
instructions a CPU really executed; past that the walk goes straight on and
stops at the first RET or unconditional jump. And a start in a 256-byte
page where nothing at all executed is dropped, which loses a genuinely
unreached routine in an untouched page and is worth it.

The gain came down from +9905 to +1024, and that number is worth more.

events.title: image: address the scroller's frame offset through a table
events.message:
image: address the scroller's frame offset through a table

The blit computed a frame's offset with mulu #kFrameStride,d2, but
kFrameStride is the whole frame's byte count across every block type: a
160x80 phase with masked, shifted-masked and eight pre-shifts comes to
86,400, and MULU has no long-immediate form. vasm rejects it (error
2037, immediate operand out of range), so the export reported success
and handed the user a .s that could not be built.

Emit a longword table (kFrameOffsets: dc.l kFrameStride*N) in the data
section and index it: lsl.w #2 then move.l 0(a0,d2.w),d2. The obvious
PC-relative form does not work — 68000 displacement is a byte and the
table is ~160 lines away, which vasm reports as error 2030 — so a base
register is required; a0 is free there because the block's own lea
reassigns it two lines later, which the generated comment now says.

The new test builds a phase whose stride is over 16 bits, asserts the
stride really is over 16 bits (otherwise it proves nothing), that no
mulu on the stride is emitted, and assembles the pair with real vasm
warning-free. kCopyStride is not exposed: it is one block's size,
bounded by the 320x200 screen.

A crafted BPB pushes firstDataSector * sectorSize past INT_MAX, and the
wrapped — often negative — product sailed through the bounds check
written to contain it, so parseGeo accepted a geometry that describes
nothing. Signed overflow is UB regardless of what the wrap happens to
produce; UBSan flags it at FloppyImage.cpp:360 on the new test's image.

Validate the whole layout in 64-bit in parseGeo (data start inside the
image, at least one cluster of data area, total sectors inside the
image), keep geoClusterOffset 64-bit until the final mid(), and share
one rootDirBytes() between listRaw and readFileRaw — the latter had no
root-directory bounds check at all, resting on QByteArray::mid
tolerating an out-of-range offset.

Verified red under a UBSan build (signed integer overflow: 16711433 *
512), clean after: the whole parsers suite runs with no runtime errors
under -fsanitize=undefined.

events.title: Find code by following branches as well as by running it
events.message:
Find code by following branches as well as by running it

codemap.py decodes instructions and follows every call, jump and
fall-through out from addresses already known to be code. It never guesses:
an address is only marked because something already known to be code goes
there. That is the opposite failure mode to the execution map, which cannot
contain a false positive but only ever finds what the playthrough reached
-- so the two are combined rather than one replacing the other. It adds
1119 instruction starts to The Hobbit's 4406, a quarter as many again.

Seeding from the execution map is the point. Recursive descent stops dead
at an indirect jump, and descent from $6C00 by itself reaches only about
two thirds of what actually ran, so it cannot stand on its own; seeded, the
real targets of every dispatch a CPU ever took are already in hand.

A heuristic pass -- mark anything that decodes plausibly -- is what the
build scripts reject, and the round-trip check is no defence against it:
data disassembled as instructions reassembles to exactly the same bytes, so
the verify stays green while the listing fills with fiction. The safety has
to come from the method.

Which is why the hand-written length table is checked against the execution
map on every build: thousands of addresses a real CPU fetched as
instructions must all come out of this decoder as instruction starts too.
It failed the first time it ran, on 62 addresses, and the cause was real --
a DD or FD prefix on an opcode naming (HL) makes it (IX+d), which carries a
displacement byte, so it is two bytes longer than the plain form and not
one. Nothing downstream would have noticed.

It then failed once more, at $8113, which turned out not to be a bug: a JR
aims at the second byte of an ED 52, so falling in runs SBC HL,DE and
jumping in runs the $52 as a one-byte no-op that skips it. Both readings
are code. The check now separates the two cases by asking whether anything
deliberately branches to the address, and only the other kind is fatal.

events.title: Trace the inflection flags back to subject agreement
events.message:
Trace the inflection flags back to subject agreement

$B6EA holds who the sentence is about, and zero means the player, so the
test PRINT_WORD makes really is subject agreement: while the game narrates
you it is zero and no verb inflects, and while it narrates anybody else it
holds that character's identifier and the inflectable verbs take their -s.
$B6E8 is a second participant, and flag $10 is how a word is made to agree
with that one instead.

Watched rather than argued: a breakpoint on PRINT_WORD, reading DE and both
variables at every call, reconstructs each sentence word by word as it is
composed. The opening runs with $B6EA zero throughout; a turn of narration
about other characters walks it through a run of consecutive identifiers
while repeating the same verb, which is a group being described one after
another.

That the identifiers are character numbers rather than flags is what the
writers say: $FF at $79B6, loaded from tables at $7956 and $7942 elsewhere,
and compared against list entries with CP (HL) at $7A73.

events.title: Work out the word reference's inflection flags
events.message:
Work out the word reference's inflection flags

The top four bits of a word reference decide whether the word is inflected,
and that is all they do: $40 always adds the suffix, $50 never does, $10
adds it when $B6E8 is non-zero, and any other value adds it when $B6EA is.
The word has the final say either way -- the suffix only goes on if bit 7
of its second byte is set, which is what marks an entry as able to take it.

Measured rather than read off the listing. PRINT_WORD was called directly
with each of the sixteen flag values and the buffer read back, then the two
variables were toggled by hand to test the dispatch; the word at $6AC1
comes out inflected or not exactly as the rule predicts in all six cases.
Nothing in the indexed list inflects, which fits: that list is what the
parser matches against, and nothing is ever printed from it.

The first attempt at this reported that no flag did anything to any word,
which was the harness and not the game -- the register indices were guessed
rather than taken from skoolkit.simutils, so DE was never actually set and
every call expanded whatever was already there. Worth remembering that a
result identical across every input is a broken experiment, not a finding.

What sets $B6E8 and $B6EA is still open. Two variables deciding whether a
verb takes its -s reads like subject agreement, but that is an
interpretation of the mechanism rather than anything traced to a writer.

events.title: Nothing in Paradroid is multicolour: the sprites are hires too (KC)
events.message:
Nothing in Paradroid is multicolour: the sprites are hires too (KC)

KC, 2026-09-18, correcting two docs at once. This is the THIRD time a
colour-format model in this project has been believed, written down and
built on without being checked against the data, so both corrections
are recorded in place rather than quietly rewritten.

graphics.md section 3 said:

  "The game sprites are multicolour. The multicolour renderings show
   coherent droid shapes; the hires renderings look fragmented."

That is a reading of how a ripped render LOOKED, not a measurement, and
it is wrong. The game sprites are HIRES - 1 bit per pixel, 63 bytes + 1
pad, 24x21 mapping 1:1 onto MODE 1.

decisions.md's "Why MODE 1" was wrong in every particular. It claimed
"both the tiles and the sprites are C64 multicolour" and derived the
mode from one multicolour pixel being exactly two MODE 1 pixels, with
table rows for "Multicolour pixel | 2 screen px | exactly 2 px" and
"Colours per cell | 4 | 4". The deck has been known to be hires since
2026-08-18 (layer-1, after THREE successive wrong models), so that
section had been stale for a month and nobody re-read it.

Worse, its own correction note had the map backwards - it said an
earlier version "described the map as 1bpp hires ... both were wrong",
when 1bpp hires is the answer layer 1 arrived at. Deleted.

THE DECISION ITSELF IS UNAFFECTED. MODE 1 is still right and the 1:1
mapping still holds - only the reason changes, and the correct reason
is simpler: 320 pixels across either way, so a C64 pixel IS a MODE 1
pixel, a character is 8x8 either way, a tile 32x32, a sprite 24x21.
Nothing is scaled and no artwork is redrawn.

The rewritten section states what the cost actually is - per-cell
foreground out of a 12-slot palette collapsing to four global logical
colours - and the counting that makes it survivable: over the tiles a
deck PLACES, weighted by placement, every deck wants the background
plus three colours and the fourth-most-used appears 2 to 40 times
against the third's hundreds. Nothing is merged. Logical 1 is black on
all sixteen decks, which deckPalette confirms: every one of the sixteen
4-byte records has &00 in slot 1.

The standing lesson, which graphics.md now carries at the site:
do not state a colour format from how a rip renders.

events.title: ui: answer a refused build, and reset session state in one place
events.message:
ui: answer a refused build, and reset session state in one place

Three related gaps in MainWindow's state, each user-visible:

A build that refused to start (no source, failed save, missing linker)
emitted nothing, so a remote-control build sat out its full 120 s
timeout for an answer known in microseconds, and run() could leave
m_launchAfterBuild armed for a build that never started — the next
plain Build then launched an emulator nobody asked for. refuseBuild()
is now the single exit for every refusal: it drops the launch intent,
logs, and emits buildCompleted(false) before showing the dialog. run()
lost its duplicate no-source check and always delegates to build().
RemoteControl's run wait also quits on buildCompleted(false), and
starts the operation from a zero timer so the wait loop is running
when a synchronous refusal emits — a quit() before exec() is lost.

m_lastState was written on every state update and never reset, so the
remote state command answered with the previous session's registers:
a plausible, wrong register file rather than 'no session state'.
resetSessionState() now owns every per-session member (arming state,
resolved bases, cached state, pending remote command) and is called
from both ends of a session's life — launch and runningChanged(false).

build.assemblerPath was persisted, shown in the settings dialog and
recommended by the setup dialog, but never passed to findAssembler();
the emulator probe had the same gap. Both now take the project
override, and refreshToolchain() runs after the settings dialog and
when a loaded project names a tool path, so an override works without
a restart.

Each fix has a regression test verified red against the pre-fix
sources: the remote run wait measured 120,320 ms empty pre-fix and
549 ms with an error after; the refused build emitted nothing; the
assembler path resolved to discovery instead of the override; and
state summary returned a dead session's pc/d0-a7/sr.

events.title: build: bound the floppy listing walk and sanitize entry names
events.message:
build: bound the floppy listing walk and sanitize entry names

A crafted image can make many directory entries name the same cluster,
or make directories point at each other in a cycle: the listing walk
had only a depth cap, and readChain's cycle detection is per call, so
two self-referencing entries per level expanded without bound on the
GUI thread — mounting such an image, or copying onto it, hung the app
until the memory ran out.

The walk now carries a visited-cluster set across the whole recursion
(expand a directory cluster at most once) plus a total-entry budget, so
a degenerate tree lists its unique entries and stops.

The same walk produces the entry paths the copy-out destinations are
joined from, and the on-disk 8.3 bytes are untrusted: display83 now
drops control characters and both separators from each component, so a
crafted name like '../evil' lists as '__evil' and cannot smuggle a
traversal or an absolute path past the join. The extraction path in
FileBrowser additionally refuses any destination that resolves outside
the folder the user chose.

The cycle regression test was verified red under a 2 GB ulimit (the
walk dies of std::bad_alloc) and green after the fix; the name test
was red with F/../evil listed verbatim.

events.title: build: keep the floppy image recoverable when the replace fails
events.message:
build: keep the floppy image recoverable when the replace fails

updateImage removed the original image before renaming the staged one
into place, so a failed rename (an emulator holding the image open on
Windows, AV/ACL interference, a full directory) lost the user's disk
image outright — despite the API's promise that a failure never
truncates the original, and with QFile::remove's return discarded so
the failure was indistinguishable from success.

The replace is now a same-directory rename dance: the original is set
aside as a .bak beside it, the staged image is renamed into place, and
the backup is removed only on success. A failed final rename rolls the
backup forward again, leaving the image exactly as it was; a failed
set-aside fails loudly with the original untouched. The round-trip test
now also asserts no staged or backup file survives a successful update.

events.title: editor: make sprite undo address the phase it was made in
events.message:
editor: make sprite undo address the phase it was made in

PaintCommand and LayerPixelsCommand recorded the frame and layer but not
the phase, and their undo resolved both through whatever phase was
current at undo time — so painting on one phase, clicking another, and
pressing Ctrl+Z wrote the undo into the wrong phase: silent corruption
of the phase on screen (in range whenever cell sizes match, the common
case), and the actual edit kept. SnapshotCommand assigns the whole
document, which is why structural operations were immune.

ImageDocument::editFrame(phase, frame, fn) runs fn with the recorded
phase and frame current and restores the previous selection afterwards,
skipping a phase or frame deleted since the push; both commands wrap
their undo/redo in it. The stroke captures its phase at first paint, so
a phase switch mid-drag cannot misattribute it.

The regression test draws and flips on phase A, undoes from phase B,
and asserts both phases' pixels. Its first draft failed identically
before and after the fix: addPhase leaves the new phase current, so the
stroke landed on B and the assertion read a pristine A. The corrected
draft was verified red by stashing the fix and rebuilding.

export path: anything over 729,088 bytes (712 clusters, after AUTO's
cluster 2) ran past the end of the 720 KiB image vector, and past ~1 MB
off the FAT copy as well. A game with incbin'd assets plus a pre-1.04
TOS ROM — the AUTO-folder fallback's exact audience — hit heap
corruption instead of an error.

The check mirrors allocateClusters' refusal, and the same bound keeps
the highest written cluster at 714, inside the 1024-entry FAT, so one
check closes both overflows. MainWindow's existing error path shows the
message.

The regression test pins both sides of the boundary: exactly 729,088
bytes succeeds, one byte more is refused with no partial image left
behind. Red under ASAN before the fix (one-byte heap-buffer-overflow).

events.title: control: fix remote-control use-after-free when a peer disconnects
events.message:
control: fix remote-control use-after-free when a peer disconnects

Blocking commands (build/run/cmd) spin nested event loops, and several
branches pump events before replying (modal dialogs from open and the
build refusal paths, screenshot's processEvents). A peer disconnecting
inside one of those loops is deleted by the disconnected -> deleteLater
in onNewConnection, and any later use of the raw socket pointer is a
use-after-free.

Two things were needed. Every reply in execute() now goes through a
QPointer, and commands execute one event-loop hop after readyRead via a
queued invocation rather than inside the socket's own dispatch: the
nested loop used to deliver the deferred delete while the socket
notifier frame that dispatched the readyRead was still suspended beneath
it, so Qt itself resumed into a destroyed socket (proven by a gdb
backtrace of the regression test crashing under both Debug and Release).

The regression test aborts the peer from a timer so the disconnect is
delivered inside the nested wait, the way a real peer's arrives; it was
red under ASAN before the fix (SIGSEGV in QIODevice::write through the
freed vtable).

the repository on purpose.

events.title: Find what reads The Hobbit's second word list
events.message:
Find what reads The Hobbit's second word list

It is the vocabulary the game's messages are composed from, as against the
one it searches when you type. PRINT_WORD takes a 12-bit offset from $6000
and expands whatever entry it lands on, so a word is only ever named by its
own offset and nothing holds the list's address at all -- which is why
searching the image for a pointer to $67AB, absolute or as an offset, finds
nothing, and why guessing from the bytes was going nowhere.

Found with a read watchpoint over the range while the game played, on a
second server so the one in use was left alone. The list stays untouched
through the opening, LOOK and INVENTORY, and is first read on a command
that composes a sentence about an object. A control watchpoint on the
indexed list was used first to show that a read watchpoint fires at all,
which it does: it stopped on the L bucket the moment a word beginning with
L was typed.

Both ends of the format are now the game's own account rather than mine.
MATCH_WORD turns typed ASCII into 5-bit codes with AND $1F -- the codes are
the low five bits of the letters' ASCII, which is why that works -- indexes
$6000 by the first letter doubled, and walks the bucket until an entry's
initial letter stops matching, confirming the linear scan the loose
ordering within a bucket implied. PRINT_WORD states the awkward rule
outright: it stops on a byte with bit 7 set unless only two letters have
been emitted, because the first two bytes carry the part of speech. A
decoder that stops at the first bit 7 splits ATTACK into AT and TACK.

events.title: window: a native picker no longer runs under the winit callback on macOS
events.message:
window: a native picker no longer runs under the winit callback on macOS

On macOS 27, opening any native file picker and resizing it aborted the
emulator: "tried to handle event while another event is currently being
handled", raised in a frame that cannot unwind.

The blocking rfd picker was run from inside the winit event callback.
While a callback is on the stack winit does not deliver further events;
it queues them as blocks on the main run loop in kCFRunLoopDefaultMode,
on the reasoning that a modal panel runs in NSModalPanelRunLoopMode and
a panel resize in NSEventTrackingRunLoopMode, so the blocks wait until
the callback has returned. macOS 27 breaks that: a mouse-down on the
panel is routed through the new gesture environment, and
_NSGestureRecognizerSortAndSendDelayedEvents spins
-[NSRunLoop runMode:beforeDate:] from inside -[NSSavePanel runModal].
The queued block runs there, under our callback, and winit panics. A
minimal winit 0.30.13 + rfd 0.17.2 program reproduces it; the same
program with rfd's async dialog does not.

A picker is now asked for with a PickRequest and a continuation
(App::pick_path / App::pick_paths) rather than called for its return
value. On macOS the request opens as a sheet on the window and returns
at once; the window loop collects the answer on a later pass and runs
the continuation then, so no callback is on the stack while a panel is
up. Windows keeps the picker thread and message pump from 54b08b2f and
Linux the direct call, with the same continuation run as soon as the
picker returns. All 19 call sites are converted; the larger ones keep
their bodies in a helper that takes the chosen path.

While a sheet is up the machine is held, as it is for the life of a
blocking picker, a second picker is refused, and the pad does not walk
the panels. A netplay session runs on behind the sheet so the peer is
serviced. Live audio is suspended and the realtime clock re-anchored
around every picker now; the SoundFont, MT-32 ROM and cover art pickers
did neither before. load_state_from_dialog no longer sets the control
flow itself: about_to_wait settles it from the run state after every
pass.

Verified on macOS 27 (M5 Max): every launcher and menu picker opened
and resized, the two-sheet Kickstart sequence, cancel paths, pacing and
audio after the sheet closes. Verified unchanged on Windows 11 ARM64
and Ubuntu ARM64. cargo test --locked: 3,879 passed, 43 ignored; six
new tests in native_dialog cover the held machine, single delivery,
cancel, a chained sheet and the refused second picker. cargo fmt
--check, clippy --all-targets --all-features -D warnings, and the
--no-default-features and frontend,cpu-jit checks are clean. No
user-visible surface or documentation changes.

events.title: Disassemble The Hobbit from its tape, verified byte-for-byte
events.message:
Disassemble The Hobbit from its tape, verified byte-for-byte

The fifth game here, and the first adventure. One 40000-byte payload at
$6000 entered at $6C00, no tape protection, so the disassembly comes
straight off the tape -- but a large part of those bytes is the database
rather than code, and a heuristic pass reads much of it as plausible
instructions. So the code map is built the Atic Atac way, by running the
game and recording what executes; unlike Atic Atac, random keys get
nowhere, so a walkthrough is typed in through real port reads.

The dictionary is decoded rather than described: a 26-letter index at
$6000 and 355 words from $6040, one 5-bit letter per byte, part of speech
in the spare top bits of the first two, and a bit-6 terminator introducing
a 2-byte synonym link. Every bucket and every synonym is checked to land
on an entry start, which is what makes the format proved rather than
merely plausible -- GET -> TAKE, KILL -> ATTACK, I -> INVENTORY.

The annotations cover the picture pipeline: a vector opcode stream (move,
line, flood fill, paint attributes) over a 256x128 canvas, its table at
$CC00, and the routines that draw it. Timings there are measured, not
estimated -- a room costs about 6.9 seconds and PIXEL_ADDRESS is 52% of
it, recomputed per pixel by both the line drawer and the fill.

Two things are deliberately left undone and say so: the second word list
at $67AB, which nothing in the index reaches and which should be found
through its reader rather than guessed at, and the drawing speed itself.

check_annotations is ported from build_aticatac.py and extended to catch a
comment whose start address is mid-instruction, not just its length. That
is the mistake counting bytes down a listing actually produces, and it
shifts every address after it while the round-trip check reports only a
byte count slightly too large.
