events.title: editor: find and replace, from a Search menu
events.message:
editor: find and replace, from a Search menu

Ctrl+F opens a find bar along the bottom of the editor (the viewport gains the
margin, so nothing is hidden behind it) and Ctrl+H opens the same bar with the
replace row. Searching is incremental: every hit is highlighted through the
extra selections as the needle is typed, and the bar's label counts them. Enter
or F3 goes on, Shift+Enter or Shift+F3 back, both wrapping; match-case and
whole-word options are toggles, and Escape closes the bar, drops the highlights
and returns the caret to the text.

Replace writes one hit at a time, stepping on to the next, and Replace All goes
back to front inside a single edit block so the whole lot undoes in one step —
which also means it does not walk over the positions it has yet to do.

The hits live in CodeEditor, and the Search menu in MainWindow acts on the
focused editor, so a session with an image tab has nothing for them to do and
they grey out with it. That needed the per-tab pass to run once at the end of
the window's construction: the pristine tab is added before the actions exist,
so Find was otherwise dead until the first tab switch.

tst_gui covers the incremental hits and their wrapping, both options, replace
one and replace-all-as-one-undo, Escape, Shift+Enter, the shortcut keys
themselves, and the actions following the tab type.

events.title: image: choose which palette colour the export masks out
events.message:
image: choose which palette colour the export masks out

The mask treated ST colour 0 as the background, hard-coded. Which colour a
sprite is cut against is the artist's call, so the export dialog now picks it
from the document's active palette — shown as its swatch — and starts on the
document's own background register. "None" leaves only the unpainted pixels
out, so every painted colour, colour 0 included, is opaque.

A colour left out is absent from the planes as well as the mask, so a blit
keeps the screen there and has nothing to OR over it; the generated scroller
says in its header which colour that is.

Also give the file map a fixed width and no wrapping: the columns were
breaking onto their own lines once a phase had frames to report.
events.author: idontwantyourspamthanks

events.title: image: export a phase's bitplanes as .dat, with an optional scroller
events.message:
image: export a phase's bitplanes as .dat, with an optional scroller

File → Export Bitplane Data… writes the blocks you tick — palette, sprite,
masked sprite, pre-shifted copies — for every frame of a chosen phase, as raw
ST screen-format bitplanes. `bitplaneLayout()` produces the byte map and the
encoder walks it, so the offsets the dialog prints are the ones the file has,
and the blocks are uniform: a pre-shift is `base + k*kCopyStride`, a frame is
`base + f*kFrameStride`.

The dialog picks the phase from the document's list, the blocks and the
pre-shift count, and prints that map (the full per-label `equ` list goes to the
console, and the map is a scrolled view since an 8-frame phase runs long).

"Also write a scroller (.s)" adds a ready-to-assemble `-Ftos` program beside
the `.dat` that `incbin`s it — vasm looks for an incbin beside the source it is
assembling, so the pair travels together and PiST's F7 build finds it — and
addresses each block through those same `equ`s. It takes supervisor mode (the
ST bus-errors user-mode access to the hardware), installs the palette, clears
the screen, then animates and scrolls across it until a key is pressed, when it
restores the palette and returns. On a screen that is not 320×200 with four
planes it says so and waits rather than drawing, and it asks before replacing
an existing `.s` (the path is derived, not chosen).

Verified against a real Hatari run: the sprite draws, animates and scrolls, a
keypress returns cleanly to GEM, and the non-low-res bail prints and waits.
tst_image covers the layout, the frame and copy strides, the phase plumbing and
a warning-free vasm assemble of the `.s`+`.dat` pair from two working
directories; tst_gui covers the dialog's phase list, map and gating.

events.title: Serialize the second RGA conflict pointer
events.message:
Serialize the second RGA conflict pointer

save_custom_slots()/restore_custom_slots() wrote only the p and
conflict pointers of each RGA slot, so a savestate captured during a
copper/blitter address-pointer conflict lost conflict2 on restore:
either the conflict vanished (slot had NULL) or a stale pointer from a
previous slot use survived. Serialize conflict2 through the previously
reserved slot field, encoded as the register index plus one so old
savestates, which hold a zero there, still restore a clean NULL.
events.author: midwan

events.title: Detect overlap on zero-pitch repeated lines in transparent blits
events.message:
Detect overlap on zero-pitch repeated lines in transparent blits

The transparent blit templates chose the backward branch with
src + h * srcpitch > dst, which is never true when BytesPerRow is zero
(the repeated-line RenderInfo that validatecoords2 explicitly allows),
so a rightward overlapping copy on that line ran forward and overwrote
source pixels before reading them, smearing the row. Use the row's
pixel width as the span when the pitch is zero, in both the 24-bit and
the generic template.
events.author: midwan

events.title: Print the exclusive end of the searched range
events.message:
Print the exclusive end of the searched range

The byte-search status line printed the user's endaddr as the last
searched address, but the loop stops before comparing at endaddr, so a
match there was never found despite being advertised. Print endaddr - 1,
matching the other search message in this file.
events.author: midwan

events.title: Resume immediate blits when DMA is re-enabled
events.message:
Resume immediate blits when DMA is re-enabled

When an immediate blit's event fired while blitter DMA was disabled,
blitter_handler() parked it with a positive blit_stuck countdown
(~3 frames of hsyncs). Re-enabling DMA calls blitter_check_start() from
DMACON(), but it only resumed negative (non-immediate) stuck states, so
the immediate blit and its completion interrupt stayed delayed until
the countdown expired. The DMACON call site already gates on
dmaen(DMA_BLITTER) and a nonzero blit_stuck, so resume any stuck state
there.
events.author: midwan

events.title: Mask unused pixel bits when matching the transparency key
events.message:
Mask unused pixel bits when matching the transparency key

The 16/32-bit transparent loops compared the source pixel against the
key at full width, so a pixel with the same visible color but a
different unused bit (the high bit of 15-bit formats, the alpha byte of
32-bit formats) was treated as opaque and overwrote the destination.
rgbmask exists exactly to exclude those bits and is already applied
throughout the logical blit macros; apply it to both sides of the
transparent comparison in both directions.
events.author: midwan

events.title: Compare against the actual positive int32 boundary
events.message:
Compare against the actual positive int32 boundary

fpu_precision_valid() rejected the negative int32 conversion endpoint
but the positive check compared against 0x7ffffffff (nine hex digits),
which no int can ever equal, so values that overflowed
floatx80_to_int32() to the positive endpoint passed validation in
precision-limited FPU tests. Compare against 0x7fffffff like the paired
0x80000000 check.
events.author: midwan

events.title: Apply suffix-based AROS detection to the MAPROM guard
events.message:
Apply suffix-based AROS detection to the MAPROM guard

load_kickstart() recognizes the built-in AROS replacement ROM both as
the exact path ":AROS" and as a path ending in ":AROS" (what a
relative-path expansion produces), but the MAPROM guard in
memory_map() still compared only the exact string. A relative-path
":AROS" therefore took the shadow-ROM mapping path that canonical
":AROS" explicitly skips, mapping AROS's split main/extended ROM
inconsistently. Both decisions now use one is_builtin_aros_rom()
predicate.
events.author: midwan

events.title: Keep long access for 24-bit transparent blits, special-case the last pixel
events.message:
Keep long access for 24-bit transparent blits, special-case the last pixel

Rework the 24-bit BLT_NAME_TRANS loops back to 32-bit long access for
the bulk of each row (read-modify-write that preserves the fourth byte,
as before) and use byte access only for the final pixel of the row,
whose 4-byte window would otherwise pass the row/buffer end. Direction
from the WinUAE upstream review of the same code. Both directions keep
the exact value composition of the previous byte-wise version, and no
access leaves the row's w*3 bytes.
events.author: midwan

events.title: Clear conflict2 when recycling RGA slots
events.message:
Clear conflict2 when recycling RGA slots

clear_rga() reset conflict but left conflict2 behind, so a recycled
slot kept the second pointer of an earlier DMA address conflict. When
the slot later took part in a sprite/blitter collision, which sets only
conflict, process_blitter() saw both pointers non-null, treated the
collision as a copper conflict, and wrote the derived copper address
through the stale pointer. Reset conflict2 alongside conflict.
events.author: midwan

events.title: Include demux hook 40 in the obsolete-hook guard
events.message:
Include demux hook 40 in the obsolete-hook guard

While the uaegfx card is installed, uaelib hooks 16-39 are rejected so
legacy callers cannot switch the emulator into uaegfx_old mode, but the
new transparent-blit hook 40 sat outside the guard: a legacy caller
invoking it set uaegfx_old = 1, silently disabling RTG hardware
interrupts and the built-in card allocation. Extend the guard through
hook 40; BlitRectTransparent is reachable through its BoardInfo
callback instead.
events.author: midwan

events.title: Fix zero random FPU divisor in cputest fpu_random
events.message:
Fix zero random FPU divisor in cputest fpu_random

With fpu_max_precision enabled, fpu_random() divided by
((rand8() + 1) & 7), which is zero whenever the low three bits of
rand8() are 7 — one draw in eight, compounded across the ten loop
iterations, so most values came back as infinities. fpuregchange()
filters those through fpu_precision_valid(), but the fill_memory_buffer()
path accepts fpu_random() results directly, so precision-limited FPU
tests filled their memory operands with infinities instead of finite
values. Form the divisor as (rand8() & 7) + 1, range 1-8.
events.author: midwan

events.title: Fix quoted argument splitting in the debugger command parser
events.message:
Fix quoted argument splitting in the debugger command parser

debug_line() swapped the active quote delimiter whenever it saw the
other quote character, so `s "don't";r` stayed quoted after the closing
double quote and swallowed the `;r` into the search arguments, while a
string with two apostrophes could be split on a semicolon still inside
double quotes. Only open a quote when none is active and only close on
the matching delimiter.
events.author: midwan

events.title: Fix BlitRectTransparent RenderInfo register and install its BoardInfo callback
events.message:
Fix BlitRectTransparent RenderInfo register and install its BoardInfo callback

The uaelib demux handler for BlitRectTransparent read the RenderInfo
from A0, which holds the BoardInfo in every Picasso96 callback
(FillRect, BlitRect, BlitRectNoMaskComplete all take it from A1), so
case 40 blitted from a BoardInfo structure misread as a render buffer.
The dead srcri/dstri register reads left over from the
BlitRectNoMaskComplete layout are removed with it.

events.title: Fix RTG transparent blits (BlitRectTransparent)
events.message:
Fix RTG transparent blits (BlitRectTransparent)

Four defects in the transparent blit path:

- do_blitrect_frame_buffer_transparent() had no BLIT_SRC case in any of
  its pixel-size switches, while picasso_BlitRectTransparent() always
  calls it with BLIT_SRC: the operation was a silent no-op. Add
  BLIT_SRC_{16,24,32} template instantiations (8-bit already existed)
  and dispatch BLIT_SRC in all four switches.
- The 8/16/32-bit forward branch of the BLT_NAME_TRANS template
  advanced src2/dst2 after the row loop instead of inside it, so every
  row re-processed row 0 and rows 1+ were left untouched. Move the
  pitch increments into the loop, matching the 24-bit variant.
- The 24-bit transparent loops loaded and stored 32-bit words at
  3-byte pixels, over-reading/writing one byte past the final pixel of
  a tightly packed region. Compose and store the three bytes instead.
- transparentcolor was compared against host-order pixel loads without
  the endianswap() used by every other pen-taking path, so 16/32-bit
  keys virtually never matched. Normalize with endianswap(Bpp).

Verified with a standalone harness instantiating the generated
BLIT_SRC_TRANS functions for all four depths: forward multi-row
copies, transparent-key skipping, overlapping blits in both
directions, and guard zones past tightly packed regions all pass
(failing before the template fixes).

events.title: Keep the window alive past the present worker's join
events.message:
Keep the window alive past the present worker's join

Closing the window (the title-bar button or Cmd+Q) hung with a beach
ball since the present worker arrived. Render drops its fields in
order: the window Arc, the reclaimed GPU side, then the worker, whose
Drop joins the copperline-present thread. That thread's closure held
the last Arc<Window>, and on macOS winit drops a Window through a
synchronous dispatch to the main thread -- the thread blocked in
pthread_join on the worker. A sample of the hung process shows exactly
that pair: main in JoinInner::join, the worker in Arc<Window>::drop_slow
waiting on the main dispatch queue.

PresentWorker now keeps its own reference to the window, so the
thread's clone is never the last one; the window drops on the main
thread after the join, as it did before the worker existed. Verified by
clicking the close button on a windowed CD32 session: the fixed build
exits with status 0 where the previous one sat in the join.
events.author: LinuxJedi

events.title: Make the CD32 FMV module opt-in
events.message:
Make the CD32 FMV module opt-in

The CD32 profile has fitted the bundled open FMV cartridge by default
since the open ROM landed (6eb61d649, in 0.19.0). A stock CD32 has no
cartridge, and fitting one is not free for the guest: the module's
resident ROM moves the heap and shifts boot timing. Kang Fu's GREED
intro is the case that surfaced it. The game clears 36 words by 356
rows with the blitter from a buffer it allocated, and with the module
fitted the effect-slot table it renders its bouncing ball from sits 22
bytes inside the tail of that clear. The ball's sprite pointers are
then rebuilt through a NULL record, pick up the ROM vector at $108,
and the ball vanishes behind a frame of sprite streaks. The clear is
the game's own bug; the default decided what it hit. v0.18.0, which
never fitted the module, keeps the ball, and so does 0.20.0 with
fmv_rom = "".

The cartridge slot is now empty unless asked for. A new top-level
fmv = true fits the module with the bundled open ROM; fmv_rom = "path"
fits it with that image and implies the switch; fmv_rom = "" keeps its
older meaning of an empty slot, and the two keys must agree. The
machine profile no longer seeds the bundled ROM. In the launcher the
FMV row starts as an empty slot with a Fit action, fits the bundled ROM
on Fit (saved as fmv = true), takes a chosen file as before, and offers
Remove once fitted; clearing a chosen file keeps the module on the
bundled ROM. The configuration guide, UI guide, peripherals chapter,
example config and the FMV asset README describe the switch.

Verified from a cold boot of the Kang Fu CD on the CD32 profile: with
the stock config the boards and frames match the earlier fmv_rom = ""
run byte for byte and the ball keeps bouncing past 120 s; with
fmv = true the FMV board autoconfigures at $200000 and the frames match
the previous default byte for byte.

events.title: Revert the Microsoft Store packaging
events.message:
Revert the Microsoft Store packaging

The Store refused the submission under policy 10.13.10:

  Products that emulate a game system or game platform are not allowed on
  any device family.

There is no exception in that policy for emulators of general-purpose
computers, and Copperline emulates the CD32 and CDTV alongside the
machines, so the classification is not one a reworded listing would
change. Windows distribution stays the portable zip until a code-signing
certificate is in hand, at which point a signed package can be built and
distributed directly, with no Store involvement and none of the
constraints the Store imposed.

This reverts the merge of #696 in full: the MSIX manifest and builder, the
Store logos and listing text, the Partner Center identity, the packaging
job, the shared payload staging, and the install and release
documentation. packaging/windows, RELEASE.md and the Windows workflow are
byte-identical to before that work.

The console-window section added since is kept, less its mention of the
Store as a way to start Copperline.
events.author: LinuxJedi

events.title: Address the review: chrome under the GPU picture, launcher hidpi, bound staleness
events.message:
Address the review: chrome under the GPU picture, launcher hidpi, bound staleness

Five findings from review, all real.

The scaler's picture draw sampled only the picture through its map and
clamped rows past it to the last picture row. That was right for the
autocrop layout, whose display draw covers the picture alone, but the
classic layout -- autocrop off, which is the default -- is one draw
over the picture and the status-bar band together, so the band showed
the last picture row. The picture shader now samples the composed
texture itself for the rows below the picture (a textureLoad on the
sRGB-typed texture already yields linear light, like the sampler), and
the GPU comparison covers the classic single draw with a chrome band:
point sampling is bit-identical there too. The sharp filter's tolerance
is now stated in linear light, where the difference lives -- near black
the steep foot of the sRGB curve turns a 0.4/255 linear difference into
five encoded LSBs.

A machine started from the launcher applied the configured aspect,
scaling, vsync and autocrop but not hidpi_texture; App::apply_hidpi_
texture sets the global and replans the backing texture.

The Copper wake bound assumed the line and frame lengths it was
computed under. A frame that wraps earlier -- shortened by an ECS
VTOTAL/BEAMCON0 write or a LACE change -- left the bound standing over
the restarted Copper, and a shortened line made the position arrive
before it. The wrap itself now drops the bound, as does any write to
the beam-timing registers (HTOTAL through HCENTER).

The present worker gave the window's pre-present hint on the main
thread at hand-off, before the surface was acquired or the frame drawn,
which on Wayland arms a frame callback for a buffer that may never be
committed. The worker now passes the window to the presenter itself off
macOS, keeping the established order (after the draw, before the
present); on macOS, where every winit window method waits on the main
thread and the hint is a no-op, it passes none.

The clip ring's repeat key omitted the pixel aspect, though the built
picture's height follows it; an aspect change on a static screen kept
the old-sized frame. The key carries the capture's row count.

Same checks as before: save state and frame dumps identical, the
timing-test golden renders unchanged, and the headless core benchmark
unmoved by the extra invalidations.

ui: imported sheets open as untitled documents; sheet source toggle

Hitting Save after importing a .pi1 did not save: the import adopted
the file as the document path, so Save silently recomposed and
overwrote the imported file — no dialog, no .pim, and the source art
gone. Under the sheet model an imported image is a sheet target, not
the document: importing now leaves the document untitled, so Save asks
for a .pim name and reports it, and Export Sprite Sheet is the explicit
act of composing back to the sheet. Exporting a sheet that came off a
mounted floppy writes the recomposition back into the disk image

events.title: ui: placement auto-slices the sheet under a phase, moves re-slice
events.message:
ui: placement auto-slices the sheet under a phase, moves re-slice

The import journey users actually take never reached the slice dialog:
drag the staged phase onto the sheet, add frames by hand, attach the
sheet in the panel — and every frame stayed empty because nothing
sliced. Placement now slices the art under a phase automatically:

- dropping a staged strip on a sheet fills its empty frames from the
  cells under them;
- moving a placed strip re-slices frames that still match the cells
  they were cut from — the strip is a window onto the sheet until a
  frame is edited, and edited frames keep their pixels;
- adding a frame to a placed phase slices the next cell of the strip.

The explicit slice dialog remains for bulk cuts.
events.author: idontwantyourspamthanks

events.title: Skip a sleeping Copper's comparator until its WAIT can release
events.message:
Skip a sleeping Copper's comparator until its WAIT can release

The CPU-idle fast-forward already computes a sleeping WAIT's exact
wake deadline once and leaves the comparator dormant until then; the
ordinary CPU-driven path evaluated the comparator on every eligible
slot of every colour clock, 3.8% of the core in the Copper slot stepper
plus the WAIT release test and its free cycle, because its spans were
thought too short for the prediction to pay for itself.

The same invariant now rides along as a cached absolute bound
(CopperWakeBound on the bus, consulted by every bus quantum through
advance_one_chip_bus_quantum_limited). Once a WAIT is in its steady
comparator phase, the earliest clock at which it could release -- the
nearest of its position, a pending frame restart and the field wrap,
with the end-of-list WAIT bounded by the wrap alone, which the idle
deadline never covered -- is computed once. Quanta strictly before it
skip the comparator; at it, the comparator runs every eligible slot
again and wakes the Copper at the slot it always would. A WAIT already
at its position gets no bound, so the wake slot and the blitter-finished
condition stay with the per-clock path, and a running Copper gets none.

What can move the wake drops the bound: the COPJMP strobe, VPOSW and
VHPOSW, a DMACON write that changes the Copper's own DMA gate, a
sleep/wake transition in the slot stepper, reset, and a state load (the
field is not saved). The first cut invalidated on every DMACON write and
every Copper step and ran 30% slower than no bound at all: the position
scan walks the beam clock by clock, and games and lists write DMACON
constantly. A bound cache lives or dies by invalidation frequency times
recompute cost.

Exactness: a save state 12 s into the Kang Fu slide is byte-identical
apart from the header's save timestamp, frame dumps match, and the
timing-test golden renders pass unchanged. Headless core benchmark, 30 s
emulated: M5 7.78 s -> 7.16 s (-8%, -14% from the start of this
series); the 2020 Intel MacBook Pro ran 23.1-24.1 s against 24.9-26.3 s
for the branch before the core work, in a noisier session.

events.title: Settle the per-colour-clock early-outs before the register decodes
events.message:
Settle the per-colour-clock early-outs before the register decodes

Line-level profiling of the AGA workload (samply on a line-tables
release build, symbolicated with atos inline chains) put 17.6% of the
core's time on one line of the per-colour-clock bus quantum: the
inlined advance_beam(cck), whose callees re-derived per clock what only
changes on register writes -- the display start from the DIW registers
(twice per clock), the effective BPLCON0 with its write-landing delay
decoded into a display mode, the effective DMACON -- before reaching
the checks that reject the vast majority of clocks. The m68k crate
itself is 11% of the core; the chip bus arbitration and the beam
bookkeeping are where the time goes.

Four reorderings, each exact, each pure computation moved after a
cheaper test it was gating nothing for:

- advance_beam resolves the display start once per quantum; nothing
  between its two uses changes the DIW registers or the frame geometry.
- The DDF sequencer's bitplane capture consults the line's slot table
  before decoding BPLCON0 and the framebuffer row, so a clock with no
  plane slot -- most of them -- costs one table load.
- The sprite capture settles its vertical gate (vpos at or past the
  display start) before the effective BPLCON0/DMACON lookups and the
  timing probe it then never uses.
- fixed_dma_owner_at answers bitplane-or-nothing straight away for
  hpos >= 0x034 off the line-end refresh pair: refresh, audio, disk and
  sprite slots all sit below 0x034 or at 0x0E2/0x0E3, so their four
  tests can only fail there.

A save state written 12 s into the Kang Fu slide is byte-identical to
one from the previous binary apart from the header's save timestamp,
the frame dumps match, and the timing-test golden renders pass
unchanged. Headless core benchmark of that scene, 30 s emulated: M5
8.24 s -> 7.78 s (-5.3%); 2020 Intel MacBook Pro 24.9 s -> 23.3 s
(-6.3%).

phases and writes it in any still-image format. The floppy image flow
test now follows the real journey — open the .pi1 off the disk, slice a

events.title: image: phases own their frames — the sprite-set model, v2 .pim
events.message:
image: phases own their frames — the sprite-set model, v2 .pim

A phase is now an animation with a home: it owns its frame stack outright
and carries a cell size (cellW x cellH), so one document can hold 32x32
characters next to a 64x64 boss — the thing the old shared-frame-list
model could not express. Phases additionally carry sheet placement
(sheet index + x/y), and a document holds sprite-sheet targets (path +
size). Frame and canvas accessors delegate to the current phase.

composeSheet() builds a sheet's 320x200 image from its placed phases;
sliceSheetCells() cuts imported sheets back into phase frames. The
old range-based phase helpers and the region experiment (model, export,
tool, panel) are gone; the .pim format moves to version 2 and v1 files
are rejected outright, per decision — no users yet.

The editor keeps compiling against the new model with a minimal phase
panel (name, cell size, placement); the full spritesheet mode follows.

events.title: Sample the presentation buffer on the GPU when nothing composes over it
events.message:
Sample the presentation buffer on the GPU when nothing composes over it

With the present worker in place, the largest frontend cost left on
the main thread was copy_window_present_frame: the CPU copy of the
presentation buffer into the 2x texture, resolving the TV glass column
blend and the row selection per texel, ~1.8 ms of a 27 ms frame on the
2020 Intel MacBook Pro, plus the 6 MB upload of the result. That copy
is a resample, which is what the scaler pass already does.

The scaler's display draw can now sample the presentation buffer itself
(ScalerDraw::picture, PresentScaler::upload_picture): the buffer goes up
at the canvas's own size, and the shader reproduces the CPU copy per
texel of the texture it stands in for -- the same row selection and the
same 8.8 two-column glass blend in the same integer arithmetic on the
encoded byte values (picture_texel, from the PictureMap that
present::picture_map builds from the copy's inputs), then the same
clamp-to-edge bilinear filter in linear light that the sampler applies
to the composed texture. Point sampling is bit-identical to the CPU
path; the sharp filter differs by the sampler's weight and sRGB-decode
precision, within two LSBs, which picture_draws_match_the_composed_
texture checks on the GPU against the CPU copy for the glass, a nudged
glass and full overscan, at an exact multiple and a fractional fit.

The redraw takes the GPU path when nothing has to be composed over the
picture on the CPU: no menu, panel, OSD, badge, guest overlay or drop
hint, no tint, and no CRT, bezel or RTG pass (those sample the composed
texture). Everything else composes the whole frame on the CPU as
before, and the chrome band below the picture always does, so the
status bar, keyboard and instrument panels are unchanged. The
presentation buffer is copied into a worker-recycled buffer for the
job, ~1.5 MB, in place of the texture copy.

Intel Mac, same save state, presenting live: 0.741x with the present
worker, 0.799x with the picture draw; 0.644x on main before this
series.
events.author: LinuxJedi

events.message: Highlight register usage on remapping panel hover

events.title: Present frames from a worker thread
events.message:
Present frames from a worker thread

The window's redraw ended at pixels' present: the texture upload, the
GPU passes and, with vsync on, the wait for the display's vblank, all on
the main thread that also turns the emulation loop. On a host that falls
short of real time that wait is a per-frame stall of the emulator; on
the 2020 Intel MacBook Pro it was ~1.5 ms of a 28 ms frame after the
copy-path fix.

Render now keeps only the window and its geometry, and the GPU side --
the pixels surface with the scaler, CRT, bezel, sticker and RTG passes,
Gpu in window.rs -- lives on a copperline-present thread while frames
are threaded. The redraw handler composes the texture image into a
buffer the worker recycles (two in flight; a third redraw marks the
presentation dirty and waits a pass) and hands off a PresentJob with
everything the passes need resolved on the main thread: scaler draws,
CRT and bezel uniforms and viewport, the RTG rect. present_job() is the
one draw path, run by the worker for the normal display and by the main
thread for a frame that carries something only it has: the RTG board's
texture upload, or the inspector's egui paint. Render::gpu_mut reclaims
the GPU side for those and for surface and texture resizes, present-mode
and shader changes and sticker loads, waiting out a frame in flight; the
next threaded redraw lends it again, and Drop reclaims it so the surface
is destroyed on the thread that made it.

The worker never calls winit: on macOS every Window method waits on the
main thread (pre_present_notify included, though it is a no-op there),
which would deadlock against a main thread waiting in reclaim. The main
thread gives the pre-present hint at hand-off instead, and
Presenter::render takes the window as an Option. Without a vsync wait in
the redraw, a polling loop with nothing running would spin; it now takes
the same 16 ms tick the vsync-off path already did.

COPPERLINE_THREADED_PRESENT=0 presents every frame from the main thread,
which is also the control for the measurement: on the Intel Mac, from
the same save state with presentation live, the committed binary runs
0.710x, the worker 0.752x, and the worker with the knob off 0.710x. The
presenter's profile line names its thread.
events.author: LinuxJedi

events.title: Resolve the TV glass column map once per frame and add [display] hidpi_texture
events.message:
Resolve the TV glass column map once per frame and add [display] hidpi_texture

On a 2020 Intel MacBook Pro (Ice Lake i5, Iris Plus, Retina) the 0.20.0
release runs AGA titles below real time. It is not GPU bound: the GPU
sits at 8%, the main thread is on-CPU 96% of the time, and the
emulation core alone takes 17 ms of the 20 ms PAL frame. The frontend
added a further ~8 ms per frame on the main thread, half of it in
copy_tv_aperture_to_window: the default "tv" overscan copy resolved the
glass column map through a per-pixel closure (tv_glass_sample, an 8.8
fixed-point two-column blend) for every one of the 769k pixels of the
2x Retina texture, every frame.

The map depends only on the column, so tv_glass_column() now yields the
(column, column, weight) triple, tv_glass_sample is one lookup of it,
and the live copy builds a frame's map once and applies it to every
row. The texture rows outnumber the aperture's, so runs of them show
one source row (the row map is monotone): a run's later rows copy the
row just built instead of resampling it, in both the TV and the
full-overscan copies. window_copies_match_a_per_pixel_reference pins
the rewrite bit-exact against the old per-pixel semantics at texture
scales 1-3, on both canvases, with the picture nudged off centre.
Measured against unmodified main on that Mac, presenting live from the
same save state: 0.644x -> 0.708x, no visual change.

[display] hidpi_texture (default true) is the knob for hosts that still
fall short: false pins the backing texture to canvas resolution and
leaves the upscale to the scaler pass, a quarter of the per-frame copy
and upload. The plan's integer multiple stands, so integer scaling
draws the same point-sampled blocks; only the smooth fit selects rows
at canvas resolution instead of the finer texture grid. Same Mac:
0.708x -> 0.741x.

Two smaller changes ride along, both correct and tested but measured as
noise on the scene above: begin_new_beam_frame swaps the promoted
capture buffers instead of taking them, so they keep their capacity
across frames; and the clip ring notes a slot whose presentation buffer
has not taken a new picture (present_fb_generation, kept per writer)
with ClipRing::repeat instead of rebuilding and comparing the frame,
which only pays on static pictures.

events.title: ui: the Degas loop — floppy images open and save back, sprite-safe export

A .pi1/.neo/.iff/.png/.pim on a mounted disk now opens like text does:
extracted to the session directory and opened as a 320×200 sheet. Saving
writes the same format back into the image entry, so a full-screen sheet
round-trips 1:1 with the file on the disk.

That required image saves to be suffix-aware: ImageEditor::saveFile on a
still-image path now exports that format instead of writing .pim JSON
into it, and addImageTab records the path importFile left unset (which
also means an opened test.pi1 no longer titles itself untitled).

Export Sprite-Safe Image… shifts the palette through
spriteSafeDocument(): colour 0 is reserved for the background (the
sheet's own background colour if free, else the first free word) and
painted colours move up, so the file re-imports losslessly with colour 0
as transparent — the exact failure demo/test.pi1 demonstrates.

emits exactly the bytes the whole-document assembler-include or raw
bitplane exporters produce for that crop.

events.title: unix: process pending input actions while paused
events.message:
unix: process pending input actions while paused

pause_emulation is toggled from AKS_PAUSE, but like all AKS_* actions it
only takes effect via inputdevice_handle_inputcode() draining the
pending-action queue (inputdevice_do_keyboard() just queues it with
inputdevice_add_inputcode()). The first Pause press works because the
normal per-frame inputdevice_vsync() path drains the queue, but once
inside the while (handle_events()) pause-wait loop in custom.cpp,
nothing drains it again, so a second Pause press queues an unpause
that's never applied and the loop spins forever.

od-win32/win32.cpp's handle_events() already calls
inputdevice_handle_inputcode() on every iteration of its own pause wait
for this reason; mirror that here.

events.title: build: share feature macros between winuae_core and Qt frontend
events.message:
build: share feature macros between winuae_core and Qt frontend

winuae_core and winuae_unix_qt_frontend both compile struct uae_prefs
through options.h, but only winuae_core gets the feature macros that
gate members of that struct. The frontend therefore compiles a different
layout for uae_prefs than the core code that initializes and writes into
it, so prefs objects allocated in the frontend and passed to core
functions overflow their allocation and corrupt the heap.

Move all of winuae_core's feature-macro definitions onto a new
winuae_unix_core_defs INTERFACE library and link both winuae_core and
winuae_unix_qt_frontend against it so both targets agree on the struct
layout.

FastFileSystem already bundled for the lide device's own tests
(test-assets/lide/wb13/Workbench1.3/l/FastFileSystem) makes the exact
same mount sequence complete cleanly with no code changes. The test now
uses that binary and passes, turning it into a real regression proving
copperhf.device correctly mounts and boots FFS media under Kickstart
1.3, with the investigation kept as documentation for the next person
who hits this with a too-modern FastFileSystem on their own disk.

events.title: toolchain: skip version probes of non-PE files on Windows
events.message:
toolchain: skip version probes of non-PE files on Windows

The toolfetch suite hung for 300 s on the Windows CI runner, killed by
QTest's watchdog with no captured output. Instrumented CI runs traced it
to probeVersion's QProcess::start on the suite's shell-script fixture
(named vasmm68k_mot.exe): starting a non-PE file stalls indefinitely
inside the OS under ctest, while the same start returns instantly under
file redirection and on Linux.

Probing such a file is meaningless on Windows — it can never execute, so
it can never answer --version — so read the MZ magic and skip the probe
instead of paying a process start. Real tools are PE and are unaffected.

Also gate vasmTarballBuildsAndInstalls on canBuildVasm(): the Windows
runner has make but no cc/gcc/clang, and the production build path
refuses to build without a compiler, so the test failed the refusal
rather than anything it exists to verify.

The Spectators select in Advanced is gone: every hosted room game now opens

host keeps its confirmed history from frame zero, so spectators can arrive

The spectator invitation is its own block with its own QR code. Both
invitations show while the host waits for player 2; once player 2's
connection opens, the spent player invitation gives way and only the
spectator invitation stays for the rest of the game. The code field offers

Join game for a player invitation, whether the link was opened or pasted.

The netplay guide, the service README and the worker, hub and room client
tests follow, and the rooms harness checks both invitations and QR codes

events.title: Let a browser host keep playing until player 2 arrives and change spectator places at any time
events.message:
Let a browser host keep playing until player 2 arrives and change spectator places at any time

Clicking Host game used to snapshot the host's media at once and lock every
machine and disk control while the invitation waited, so a host could not set
up the game it meant to share. The page now only checks that a ROM and every
inserted disk are on hand when hosting starts, keeps running as an ordinary
local page, and captures the media, replaces the machine and locks the
controls when player 2's connection opens. Guests and spectators still lock at
Join game or Watch game.

The Spectators choice was also fixed at hosting time. The select now stays
live for a room host before and during play: the spectator hub opens the
watch room on the first non-zero count and resizes it afterwards, the host
always keeps its confirmed history in room mode so late admission works
whatever the count was at frame zero, and None admits nobody new while
keeping the room, its invitation and everyone already watching. The room
service gains two owner routes for this, POST /watch/{id}/slots (0 to 8) and
POST /watch/{id}/refuse. The service only counts places still in signaling,
so a host whose places are all watching now turns surplus offers away and the
spectator's answer poll reports the refusal instead of waiting for the offer
to expire. Spectator notices hold the status line for a few seconds against
the once-a-second frame report.

The rooms harness inserts DF1 and picks the spectator count only after
hosting, refuses a second spectator when the one place is taken, and goes
from None back to two places on the same invitation; its spectator condition
accepts under a second behind, since a live spectator always trails the
players by the input delay. The netplay guide, the service README and the
worker, room client and hub tests cover the new behaviour.

events.title: emu: boot pre-1.04 TOS from a generated AUTO-folder floppy
events.message:
emu: boot pre-1.04 TOS from a generated AUTO-folder floppy

GEMDOS HD does not exist below TOS 1.04 (Hatari refuses it), so the run
path used to refuse those ROMs outright. Every TOS executes AUTO/*.PRG
from the boot floppy, so write a per-session 720 KiB FAT12 image with
AUTO/PROG.PRG (src/build/FloppyImage.cpp, geometry pinned against a real
mkfs.vfat image in tst_parsers) and boot it via --disk-a with no
positional and no -d.

On this path --debug must accompany --debug-except: the autostart
deferral arms the exception mask only on INF load, which a floppy boot
never performs, so without the startup toggle the mask stays zero and
faulting programs never break in.

Verified live against TOS 1.02: the entry breakpoint fires (program
loads at 0xCC04 rather than the GEMDOS-HD 0x12596) and an illegal
instruction breaks in with a CPU exception. Unverifiable ROMs whose
warning the user accepts take the same path. Resolves PLAN.md 9.4.

events.title: Ignore UDP connection resets so a departed spectator cannot fail the players
events.message:
Ignore UDP connection resets so a departed spectator cannot fail the players

Windows reports an ICMP port-unreachable for an earlier send as
WSAECONNRESET on the UDP socket's next receive or send. On the host's
shared socket that reset arrived as soon as a spectator left, and the
players' link failed with error 10054 (both Windows unit-test jobs). A
reset on a datagram socket is a destination that went away, not a broken
link: the transport now treats it as no packet on receive and as a sent
packet on send, leaving the protocol's own timeouts to drop the dead
link, as they do on every other platform.

events.title: release: add deb, rpm, dmg and msi installers
events.message:
release: add deb, rpm, dmg and msi installers

The installers are built with CPack from the same staged trees the
archives carry (the AppDir for deb/rpm, bundle/ for dmg/msi), so an
installer and its archive are byte-identical content: binary, bundled Qt
runtime, vasm, the hrdb-main Hatari, EmuTOS, licences and notices.
CPACK_INSTALL_CMAKE_PROJECTS="" suppresses the project's own install
rules, which otherwise doubles the payload with both trees; the binary's
rpath is $ORIGIN/../lib so a package resolves its bundled Qt from any
install prefix (verified from a sandbox extraction).

- Linux job builds deb + rpm after the AppImage and self-verifies the
  deb with --diagnose under xvfb.
- macOS job builds a dmg and asserts its contents (app bundle, ROM,
  notices).
- Windows job builds an MSI via WIX (installed if absent) and asserts it
  exists. Upload and release-attach steps now carry all assets, archives
  included.
- DEB/RPM declare no shared-library dependencies: the packages are
  self-contained by design, and a distro Qt may be below the 6.5 floor.

deb and rpm verified end to end locally: metadata, contents layout, and
the packaged pist --diagnose resolving its bundled tools and ROM.

events.message:
ui: fix memory/stack interactions and add the debug console

Memory editing fixes, from a user report ('the value returns'):

- applyDump rewrote every cell with signals live, so each setText fired a
  phantom memoryEdited → debugger write + pane refresh → new dump → an
  unbounded write/refresh storm that closed the in-progress editor and
  reinstated the dumped value. Programmatic rewrites are now
  signal-blocked; clear() and the invalid-commit restore path compose
  correctly under an outer blocker.
- A plain double-click on a cell whose 4-byte window looked like an
  address navigated instead of editing — roughly half of memory. Double-
  click now always edits; pointer-following moved to Alt+double-click
  (Ctrl is macOS's secondary-click gesture).
- Dumps whose first row is not the view's base are discarded as stale
  (navigation while a dump is in flight), so display, status text and
  edit-write addresses stay consistent; goToAddress blanks the stale
  region instead of showing old bytes under a new base.
- The table is focusable while editing, so F2 and the in-place editor
  actually receive keys; editing a second memory pane refreshes that
  pane, not the first.

Stack → memory navigation, previously unimplemented: StackView gains an
addressActivated signal — a pointer-looking value follows to its target
(return addresses), any other row follows the slot's own address — wired
into the first memory pane, which now raises itself out of the bottom
tab group on navigation (watchpoint activation too).

Debug console: the build/debug console gains an input line. Typed
commands go through IDebugBackend::consoleCommand(); the ack appears
exactly once on both transports (HRDB emits console-originated acks;
native streams stderr). The command translation table is factored into
translateCommand() shared by typed and internal commands.

debugBackend setting (SettingsDialog gains the transport combo), all

events.message:
release: bundle the hrdb-main Hatari fork as the AppImage emulator

The Linux AppImage's only emulator is now the hrdb-main fork (upstream
2.6.1 plus the remote-debug listener), pinned by commit (21aa4cb) and
tarball checksum and installed as 'hatari'. PiST's content probe selects
HRDB for it automatically; stock Hatari keeps the native backend, so a
fresh install gets typed framing, pause-while-running and one transport
everywhere with no per-project switching.

- build-hatari action gains variant (upstream|hrdb) and binary-name
  inputs, so CI builds the fork side-by-side (hatari-hrdb, exercising the
  tst_hrdb and transport-swap suites) while the release builds it as the
  bundled 'hatari'.
- The AppImage verification asserts the diagnose output reports
  'transport: hrdb', so an upstream binary shipped by mistake fails the
  release.
- collect-notices.py detects the fork in a bundle by the same probe and
  emits a pinned-commit source offer (an upstream-tarball link cannot
  satisfy GPLv2 for a patched binary); NOTICE matches.
- macOS and Windows archives are unchanged: no emulator is bundled
  there today.

The fork is never patched: it is built unmodified and driven as a
subprocess by command-line arguments, exactly like upstream.

debug: add IDebugBackend with native and HRDB implementations

Extract the debug-transport contract from EmulatorHost and implement it
twice: the native stdin/prompt transport (stock Hatari) and HrdbBackend
over the tattlemuss hrdb-main fork's typed TCP protocol (56001, 0x100a).

- IDebugBackend covers start/stop, stepping, breakpoints, memory dumps,
  state snapshots, pause, and the shared signal set. EmulatorHost is the
  native implementation.
- HrdbBackend: entry stop via the bootstrap parse file (airtight; a
  socket-armed entry bp races TOS boot), registers and live TEXT/DATA/BSS
  bases from typed regs, uuencoded mem payloads rendered as upstream 'm'
  text, BreakCond breakpoints and watchpoints, step, client-synthesized
  step-over, pause-while-running, console commands via the fork's stderr.
- HatariProbe gains a content probe (hasHrdb): the fork is
  version-identical to upstream and adds no CLI option, so only the
  listener banner string distinguishes it. Backend selection defaults to
  auto (probe decides); forced native/hrdb mismatches are refused at
  launch with the reason named.
- EmbedSocket shares the control-socket server (embed size reports,
  hatari-debug lines) between both backends.
- Native pause works via 'hatari-debug b pc ! 0 :once' over the control
  socket; hatari-stop alone only halts the VBL loop. This exposed a real
  race: a stdout prompt outrunning the stderr entry banner left
  m_awaitingEntryPrompt stale, swallowing the next stop's prompt. Fixed
  in handleStderrLine and pinned by tst_emulatorhost.

tst_hrdb (12 live tests, gated on $PIST_HRDB_HATARI) covers entry,
registers/bases, mem read/write, stepping, step-over, breakpoints, pause
and the embed-size seam, and honours PIST_REQUIRE_EMULATOR like the

events.title: Settle checkpoints before same-frame disk changes and keep feeds flowing
events.message:
Settle checkpoints before same-frame disk changes and keep feeds flowing

Review findings on spectator mode, each with a regression test:

- A disk change that lands on a 60-frame checkpoint boundary was applied
  by the browser wrapper before the checkpoint was compared, so the
  host's pre-change digest met a post-change machine and the spectator
  failed. Spectator::verify_frame now reports whether the boundary is
  settled, and both frontends apply a due change only once it is. The
  core test records a change on frame 120 and the web wrapper test
  performs one at a held boundary.
- The host page sent a whole disk image (up to 16 MiB) in one pump after
  a single buffer check. RtcWatchPeer keeps the taken buffer and an
  offset and sends one chunk at a time while the channel's buffer stays
  within FEED_BUFFER, with a bounded number of chunks per pump for a
  channel that never reports its buffer.
- The room service deleted a spectator's answer as it was fetched, so a
  response lost in transit left the spectator unable to retry. A fetched
  answer now frees the place but stays readable for a minute.
- The desktop flush serviced spectator links without reading the host
  socket, so direct-UDP acknowledgements never reached their slots and a
  long feed could be cut off at the timeout. Session::spectators_delivered
  polls the host's control link first; the flush loops on it.

(refreshToolchain), so a just-installed vasm works without a restart.

events.title: Serve netplay spectators from the browser page and room service
events.message:
Serve netplay spectators from the browser page and room service

The room service gains watch rooms: a host that admits spectators
creates a second room with its own 22-character capability, so a
spectator link never reaches a player room. Signaling runs the other
way round from player rooms: each spectator reserves a place and
offers, the host polls for offers (which keeps the room alive) and
answers them, and a fetched answer frees the place. Entries are stored
per spectator, role mismatches answer 403, and stale offers and
answers are pruned.

The page moves the shared WebRTC plumbing and connection codes into
netplay-rtc.js and adds netplay-watch.js: RtcWatch (the spectator's
offering link), RtcWatchPeer (the host's answering peer) and
SpectatorHub, which polls the watch room while the host machine runs,
serves the host media once described, requires a matching machine
fingerprint, and streams the feed in 16 KiB messages under bounded
buffering, dropping a spectator that never drains. The Advanced block
gets a Spectators count and the host a separate spectator invitation
with copy and share; a #watch= link offers Watch game.

WebEmu gains netplay_enable_spectators, netplay_identity and
spectator_feed_open/take/close for the host, and start_spectating,
spectate_receive and spectate_status for a spectator whose run loop
paces like a player or replays a backlog in bounded bursts with its
audio discarded. Every mutation and input entry point now checks a
session_active flag that covers spectating. The WASM harnesses run
two late spectators and a spectator that follows every disk change.
events.author: LinuxJedi

events.title: Add netplay spectators with a confirmed-only feed
events.message:
Add netplay spectators with a confirmed-only feed

A host can admit up to eight spectators, who follow the game without
owning a controller port and may join while it is in progress. Only the
host serves them: the guest and the CLNP input protocol are unchanged.

The host's Rollback logs each frame's inputs as they become confirmed,
and Connection::enable_feed keeps that history, the checkpoint digests
and every disk change (with the digests measured before and after it)
in a spectate::Feed. A spectator receives the same cold-boot bundle a
guest gets, replays the feed from frame zero unpaced until it is level
with the players, and then executes confirmed frames a few frames
behind them, verifying every 60-frame checkpoint and failing closed on
a mismatch. No remote emulator checkpoint is ever deserialized.

Session now serves host, guest and spectator roles. The feed rides the
reliable control channel as kind byte 4; Control checks a local/peer
role pair, holds chunks in its receive window instead of failing once
four messages are queued, shares Arc bundle parts between links, and
merges small messages with the length prefix. Direct UDP spectators
share the host's socket, demultiplexed by source address into a capped
slot table; Internet mode keeps the iroh endpoint accepting after the
player joins and admits each connection by capability, with a separate
CLNS1. spectator invitation that cannot claim the player slot. Each
connection is pumped by its own task, so a spectator's failure lands
only in its queues, and the host drops a silent link after ten seconds.

The launcher gains a Watch role, a Spectators row and a spectator-code
copy action; the CLI gains --netplay-spectators, --netplay-spectator-
invite and --netplay-watch. A spectator's window sends no input to the
machine, catch-up runs unpaced with live audio muted like a warp gate,
headless captures keep one frame per pass, and a headless host flushes
its feed to connected spectators before exiting. check-netplay.py can
launch late-joining spectator processes and requires identical PNGs.

Owner's request for a gamepad-only setup (a Steam Deck in Game Mode has
no keyboard, and the suggested controller template has nothing bound to
a numbered key or a Ctrl chord): "Can the first menu support a highlight
bar... so the player can still highlight and select a choice hitting the
A key?"

This screen actually had exactly that once, and it was removed on
purpose: D-018 (live-confirmed) found the real disk's screen polls only
for the literal Ctrl+1/Ctrl+2 chord, no cursor, no fire-select at all, and
an earlier pass deleted the invented cursor to match (FV-1c1/FV-1c2).
Reintroducing it needed the owner's own call given that history, not a
silent reversal.

on UP/DOWN and resolves FIRE to whichever SELECT_* event that row
represents, gated the whole time on `not is_original(...)` - the same
test the mouse already uses (options.pointer_allowed). render/frontend.py
draws it through the screen's existing mouse-hover highlight, no new
visual language needed.

specifically on a Deck with no keyboard at all - was declined by the
owner, citing the standing ruling on the mouse: ORIGINAL means the
original machine too, and does not bend for whatever hardware happens to
be attached. The documented answer for ORIGINAL on a Deck is a Steam

events.title: Alien (1984): a Python remake
events.message:
Alien (1984): a Python remake

A playable reimplementation of Alien (Mind Games / Argus Press Software,
1984) for the Commodore 64, rebuilt in Python by reading the original
disk's 6502 code and copying what it actually does.

Two ways to play: ORIGINAL matches the 1984 disk exactly - same rules,
same odds, same screens, no additions. UPDATED adds an optional analog
CRT look, sound effects, mouse control, a quicker boot chain, feedback
the original never gave you (a notice when an attack on the Alien lands,
for one), and true randomness for the opening death and the hidden
android where the disk always drew from a short fixed list. Everything
added is off under ORIGINAL and toggleable from the options screen.

No game data is distributed here - you supply your own disk image, and
the first run decodes the graphics, sprites, text and music out of it.
docs/re/ carries the decompilation itself: the annotated disassembly, the
memory map, the discoveries log, and the faithfulness report, so the
reverse-engineering behind the remake can be checked independently of the
remake's own code.

See the README for how to install and play, on Windows, Linux, or a
Steam Deck.

events.title: The pack loop's includes are clean's, not distclean's (#18)
events.message:
The pack loop's includes are clean's, not distclean's (#18)

hexwab, issue #18: 2fa5213 FTBFS for him, debug and release, with
`ASSERT spr_end <= SWRAM_BASE + &4000`. `make clean` did not help;
`make distclean` did. His previous build was 044b42c.

DIAGNOSED, AND IT IS A REAL FRAGILITY RATHER THAN A DOC GAP.
src/data/brfimg.asm, lowimg.asm and krimg.asm are the pack loop's own
output: gitignored, different between a DEV and a -Release build, and
- the part that bites - THEY SURVIVE A BRANCH SWITCH. --ensure only
creates them when MISSING; it never asks whether the ones on disc
belong to this tree, so the first assembly reads whatever is there.
#20 changed keyredef, so his krimg.asm was ~161 bytes wrong for bank
5.

THE LOOP CANNOT CLIMB OUT OF THAT. Its whole premise is assemble ->
pack -> assemble again, and when a stale stream overflows a bank the
assembly stops BEFORE pack_overlays runs to regenerate it. The one
state it cannot repair is the one that stops it.

The same trap cost me an hour during the rebase of this branch, and I
reported it and did not fix it. Fixed now, in both pipelines:

  make clean          removes the three includes (they leave distclean)
  ./build.ps1 -Clean  new - the same, plus build/ and the loose SAVEs.
                      build.ps1 had NO clean target at all, so Windows
                      had no recovery but deleting them by hand
  first failed pass   build.ps1 names the likely cause and the fix
                      instead of just re-throwing beebasm's error

Documented in CLAUDE.md's build block and a new section of
docs/build.md, including the part that should stop anyone worrying
about what has already shipped: A BUILD THAT COMPLETES HAS CONVERGED.
If a stale stream still fits, pack_overlays regenerates it from that
assembly's own output, sees the difference and exits 10 for another
pass. Only the failing case is dangerous, and only because it is
confusing.

Verified: ./build.ps1 -Clean empties all three, a plain build then
stubs and converges from cold ("stubbed brfimg/lowimg/krimg ...
assembling again"), and -Clean -Release chains. A pristine clone of
23a4267 also builds -Release to the same 86,016 -> 55,808 image, which
is what says the COMMIT was always sound and only hexwab's working
tree was stale.

Refs #18

events.title: Merge issue #18: OSBYTE 140, one *RUN boot, and the zero page it opens
events.message:
Merge issue #18: OSBYTE 140, one *RUN boot, and the zero page it opens

hexwab's contract correction, and what it paid for.

THE CONTRACT (layer-13 DECISION 4). There are two problems with two
different answers and the port gave the loader's answer to the game. A
LOADER still needs to load, so it borrows the filing system's workspace
and must own the machine to do it. A GAME that has finished loading
calls OSBYTE 140 and has the filing system detach, hand its hooks back
and stand its NMI hardware down - and only then is the workspace ours.
We were the second case behaving as the first while making OS calls
anyway. Acorn's DFS does not hook them, which is the only reason it
ever ran; hexwab's Opus 1770 with DDOS 3.45 hung at the deck plan.

EVERY DISC BOOTS BY *RUN NOW, which is not tidying but the
precondition: the game runs inside DFS's workspace at &1100-&1900, and
*EXEC writes there - as does closing an exec file, which is an implicit
*EXEC. The dev disc's *EXEC !BOOT had DFS scribble over the very
instructions executing OSBYTE 140.

THE ZERO PAGE (DECISION 5). Every absolute-mode data reference in the
build was counted per operand and attributed to the bank making it.
abs -> zp saves a byte per reference always and a cycle only when not
indexed, so scalars pay and arrays do not: drIdx is 45 references in one
byte where drEnergy is 51 in fourteen. Three tiers, 27 bytes of zero
page:

  main RAM   39 ->  91 B      bank 6  260 -> 303 B
  bank 4     64 -> 129 B      bank 7   86 ->  90 B, pad 5 -> 236
  bank 5    148 -> 149 B

405 bytes across five regions. &D0-&E6 was measured free on top of that
- the VDU driver's workspace, which OSBYTE 140 does NOT free, but which
nothing touches while the game owns IRQ and issues no VDU call.

ONE REGRESSION, FOUND BY KC AND FIXED IN b36d73a: score is not loaded
any more, and &CC-&CF is DFS's old workspace, so the briefing panel
showed 24001300. Zeroed once at boot. The reasoning that let it through
- "SKIP 4 means CombatInit is its only initialiser" - was wrong, because
SKIP inside a SAVEd block emits zeros into the disc file, and it is
corrected everywhere it was written down. The other 22 moved variables
were then audited against the same fault with read breakpoints across
the OSBYTE 140 -> ZpSeed window, and are clean.

Docs re-read from a fresh label dump rather than adjusted, which turned
up three main-RAM rows that were WRONG rather than stale (keyTab and
DECK_DONE were listed above code_end) and two figures on main that were
already stale before this branch touched them.

Release Candidate #8 (zero page) built and smoke-tested from the
shipping 204,800-byte image: autoboot, stamp with no DEBUG line, probe,
intro, title, briefing with the score at 0, and into play.

NOT DONE, and both are cheap for someone with a POSIX box and a few
minutes of play: `make check-ps1` has not run since both build pipelines
changed, and Tier 2's transfer minigame board and lift side view were
never driven.

Issue #18's &0D9F question and hexwab's warning that filing-system

events.title: Fix: score showed DFS leftovers in the briefing panel (#18)
events.message:
Fix: score showed DFS leftovers in the briefing panel (#18)

KC: "on boot, the briefing shows a very large number in the panel".
It read 24001300, and &CC-&CF read `24 00 13 00`. Reproduced, fixed
and the rest of the moved variables audited for the same fault.

MY BUG, AND MY STATED REASONING FOR IT WAS WRONG. Tier 1's note said
score needed no seeding because it "was SKIP 4, never an EQUB, so
CombatInit has always been its only initialiser". SKIP inside a SAVEd
block emits zeros into the disc file - so score was LOADED as zero and
stayed zero from boot until CombatInit, and the panel drew 0 on the
title and the briefing, both of which come long before any CombatInit.
Zero page is not loaded, and &CC-&CF is inside &B0-&CF, which is DFS's
own zero-page workspace, so after the boot loads it holds DFS's
leftovers.

FIXED by zeroing score once in .start, beside OSBYTE 140 - nine bytes,
reproducing exactly what loading the image used to do. NOT in ZpSeed:
that runs on every route into play and GoTitle reaches TitleSeq, so
seeding it there would tie it to HsEntry still being ordered BEFORE
ts_loads, and a future reordering would silently wipe the score out
from under the high-score entry. Zeroing at boot has no ordering to
break.

THE OTHER TWENTY-TWO ARE CLEAN, and that was measured rather than
argued. The exposure window is OSBYTE 140 to the first ZpSeed, and
InfoCall and FillPanel both run inside it - they are ts_loads calls
that precede ZpSeed, and infoscr.asm and panel.asm do reference the
moved names. Read breakpoints on sndFx1, moveMode, dbCap, pnTmp and
pnCol across that window ALL lost the race to ZpSeed's execute
breakpoint, twice over: nothing reads a seeded byte before it is
seeded. InstallIrq is the last call in ts_loads, well after ZpSeed, so
the sound tick cannot reach sndFx1/2, snCvH or snTm2 early either.

Verified in jsbeeb (B/DFS 1.2), both directions: a cold boot now shows
0 in the briefing panel where it showed 24001300, and a game played
with CTRL+C scored 1305 (&CC-&CF = 00 00 13 05), so the boot zeroing
does not touch a live score.

  main RAM  100 -> 91 B  (code_end &2F9C -> &2FA5)

The wrong reasoning is corrected everywhere it was written down -
main.asm's zero-page map, combat.asm, droid.asm's ZpSeed header,
CLAUDE.md, memory-map.md and layer-13 DECISION 5, which now carries
the whole story including the audit.

events.title: Size the libretro state envelope from the machine it was built for
events.message:
Size the libretro state envelope from the machine it was built for

retro_serialize_size() reported a flat 64 MiB for every session, while
a stock A500 with one floppy writes 4.3 MiB of state. The frontend
takes that number at face value: RetroArch allocates it for every
rollback slot and, with netplay's per-frame check, checksums a whole
buffer each frame. Measured on this core, that checksum alone cost
1.43 ms a frame against the 2.7 ms it takes to emulate the frame.

The bound is computable, because what a checkpoint holds is: each RAM
bank and ROM image once, chip RAM twice more (the BUS chunk carries
current_frame_chip_ram and last_frame_chip_ram, whole copies, which is
the entire size difference between an OCS and an AGA machine), the
drive's disk image, this core's own copy of every disk slot, and the
chipset scratch -- registers, the Copper and blitter, and the per-line
beam events the renderer replays. Only the last of those is measured
rather than derived; across nine OCS and AGA titles it stayed under a
megabyte, and 4 MiB is reserved for it. WHDLoad's hard-disk overlays go
on top as they did before.

An A500 with one floppy now reserves 14.0 MiB, an A1200 18.0 MiB and a
CD32 11.2 MiB, and the same nine titles peak at between a third and a
half of their envelope over 2,500 frames each. The per-frame checksum
falls to 0.31 ms, and RetroArch's rollback ring shrinks with it.

Two things follow from paying per disk slot. A floppy session reserves
its playlist and two spares, because each slot costs a whole image in
every checkpoint, and add() now refuses past that naming the session's
limit; a CD session, whose slots hold a reference rather than an image,
keeps all sixteen. And retro_unserialize can no longer insist the
buffer be no larger than this session reserves, or state files written
when every session reserved 64 MiB would stop loading: they are mostly
trailing zeros, and the payload length in their own header is what has
to fit.
events.author: LinuxJedi

events.title: Judge the netplay check by the workload, not RetroArch's exit
events.message:
Judge the netplay check by the workload, not RetroArch's exit

The Libretro job failed 12 of its last 76 completed runs, always in the
same step and always with "netplay test timed out". In every one of
those runs the client's log already said

    Content ran for a total of: 00 hours, 00 minutes, 24 seconds

which is the 1,200 frames it was asked for at 49.92 fps: the whole
workload, every per-frame CRC exchanged and every one agreed. Eleven of
the twelve never reached the monitor-refresh line that ends the log of
every passing run, so the client had wedged in RetroArch 1.18's driver
teardown and never exited, and the harness sat on client.poll() until
its 600 second budget ran out. The check has never once failed on a CRC
mismatch.

That teardown is the frontend's business, not the core's, and this file
already made the same allowance for the host, which stops answering
quit requests once its peer disconnects. Make it for the client too:
wait for the completion marker, compare the emulated seconds it reports
against the frames that were asked for, so a run cut short still fails,
and then allow --exit-grace for the process to leave before cleanup
stops it like the Xvfb servers. A timeout now prints the tail of both
peer logs, which is what the log artifacts were being fetched for.

The two subsystems the run never uses are switched off in the generated
configuration while here; MIDI was failing to initialise on every run
and saying so.

events.message:
Record the zero-page measurements (#18)

Docs only; no code. Three places, because CLAUDE.md's own warning is
that the budget table goes stale and the addresses must come from the
build rather than from any document.

MEASURED AGAINST main, after this branch was moved off dither. The
tier commits' own figures were taken on the pre-#20 base and are
superseded by these; DECISION 5 says so rather than leaving two sets
of numbers to be reconciled by whoever reads it next.

  main RAM   39 -> 100 B   +61  (the tiers gave 70, OSBYTE 140 spent 9)
  bank 4     64 -> 129 B   +65  (less 23 for ZpSeed's seed table)
  bank 5    148 -> 149 B    +1
  bank 6    260 -> 303 B   +43
  bank 7     86 ->  90 B    +4  tail, and the ALIGN pad 5 -> 236  +231
                          -----
                           +405

BANK 7 IS THE WORKED EXAMPLE for the standing rule about quoting a
bank's pad and tail as a pair: of Tier 2's 235 bytes the tail shows
four. planChars went &AFFF -> &AF18 and plandata.asm's pad absorbed
the rest.

Two of main's own rows were stale and are corrected in passing: bank 6
measured 260 rather than the 255 claimed, and bank 7's pad 5 rather
than 29.

CLAUDE.md
  - the zero-page row: &A0-&BF and &CC-&CF spent, 35 bytes free, and
    the whole claim conditional on .start's OSBYTE 140 - without it
    &B0-&CF is the filing system's and the deck plan hangs on a
    third-party DFS.
  - the five budget rows, and bank 4's records that ZpSeed's table
    lives there, so every future tier costs it a byte a variable.

docs/layer-13-compatibility.md, DECISION 5
  the rule that decided it (abs -> zp is always a byte, only a cycle
  when not indexed, so scalars pay and arrays do not), the three tiers,
  why score sits above the seeded run, the &D0-&E6 measurement, and -
  explicitly - that Tier 4 was costed and REJECTED so it is not
  re-litigated without a region that is tight again. Names the two
  screens never driven.

docs/memory-map.md
  the zero-page outline and group tables, and the code_end row.

THE &D0-&E6 MEASUREMENT is the new fact. KC's argument was that the
MOS's VDU driver workspace should be fine while the game owns IRQ and
issues no VDU command. OSBYTE 140 does NOT free it - it is the VDU
driver's, not the filing system's - so it needed measuring rather than
inferring. All 23 bytes seeded &A5 and read back untouched through
title, briefing, play, movement, firing, a CTRL+] deck change, ESCAPE,
the death sequence, the game over, the high-score entry with initials
typed, and back to the title and briefing including GoTitle's
OSBYTE &0F. The same dump shows &E7 up carrying live OS data, so the
boundary is confirmed where it has always been claimed.

  00D0  A5 A5 A5 A5 A5 A5 A5 A5 A5 A5 A5 A5 A5 A5 A5 A5
  00E0  A5 A5 A5 A5 A5 A5 A5 01 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 13

Caveats recorded with it: Acorn DFS 1.2 with no other ROM claiming
vectors, and the boot VDU 22 runs before ZpSeed, so anything put there
is safe only because it is seeded on every route into play.

Tier 2: bank 7's scalars into zero page (#18)

Twelve more, all of them bank 7's, all plain (never indexed) reads so
each reference saves a byte AND a cycle:

  xfTmp2 30  xfColTmp 25  dbType 20  xfPlyColor 19  dbCol 15
  lvPos  15  xfPlyY   14  xfColV 13  xfTime     13  poB   12

THE SAVING IS IN THE ALIGN PAD, NOT THE TAIL, and quoting the tail
alone would have said the change did nothing. plandata.asm's ALIGN
absorbs anything assembled in front of it, so xfer_end did not move at
all: planChars went &AFE7 -> &AF18 and THE PAD GREW 29 -> 236. Bank 7
has 88 B at the tail plus 236 in the pad, against 88 plus 29 before.

SCORE MOVED &B2 -> &CC, and that is the structural half of this commit.
It was sitting in the middle of what wants to be one contiguous seeded
run, and Tier 1 had to stop the run short to step over it. It is above
the run now, so ZpSeed can keep growing a tier at a time without ever
having to skip a hole - LDX #17 -> #29, seed table +12, no new code.
Everything about WHY score is not seeded is unchanged and restated
where it lives.

Verified in jsbeeb (B/DFS 1.2). Two proofs, because this is a bulk
mechanical edit and the screens it touches are not on the smoke path:

  MECHANICALLY, via tools/listing_stream.py: 22,638 instructions before

  every one of the 199 differences is a same-mnemonic abs -> zp

NOT DRIVEN: the transfer minigame board (xfTmp2, xfColTmp, xfPlyColor,

events.title: Tier 1: the hot scalars into the reclaimed zero page (#18)
events.message:
Tier 1: the hot scalars into the reclaimed zero page (#18)

OSBYTE 140 made the second half of the zero page legitimately ours
(61500a8, hexwab's contract). This spends thirteen bytes of it on the
measured top of the reference list.

MEASURED, NOT GUESSED. Every absolute-mode data reference in the build
was counted per operand and attributed to the bank of the code making
it. abs -> zp saves ONE BYTE PER REFERENCE always, and one cycle only
when the reference is not indexed - abs,X and zp,X are both 4 cycles.
So scalars pay and arrays do not: drEnergy is 51 refs but 14 zp bytes
(3.6:1) where drIdx is 45 refs in one byte (45:1). Arrays are left
where they are, deliberately.

  sndFx1 &A9  sndFx2 &AA  joyYDir &AB  numDoors &AC  moveMode &AD
  drIdx  &AE  drCount &AF snCvH   &B0  snTm2    &B1  score    &B2-&B5

ZERO PAGE IS NOT LOADABLE, and it does not survive the front end, so
every EQUB initial value these carried in the code image had to be
re-established at run time. SprSeedYcol already did exactly that for
drYcol0-2, so it is now ZpSeed and the nine seeded scalars are simply
an extension of its table: eighteen bytes, one run, one loop, and the
count is ASSERTed against the last symbol. moveMode's MM_MOBILE is the
only non-zero seed and the reason this is a table, not a fill.

SCORE IS DELIBERATELY NOT SEEDED, and that is a correctness point
rather than an oversight. It was SKIP 4, never an EQUB, so CombatInit
has always been its only initialiser. ZpSeed runs once per route into
play and the briefing's fire exit is one of those routes, so seeding
score there would be a silent wipe. It sits one byte past the run.

FONTCODE_BYTES 201 -> 185: DoScore is in the PARAFNT block and lost 16
bytes to zero page. The ASSERT caught it, which is what it is for.

  main RAM   30 ->  100 B   (code_end &2FE2 -> &2F9C)   +70
  bank 4     25 ->  129 B   (ends &BFE7 -> &BF7F)      +104
  bank 5    342 ->  345 B                                +3
  bank 6    254 ->  263 B                                +8
  bank 7     84 ->   88 B                                +4
  PARAFNT                                                +16

193 bytes of the five tight regions for thirteen of zero page, and
~180 cycles a pass off the non-indexed reads.

Verified in jsbeeb (B/DFS 1.2), and the seeding was tested the way

events.title: OSBYTE 140 when loading is done, and one *RUN boot (#18)
events.message:
OSBYTE 140 when loading is done, and one *RUN boot (#18)

hexwab's contract correction. There are two problems with two different
answers, and the port gave the loader's answer to the game:

  a LOADER still needs to load, so it borrows the filing system's
  workspace and must OWN THE MACHINE to do it - claim the NMI, let no
  OS code run, because regaining control is the only way the filing
  system can find out;

  a GAME that has finished loading calls OSBYTE 140 and has the filing
  system detach, hand its hooks back and stand its NMI hardware down.
  Only then is the workspace ours - &B0-&CF in the zero page, and
  &0E00 up to OSHWM, where the low overlay lives.

We were the second case behaving as the first while making OS calls
anyway: OSBYTE 229 per game start, &0F at the game over, 19 at every
rupture align, all after PageLowIn has buried the workspace. Acorn's
DFS does not hook those, which is the only reason it ever ran; hexwab's
Opus 1770 with DDOS 3.45 hung at the deck plan. 044b42c blamed the
memory map - that change stands, the deck plan's pointers cost nothing
where they are, but its reasoning does not and the note is corrected.

The call goes after the PARXFER load, the last load on any path, and
before the OSBYTE 143 that was already there. The NMI claim stays:
hexwab calls it belt-and-braces, and it is eight bytes against an
unrecoverable jump through stale 6502.

AND EVERY DISC BOOTS BY *RUN NOW, which is not tidying - it is what
makes the above possible. THE GAME RUNS INSIDE DFS's WORKSPACE:
&1100-&1900 is the random-access file buffer area, and living there
works only because *LOAD, and *RUN which is *LOAD plus a jump, never
touch it. *EXEC does. So does CLOSING an exec file, which is an
implicit *EXEC: a first attempt put OSBYTE 119 in front to close it
politely and hung identically, the close being itself a write into the
region it was meant to make safe. The dev disc's *EXEC !BOOT therefore
had DFS scribble over the instructions executing the call - boot

events.title: Put away the console window a desktop launch opens
events.message:
Put away the console window a desktop launch opens

Starting Copperline from Explorer, the Start menu or the Store package
left a console window sitting behind the emulator.

The obvious answer -- windows_subsystem = "windows" -- is the wrong one.
copperline.exe is one binary doing two jobs, and the console subsystem
is what the command-line half needs: a shell waits for a
console-subsystem process and its output lands in the terminal, where a
GUI-subsystem one hands the prompt straight back and prints nowhere
anybody is looking. Every scripted --screenshot-after run, and the
functional-coverage CI jobs, would read their results before the run
they asked for had finished.

So the subsystem stays as it is and the window goes instead, and only
when it is ours to take away: GetConsoleProcessList reporting this
process alone means Windows made that console for this launch, where a
shell -- or cargo run -- would still be attached to it and keeps every
byte Copperline writes. The standard handles are pointed at NUL before
FreeConsole, because Rust fetches them per write and println! panics
when the write fails.

The window can still flash: Windows puts it on screen before any of this
code runs, and hiding it first is the earliest that can be cut short.
events.author: LinuxJedi

events.title: Give copperline.exe the Copperline icon
events.message:
Give copperline.exe the Copperline icon

winit's with_window_icon dresses the window at runtime, but says nothing
about the file on disk, so Explorer, the taskbar, the Start menu and the
Store package all drew the generic default executable icon.

Link the icon in as a Win32 resource instead. Resource id 1 is what the
shell draws -- the lowest icon id in a binary wins -- and it names the
same multi-size .ico the window already loads, so the executable and the
window it opens agree. The script sits beside the icon it names, which
is where the resource compiler looks first; build.rs passes the
directory as an include path as well, for the toolchains that do not.

Scoped to the one binary that is the app: copperline-ctl and
copperline-import-uae ship beside it but are not Copperline. A toolchain
with no resource compiler is not fatal either -- it warns and builds an
emulator with the default icon.
