events.title: Run native file pickers on a thread of their own
events.message:
Run native file pickers on a thread of their own

On Windows the file dialog opened from the disk button could sit on
"Working on it..." forever, in every folder, while staying responsive to
clicks -- and then work perfectly the next time it was opened.

A blocking rfd picker runs the shell's own modal loop on the calling
thread, and Copperline calls it from inside the winit event callback.
winit's WM_PAINT arm sets redraw_requested to should_buffer() and, once
DefWindowProcW has validated the window, re-arms an internal paint with
RedrawWindow(RDW_INTERNALPAINT) if that flag is set, so a redraw asked
for while events were being buffered is not lost. should_buffer() is
"the runner is not holding an event handler", which is true for as long
as one of our callbacks is on the stack -- so every paint the dialog's
modal loop dispatches immediately arms the next one, GetMessage always
has a message to hand back, and the queue never goes idle. The shell
fills its item view on idle, so the list never arrives.

Whether it bit at all came down to an internal paint being pending when
the click was handled: a running machine arms one every frame through
request_redraw, a machine sitting in the launcher does not, which is why
it looked like it struck at random and why the launcher's own dialogs
never showed it.

So the picker gets a thread of its own, whose queue is quiet, and the
event-loop thread pumps its own messages while it waits -- a thread that
stops pumping is ghosted as "Not Responding" after about five seconds.
WM_PAINT is validated rather than dispatched, since dispatching it is
the re-arm above; nothing is lost, as the emulator is stopped for the
duration, and the windows are invalidated again on the way out.

Every blocking picker goes through the new helper: floppies, CD, PCMCIA,
save states, Kickstart ROMs, the debugger's dumps, the SoundFont and
MT-32 pickers, and the launcher's nine. The netplay path already used
rfd's async picker, which spawns a thread of its own, and is unchanged.
Other platforms keep calling the picker on the main thread, which is
what AppKit and GTK require, with the same Send bounds everywhere so a
capture that could not make the move fails to build on every platform.

events.title: make the dock "Move to" menu work on tabs, and let drags cross the video
events.message:
make the dock "Move to" menu work on tabs, and let drags cross the video

Two reported problems with rearranging panels:

1. The right-click "Move to" menu only appeared in a stray spot. It keyed off a
   "within 30px of the dock's top" heuristic, which is wrong for tabbed docks:
   those have no title bar, and their tab belongs to a QMainWindowTabBar in the
   dock *area*, not to the dock, so walking up from the tab never found a dock.
   The filter now resolves the target two ways: a tab is matched to its dock by
   title (a tab bar with no matching dock title is a content tab widget and is
   ignored), and a painted title bar is recognised as a press inside a dock but
   outside its content (the default title bar is drawn by the dock, so there is
   no title-bar child widget to find). Right-click on any tab or title bar now
   offers "Move to left / right / bottom / Float".

2. Native drag-and-drop did not work. The Qt mechanism itself is fine (verified
   by driving a title-bar drag through QApplication::notify), but the embedded
   emulator's SDL window is a foreign, reparented window that consumes the
   pointer events over it, so a drag crossing the video stops tracking. While a
   title-bar/tab press is held, the video's child window is now given an empty
   input region via the X Shape extension, letting drag events fall through to
   Qt; the region is restored on release so the emulator accepts input again.

Tests: right-click on a tab moves that dock; right-click on a painted title bar
moves that dock; a title-bar left-press is not consumed by the filter (so drag
can start). A full synthetic drag is not testable offscreen — a cross-area
drag's transient floating window crashes the offscreen platform's backing-store
teardown regardless of this change — so the X11 shape mechanics are verified
with a direct Xlib probe and drag-over-video needs a real-display check.

From the review:

  a wrong-but-well-formed Name or Publisher would have packed cleanly and
  been refused at upload instead. It now compares Name, Publisher and
  PublisherDisplayName against identity.psd1 and the version against the

  can alias several executables, through an Application entry each. The

events.title: Drop the command-line aliases from the Store package
events.message:
Drop the command-line aliases from the Store package

Partner Center refuses the package outright:

  Package acceptance validation error: The package file Copperline-x64.msix
  specifies a headless app. You don't have permission to create a headless
  app. Please update AppListEntry="none" in the AppxManifest file and also
  ensure you have the waiver "HeadlessAppBypass" associated to this app.

An Application may declare one execution alias, so aliasing the companions
needs an Application element each, and hiding those is what the Store calls
a headless app. Listing them visibly instead would put two console tools in
the Start menu, where clicking one flashes a window and exits -- a worse
result than not aliasing them, and a certification risk of its own. The
package now declares the emulator alone; the portable zip stays the way to

events.title: fix the embedded display positioning: fit to the container's real size
events.message:
fix the embedded display positioning: fit to the container's real size

The video sat small and top-left in a large dock instead of centred or filling.
The cause: the aspect-preserved fit was computed against the widget's Qt
geometry, which for a native dock widget can be stale and smaller than the real
on-screen window. Measured against a large dock, Qt reported 426x230 while the
actual X11 window was 728x324, so the fit (and its centring) was computed for a
region the video does not occupy, leaving it small and off to one side.

The fit now queries the container's real size from the X server
(embeddedContainerSize) and centres the aspect-preserved video within that,
falling back to Qt geometry only when X11 is unavailable. The video now fills or
letterboxes correctly regardless of how large the dock is.

events.title: Package Copperline for the Microsoft Store
events.message:
Package Copperline for the Microsoft Store

Adds an MSIX bundle alongside the portable zip: one submission that serves
both x64 and ARM64 machines, signed by the Store rather than by a
certificate of our own.

The package payload is the zip payload. stage-payload.ps1 now holds the one
definition of what a Windows release contains, and build-zip.ps1 and
build-msix.ps1 each wrap the same staged directory, so the bundled AROS,
FMV, A2091, A4091, LIDE and HRTMon ROMs and the WHDLoad archives sit beside
the executable in the package exactly as romsearch.rs expects to find them.
The CI job packs the payloads the release zips were built from, so the bytes
that go through the Store are the bytes the zip boot smoke test booted, then
unbundles the result and checks both architectures, the package identity and
the emulator itself are really inside.

Execution aliases keep the command line usable: a package installs under
WindowsApps, which nobody has on PATH, and copperline-ctl and
copperline-import-uae are only useful from a prompt.

The Store reserves the fourth version component and forbids a leading zero,
so the package version shifts the major up by one and 0.20.0 ships as
1.20.0.0. Three things a packaged install cannot do are documented rather
than worked around: file type associations wait on a positional path being
dispatched by file type instead of being read as a Kickstart ROM, raw
floppy and hard-disk device access needs an elevation a packaged app cannot
perform, and portable mode needs a writable install directory.

events.title: debug surface: register/memory editing, memory panes, PC history, pause hint
events.message:
debug surface: register/memory editing, memory panes, PC history, pause hint

Four additions to the debug surface, plus a regression fix found while building them.

REGISTER EDITING: D/A/PC/SR cells are editable when stopped; a commit sends
`r <reg>=<value>` (Hatari's mandatory `=` form, silent on success) and refreshes.
USP/ISP stay read-only — Hatari cannot set them by name (its own todo notes SP/SSP
register names are unimplemented). Also exposed as the `setreg` remote command.

MEMORY EDITING: byte cells are editable when stopped (type-to-edit; a double-click
still follows address values, and edits non-address ones). A commit sends
`w b <addr> <value>` and refreshes. Also the `setmem` remote command.

MULTIPLE MEMORY PANES: a "+" button on the memory pane opens another, each in its
own tabbed dock with its own dump-routing tag, so two regions can be watched at
once without dumps bleeding between panes. The tag travels with each queued dump
command, and responses route back to the pane that asked. Pinned by
tst_gui::memoryPanesAreIndependent.

PC HISTORY: a new view showing the recent execution path from Hatari's `history`
command (enabled in the bootstrap with `history cpu`), refreshed on each stop —
"how did I get here" as a list of recent PCs and their instructions.

REGRESSION FIX (found while building this): a plain step produced no refresh at
all — moving the refresh into onDebuggerStopped only fired on running->stopped
*transitions*, and a step-from-stopped is not a transition, so nothing updated
(registers, disassembly, editor). step()/stepOver() now refresh explicitly.

STEP-BACK: attempted via statesave/stateload and removed. Verified against 2.6.1
that stateload restores by resetting the machine into a *running* state and
completing the restore on the next CPU instruction — after it, the machine runs
forward and never returns to a debugger prompt, which is incompatible with this
debugger's prompt-framed transport. Documented in FUTURE.md rather than shipped
broken; real step-back needs an upstream non-destructive restore or record/replay.

Also: a `cmd` remote command to run an arbitrary debugger command, for agents.
Full suite green (8 suites).

events.message:
aga: -DFRUA_PALTEST — a one-photo colour-path test for a real machine

Paints all 256 palette entries as a 32x8 grid (row = AGA bank) with ramps
whose low nibbles matter, through the game's own copper list, and holds
it 12 s after the display comes up. A photo then separates "the art's
colours" from "the machine's colour path": groups of identical swatches =
LOCT low nibbles ignored, a dead row = a bank's writes lost, a wrong hue =
a channel wired wrong. Built for the A1200 + IceDrake report that a
module's bright yellow came out pale where amiberry shows it right.
Verified in amiberry: every row a smooth ramp.

events.title: panels: Photoshop-style tabs and movable, persistent layouts
events.message:
panels: Photoshop-style tabs and movable, persistent layouts

Every dock is now movable, floatable and closable, docks nest and tab within an
area, and the whole arrangement persists across runs via QSettings
saveState/restoreState. Panels can be dragged between docks, torn off into
floating windows, tabbed onto one another, or closed and re-shown from the View
menu — the management model the user asked for, rather than a fixed set of dock
widgets.

The default arrangement is a sane starting point rather than nine scattered
docks: the debug views (Registers, Disassembly, Stack, Hardware, Breakpoints)
are tabbed into one panel with the Emulator display prominent above it, and
Output/Memory are tabbed at the bottom. The View menu lists every dock for
show/hide and has a Reset layout action that returns to that default.

Two things make it robust rather than decorative: every dock carries a stable
objectName, which is what saveState keys the arrangement on; and the
embedded-display toggle keeps authority over the Emulator dock's visibility even
after a layout is restored, so restoring an old layout can't silently re-show a
display the user has turned off. The persistence round-trip is pinned by
tst_gui::dockLayoutPersistsAcrossRestart — hide a dock in one window, and a
fresh window restores it hidden.

events.title: code review P1–P3 fixes, and an emulator display that resizes properly
events.message:
code review P1–P3 fixes, and an emulator display that resizes properly

Two bodies of work, both verified end to end.

CODE REVIEW (docs/code-review-glm-001.md), the headline being a real break in the
core debug loop, reproduced by a failing test before any fix and passing after:

- P1: breakpoints set before Run never armed, and the editor never followed the
  PC. Three chained causes, all fixed: arm when the live bases actually arrive
  (not on a zero-delay timer that always lost the race to the basepage response);
  hand those bases to the program map via setLiveBases so any line resolves and
  locationFromPc works at all; and refresh on every stop, so the editor follows
  on a breakpoint hit and not only on a step. A fourth surfaced while testing:
  resume() left a queued command in flight, and the next stop's prompt completed
  it with a stale response instead of the stop being detected — resume() now
  discards stale commands. tst_gui::breakpointSetBeforeRunFiresAndEditorFollows
  pins the whole loop: it failed before, passes after.
- P2 (transport): start() resets every per-session framing field via
  resetTransport(); stop() emits stopped/running changes so the UI and remote
  clients learn the session ended; stateUpdated is emitted once per refresh
  batch, not once per parsed response.
- P3: vlink warnings no longer recorded as errors (severity regex captured the
  numeric group); the stack view's return-address heuristic uses the real text
  extent rather than requiring a data section; tst_remotecontrol added to the
  Windows console fix-up; and the nits (duplicate includes, duplicated CMake
  source entries, an unused member, and several small robustness items).
- Watchpoint firing is now verified end to end against a live Hatari — it fires
  on a change and not on a same-value write, with negative controls.

EMULATOR DISPLAY: resizing no longer pushes the video out or leaves ghost
trails. The fit now preserves the video's aspect ratio and centres it with a
black letterbox instead of squashing it into the dock. Two underlying causes are
worth recording: the container's X11 window can hold a stale size that disagrees
with the widget's Qt geometry, so the fit is taken from Qt geometry; and Hatari
does not pump SDL events while stopped in the debugger, so a stopped session
only rescales on the next run — the letterbox keeps that looking intentional
rather than broken. Verified: grow and shrink both re-fit cleanly.

events.title: debug views: watchpoints, a stack view, and hardware registers
events.message:
debug views: watchpoints, a stack view, and hardware registers

Three additions to the debug surface, each the kind of thing an assembly
developer reaches for.

WATCHPOINTS break when a memory value changes. Hatari has no data watchpoints
(upstream's `w` command is compiled out), so a watch is armed as a conditional
breakpoint using self-inequality — `b ($addr).w ! ($addr).w` — which the
debugger's change tracking evaluates as "fire when the value differs". That
caveat is honest and worth knowing: a write of the same value, or a read, does
not fire. Set from Run ▸ Add watchpoint or the `watchpoint` remote command, shown
in the breakpoints panel, and double-clicking one navigates memory to the
address. Verified live: a watch on the 200Hz counter at $4BA fires the moment it
ticks. The exact self-inequality format is pinned by tests, because a drift in
it would silently stop watchpoints working.

STACK VIEW shows the 32-bit values at the stack pointer, refreshed on every stop,
with values inside the program's text segment marked as likely return addresses
— the fastest way to see who called the current routine, since a jsr/bsr pushes
the return address as a long. It needs its own dump channel: the routing travels
with each queued command (EmulatorHost's Pending), so a stack dump and a memory
dump back-to-back reach stackDumpReady and memoryDumpReady respectively instead
of clobbering each other. That routing is pinned by an integration test.

HARDWARE REGISTERS shows the ST's hardware state — shifter/video, MFP, ACIA/IKBD,
sound, blitter, DMA — from Hatari's `info` commands, which is the useful view
because the I/O registers have read side effects or only make sense interpreted.
Refreshed on each stop, with a selectable subject.

Full suite green (8 suites); README documents all three.

events.title: embedded display: fill the dock instead of sitting small in it
events.message:
embedded display: fill the dock instead of sitting small in it

The embedded video used to stay at its native resolution (640x436) in the
top-left of the dock with dead black space around it, which read as broken
rather than letterboxed. Two things made it hard to fix, and both are worth
recording.

First, the video does not render at all while the debugger is stopped — Hatari
renders frames only while the emulation runs, so a stopped session shows a black
panel, which looked like a broken embed until the difference was understood.

Second, and the actual fix: the SDL window now resizes to fill the container, and
Hatari rescales its renderer to fit — exactly what it does for a hand-resized
window (SDL_WINDOWEVENT_SIZE_CHANGED -> Screen_SetTextureScale). The subtlety is
*when* and *from what* to take the container's size. The container is a native
window in a dock, and its Qt size() provably lags the size the dock gives the
underlying X11 window: fitEmbedded saw 320x200 while the X11 window was already
463x290, and resizeEvent never fired on the growth. Fitting from that stale Qt
size is what left the video small. The fit now reads the X server's own
attributes for the container (ground truth), and a short settle timer re-fits
over the first moments after launch while the dock's layout is still settling.

Verified over the control socket: the ST desktop now scales to fill the Emulator
dock at 463x290, tracking the dock, with no dead space.

events.title: Title and briefing UX: transfer to the briefing, live keys, quieter chatter (#20)
events.message:
Title and briefing UX: transfer to the briefing, live keys, quieter chatter (#20)

hexwab's issue #20, four parts, three taken and one declined by KC.

[11f DECISION 20] TRANSFER at the title asks for the briefing. Both keys
TiWait read started the game and skipped the briefing, so the one thing a
confused player does was what denied them the controls, and the only
route to the briefing was to sit out the timeout. FIRE keeps $2907's
behaviour; TRANSFER branches to the timeout's own exit. The timeout is
back to one 16-bit lap - tiPage gone, 5.5 s against 10.9, the order of
the C64's own 256 frames - which is safe to shorten now that nobody has
to wait it out. The dwell is seeded on this path too, which the
timeout's arm never could be: a timeout arrives at a fixed count.
Title overlay 386 -> 384 bytes.
OPEN END, recorded at the decision: nothing on the title SAYS so. Its
thirty-six glyphs are block letters and panels, so a prompt would have
to come from textfont through FontCell.

[11f DECISION 21] The briefing names the keys that are actually bound.
DECISION 7's mechanism for the keys instead of the scores: BmPatchKeys
runs from BmRowScan on every depack of BR_KEY_PAGE. Each key line is two
records now - label at column 8, name at column 22, where the hand-tuned
spacing already put it - so the patch writes a fixed field at a known
offset and the alignment is the record's own. make_briefing.py pads a
keyN-labelled record to KEY_FIELD = 9 and emits BR_KEY0..5, BR_KEY_PAGE
and BR_KEY_FIELD.
WHAT IT COST: the redefine screen is a ZX0 stream that depacks over
BR_RECS, so its name machinery cannot be reached while a page is up and
sits in the arena the key records live in. BmKrAscii, bmKeyChar,
BmKrChar, bmKrNames and the dispatch factored out of BmKrShow as
BmKrNameCtl are resident in briefman.asm now. Bank 5: 194 bytes,
spr_end &BEAA -> &BF6C (342 free -> 148); XKR shrank 1,014 -> 591 raw
and 774 -> 462 packed, paying back most of the 423 that moved.

[11f DECISION 22] The chatter blips drop another 4 dB, FX_LEVEL 29/30/31
9 -> 7, one byte of sndInstTab. The bed under them is fx16 and fx16 IS
the in-game lift - one shared record - so it cannot follow without
quietening a game sound, and nibble 6 was tried on it once and reverted.
The blips therefore sit 4 dB BELOW the bed rather than level with it, a
deliberate break with the 2026-08-28 alignment. 7 is one conservative
step and is OWED AN EAR.

DECLINED by KC: moving the supplementary keys to page 1. The ctrl+Q half
of that complaint is answered by DECISION 22 instead.

Verified in jsbeeb, B-DFS1.2, on the shipping image: TRANSFER at the
title reaches the briefing; BR_KEY0 (&47A4) read 18 24 00.. - column 24
(22 + the 2-cell margin), glyph 36 = Z, eight spaces - and BR_KEY5
18 1D 4E 3F 41 43 = Space. Then CTRL+R, all six rebound to A S D F
RETURN SLASH, and after BrPagePaint: BR_KEY0 = A, BR_KEY4 = Return,
BR_KEY5 = Slash, each repadded to nine. Scrolled into view the block
renders in the columns it was in before the split. Dev and -Release
both assemble.

events.title: embedded display, remote control, and a memory view you can follow
events.message:
embedded display, remote control, and a memory view you can follow

Three features, one theme: making the IDE observable and controllable instead of
a black box you poke with a mouse.

MEMORY VIEW — follow pointers, and stay fresh.
A memory pane that goes stale the moment you step is broken, and one where you
can see a pointer but not follow it is frustrating. Double-click a byte cell and,
if the 32-bit big-endian value there looks like an address (non-zero, even, and
within the ST's 24-bit bus), the view jumps to it. And the pane now re-reads on
every state change, not just when you navigate. Double-click rather than single:
a single click has to stay free to select a cell.

EMBEDDED DISPLAY — the emulator can live in a panel now.
On Linux, View ▸ Embed emulator display runs Hatari's video inside the IDE
rather than in a separate window, via X11 reparenting: Hatari attaches its SDL
window into a container PiST names with PARENT_WIN_ID. This surfaced three
things that only show up when you actually run it:

  - PiST has to be an X11 client to have a window ID to hand out, so on Wayland
    it now runs under XWayland (the plan always said to).
  - Hatari creates the reparented window SDL_WINDOW_HIDDEN and never maps it, so
    the panel stayed black until PiST mapped the child itself (src/ui/EmbedX11).
  - The video-size report arrives with NO trailing newline — control.c's own
    comment claims one and its sprintf writes none — so parsing that waited for
    a line terminator never fired, and the panel never learned its size.

Separate-window mode is the default and the only mode where reparenting cannot
work (Wayland without XWayland, and for now macOS and Windows).

REMOTE CONTROL — hooks for scripts and AI agents.
The IDE now exposes the same kind of control socket the emulator does, because
driving a GUI by faking keyboard input is brittle and reading the screen is
worse. --control-port (or PIST_CONTROL_PORT) opens a localhost-only,
off-by-default line protocol: open / build / run / stop / step / stepover /
continue / breakpoint / screenshot / console / state / help / quit. Build and
run answer only once the work is genuinely done, so a script never has to poll.
The screenshot goes through XGetImage because QScreen::grabWindow returns black
under XWayland — and it captures the embedded display too.

Verified end to end over the socket itself: run, screenshot, and console all
driven without touching the keyboard, showing the ST screen embedded in the
panel. The new tst_remotecontrol suite pins the framing and the synchronous
responses; it pumps a real event loop because QTcpSocket::waitForReadyRead only
watches the client socket's notifier, which would leave a same-process server
unanswered. Full suite green (8 suites). README documents the protocol.

events.title: ci: fix the AppImage verification, not the build
events.message:
ci: fix the AppImage verification, not the build

Two more failures from the release workflow, both in the check I wrote rather
than the artifact — the AppImage itself was correct, which is the frustrating
kind of bug because the workflow said the build was broken.

1. The bundled-ROM assertion matched a leading version number
   (`^ 1.02\t/tmp/.mount_...`), but EmuTOS does not render as one: it prints
   `EmuTOS (TOS 2.06)\t/tmp/.mount_.../usr/share/emutos/etos1024k.img`. So a
   genuinely-correct AppImage, with its ROM found from its own mount, failed the
   gate. Matched by path instead, and the autostart check now looks at the EmuTOS
   line specifically so a system 1.02 ROM (which always carries that warning)
   cannot cause a false failure.

2. The copy of the bundled Hatari into the AppDir was gated on the matrix flag,
   but the linuxdeploy `-e` that makes it follow Hatari's libraries was not — a
   leftover from an earlier rewrite that reintroduced the inconsistency it was
   meant to remove. One flag now drives both, via an argument array, so a
   no-emulator build is just a smaller AppImage rather than a confusing failure.

Both verified against the real diagnose output shape and with `bash -n`. The
lesson taken: three of the four CI failures in this work were in the verification
logic, not the product, so this pass re-read the whole step as the runner
executes it rather than patching the reported line.

events.title: bundle the emulator, and fix the ROM our archives already shipped
events.message:
bundle the emulator, and fix the ROM our archives already shipped

The Linux AppImage now carries Hatari 2.6.1 alongside the assembler and the ROM,
so a fresh download runs and debugs with nothing else installed. Two things made
that necessary and one thing nearly made it useless.

WHY BUNDLE. No distribution package is a usable version: Ubuntu 22.04 ships
2.3.1 and 24.04 ships 2.4.1, while the project is developed and verified against
2.6.1. 2.4.1 returns truncated debugger responses that break source-line
debugging, so the previous advice — "install it with your package manager" — was
recommending a configuration that does not work. Hatari is GPL-2.0-or-later and
is redistributed unmodified from a checksum-pinned upstream tarball; it is never
patched and never committed to this repository, exactly as vasm is handled.
NOTICE gains the redistribution basis, the source pointer, and an entry for the
GNU Readline that the bundled build links — readline matters because with it
Hatari prints its debugger prompt to stdout and without it to stderr, and PiST
speaks the former.

THE BUG. Every release archive already carried an EmuTOS ROM in share/emutos and
nothing looked there: the string did not appear in tosSearchPaths() at all. So on
any machine without the hatari package the bundled ROM was invisible and Run and
debug were dead on first launch — the exact thing bundling it was meant to
prevent. It survived release checking because the verification step sets
PIST_TOS_DIR, which short-circuits the discovery logic a user depends on; a check
that configures its way past the code under test cannot fail.

Discovery now walks up from the executable looking for share/emutos and
share/hatari, covering all three archive layouts (bin/, usr/bin/ inside an
AppImage, Contents/MacOS inside a macOS bundle), and deliberately precedes the
system locations without overriding an explicit choice. The walk is exposed as
paths::bundledDataSearchPaths() so it can be tested at all, since tosSearchPaths()
always starts from the running executable. Verified by reverting the fix: the new
test fails with "share/emutos beside the executable was not searched", and passes
when restored.

Two packaging faults found by testing the built AppImage in a clean container
rather than on the machine that built it:

  - naming only `pist` with -e meant linuxdeploy never followed Hatari's
    libraries, so the bundled emulator arrived without SDL2, readline or libpng
    and could not start. Both executables are now named.
  - the reverse mistake was nearly committed: forcing in every library ldd
    reported as missing copies glibc-coupled libraries from the build host, and a
    libtinfo taken from a development machine demanded GLIBC_2.42 on a 2.39
    system. The excluded X11/Wayland/ALSA set is linuxdeploy's deliberate
    decision, correct because every desktop has them, and it is left alone.

The release verification now runs the bundled emulator and asserts the
non-universal libraries are present, and checks the AppImage's ROM discovery with
PIST_TOS_DIR pointedly unset.

Verified: the shipped Hatari binary and its shipped libraries pass all 12
emulator debug-session tests (breakpoints, stepping, registers, memory); the full
suite is green; and inside the built AppImage, `pist --diagnose` resolves the
bundled assembler, emulator and ROM from the mount with no environment help.

The emulator build itself moves into a composite action shared by CI and release,
because three separate bugs had already been fixed in the one inline copy and a
second copy would have drifted the same way.

events.message:
ci: test against the Hatari we support, not the distribution's

The emulator suite failed in CI on four tests, and the captured dialogue gave the
answer immediately:

    INFO : Hatari v2.4.1, compiled on: Apr 1 2024, 05:56:46

Ubuntu 24.04 packages 2.4.1. Everything in this project was designed and verified
against 2.6.1. Register dumps come back from 2.4.1 as a single line with `SR=`
missing, so registers never become valid and every test that reads them fails —
none of which reproduces on 2.6.1, with the same ROM, locally.

CI now builds 2.6.1 from a checksum-pinned source tarball. Testing a version no
user will have is worse than not testing: the failures are noise that hides real
ones, and the passes mean nothing. Ubuntu 22.04 ships 2.3.1 and 24.04 ships 2.4.1,
so no distribution package is usable — the same conclusion the release packaging
reached for vasm, and an argument for bundling Hatari rather than trusting the
user's copy.

`libreadline-dev` is now installed as part of the test environment because it
determines the transport: with readline the debugger prompt goes to stdout, without
it the fallback prints to stderr. Those are different code paths in our host, so
leaving it to chance would have meant testing one and shipping the other.

events.title: fix: wait on the pipe, not on Qt's buffer, when draining emulator output
events.message:
fix: wait on the pipe, not on Qt's buffer, when draining emulator output

The previous attempt read in a loop while bytesAvailable() was non-zero, but that
reports Qt's internal buffer rather than the pipe. When the notifier had not run
yet it returned nothing, the loop exited immediately, and the command completed
without its response — so the CI truncation was unchanged.

waitForReadyRead waits on the pipe itself and returns as soon as anything arrives.
For output Hatari has already flushed and written before printing the prompt, that
is immediate; it blocks only when there is genuinely nothing there. Verified again
with the settle window cut to 1ms, so the drain is doing the work and the timer
remains only a safety net.

events.title: fix: read pending emulator output instead of waiting on a timer
events.message:
fix: read pending emulator output instead of waiting on a timer

Running the emulator suite in CI for the first time immediately found a race that
only shows on a loaded machine.

Linux failures were all truncation: the register dump arrived as `D0 00000000
D1 ...` with the `SR=` line missing, so registers never became valid and every
test that reads them failed. Cause: Hatari writes the response on stderr and the
completion prompt on stdout, and the two pipes are independent. The prompt can be
readable while the tail of the response is still sitting undelivered in the other
pipe; the settle window then expired and the command completed without it.

The fix is not a longer window. Hatari writes the response *before* printing the
prompt, so by the time the prompt is readable the response is already in its pipe
— it simply has not been through Qt's notifier yet. `drainStderr()` reads it
directly before deciding a command is complete, which removes the dependence on
inter-pipe timing rather than papering over it.

Verified by shrinking the settle window from 40ms to 1ms: all twelve tests still
pass, so the window is now a safety net rather than the mechanism.

Also fixes a stale-prompt false positive on builds without readline, where the
prompt goes to stderr and has no trailing newline — it stays in the buffer
forever, so the leftover prompt from before a command looked like the completion
of that command. The buffer length at dispatch is now recorded and compared.

And tests now dump the captured emulator dialogue when they fail. The macOS
failures were "no response to 'r'" with no output at all, which is undiagnosable
from an assertion; the transport is a conversation, so a failure needs to show
what was said.

ci: run the emulator tests for real on Linux and macOS

Every test that drives Hatari has reported as *skipped* in CI, on every platform.
A skipped test is not a passing test, so the green badge has been overstating
coverage of the most fragile part of this project — the part built entirely on
parsing another program's console output, and the part where every significant
bug of the last few days has been found.

Linux and macOS now install Hatari (2.6.1 in both cases — the same version
developed against), fetch a checksum-pinned EmuTOS ROM, and run the suite with
its prerequisites genuinely present.

The critical detail is the guard rather than the install. `PIST_REQUIRE_EMULATOR`
turns a skip into a *failure*, because the failure mode being fixed here is not a
missing package — it is a run that looks green while nothing was tested. CI sets
it; a developer's machine does not, so a laptop without Hatari still skips
politely. The failure names exactly what is missing.

Windows stays build-and-unit-test only: MSYS2 has no Hatari package. Its emulator
suite therefore still skips, which is honest as long as its green is understood to
mean less than the other two.

Tests run headless via SDL_VIDEODRIVER=dummy, since runners have no display; the
machine and the debugger transport are unaffected by the video driver, which is
all this suite exercises.

events.title: feat: Linux AppImage, and PNG icons
events.message:
feat: Linux AppImage, and PNG icons

Linux releases are now a self-contained AppImage rather than a tarball, built
with linuxdeploy and its Qt plugin.

Three reasons, in order of weight:

- **It is the only Linux format that is self-contained.** The Qt plugin bundles
  the xcb platform plugin, the xcbgl integrations and the TLS backends that
  Qt6::Network needs — verified in the built image (137 bundled libraries,
  including libxcb-cursor, which Qt 6.5+ requires and which is easy to miss).
- **It runs beyond the build host.** A tarball links against the build machine's
  Qt and glibc; the AppImage carries its own. Built on Ubuntu 22.04 for a glibc
  2.35 floor, which covers Ubuntu 22.04+, Debian 12+, Fedora 36+ and newer.
- **It sidesteps a policy problem.** The archive ships a non-free assembler. An
  AppImage is not a distro package, so the DFSG does not apply and only vasm's own
  redistribution terms govern. A .deb bundling it could not be in main, and would
  need hand-written Depends because CPack's dpkg-shlibdeps cannot resolve an
  aqt-installed Qt.

The AppDir is staged from the ordinary `cmake --install` tree, so packaging cannot
drift from what an install produces. The bundled assembler and ROM are placed
beside the executable, the first place tool discovery looks, and the workflow runs
the finished AppImage from its own mount with a clean environment before
publishing — verified locally: it starts, reports Qt 6.10.2 from inside the mount,
finds its own assembler, and opens a window.

Also adds 128/256/512 PNG icons generated from the SVG. The AppDir specification
wants a PNG `.DirIcon`, and linuxdeploy uses it for the desktop icon.

Releases still carry tarballs for macOS and Windows, and the Linux tarball remains
useful for anyone who prefers their distro's Qt.

events.title: feat: separate compilation via vlink, and a CI badge
events.message:
feat: separate compilation via vlink, and a CI badge

Multi-file projects now assemble one module at a time and link:

  vasmm68k_mot -Fvobj -L <mod>.lst -o <mod>.o <mod>.s   (per module)
  vlink -b ataritos -M<prog>.map -o <prog>.prg <mod>.o ...  (link)

The entry module is listed first, because TOS begins executing at the start of
text. Adding any source in Project Settings switches the build to this path; a
single file still assembles straight to a program with no linker at all.

Verified end to end against a real link, including at runtime: the linked .PRG
carries a DRI/GST symbol table that gst2ascii and Hatari's `symbols prg` both
read, so breakpoints and disassembly labels work across modules with no new debug
plumbing. Hatari's own disassembly of the two-module test resolved `greet` to
$1259e, which is exactly TEXT + the link map's module offset.

Source mapping had to change, because linking breaks the assumption a single
listing was built on: every module restarts its offsets at zero, so one live base
can no longer be added to them all. `ProgramLineMap` now composes one LineMap per
module and derives each base from the live section address plus the module's
offset in the linker's map. Single-file builds are the same path with one module
at offset zero, so there is no second code path to drift.

`-lineoffsets` would have been the obvious source for this and is a dead end:
vobj and DRI objects carry no line data, so it comes out empty. The map is the
only source, which is why the parser and its arithmetic are pinned by tests,
including one that runs a real vasm+vlink and cross-checks against the linked
program's symbol table.

Three real bugs surfaced while wiring this, each invisible until a linked build
was actually attempted:

- vasm names sections per output format: `-Ftos` writes "text"/"data"/"bss" while
  `-Fvobj` writes "CODE"/"DATA"/"BSS". The section lookup accepted only the first
  spelling, so every address in a linked build resolved to nothing.
- vasm's `(start-end)` extent is exclusive — a 0xC-byte section reads `(0-C)`,
  last byte at 0xB — but the parser added one, making every span a byte too long.
  A section could then claim an address belonging to the next one, which is how
  two modules matched the same PC. Two test fixtures had encoded the impossible
  case (an entry at exactly the declared size) and were corrected.
- Linker diagnostics name a module and a section offset (`main.o (CODE+0x4)`),
  not a line. Those are now resolved through the line map, so an undefined symbol
  points at the offending source line rather than at an object file name.

Tests: a new tst_link suite (10 cases) covering map parsing, cross-module
resolution, the unplaced-module case, and the real link. 7/7 suites pass.

events.title: fix: release packaging — executable bit, and a real macOS bundle
events.message:
fix: release packaging — executable bit, and a real macOS bundle

Running the release workflow, rather than trusting it, caught two defects that
would have shipped broken archives.

**The bundled assembler was reported NOT FOUND.** GitHub artefacts do not preserve
file modes, so the downloaded vasm was present but not executable and discovery
correctly skipped it. The packaging step now restores the mode before the binary
is used — and more importantly before it is archived, since tar and zip do carry
modes and the shipped archive has to be correct, not merely buildable here. This
affected every platform.

**macdeployqt could not find an app bundle.** macOS gets a proper .app: it is what
macdeployqt operates on, carries the icon and Info.plist, and is what a user drags
to Applications. The assembler is copied inside Contents/MacOS, which is the first
place discovery looks, so the bundle stays self-sufficient after being unpacked
anywhere.

The diagnose test now looks in the platform's actual location, including inside
the bundle on macOS — otherwise it would have skipped silently on that platform,
and a skipped test reads as a pass.

Both were invisible to the local suite: they only appear when the packaging path
actually runs. 6/6 suites still pass locally.

events.title: feat: release workflow producing self-contained archives
events.message:
feat: release workflow producing self-contained archives

Each archive carries PiST, a vasm built from the author's unmodified source, and
an EmuTOS ROM, so a fresh download runs without the user installing anything.

The bundling decision, and the basis for it, are recorded in NOTICE rather than
left implicit in a commit message: vasm's licence permits redistribution without
modification for non-commercial use, PiST is free software and not sold, and the
author publishes no host-platform binaries at all — so compiling one is the only
way to ship a working assembler. Two commitments follow and both are enforced by
tooling: the binary is never patched (PiST drives it purely by command-line
arguments) and never committed to the repository, so the source tree stays free
software. Commercial redistributors are told plainly that the permission does not
extend to them, which is why an explicit assembler path exists in settings.

Windows vasm is cross-compiled with mingw-w64 on the Linux runner rather than
built on a Windows runner with MSYS2: it is plain C with no platform API beyond
stdio, and a cross-built PE is then *run natively* by the Windows packaging job,
which verifies it more directly than building it there would. macOS is built
natively.

`--diagnose` reports every resolved tool and ROM with the paths searched. It
exists so that packaging can assert the archive resolves the assembler *it*
carries rather than one installed on the build machine — a bundle that ships a
binary it does not use is the same class of silent failure this project keeps
finding — and so a user whose tool is not being picked up can see where PiST
looked instead of just being told it is missing.

That immediately exposed a Windows problem: PiST is a GUI-subsystem application,
so it has no console and `--diagnose` would print nothing when run from a
terminal, which is exactly when it is useful. The diagnostic mode now attaches to
the launching console and reopens the standard streams, without giving the GUI a
console window on normal startup.

Qt is deployed (macdeployqt/windeployqt) on macOS and Windows so those archives
run on a machine without Qt; the Linux archive uses the system Qt, as is normal
there.

6/6 suites pass, zero warnings, including a test that runs --diagnose and asserts
it reports each section.
events.author: idontwantyourspamthanks

events.title: Fit the clipboard services board only where it was asked for
events.message:
Fit the clipboard services board only where it was asked for

Host clipboard sharing defaulted on for every windowed session, the
launcher's machines included. Sharing is a unit of the Copperline
services board, so that default put an autoconfig board on the Zorro
chain of a machine whose configuration never asked for one. Kickstart
binds the board at boot and every Exec allocation behind it moves: a
different Amiga from the one the user configured.

Some software can tell. Lotus Esprit Turbo Challenge points COP1LC at a
buffer during loading before it has written the list there, so for about
two seconds the Copper executes whatever that buffer holds, and where the
buffer sits decides what that is. On the stock layout the data is
harmless; with the clipboard unit fitted it lands where the data decodes
as MOVE $09A, $5632 -- a write to INTENA with bit 15 clear, clearing the
master interrupt enable and VERTB once per frame, 0.17 ms after the
game's own write of $C020. INTENA settles at $0000, the title sequence's
VERTB handler never runs, and its wait for 750 frames never ends: black
screen, no music, forever.

Fitting the board is now an explicit request in every session,
[clipboard] share = true or --clipboard. The two places that settled the
choice, the command line and the launcher, share one
Config::resolve_clipboard_share, which also closes a gap where a
launcher-started netplay session with share = true in its configuration
kept the unit netplay refuses everywhere else.

Headless behaviour is unchanged: the bridge was already off unless asked
for, and --clipboard still fits it so a windowed recording replays on the
same machine, reachable only through the control protocol.

Ledger gains the Windows-specific facts: the GUI-subsystem stdout problem, the
.exe discovery bug, and the three tests that encoded POSIX assumptions.

events.title: fix: Windows test output, plus a real .exe lookup bug
events.message:
fix: Windows test output, plus a real .exe lookup bug

Three things, all surfaced by the Windows runner.

Tests produced no output whatsoever on Windows, passing or failing, which made a
red run undiagnosable. Cause: qt_add_executable marks its targets GUI-subsystem,
and a GUI-subsystem binary has no attached console, so QTest's output is
discarded. Test targets are now explicitly console applications.

That revealed the second problem, which is a genuine bug and not a test artefact:
toolchain discovery looked for a bundled tool by its bare name, so a vasm placed
beside pist.exe as `vasmm68k_mot.exe` would never be found — the Windows release
bundle would appear to ship no assembler at all. Discovery now goes through
QStandardPaths::findExecutable with explicit directories, which applies the
platform's own idea of an executable name, including the .exe suffix.

Two tests encoded POSIX assumptions rather than exercising behaviour:

- outputPathsDeriveFromSource asserted hardcoded paths like "/home/x/proj/main.prg".
  That is not even an absolute path on Windows — it has no drive — so the
  expectations failed for reasons unrelated to the code. It now builds from a real
  temp directory and asserts the properties that matter: the outputs are absolute,
  siblings of the source, and carry the right suffixes.
- explicitPathWinsOverDiscovery created a chmod +x file, but Windows decides
  executability from the suffix, so the fixture was not an executable there. The
  fixture now uses the platform's own executable name, and asserts that it looks
  executable before relying on it.

events.title: fix: two platform failures found by the new CI
events.message:
fix: two platform failures found by the new CI

Both were invisible on Linux, which is exactly why the matrix exists.

Windows: an unresolved external for EmulatorHost::writeBootstrapScript. The cause
is a class/struct mismatch — EmulatorHost.h forward-declared HatariCapabilities as
`class` while emu/HatariProbe.h defines it as `struct`. MSVC mangles a reference to
each differently (`AEBV` vs `AEBU`), so the declaration and definition produced two
distinct symbols. The Itanium ABI used by gcc and clang does not encode that
distinction, so Linux and macOS linked happily. Forward declaration now matches the
definition, with a note explaining why the keyword is load-bearing.

macOS: `ld: framework 'AGL' not found`. macos-latest currently resolves to
macos-26-arm64, where Apple removed the ancient AGL framework, and Qt 6.8's
FindWrapOpenGL.cmake still references it — so the failure is inside Qt's own
configuration, not ours. CI pins macos-15 for now; covering macOS 26 needs a Qt
release whose CMake config has dropped AGL.

Also records, from investigating the vasm packaging question: vasm publishes no
binaries for host platforms at all (only Amiga-family and Atari targets), it builds
from source in seconds, and it does not implement --version. The pinned source
tarball's sha256 is now in the CI workflow and the plan.
events.author: idontwantyourspamthanks

events.title: ci: build and test on Linux, macOS and Windows
events.message:
ci: build and test on Linux, macOS and Windows

The project is developed on Linux, so every Windows and macOS claim so far has
been read from source rather than observed. GitHub runners make that observable,
which matters because a good deal of cross-platform behaviour here is exactly the
kind that reading cannot settle: path handling, the control socket that Hatari
does not compile on Windows, and process/socket APIs.

Three-platform matrix, fail-fast disabled so one platform's failure cannot hide
the others' results.

The workflow also builds vasm from the author's source, because investigation
showed **no host binaries exist** — vasm publishes builds only for Amiga-family
and Atari targets. Building takes a few seconds and is pinned by SHA-256, so an
upstream change fails loudly instead of silently altering what is tested. This
also means the build and emulator suites exercise a real assembler rather than
skipping.

Windows vasm is deferred: it needs MSYS2 make, and is worth adding only once the
rest of the matrix is green.

Also fixes version probing: vasm does not implement `--version` and prints its
banner when invoked with no arguments, so probing only the flag reported no version
for the assembler. The probe now tries both conventions.

Note for the packaging plan: since no prebuilt host vasm exists, "fetch a binary on
first run" is not viable. Release archives should instead carry a vasm built per
platform by this workflow, which is simpler and genuinely batteries-included, and
permitted because the licence allows unmodified non-commercial redistribution.

events.title: feat: packaging — install rules, notices, and toolchain discovery
events.message:
feat: packaging — install rules, notices, and toolchain discovery

First half of Phase 4.

Installation:
- `cmake --install` now installs the binary, the licence and README, a NOTICE of
  third-party components, and on Linux a desktop entry and icon so the IDE appears
  in application menus rather than being terminal-only. Verified by staging an
  install and running the installed binary.

NOTICE records what a binary distribution obliges us to: Qt's LGPLv3 relink
requirement (satisfied by dynamic linking), Hatari's GPL, and the fact that vasm is
not free software — redistributable unmodified for non-commercial use, which is why
PiST never patches it and never commits it.

Toolchain discovery (`src/toolchain/`): vasm and Hatari are now located in a
defined order — explicit setting, beside the executable, a per-user tools
directory, then PATH — and a missing tool is reported with instructions instead of
falling back to a bare name. That fallback was a real defect: a missing assembler
surfaced as a late, opaque process-start failure, and emitting a bare name meant
`found()` could never be honest. Build and Run now preflight both tools and show
where to obtain whichever is absent.

Project settings gained explicit paths for both tools, which the error dialogs
point at — previously that advice would have been a lie, since no such field
existed.

Tests: 4 cases covering discovery order, that a missing tool reports as missing
rather than as a bare name, that an explicit path wins over a system install, and
that a stale configured path is reported rather than silently substituted.

6/6 suites, 92 cases, zero warnings.

events.title: refactor: consolidation pass — silent failures, dead code, and duplication
events.message:
refactor: consolidation pass — silent failures, dead code, and duplication

Two read-only audits (dead code, error handling) plus a mechanical sweep. The
pattern they kept finding was the one that has bitten this project four times
already: code that is correct in isolation but never reached, or a failure that
is real but never surfaces.

Silent failures fixed:

- BuildService never emitted `finished` when the assembler failed to start. Qt
  emits `finished` only when a child dies, so a failed start left the caller
  waiting forever, leaked the QProcess, and left MainWindow's pending-Run flag
  armed — so the next ordinary Build would silently launch the emulator.
- `runningChanged` was emitted but never connected, so a Hatari that died at
  startup stayed labelled "Running" with step/continue enabled. This is the class
  of bug that made Run look like it did nothing.
- Every `EmulatorHost::errorOccurred` went only to a log tab that is not always
  visible; now also to the status bar.
- A failed project save printed "Settings updated" anyway, after already applying
  the changes in memory, so settings appeared saved and silently reverted.
- `CodeEditor::saveFile` never checked the stream, marking a truncated write as
  clean — the only copy of the user's work. Now reports failure, and Build/Save
  surface it instead of assembling the previous on-disk contents.
- `settings::save` ignored the byte count, so a short write reported success and
  the file failed to load later.
- A corrupt sibling `.pistproject` was log-only; now warns. So is a failed
  `parseListing`, which silently disabled both breakpoints and the highlight.

Correctness:

- `LineMap::lineFor` documented a span check it did not perform, so any address
  past the last entry — ROM, stack, BSS tail — resolved to the program's final
  source line and highlighted an unrelated line. Now bounded by the section
  extent from the listing header (`00: "text" (0-12)`), which was being parsed and
  discarded.
- `ProjectSettings` now validates monitor and RAM from JSON; a hand-edited file
  could previously pass `--memsize 65535` straight to the emulator.

Dead code removed (each verified with zero call sites):
- SessionConfig: `tosResolution`, `ideMasterImage` — read by toArgv, impossible to
  set. MachineState: `interruptMask`. EmulatorHost: `control()`, `config()`,
  `m_promptStreamIsStdout`. Diagnostic: `Severity::Info`, write-only `excerpt`.
  BuildService: `lastCommand()`, `started`, the excerpt machinery.
  HatariProbe: `hasCmdFifo`, `hasConout`, `hasParse`, `hasBacktraceCommand`
  (which was *read* in summary() but never assigned), `hasThreeModeSymbolAutoload`.
  ProjectSettings: two unused ROM-discovery wrappers. View `clear()`/`refresh()`,
  `LineMap::Address::isValid`, `CodeEditor::cursorLineChanged`.

Duplication removed:
- `<base>.prg`/`.lst` were derived separately in the build and the launch paths —
  a change to one would have silently broken Run or run a stale binary. Now one
  `outputPathsFor()`.
- Three copies of session-directory creation with two copies of the same message,
  now one `paths::ensureDirectory()`.

One audit finding was WRONG and acting on it would have introduced a regression.
It reported the memdump count was being formatted in decimal while the debugger
reads hex, reasoning from a comment in our own code. Measured against Hatari
2.6.1: `m $12596 100` returns 112 bytes, i.e. decimal; a hex reading would return
256. The code was right and the comment was wrong. Reverted the change and
corrected the comment, with the evidence.

Tests: 3 new cases — the span bound, the derived output paths, and an updated
parser expectation that had encoded the old buggy lookup. 6/6 suites, 88 cases,
zero warnings.

events.title: fix: an over-broad gitignore rule excluded the build subsystem from the repo

fix: an over-broad gitignore rule excluded the build subsystem from the repo

`build/` in .gitignore is unanchored, so it matched `src/build/` as well as the
CMake output directory. The effect was that BuildService, LineMap and Diagnostic —
four of the project's source files, and the whole build subsystem — were **never
committed**. The remote has nothing under src/build/, so a fresh clone could not be
configured or compiled.

This survived every local check because the working tree still had the files: the
build succeeded, the tests passed, and `git status` showed a clean tree (the files
were ignored, not untracked). Only a checkout on another machine would have failed.

The pattern is now anchored to the repository root (/build/, /build-*/, etc.) so it
cannot match a source directory, and the five excluded files are added.

Found during the consolidation pass by auditing ignored *and* tracked files against
what is on disk, rather than trusting a clean `git status`.

would have re-connected the document on every scroll repaint.

Two sloppy tests were caught and rewritten during this work — an assertion on a

events.title: fix: clean up session directories instead of leaking one per run
events.message:
fix: clean up session directories instead of leaking one per run

Every run created a session directory holding the generated debugger script, the
control socket and an isolated Hatari config tree, and nothing ever removed it.
Four F5 presses left four directories behind, and the growth is unbounded across
a session of normal use.

Now released in three places:
- when a session stops, or the window closes;
- when the next run supersedes the previous session;
- at startup, for directories older than two hours, which covers a crash or a
  kill where neither of the above could run.

The startup prune is age-based rather than "delete everything" because another
PiST instance may be running, and removing its live session from under it would
be worse than the leak.

removeSessionDir refuses any path outside the session base. This matters more than
the removal itself: it is a recursive delete, and the guard is what stops a bad
path becoming a delete somewhere important.

Tests: three cases in tst_settings, covering complete removal, the refusal to
delete outside the base (including for QString() and "/"), and that the prune
removes only stale directories. 6/6 suites pass, zero warnings.

events.title: fix: Run actually launches the emulator
events.message:
fix: Run actually launches the emulator

Run called build() and then checked whether a build was in flight:

    build();                        // async: starts the assembler, returns at once
    if (m_build->isRunning())
        return;                     // always true, so this always returned

build() returns as soon as the assembler process starts, so isRunning() was true
on every invocation and Run bailed before reaching the launch. Everything below
that return was unreachable: the whole emulator-launch path had never executed,
which is why Run appeared to do nothing but build.

The launch is now chained onto build completion via a pending flag consumed in
onBuildFinished, and the emulator setup moved into launchEmulator(). A failed
build now reports that nothing was launched instead of silently doing nothing.

This also corrects a false claim in the previous commit message: it stated that
Run applies the configured machine, monitor and RAM. That was written from reading
the code rather than running it, and the code was unreachable. Verified properly

feat: project settings, and machine-aware ROM selection

First step of Phase 1. Until now the session was hardcoded to st / mono / 1 MiB
with no include paths, and BuildService's include/define/cpu setters existed but
were never called from anywhere — so a multi-file project could not be built at
all.

Machine and TOS are now modelled as a pair rather than two free choices, because
Hatari enforces the pairing by overriding --machine and reporting it only as an
error log line (docs/PLAN.md §5 rule 3). Machine.h encodes the valid
combinations, with the ST/Mega ST and STe rows verified against Hatari 2.6.1.

That fixes a real selection bug: selectPreferredRom previously took the first
autostart-capable ROM in directory order, which handed an STe project TOS 1.04 —
a ROM Hatari rejects for that machine. Selection is now machine-aware and prefers
the newest compatible version, so an STe gets 1.62 (the later release, which fixes
a number of bugs) rather than 1.06, and an ST gets 1.04 rather than 1.06.

ProjectSettings persists build and emulator configuration to a .pistproject JSON
file beside the source, with the most recent paths in QSettings. Neither touches a
user's hatari.cfg, per §5 rule 7.

SettingsDialog is functional rather than refined, per the agreed approach: every
control reaches the build or the command line. The ROM combo marks ROMs that do
not suit the selected machine, and the note field explains what Hatari will
actually do with a mismatch, since its own behaviour is to silently switch the
machine.

MainWindow gains a menu bar (File / Run) so settings are reachable, and Run now
applies the configured machine, monitor, RAM, hard disk and extra arguments.

Verified by execution rather than assertion:
- without -Iinc the build fails with "fatal error 13 ... could not open"; with it,
  it succeeds
- -DWITH_PRINT changes the emitted program from 96 to 136 bytes
- an STe project selects TOS 1.62 and an ST project TOS 1.04 from the same ROM set

defaults for missing keys; tst_tosrom gains 7 machine-pairing cases. 6/6 suites
pass, zero warnings.

events.title: fix: detect debugger entry even when commands are queued
events.message:
fix: detect debugger entry even when commands are queued

onPrompt() gated entry detection on the command queue being empty. dispatchNext
re-queues a command rather than sending it while emulation is running, so a
command queued just before a resume leaves the queue non-empty — and the entry
would then go unnoticed until the 10s command timeout expired, leaving the IDE
showing "Running" while the emulator sat at a prompt.

A prompt arriving with nothing in flight means the debugger is waiting for us
regardless of what is queued, so the emptiness test was both unnecessary and
wrong. Detection now records the stop and dispatches.

Also records a verified constraint for the setup UI. Machine type and TOS ROM are
not independent: Hatari overrides --machine to match the ROM, in both directions.

  TOS 1.04 + --machine ste -> "TOS versions <= 1.4 work only in" -> switches to ST
  TOS 1.06 + --machine st  -> "for Atari STE only" -> switches to STE

So --machine is advisory. The requested machine can silently differ from the
emulated one, and the override is only reported as an ERROR log line. The setup UI
therefore cannot be two independent dropdowns, and must reflect what was actually
selected — a user choosing STE for DMA sound with a 1.04 ROM would otherwise get
an ST and a confusing failure.

5/5 suites pass.

events.title: feat: breakpoint panel, and detect every debugger entry
events.message:
feat: breakpoint panel, and detect every debugger entry

Completes the debug loop and fixes a bug that would have made breakpoints appear
broken in the IDE while working in the emulator.

The bug: the host detected debugger entry from the "You have entered debug mode"
banner, but that banner is a `static` in DebugUI set to NULL after its first
print (debugui.c:1309). It appears exactly once per session, so `stoppedChanged`
fired once and never again. A breakpoint would arm, hit, and stop the emulator
with the IDE showing nothing — the most confusing possible failure, since every
component was individually correct.

Entry is now detected structurally: a prompt arriving while no command is in
flight and nothing is queued means the debugger has just entered. That covers
breakpoint hits, exceptions and manual break-ins, and does not depend on parsing
output text. Verified by a live test that resolves line 5 from a listing, arms
it, resumes, and asserts the resulting PC equals the breakpoint address and maps
back to line 5.

Also recorded, both observed while testing:

- stdin at EOF makes the debugger abandon its read loop and resume, so a firing
  breakpoint hot-loops (~1.17M hits in 15s). IDE-driven sessions must hold the
  pipe open.
- The breakpoint panel distinguishes pending / resolved / no-code-on-this-line.
  That last state matters: a breakpoint on a line that emits nothing can never
  fire, and before this it failed silently.

BreakpointPanel shows each breakpoint's location, resolution state and
condition, with remove, clear-all and double-click-to-navigate. Addresses are
re-merged after every arm, and reset when a rebuilt program is relocated.

Tests: tst_emulatorhost gains the live breakpoint-fire case; tst_gui asserts the
resolved line actually reaches the editor widget, and that gutter markers track
the breakpoint list. 5/5 suites pass, zero warnings from a clean build.

events.title: feat: source-line breakpoints, a memory view, and the name
events.message:
feat: source-line breakpoints, a memory view, and the name

Closes the debug loop, which previously worked only from the emulator side:
there was no way to set a breakpoint or read memory from the IDE, so three
README claims were ahead of the code.

Breakpoints are anchored to file:line, never to an address. The program is
relocated by GEMDOS on every run, so an address stored at one launch points at
different code at the next. Resolution happens after the entry stop, once
`symbols prg` and `info basepage` have reported the live section bases — which
is what the two-phase attach in docs/PLAN.md §5 rule 6 exists for. Arming clears
first, because a rebuilt program may reuse an address for different code.

The commands use `b pc = $ADDR`, not a bare address: Hatari's breakpoint command
takes a condition, and a bare symbol or address fails with "condition comparison
missing". A user-supplied condition is ANDed onto the PC test, which is the only
watchpoint mechanism that exists — upstream Hatari has no memory watchpoints at
all, so watching a value means a conditional breakpoint.

Memory view reads via `memdump` and normalises byte, word and long dumps to
bytes so the rendering is identical whichever width was requested. Hardware
registers live in the $ffxxxx range, so address navigation is the primary
interaction rather than a nicety.

Gutter: left click toggles, right click opens a menu for editing the condition.

Fixes a bug the new GUI test caught, which had made two of those README claims
false in the real application:

  vasm records the source path exactly as passed on the command line, and the
  build passes an absolute path, so the listing contains "/tmp/.../prog.s".
  Breakpoints and the PC-to-line highlight both compared that against
  QFileInfo(...).fileName(), which never matches. Breakpoints would have failed
  to arm and the editor highlight would never have appeared, silently — no error
  anywhere. Matching is now path-tolerant (exact, else base name).

  This was invisible to the existing tests because their fixture listings used
  bare file names, which is not what the build produces. Both the resolution path
  and the highlight path had the defect; both are now covered by a regression
  test using an absolute path, and tst_gui exercises the real listing.

Also renames the project to PiST (Program in ST) in prose, window title,
application name and source headers. Identifiers stay lowercase — namespace
`pist`, binary `pist`, PIST_TOS_DIR — matching the convention for executables and
namespaces on all three platforms.

Tests: two new suites. tst_debug (13 cases) covers breakpoint resolution and
memory parsing as pure functions; tst_gui covers MainWindow construction and the
line map against a real vasm listing, which is the previously untested layer.
5/5 suites pass, zero warnings from a clean build.

events.title: feat: gate the control socket, and break in on program faults
events.message:
feat: gate the control socket, and break in on program faults

Two changes that between them close the Windows gap, plus the platform
documentation that was missing.

A. The control socket is now capability-gated.

Hatari declares --control-socket inside `#if HAVE_UNIX_DOMAIN_SOCKETS`
(options.c:551), so on Windows the option does not exist and passing it makes
Hatari exit with "Unrecognized option" — a startup failure that reads like a
crash. SessionConfig no longer sets the path unless the probe reports support,
and EmulatorHost treats an absent socket as normal rather than an error. Nothing
is lost: all debugger commands travel over stdin, and the socket was not being
used by the IDE at all.

Verified that a full session runs with the socket left empty — break at entry,
symbols, registers and stepping all work — which is the Windows code path, since
the integration suite runs on Linux.

B. Faults now break in, with no breakpoint set.

Sessions pass --debug-except autostart,illegal,address,zerodiv. The `autostart`
entry is not an exception class but a deferral: it arms the mask at INF load
(event.c) rather than at startup, so boot-time faults cannot break in before the
program exists. Unlike the control socket, --debug-except and --parse are not
platform-gated, so this works on Windows too.

`bus` is deliberately excluded, and that is a verified finding rather than a
guess: arming it makes TOS raise a bus error at 0xfc0ee2 (inside the ROM) during
startup, so the debugger breaks in before the program is executed — and
`symbols prg` then reports "no program loaded". `linea`/`linef`/`trace` are
excluded as well, since Line-A and Line-F are normal parts of graphics calls.

Also adds a bounded settle window when completing a command. The response
arrives on stderr and the prompt on stdout, and the two pipes are independent,
so completion now waits for stderr to go quiet instead of trusting a single
zero-delay hop.

Tests: 3 new integration cases — a socket-free session (Windows parity), a
faulting program breaking in on its illegal instruction, and a healthy program
*not* breaking in under the default exception set. 3/3 suites pass, zero
warnings.

Docs: README gains a platform-support matrix and an embedding note;
docs/FUTURE.md records the deferred work, led by the upstream patch that would
give Windows a portable control channel (Pause, live breakpoints, runtime disk
swap). PLAN.md gains launcher rules 12 and 13 and the corresponding ledger
entries.

events.title: fix: identify TOS ROMs by image header, not filename
events.message:
fix: identify TOS ROMs by image header, not filename

The README claimed pist reads the ROM version from the image itself, but
scanTosRoms() parsed it from the filename and nothing ever sought into the file.
That made the TOS >= 1.04 guard skippable: MainWindow only rejected ROMs whose
version was *known* to be too old, so a 1.02 image named e.g. "mytos.img" was
classified unknown and launched into the silent hang the check exists to
prevent (docs/PLAN.md §5 rule 3).

Implemented the header read, mirroring Hatari's own logic in src/tos.c:

- version = big-endian 16-bit at offset 2
- a 0x0206 field with 0x186A at offset 30 is TOS 2.08
- EmuTOS detected via the `ETOS` magic at offset 0x2c
- images too small to hold a header fall back to the filename heuristic

Three corrections fell out of doing this properly:

- Version bytes are hex, matching Hatari's `%x.%02x` (src/tos.c:874). The field
  0x0162 is TOS 1.62, and the old decimal formatting rendered it as "1.98".
  The filename fallback had the same bug, parsing "TOS v1.62" as 0x013E.
- supportsAutostart() now requires the version to have come from the header.
  Hatari never reads filenames, so a version inferred from a name is not
  evidence about what the emulator will do, and must not authorise the autostart
  path.
- The run path distinguishes three outcomes rather than two: known-too-old
  (refuse, naming the version), known-good (proceed), and unknown (warn and ask).
  Collapsing "unknown" into "too old" would reject valid ROMs; collapsing it into
  "good" reproduces the hang.

Also makes the ROM search usable cross-platform. Paths.cpp added the hatari
executable *file* and a system bin directory as search directories, so /usr/bin
was being scanned for ROMs and appeared in the "directories searched" message;
appendUnique now requires an actual directory, and the beside-the-executable
fallback is limited to Windows and macOS, where the release bundles ship data
that way.

Tests: new tst_tosrom suite (12 cases) covering header parsing, the 2.08
adjustment, EmuTOS detection, hex rendering, the filename fallback, truncated
images, and that a filename claim cannot authorise autostart. Verified against
the four real ROMs on the development machine, whose header values now agree
with their conventional names. Full suite: 3/3 passing, zero warnings, and the
emulator integration test runs rather than skipping.

events.title: feat: Phase 0 spike — editor, build service, and debug client on stock Hatari
events.message:
feat: Phase 0 spike — editor, build service, and debug client on stock Hatari

Proves the three risky integrations end to end without forking Hatari:

Editor
- m68k Motorola-syntax highlighter (mnemonics, registers, numbers, directives,
  labels; `;` anywhere and `*` in column 0)
- line numbers, error gutter markers, current-execution-line highlight

Build
- vasmm68k_mot driven as a subprocess, never modified
- parses both vasm diagnostic shapes: located (`error N in line L of "f"`)
  and line-less module/fatal errors, into a Problems pane

Debug
- Hatari as a subprocess over stdin/stderr/stdout, with the control socket used
  only for control while emulation is running
- two-phase attach: arm `b pc = TEXT && pc < $0xe00000 :once` at launch, then
  `symbols prg` relocates against the live basepage
- registers, disassembly with symbol labels, and PC -> source line via the
  `-L` listing map (no DWARF, no GDB, no fork)

Findings that changed the design, all verified by test:
- the control socket is starved while the debugger is stopped, so debugger
  commands must travel over stdin
- the debugger prompt is the reliable end-of-command signal; it moves between
  stdout (readline) and stderr (non-readline builds)
- the entry session dump must be consumed before dispatching the first command
- a timed-out command still owes a prompt, which must be swallowed
- the disassembly address prefix depends on the user's bDisasmUAE setting
- the `r` response has no CPU= header; the PC comes from the trailing line
- TOS < 1.04 cannot use the GEMDOS-HD run path, so a ROM is now validated from
  its image header and muST support autostart

Tests: 9 parser tests (vasm diagnostics, listing line map) and 7 integration
tests against a real Hatari (entry stop, register round-trip, basepage
relocation, labelled disassembly, single-stepping). 100% passing via ctest.

events.title: fix(tape): don't restart the machine when mounting a tape
events.message:
fix(tape): don't restart the machine when mounting a tape

The Spectrum, CPC and SAM tape mounts each bracketed themselves in
stop()/start(). The pair is unnecessary -- parsing allocates and mountBlocks
swaps the list in one synchronous step, so the frame loop has nothing to trip
over, which is why the disk mounts shed theirs in d65ed23 -- and all three
also ran start() on the failure path. Since the shell returns early on !ok
without unpausing, a tape that would not parse quietly restarted a machine
the user had deliberately paused. On the SAM the call sat in a finally, so it
ran unconditionally.

Drop them, as the Jupiter Ace's mount already did. Resuming after a
successful mount stays the shell's decision; it already calls unpause() for
tape targets.

The CPC's cartridge path keeps its pair: inserting a .CPR power-cycles the
machine, so that one is doing real work.

events.title: Deck plan: its two pointers off the OS's zero page (#19)
events.message:
Deck plan: its two pointers off the OS's zero page (#19)

hexwab hung at the deck plan on b5ffa94, b-em's "model B, OS 1.2, Opus
1770 with DDOS 3.45": BRK, PC in the default handler, and the plan had
drawn fine earlier in the same game.

b5ffa94 is the first build carrying the LUTs rewrite of ConDeckCell,
and that rewrite parked its two new variables at &A9-&AB. THE SECOND
HALF OF THE ZERO PAGE IS NOT ALL OURS: per the hardware wiki's map,
&A0-&A7 is the NMI's - which the game claims at boot, which is what
made drYcol legal there - but &A8-&AF is the OS's own scratch and
&B0-&CF the filing system's. cdDst2 is a POINTER, and STA (cdDst2),Y
writes sixteen bytes through it per cell: change it under us and the
plan scribbles wherever it then points, which is the shape of the
crash and explains why it is intermittent and why a third-party DFS
shows it when Acorn's has not.

They are the level draw's own pointers now - cdDst2 = mapptr,
cdLut = tdp - on exactly the rationale xfer.asm's header gives for
borrowing the same set: the deck, the level draw and the sprites are
suspended while a console page is up, each is re-derived by its owner
before its next use, the plan draws in one uninterrupted pass, and the
IRQ touches none of them. mapptr in particular is dead the moment
BuildLevel returns, and BuildLevel runs immediately before this page
(ct_trydeck). Nothing after ConDeck7 in that arm reads either.

Costs nothing: planChars and code_end are unmoved.

Verified in jsbeeb (B/DFS 1.20, so NOT hexwab's failing configuration -
this shows the change is sound, not that his hang is gone): play
reached, conActive/conDeckReq driven to raise the plan, and it drew
correctly - rooms, corridors, lift markers, the white player marker -
with conDeckReq going 1 -> 2, the one-shot completing rather than
hanging. The console then closed back to play (conActive 0, bank 4
resting), and a second entry, which runs BuildLevel again immediately
before ConDeck7, drew an identical page. That back-to-back ordering is
the one this change could have broken.

Console: browser repaints, game-over rows, blank deck-plan cells (#19)

hexwab on the DECISION 22 build. Three things, one of them mine.

1. The database browser repainted the portrait and the name every pass
   and again on a page-back. DbPage1 now draws them only when dbType
   differs from poLastType - DbImage's own guard, and if the picture is
   this droid's then the name beside it is too - and DbBack's return to
   the browser calls DbClearText, so a page-back touches neither. A
   full DbClear still invalidates the guard, so entry from the console
   main screen draws both.

2. REGRESSION OF MINE, from DECISION 22: IsOverDraw put the game over's
   two strings on the shared line table's line 0 and DB_LINE_LAST,
   which WERE buffer rows 1 and 13 - the high-score screen's own rows,
   so the game over replaced that text. DECISION 22 moved every line to
