events.title: Sell bank 6's SCANSTEP tail fold back: -613 B, +3 cycles a compiled row
events.message:
Sell bank 6's SCANSTEP tail fold back: -613 B, +3 cycles a compiled row

Issue #2, KC's route A. The fold is now per bank - export_droids.py grows
a FOLD_TAIL tuple and it is (0,). Bank 5 keeps its fold, bank 6 unfolds.

THE LEDGER FIGURE WAS WRONG AND HAD BEEN SINCE THE DAY IT WAS WRITTEN.
docs/no-load.md 11j records 70 sites a bank and 756 bytes. 11k's
interning of the duplicate compiled blocks landed the SAME DAY and
collapsed 13 of those sites onto shared copies; nobody netted the two off
against each other. Counted and then measured on today's tree:

                       sites/bank   bytes/bank
  11j as recorded          70          756
  actual, after 11k        57          613

Measured rather than derived - the exporter was unfolded wholesale, the
bank asserts commented out and the gauge read: bank 5 &BFA8 -> &C21B and
bank 6 &BB9A -> &BE0D, both 627, which is 613 plus the 14-byte tail that
is then dead. 57 x 11 = 627 exactly. The 17-byte SCANSTEP in the drRHalf
accounting was stale too (the macro has been 13 since the deferred carry
of 2026-09-01) and is corrected.

The cycle side is untouched by any of that, because interning changed
which copies exist and not how many rows execute: 3 cycles per compiled
row DRAWN, 20 rows a sprite a pass, ~480 with a full pool of eight.

WHY ASYMMETRIC. Because the banks are:

  bank 5  droids.asm   shifts 0/1 px    88 free  - keeps the fold
  bank 6  droids2.asm  shifts 2/3 px  1,126 free - unfolds, 513 left

A sprite picks its bank on sub-pixel X, so about half the pool draws
through the faster copy: ~240 cycles a pass at eight slots. Nothing in
the blitter cares which way a bank went - the tails were already per bank
(a JMP cannot reach the other), every block is entered through a dispatch
table, and the tables are the same size in both files by construction,
which is what main.asm's address asserts check.

Unfolding bank 5 as well needs 525 more. Its only movable content is a
briefing page stream, and the evicted stream then has nowhere to land:
bank 6 after its own unfold has 513 and brstream3 is 566. Fifty-three
bytes short - a bin-packing failure, not a space one, with 384 bytes of
total machine slack. Not done, and not only because of that: the port
holds 50 passes in 100 fields, so this buys headroom and nothing visible,
and taking banks 5 and 6 back to 41 and ~0 is not worth 240 cycles until
something wants them. 11l has the working.

VERIFIED BY TEXTUAL EQUIVALENCE, which the usual two checks cannot do -
the buffer oracle NOPs the sprite draws and the listing stream changes
instructions by design. Expand every `JMP xScanStepRts` in the OLD
droids2.asm to SCANSTEP + RTS, drop the dead tail, diff against the new
file: 2,388 lines -> 2,442, identical to the new file's 2,442. The
generated code is provably the same program. droids.asm is byte-identical
to before. Then built and played - title, into a deck, a long run right
with the deck scrolling clean behind the droid.

CLAUDE.md's memory table was stale in four rows and is corrected from the
gauge: code image 108 B (&2F94), bank 5 88, bank 6 513, bank 7 171.

events.title: A POSIX Makefile, and the tools stop naming .exe (issue #3)
events.message:
A POSIX Makefile, and the tools stop naming .exe (issue #3)

hexwab's issue #3. build.ps1 stays the Windows build; the Makefile is the
same pipeline as a dependency graph, so a partial build does only what
changed and `make -j4` runs the five bank compressors at once.

  build.ps1                  7.9 s
  make, serial, from clean  18.2 s
  make -j4, from clean       9.2 s
  make, nothing changed      0.23 s
  make, one src/*.asm        3.1 s

The two produce the SAME DISC, and it is checked rather than asserted:
tools/compare_ssd.py compares per file out of the DFS catalogue, masking
!BOOT's build timestamp. Identical on both, debug (8 files) and -Release
(12). The Makefile's image boots to the title in jsbeeb.

POSIX.1-2024 make - ?=, .PHONY, .NOTPARALLEL and -j are all in Issue 8,
and GNU make and bmake have had them for years. No $(wildcard), no ifeq,
no % rules: every source is listed explicitly, which is what the issue
asked for. Slashes throughout, every filename in the case it has on disc,
and no `.exe` written down anywhere - tools/zx0tool.py resolves the
compressor for the five Python tools that shell out to it ($ZX0, then
bin/, then $PATH), and build.ps1 now reads $env:PYTHON / $env:BEEBASM so
`make check-ps1` can hand its own tools over.

PARALLEL COMPRESSION cost make_disc.py a split: --extract-file drops one
bank out of the raw image as build/pack/NAME.bin, a .bin.zx0 inference
rule compresses it, --packed-dir consumes the streams. A stream from
outside is NOT trusted - same zx0.py round-trip against this build's
bytes, same in-place margin test - so a stale .zx0 fails the build
instead of shipping a broken disc.

THREE PARTS OF THE PIPELINE ARE NOT A DAG (docs/build.md has all three):

- The pack loop is a fixpoint. It stays a shell loop in the $(RAW)
  recipe, and brfimg/lowimg/krimg.asm are prerequisites of nothing - list
  them and every build finds the image stale against its own output.
- A config STAMP FILE was wrong, and instructively so: make counts a
  target whose recipe RAN as updated whether or not the file changed, so
  a stamp rewritten every build made a no-op `make` reassemble and
  recompress the lot. Replaced by a phony `config` that deletes $(RAW)
  when RELEASE/INTRO change, ordered by the recursion in `all`.
- Multi-output exporter rules race under -j: serial, make re-stats and
  export_bbc.py runs once; under -j4 four copies ran concurrently over
  the same files. mk/data.mk declares .NOTPARALLEL.

The exporters live in mk/data.mk, NOT the Makefile, so they cannot creep
into the default build - the first version had them inline and adding one
tool file made `make` try to regenerate all the artwork. src/data stays
committed for the reasons in the gitignore; `make data` and `make world`
are explicit.

paradroid_ce.lst is committed (KC, on the issue), which is what makes
`make data` possible at all.

TWO BUGS FOUND ON THE WAY:

- src/data/sndchat.asm carried a hand edit export_sound.py did not know
  about. BR_CHAT_PRE moved to main.asm in no-load step 5 and its old home
  became `ASSERT BR_CHAT_PRE == 5`; the exporter still emitted the
  definition, so regenerating would have given beebasm the symbol twice.
  Exporter fixed - and the other 21 generated files came back
  byte-identical, which is the first proof that the exporters are
  deterministic and the committed data does match the listing.
- distclean ate the compressor: `rm -f bin/zx0` under MSYS resolves to
  bin/zx0.exe. It no longer touches bin/ at all.

Known rough edge: `make check-ps1` will not run under MSYS2's make here,
because PowerShell launched from MSYS sh cannot execute the Microsoft
Store Python alias. It works from a normal Windows shell; the equivalence
it checks was verified by hand.

events.title: partial-register-write: ask which bits are undefined, not whether one write is whole
events.message:
partial-register-write: ask which bits are undefined, not whether one write is whole

The rule suppressed a partial write only when some single instruction wrote the
register whole. That misses how registers are actually built: `move.w d3,d4`
then `move.b d2,d4` defines the whole low word between them, and the byte write
preserving bits 8-15 is the entire point of writing it that way.

So instead of asking whether the register is ever written whole, accumulate the
bits the routine writes at any width, subtract them from the preserved bits,
and ask only whether what is left -- the bits nothing ever defines -- is read.
Populating a register across several narrow writes is construction; only
effectively undefined bits are worth reporting.

On the corpus this takes `respect` from 3249 reports to 7, and the three
projects measured for the EXT fix from 55 to 41. The 3240 that dominated the
count were one generated file using the low and high byte of a register as two
independent accumulators, which is exactly the shape this now understands.

The survivors look like the real thing: a `move.w` feeding an `add.l`, and one
site whose preceding line is a commented-out `ext.l` on the same register.
Reading past what the narrow writes define is still reported.

events.title: Model EXT/EXTB as reading their source width, not their result width
events.message:
Model EXT/EXTB as reading their source width, not their result width

EXT and EXTB name the width of the result, not of the operand read out of the
register: EXT.W reads the low byte and writes the low word, EXT.L reads the low
word, EXTB.L reads the low byte. The bits analysis read them at the result
width, so the bits the instruction is about to overwrite looked observed.

That made partial-register-write report the ordinary sign-extension idiom --
`move.b (a0)+,d0 / ext.w d0 / muls.w #40,d0` -- as a partial write whose
preserved bits are consumed. Across three corpus projects the fix removes 34 of
89 reports from that rule, all of them this shape.

It narrows what EXT is taken to read; it does not excuse the register.
`move.b` then `ext.w` then `move.l` is still reported, because EXT.W defines
bits 8-15 and no further, so reading the long still observes whatever bits
16-31 held on entry -- which is the bug the rule is for. The DIVU/DIVS case
just above already handled the same mismatch in the other direction.

events.title: Gate combine-loads-into-movem to the targets the win is measured on
events.message:
Gate combine-loads-into-movem to the targets the win is measured on

68kcounter models the 68000 and the 68020, and both agree that MOVEM wins from
three registers up. It does not model the 68040 or 68060, where MOVEM is not
the fast path -- and the code this rule fires on most in the corpus is Kalms'
c2p routines, which target exactly those parts. Assuming the 68000 result
carried over would have made the rule most active precisely where it is least
justified, so 040/060/CPU32 are excluded until someone measures them.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Add combine-loads-into-movem
events.message:
Add combine-loads-into-movem

A run of postincrement loads through one pointer is what MOVEM does in a
single instruction: `move.l (a0)+,d0 / (a0)+,d1 / (a0)+,d2` is
`movem.l (a0)+,d0-d2`. This is the load direction the shelved MOVEM plan
deferred, which the corpus says is the one worth having -- 188 foldable runs
against 12 for the store direction.

Two things measurement decided, both contradicting the original plan:

- Three is the floor, not two. On 68000 a pair of loads is the same 4 bytes as
  the MOVEM and 4 cycles faster, so folding a pair is a regression. From three
  it turns over: 6 bytes/36 cycles become 4/36, and eight registers go from
  16 bytes/96 cycles to 4/76.
- Long only. MOVEM.W sign-extends each word into the whole register where
  `move.w (a0)+,d0` leaves the top half alone, so a word run would first have
  to prove those bits dead. 169 of the 188 foldable runs are long anyway, so
  the word case is left for later rather than guessed at.

Registers must ascend in MOVEM's own D0-D7/A0-A7 order, though the numbers need
not be contiguous since the list is a bitmask -- `d1/d3/d5` is one instruction.
A run will not load into the pointer it is walking, and the flags are gated
because each MOVE sets N/Z/V/C while MOVEM sets none.

events.title: Add combine-consecutive-bit-ops
events.message:
Add combine-consecutive-bit-ops

A run of single-bit operations on one register is one masked operation:
`bclr #0,d0 / bclr #4,d0` clears the same bits as `and.b #$ee,d0`. Mined 38
sites, and it is the largest per-site win found so far -- on 68000 a two-long
chain goes from 8 bytes and 28 cycles to 4 and 8, and the four-long CACR
cache-control chains in real boot code go from 16 bytes and 56 cycles to the
same 4 and 8. Wins on 68020 too, so no CPU gate.

Details that needed care:
- BCHG is its own inverse, so its bits cancel out of the mask rather than
  accumulating; a run that toggles the same bit twice has nothing to suggest.
- The mask is sized to the highest bit touched (.b/.w/.l), which is safe
  because a bit instruction on a data register only alters the bits named.
- `& limit` operates on a signed 32-bit value, so the unsigned coercion has to
  come last or a mask reaching bit 31 renders as a negative number.
- Symbolic bit numbers are kept as parenthesised shifts, so the mask does not
  rely on the assembler agreeing with C about how `<<` and `|` bind.
- Flag gating matches bit-op-low-word: BCLR sets Z from the bit it tested,
  AND sets N/Z from the whole result.

Verified against the corpus, including that a run is not merged across
conditional-assembly arms -- the code this was found in puts the ELSE branch's
BCLRs directly after the IFEQ branch's.

events.title: Merge the two fold rules into fold-redundant-intermediate
events.message:
Merge the two fold rules into fold-redundant-intermediate

There was no code duplication -- both came from one factory -- but the split
was weakly justified and leaked into the matching logic.

The rule id split was my own assertion that a memory-to-memory move is "a
style choice some codebases would rather not have suggested", which I never
checked; memory-to-memory MOVE is thoroughly idiomatic 68k. It is one
transform, so it is now one rule id, named for the concept rather than the two
shapes it happens to take.

The leak mattered more. The body asked `kind === "copy"` to decide whether a
memory destination was reachable, phrasing an encoding fact as a question about
which rule was running: arithmetic has only an `<ea>,Dn` form and MOVE is the
one that reaches memory, whichever rule matched. That check now reads the
mnemonic, so the body no longer knows which rule it belongs to.

The audit keeps both shapes as separate measured cases under the one id.

events.title: Generalise the fold to any source, and add zero-store-to-clear
events.message:
Generalise the fold to any source, and add zero-store-to-clear

Two things came out of the corpus that the first fold rules were too narrow for.

Generalise the intermediate-register fold from memory sources to any source,
so a register copy or an immediate that only feeds the next instruction folds
too: `move.w d2,d1 / add.w d1,d0` is `add.w d2,d0`, and `move.w #$7fe,d3 /
and.w d3,d0` is `and.w #$7fe,d0`. Each measures 2 bytes and 4 cycles better.

The exclusion matters more than the extension. The single most common shape in
the corpus (1394 sites) is `moveq #-1,d0 / move.l d0,bltafwm(a6)` -- the
MOVEQ-via-scratch idiom that move-immediate-via-scratch actively recommends,
because MOVEQ carries its value in the instruction word. Folding those back
measures 2 bytes and 4 cycles WORSE, and the word-sized case is an exact wash.
So an immediate only folds when it pays for its own extension word either way
and MOVEQ could not have carried it.

zero-store-to-clear covers `move.w #0,<mem>` -> `clr.w <mem>`: 2 bytes (4 for a
long), identical cycles and bus cycles, identical flags. Kept as a review
rather than a safe fix because a 68000 CLR reads before writing, so a
write-only register briefly holds bus noise between the two cycles -- harmless
where nothing samples it in between, which is the usual case for things like
blitter modulos. Declares no `serves` goal: the project's own goal-filtering
test caught that a rule costing nothing must not declare one.
events.author: grahambates

events.title: No loads after boot: the font goes boot-only and dfsSave dies with it
events.message:
No loads after boot: the font goes boot-only and dfsSave dies with it

The PARAFNT load lived in ts_loads, which every route to the front end
runs -- boot, the game-over title and the briefing's fire exit --
because the title overlay was MODE 1 artwork at &3000 and ate the font
every time it was shown. no-load step 3 moved that overlay to &0900;
step 5 took away the last thing that staged over &3000, PARMAN's
stream at DEPK_STREAM. Nothing destroys the font any more, so it is
loaded once, in .start.

Its position is load-bearing on both sides: after SetupMode because
VDU 22 clears &3000-&7FFF, after BootBanks because PARADAT's stream
stages from &3200 to &5C0F over it, before TitleSeq because a filing
call needs the MOS still to own the machine. It also makes PARAFNT
resident for HsEntry, which was an invariant no ASSERT could check.

THAT FORCES THE TERMINAL DIVIDEND, because SaveDfsWs had exactly one
call site and removing it would leave RestoreDfsWs restoring a
snapshot nobody took -- garbage over &0D60-&0DEF and &0E00-&10FF. So
the whole machinery goes: SaveDfsWs, RestoreDfsWs, the DFSWS
constants, both call sites in GoTitle and BrDispatch, and dfsSave's
912 bytes of bank 6. The rule they enforced still holds -- the low
overlay does still bury DFS's workspace and the MOS's extended vector
table -- but nothing has to obey it, because nothing makes a filing
call after PageLowIn. UnpackBankIn and BootBanks stay: they are the
boot loads.

  filing calls after boot   1 -> 0
  main-RAM code image free  28 -> 108   (code_end &2FE4 -> &2F94)
  bank 6                    212 -> 1,126

11h estimated the dividend at 241 bytes of scattered main RAM; 80 is
what it actually yields, because the boot loads still need
UnpackBankIn, BootBanks and the loadfnt string. Its 912 for bank 6
held up exactly.

Verified on the shipping image in jsbeeb, B-DFS1.2, two cold boots:
title, fire, game, ESCAPE, death, game over, high-score entry, three
initials, title again (now with no RestoreDfsWs in front of it), fire,
game again -- which runs ts_loads and PageLowIn a second time; and
boot, title, timeout, briefing, which is BrTimeout RTSing into the
font-less ts_loads.

events.title: The briefing goes resident: post-boot loads 3 -> 1
events.message:
The briefing goes resident: post-boot loads 3 -> 1

PARMAN is gone. Its text is the five ZX0 page streams of stage 1,
depacked one page at a time into the arena; briefman, sndchat and
brExtra are bank-resident in bank 5; keyredef is a ZX0 stream
assembled at BR_RECS and depacked over the page it replaces.
BrTimeout makes no filing call and BrDispatch reloads PARASPR on
neither exit, because bank 5 is never evicted now. PARAFNT is the only
post-boot load left.

The renderer got simpler, not more complex. BrRowList's per-page walk
through brPageLLo/LHi/HLo/HHi -- four indexed loads to keep every index
8-bit across 285 rows -- is two loads from main RAM, because the
depacked page carries one page's tables at a fixed address. PARBRF
shrank 1,012 -> 967 on that alone.

arena's now and only the page that is up exists, so BrFerryScores
carries bank 7's fourteen bytes into brSc once and BmRowScan applies
them on every depack of BR_SCORE_PAGE.

- Page 5 came up as pure noise. PoDraw depacks a portrait chunk into

  disc image       47,872 -> 45,312
  bank 4  225      bank 5  2,650 -> 88
  bank 6  442 -> 212 (via 16's +461)   bank 7  775 -> 171

events.title: The build grows a pack pass: brfImg and lowImg ship ZX0, +461 in bank 6
events.message:
The build grows a pack pass: brfImg and lowImg ship ZX0, +461 in bank 6

beebasm cannot compress its own output, and two of the things bank 6
carries are assembled code copied down to run elsewhere: the PARBRF
briefing driver at &0400 and the low overlay at &0E00. main.asm now
SAVEs each block under an X-name, tools/pack_overlays.py reads them
back out of the image, ZX0s them and writes src/data/brfimg.asm and
lowimg.asm for the next assembly, and build.ps1 assembles again if
anything changed.

  brfImg  1,012 -> 769
  lowImg    919 -> 731
  bank 6     33 -> 494   (+461: 431 packing, 30 shorter copiers)

BrfResident and LowResident become depacks rather than
three-page-and-a-tail copies. Zx0Unpack is main RAM, so calling it
from bank 6 is the ordinary direction and the stream stays paged.

THE LOOP IS NOT BELT AND BRACES. A stream that changes size moves the
bank around under the very block it came from, so the extracted bytes
could be from a layout that no longer exists. The exit code (0
unchanged, 10 rewrote) makes convergence a build-time fact. Measured
from a cold start with both generated files deleted: stub, assemble,
pack, assemble, unchanged -- two assemblies, and the second proves the
overlays' bytes did not depend on the bank layout. Steady state is one.

Two details worth keeping: the X-files never reach the disc, because
make_disc.py writes only the names in its LAYOUT; and the size ASSERT
lives in the generated file rather than main.asm, so the bootstrap
stub can omit it and still assemble while every real stream carries
it.

WHY NOW (docs/no-load.md 16): the handover's stage 2 cannot be built.
PARMAN loads OVER bank 5 and three of the five page streams have to
live in bank 5, so the load that delivers the renderer would evict the
text it reads. Stages 2 and 3 merge, and merged the packing is 194
short -- bank 4's 225 can hold nothing, bank 6's 442 absorbs one item.
The pass that fixes it was already required: 3A, keyredef shipped
packed, is impossible inside one beebasm run for exactly the reason
above. Both agreed with KC.

It costs disc space: 47,872 -> 50,176, +2,304. A ZX0 stream inside
PARSPR2's own ZX0 stream compresses worse than the raw code did.

Verified on the shipping image in jsbeeb, B-DFS1.2 -- the whole
front-end loop, which is the right test because LowResident delivers
the IRQ, the rupture and the keyboard and BrfResident delivers
BrDispatch: cold boot, title, fire, game, ESCAPE, death, game over,
high-score entry, three initials, title again through GoTitle after
RestoreDfsWs, briefing on the timeout.

events.title: Extend the load fold to copies, giving memory-to-memory moves
events.message:
Extend the load fold to copies, giving memory-to-memory moves

`move.w (a1,d1.w),d3 / move.w d3,(a0)` is one `move.w (a1,d1.w),(a0)` on the
68k. Mining found 233 candidate sites, more than the arithmetic case the rule
was built for, and 68kcounter puts the fold at 2 bytes and 4 cycles better.

Split under its own rule id rather than folded into the arithmetic one: a
memory-to-memory move is a style some codebases would rather not be nudged
towards, even though it measures strictly better, so it should be separately
switchable.

The copy case needs one guard the arithmetic case did not: a memory
destination is evaluated after the load in the original pair, so if it
addresses through the scratch register it is currently indexing with the
freshly loaded value, and folding would silently index with the old one.

events.title: A formatted disk kept its old geometry on the MTX, Einstein and SAM
events.message:
A formatted disk kept its old geometry on the MTX, Einstein and SAM

Only the Spectrum consumed the format latch. Everywhere else a completed
WRITE TRACK left formattedUnit sitting on the controller, so the drive panel
went on showing the geometry the image had when it was inserted, and the
latch was never cleared. The MTX and the SAM even had diskImageForSlot ready
for it — the half the bridge needs to re-detect an image — with nothing ever
publishing a slot to use it.

The MTX and the Einstein tick their own controllers from runFrame, so their
frameTick consumes the latch and does nothing else; ticking the FDC here as
well would decay its display state twice. The Einstein was two pieces short
rather than one and gains diskImageForSlot, without which the bridge skips
the refresh however the slot is published.

Each SAM drive is its own WD179x, so formattedUnit is always 0 on whichever
one formatted and the panel slot is the drive, not the unit. Two formats
finishing in one frame can still only report one slot, as on the Spectrum,
but both latches are cleared so neither re-fires.

The tests drive a real format stream through each controller — an ID field
and a data field per sector, at each machine's sectors-per-track — rather
than poking the latch, since the point is that the path from WRITE TRACK to
the panel is joined up.

events.title: Add fold-load-into-operation, found by corpus mining
events.message:
Add fold-load-into-operation, found by corpus mining

A load into a scratch data register that the very next instruction consumes,
and nothing else reads, is a whole instruction the operation could perform
itself: `move.w x_speed,d1 / add.w d1,d0` is just `add.w x_speed,d0`.

Mining turned up 124 candidate sites across 14 real projects. Verified with
68kcounter that the fold is always 2 bytes smaller and 3-6 cycles faster on
68000 (and no worse on 68020), so it carries no CPU gate.

Two correctness points the pattern-matching alone would have got wrong:
- EOR is excluded. The 68k only encodes EOR Dn,<ea>, so `eor.w (a1),d3` is
  not an instruction at all; 14 of the mined candidates were EOR.
- ADDA/SUBA preserve CCR, so for an address-register destination the MOVE's
  N/Z/V/C are what survives the original pair. Folding drops them, so that
  case is gated on flag liveness instead of being unconditionally safe.

Checked against the corpus: in Amiga-sources/Wave.s it fires on four blocks
and correctly declines a near-identical fifth twelve lines earlier, where a
later `swap d1` still reads the scratch.

events.title: Drive sounds for the MTX, CPC and Einstein, and the CPC's drive panel
events.message:
Drive sounds for the MTX, CPC and Einstein, and the CPC's drive panel

The synth only ever ran for the Spectrum and the SAM: every other machine
with a drive published floppySlot = -1, so the Drives pane offered a sound
toggle that could not make a sound. The MTX also had nothing to play — its
FDX drives are 5.25" half-height units, and the two profiles modelled the
3" CF2 and the 3.5".

The new profile carries the two things that make a 5.25" recognisable, both
optional so the existing profiles are untouched: a belt-driven spin-up, the
hum sweeping 42Hz up to 72 over the gain ramp, and a low sine thump under
each step, where the band stepper lands as a clack rather than a click. Its
seeks are slower to match — 12ms a track against the 3"'s 10 and the
3.5"'s 6.

The FDX's profile is fixed rather than read off the disk: an 80-track FDX
image is past the capacity where the +3's test would call a drive 3.5". The
CPC and Einstein do take that test, since a 720K drive alongside the built-in
one was common on both. It moves to floppy-sound.ts as profileForDisk, with
the profile codes and driveTypeForProfile, so the mapping lives in one place
instead of an if/else in the bridge.

The CPC's drive panel goes with it. Wiring the LEDs meant ticking the FDC:
the uPD765A latches its read/write state for 25 frames and decays it in
tickFrame, which nothing on the CPC called, so the first access would have
pinned the LED on read for good. That is the Spectrum's frameTick block, so
the CPC now takes the rest of it too — the unsupported-SCAN warning, and the
FORMAT latch that refreshes the disk metadata, which needs diskImageForSlot
on the probe or the bridge skips the refresh.

events.message:
no-load §14: step 5 measured and designed, and 2B turns out to be unnecessary

KC chose 1C, 2B and 3A. Measuring the pages first says the split is not needed:
§5's "the buffer needed is 1,082" is a page WITH its 114-byte pointer tables,
and the records alone top out at 967, which already fits the map's 1,024. The
briefing keeps its five pages, exactly as the original has them.

  page   records  +tables   ZX0(recs)  ZX0(with tables)
     0       624      738         409               474
     1       967    1,081         604               671
     2       962    1,076         574               643
     3       932    1,046         566               634
     4       435      549         292               356
           3,920    4,490       2,445             2,778

Keeping the tables in a bank costs 2,445 + 570 = 3,015; folding them into each
page's stream costs 2,778. The tables hold absolute addresses, so the second
only works if the depack lands at a fixed base — which it does, so the exporter
assembles each page as if it lived at the buffer and the pointers are right by
construction.

The arena is bigger than the map, and this is measured rather than reasoned:
seeded &4220-&460F with &A5, ran the briefing, read it back. 296 bytes written,
all of them &4220-&4347; &4348-&4600 untouched, and contiguous with the map. So
the arena is &4348-&4A00, 1,720 bytes. The 296 is more than BmSnap's rectangle
accounts for and is NOT explained, so the buffer starts at &4500 — 440 bytes
clear of the high-water mark, and still 199 spare on the largest page.

Budget: 2,778 text + 471 briefman/sndchat + 776 keyredef packed = 4,025 against
4,092 free. 67 spare, every figure measured. The next 432 are in packing brfImg
and lowImg, which needs §12a's build pass.

events.title: Add combine-consecutive-shift, discovered by mining real Amiga source
events.message:
Add combine-consecutive-shift, discovered by mining real Amiga source

Parsed 6250 .s/.asm/.i files (517k instruction lines) across ~30 real
demoscene/game projects in the sibling projects directory to find repeated
instruction shapes not covered by any existing rule, using m68k-parser
directly rather than eyeballing code (zero parse failures across the corpus).

Two consecutive same-register same-direction immediate shifts turned up
repeatedly (Planet-Rocklobster's rotzoom/blur/city/framework in particular).
Verified with 68kcounter that combining is unconditionally safe -- splitting
a shift into two steps on the same register is associative for the value
and every flag, not just usually equivalent -- and that when the combined
count no longer fits a single immediate shift (>8), routing it through
MOVEQ + a register-count shift is a real 68000 win (36 cycles -> 10 for one
real example) but a wash or slight loss on 68020's barrel shifter, so that
branch is 68000-only like its siblings in known-register-shifts.ts.

events.title: PARBRF and PARALOW stop being disc files: post-boot loads 5 -> 3
events.message:
PARBRF and PARALOW stop being disc files: post-boot loads 5 -> 3

The 4A experiment §12a asked for, and it came out yes.

THE EXPERIMENT. Move both overlays' assembly ABOVE bank 6's block, so bank 6
can COPYBLOCK them and still SAVE before bank 7 reuses &8000 — only the last
bank block can be filled after the fact, and bank 7 had 759 bytes against the
1,931 these need. beebasm resolves constants in file order, so the question
was how many the overlays use that are defined later. A static probe found
six in one pass:

  BR_PAGES, BR_ROW_LO, BR_ROW_HI, BR_XTRA0   ->  src/data/briefconst.asm, a
                                                 second generated file that
                                                 main.asm includes early
  BR_CHAT_PRE, BR_PO_UNIT, BR_PO_OFS         ->  main.asm beside UNIT_BYTES,
                                                 ASSERTed at their old homes

A first attempt moved the whole PARMAN block up instead, to carry the BR_*
constants with it, and failed on BR_PO_ROW0 = DB_IMG_ROW — which reaches into
bank 7. Splitting the four generated constants into their own file is what
avoids dragging bank 7 up as well.

The move was proved inert before anything was built on it: EVERY file in the
catalogue byte-identical to the previous build, PARBRF and PARALOW included,
with !BOOT the only difference because it carries the build stamp.

WHAT WAS BUILT. brfImg and lowImg at the tail of bank 6, sized by
`brf_end - brf_start` and filled by COPYBLOCK — no hand-maintained constant,
because the overlays are assembled before the bank now; PARTITL cannot do
that and pays for it with TITL_BYTES. BrfResident and LowResident live IN
bank 6, like TiResident lives in bank 7, so they cost the code image nothing,
and both end in main RAM's PgData because a PAGEBANK executed in the bank
would swap the RTS out from under itself.

  post-boot loads   5 -> 3   (PARAFNT, PARMAN, PARASPR)
  disc files       11 -> 9
  disc image   46,336 -> 45,568
  code image free  14 -> 28
  bank 6 free   2,447 -> 442
  bank 7 free     759 -> 775   (the title overlay lost TiLoadBrf: 397 -> 381)

Verified in jsbeeb on the shipping image, the whole front-end loop: cold boot,
title, fire, game (LowResident — the low overlay carries the IRQ, the rupture
and the keyboard, so a bad copy never reaches a screen), ESCAPE, death, game
over, high-score entry, three initials, TITLE AGAIN, briefing on the timeout,
fire, game. The second title is the one that matters for BrfResident: it
arrives through GoTitle after RestoreDfsWs, and BrDispatch — which every
post-title path runs through — lives in the bytes it copies.

events.title: Sign the dmg's companion tools before the bundle

Sign the dmg's companion tools before the bundle

The macOS package job failed at codesign: signing Contents/MacOS/copperline
makes codesign treat it as the bundle's main executable and verify every
nested code object, and copperline-import-uae was still unsigned at that
point because lipo -create strips the per-slice signatures. The local dry
run passed only because a single-arch lipo is a plain copy that keeps the
linker's ad-hoc signature.

Sign the two companion tools first and let the bundle-level --deep sign
cover the main executable. Reproduced locally by stripping the prebuilt
binaries' signatures: the old order fails with the CI error, the new order
produces a bundle that passes codesign --verify --deep --strict with all
three executables signed.

events.title: Ship copperline-ctl and copperline-import-uae in every release package
events.message:
Ship copperline-ctl and copperline-import-uae in every release package

Both tools are default-feature binaries, so every packaging job already
compiled them, but only the Homebrew formula installed them: the Windows
zip, macOS dmg, AppImage and Flatpak staged the emulator alone. The DAP
guide and the VS Code extension expect copperline-ctl on PATH, so users
of those packages could not use the debug adapter or the MCP server
without a source build.

Windows: build-zip.ps1 copies both .exe files beside copperline.exe and
the zip smoke job checks they are present and start. macOS: the build
job uploads all three binaries as its slice, build-dmg.sh lipo-joins
each into Contents/MacOS and signs the tools explicitly (codesign --deep
does not reliably reach extra executables there), and the smoke job
checks both are universal and start natively and under Rosetta.
AppImage: a single-entry-point image cannot expose a second binary, so
the tools ship as a separate Copperline-<ver>-<arch>-tools.tar.gz release
asset, smoke-tested like the net-helper tarball. Flatpak: both are
installed into /app/bin for flatpak run --command=.

Both tools returned exit status 1 for --help, which the new smoke checks
rely on; -h/--help now print usage to stdout and exit 0.

Docs: getting-started gains a Command-line tools table listing where each
package puts the tools; the DAP, VS Code, UAE import and extension READMEs
point at it instead of implying a source build is required.

events.title: Widen medium-confidence optimisation rules, verified with 68kcounter
events.message:
Widen medium-confidence optimisation rules, verified with 68kcounter

Rather than trust the earlier hedged guesses, measured each candidate
against real 68000/68020 timings before changing anything:

- known-zero-clear: every memory-destination CLR form is slower than
  MOVE from a known-zero register, not just predecrement/indexed
- lea-zero-address: the .L form is an even bigger win than .W
- arithmetic-immediate-via-scratch: AND/OR/EOR benefit at any magnitude,
  since they have no quick-immediate form to defer to unlike ADD/SUB
- known-register-shift-to-clear: a genuine win on 68020's barrel shifter
  too, unlike its 68000-only siblings in the same file which specifically
  trade instructions for cycles on a linear shifter
- added asl-byte-seven alongside lsl-byte-seven, tracking V (which ASL
  sets data-dependently, unlike LSL which always clears it)
- added cancel-subq-postincrement-move, the mirror of
  cancel-addq-predecrement-move (the read lands at the decremented
  address, so the fold needs an explicit displacement rather than
  collapsing to bare (An))

Confirmed prefer-bit-op's .L-only restriction and shift-two-adds' .W/.B-only
restriction are both already correct, not narrow: widening either would be a
measured regression, so both are left alone.

docs/no-load.md §12: the handover — where the night got to

Free bank space went from 2,201 to 6,081 in four commits, all of it in the

per compiled row (0.6% of a pass at worst; the frame lock still measures 50
passes in 100 fields).

  bank 4    225 ->   225
  bank 5    665 -> 2,650
  bank 6    552 -> 2,447
  bank 7    759 ->   759

Step 5's demand is 3,955 against 6,081, so IT FITS for the first time, with
2,126 to spare. Space is no longer what blocks the goal, and byte-hunting is
no longer the priority — it was, right up until tonight.

§12a is where I stopped and why: step 5 is a real rearrangement, and the three

block assembled, and bank 6's SAVE cannot be deferred the same way. Reordering
the bank blocks, assembling the low overlay inside bank 6's block, or adding a
build pass are all build changes; none should be picked unattended.

Also verified tonight on the folded+interned build, beyond the A/B: the
briefing round trip (title timeout, briefing, fire, game — which is the path
that evicts bank 5 and reloads PARASPR into the rearranged bank) and the

events.title: Intern the duplicate compiled blocks: +2,368 bytes, and no cycles at all
events.message:
Intern the duplicate compiled blocks: +2,368 bytes, and no cycles at all

Bigger than the tail folding it follows, and free. Every compiled block is
reached only through a dispatch table, so pointing two entries at one copy
costs nothing — no indirection, no cycles, just a different byte in a table
that was always going to be there. docs/ram-pass.md's bank-4 finding, applied
to the compiled code: what pays is redundancy, not compression.

emit_rotor_code writes every block through a pool keyed on the block's own
text and hands back the label that already holds an identical body. What it
catches:

  The two shifts' restore halves are identical — a 1 px shift does not
  change WHICH columns a row touches, and a restore is keyed on the column
  set. Eight drRHalf blocks a bank become four.

  The eight restore programs of a shift are two: the sequence depends on
  phase >> 2, so phases 0-3 share one and 4-7 the other.

  And then the programs collapse across shifts as well, because once the
  halves are shared the two drRPrg bodies are textually identical. The
  saving compounds, which is why it came out at 2,368 rather than the 2,318
  a scan of duplicate bodies predicted.

  bank 5   ends &BA73 -> &B5A6    1,421 free -> 2,650   (+1,229)
  bank 6   ends &BAE4 -> &B671    1,308 free -> 2,447   (+1,139)

Free bank space is now 225 / 2,650 / 2,447 / 759 = 6,081, and step 5's 3,955
fits with room for the first time.

Verified by the §11j recipe and against the PRE-FOLD baseline, so the folding
and the interning are proved together: seed pinned at gs_seeded, aligned on
gameTick, both machines stopped at &111E, &3E00-&8000 compared — 18,944 bytes
covering the sprite save areas, tile map, panel, LUTs and the strip. ZERO
differences at both checkpoints, one at rest and one after 150 frames right
and 110 down (which puts the player on shift 2, so bank 6's code). Frame lock
still 50 passes in 100 fields.

events.title: SCANSTEP tail folding: +756 bytes in each of banks 5 and 6
events.message:
SCANSTEP tail folding: +756 bytes in each of banks 5 and 6

The first move of no-load §11, and ram-pass.md's held reserve is spent.

Every compiled rotor row ended with the SCANSTEP macro expanded inline (13
bytes) and its own RTS. They end `JMP <tail>` (3) instead, with one 14-byte
shared tail per bank — it has to be per-bank because only one is paged at a
time. 70 sites a bank: 28 draw rows + 4 restore rows per shift, two shifts,
plus the 6 drRHalf blocks whose last row emits a SCANSTEP immediately before
the block's RTS. The emitter buffers each drRHalf block now so it can see
whether it ends that way; the other ten end on a restore and keep their RTS.

  bank 5   ends &BD67 ->  &BA73    665 free ->  1,421
  bank 6   ends &BDD8 ->  &BAE4    552 free ->  1,308

NOT the ~2,100 ram-pass.md promised. That entry predates the SCANSTEP
deferred carry, which took the macro from 15 bytes to 13 and so took 2 off
what each fold gives back; the estimate was never re-derived. 756 a bank is
the measured figure, and no-load §11c is corrected with it.

Cost: 3 cycles per compiled row DRAWN and nothing else — the JMP is on a path
that was already a JSR from its caller. Twenty rows a sprite a pass means
~120 cycles with two sprites up and ~480 with a full pool of eight, 0.6% of
the 79,872-cycle pass. FRAME LOCK UNCHANGED: 50 passes in 100 fields on both
builds, measured the same way on each.

Verified by A/B differential against the previous build, three checkpoints,
ZERO differences:

  at rest, 2 sprites, shift 1          play buffer      0 of 10,240
  +150 right +110 down, player shift 2 play buffer      0 of 10,240
  +63 left                             &3E00-&8000      0 of 18,944

The last covers SPR_SAVE, which is what the restore routines write — 32 of
the 70 folded routines are restores.

THE TRAP, and it is why no-load §11j records the recipe: two builds do not
play the same game. TiBootPal seeds drSeed from TiWait's title dwell, and the
two images differ in size, so the same key presses at the same frame counts
give a different seed, deck and droid layout. The first attempt scored 1,672
of 10,240 on a build that is provably correct, entirely from that. The fix is
to break at gs_seeded, poke drSeed identically in both (bank 4), align on
gameTick rather than frames, and stop both at the top of the main loop before
dumping.

events.title: no-load: the plan re-audited (§11), and §10's test list cleared
events.message:
no-load: the plan re-audited (§11), and §10's test list cleared

§11 is the new plan. §1a's demand arithmetic survives; its SUPPLY column
missed two things worth ~1,800 bytes, so the goal closes by ~300 rather than
missing by ~1,200:

  dfsSave is 912 bytes of bank 6 and is pure load-support (main.asm:4094).
  It is a terminal dividend — it only pays when the LAST load goes — which
  means the plan can be ~900 short right up to the final step and still land.

  "Bank content cannot live in main RAM" (§4b) is wrong. Main RAM is visible
  from every bank and bank code may call and read it freely; the one-way rule
  is the other direction. Freeing main RAM converts to bank space 1:1 by
  relocating a bank routine out.

§11a is the first per-file byte map the port has had, taken by assembling a
copy of main.asm with a PRINT after every INCLUDE. The compiled shifts are
23,777 bytes — 24% of the machine's RAM — holding ~2,400 bytes of entropy.
§11d says why a runtime generator for them is still the wrong lever, and
answers §5's rejection, which was argued on disc size rather than residency.

§11e changes step 5's shape twice: keyredef depacks into the tile map and runs
there (1,014 unpacked exceeded every free block and always would), and every
briefing depack routes through the map rather than DEPK_STREAM, which kills
&3000's second destroyer inside step 5 instead of needing a step of its own.

§10's test list is cleared in jsbeeb on this build — transfer (entry, board,
play, win, exit), the lift and its no-load exit, all four console pages and
the exit, the three straddling portrait types, the CTRL+R redefine screen, a
sound capture, and the -Release build booted through the intro to play. §9's
two outstanding items are closed with it. Real hardware, the transfer's lose
path and a systematic rotor walk remain.

The levers used to reach each screen are recorded, because they are reusable —
and DEBUG_DECK's CTRL+[ IS drivable: key_down takes inkey numbers.

events.title: Stop taking the function keys off the browser
events.message:
Stop taking the function keys off the browser

F1-F12 belong to the browser and the operating system — F5 reloads, F11 goes
full screen, F12 opens the developer tools — and an emulator has no business
hijacking them. They are now dropped at the browser boundary before anything
else looks at them, joystick bindings included, so nothing calls preventDefault
on one.

The machines that have function keys of their own keep them in their matrices:
the Einstein's F0-F7, the MTX's F1-F8, the MSX's F1-F5, the SAM's F0-F9 keypad.
Those maps also drive the MCP key tool, which runs headless with nothing to
hijack, so deleting them would have cost automation for no gain. They stay
reachable on the on-screen keyboard, and on the SAM through the numeric keypad,
which is the same set of cells.

events.message:
A floating pane moved while it was being resized

The resize grip is the browser's own, drawn by the resize property rather than
by an element, so there is nothing to hit-test and nothing to stop propagation
on. Pressing it lands on the pane, and since the whole case had just become the
drag handle, the same press started a move as well: the pane wandered off under
the pointer as it grew.

Its corner is now reserved by hand — a press within 18px of the bottom-right,
against a grip of about 16, does not start a drag. The check sits in panes.ts
rather than the component because the test environment is node, where importing
a compiled JSX module runs delegateEvents against a window that is not there.

events.message:
An undocked keyboard is the case alone, dragged by itself

Out of the layout, the pane drops its chrome: no title bar, no border, no pane
background. What floats is the machine's case and nothing else, which is the
point of taking it out of the column in the first place.

With no title bar to grab, the case is the handle — a press anywhere that is
not a key or a control starts the move, so keys still type. The resize corner
stays where it was. The dock toggle leaves the title bar for the pane's own
top-right corner: docked it lands where it always did and floats the pane,
undocked it stays invisible until the pointer comes to the keyboard.

Docked panes are untouched, title bar and all.

events.title: Keyboard cases fill the pane, and floating panes scale the face
events.message:
Keyboard cases fill the pane, and floating panes scale the face

Resizing a floating pane now works in both axes and scales the face with it.
The scene publishes the two candidate scales — what the display-scale setting
asks for, and the largest the frame can take — and the stylesheet picks: docked
takes the smaller of the two as before, floating takes the fit alone, so
dragging the pane makes the keyboard bigger as well as smaller. A floating pane
therefore carries an explicit height: its frame has to be a size container for
that fit to mean anything, and a size container without a definite height
resolves to none at all.

The 48K's legends were the last ones sized from the display-scale setting
rather than the scale the scene is actually drawn at, so they kept their full
size on keys shrunk to fit a narrow pane — and stayed small on keys enlarged in
a floating one. Every other face was converted at some point; this one was
missed.

Every case — its colour, edges, bevels and moulded grooves — now paints on a
full-bleed backdrop rather than a centred strip, following the CPC's existing
50cqw idiom instead of the second background this had grown. That needed the
container-type and the overflow clip off each scene, or the backdrop was
clipped back to the box it was trying to escape. How far it bleeds is one
variable: width only when docked, both axes when floating, where a pane taller
than its keyboard was showing the pane's own colour as bands above and below.

events.title: Upgrade m68k-parser to 1.6.0
events.message:
Upgrade m68k-parser to 1.6.0

The lockfile was pinned to 1.3.0, so this picks up several parsing fixes
that change counts rather than just messages.

The one that matters most here: `<` used to begin a lookahead for a matching
`>` that stopped only at whitespace, so in

    dc.w 1,((W+16)>>4)|(24<<6),0,((W+16)>>4)|(24<<6)

it found the `>` in a later operand and swallowed everything between as a
string literal. The line came back with two operands instead of four, and
was counted as 4 bytes rather than 8.

Also included: a parenthesised displacement such as `(WIDTH+32)/8(a0,d0.w)`
now parses as indexed addressing rather than being rejected, `equr` register
aliases are accepted as index registers, `@` is accepted in symbol names as
vasm's mot syntax allows, and macro parameter locations inside expressions
span the backslash.

The block layer added in 1.6.0 is deliberately not adopted. It reports where
blocks are, whereas Parser.ts needs to expand them - collecting macro bodies
by name and replaying REPT bodies a computed number of times - which is a
different job that the existing streaming state machine already does.

3062 tests pass unchanged.

events.title: Close a 19-rule gap in test coverage
events.message:
Close a 19-rule gap in test coverage

Audited by checking whether each registered rule's id appears anywhere in
the test suite text at all: 19 of 132 rules never did, meaning nothing
would fail if their logic broke.

Most were the untested half of a pair sharing a source file with a
well-tested sibling - style/prefer-dbf next to the tested style/prefer-dbra,
optimization/prefer-bclr next to the tested optimization/prefer-bset, and
similar pairs in narrow-address-immediates.ts and move-immediate-synthesis.ts.
Same factory function, same shared logic, but each direction has its own
alias table or trigger condition, so a typo in the untested one (a wrong
condition-code mapping, a mask polarity error) would have shipped silently.
Spot-checked three of these against their source before trusting the rest of
the list, since a false positive here would mean writing a redundant test:
in each case the sibling really does have distinct trigger logic, not just a
mirrored id.

The rest were standalone rules gated behind a specific processor
configuration nothing in the suite happened to construct (mc68030-only,
mc68060-only, 68020+-only), or narrow one-off sequences (JSR+JMP tail
dispatch, EXT.W+EXT.L combining) that were implemented but never asserted on.

Writing these surfaced two places where my own first draft was wrong, both
now recorded as comments so the next person does not repeat the mistake:
register/flag liveness across a branch is only ever "dead" with an explicit
overwrite past the point every path converges - reaching RTS unmodified
leaves it "unknown", not "dead" - and the scratch register in
compare-long-immediate-via-moveq is loaded with the value being compared,
not the value used to prove some other register dead.

132/132 rules now referenced by id at least once. 39 new tests, 652 total,
all passing.

events.title: Take block structure from m68k-parser
events.message:
Take block structure from m68k-parser

scanBlocks walked the directives itself, keeping three parallel stacks and
its own copies of the opener, alternative and terminator lists. m68k-parser
1.6.0 derives the nesting, so this becomes a reshaping of that tree into the
flat views the analyses want: a flow region per line, terminated REPT bodies,
and conditionals with their arms.

isBlockBoundary now asks blockRole rather than matching against local lists,
which is what kept those lists here in the first place. The BlockStructure
and ConditionalBlock shapes are unchanged, so cfg, symbols, project-symbols
and context are untouched.

118 lines to 95, with the parts that were easy to get subtly wrong - pairing
terminators through nesting, and which blocks count as terminated - now
shared with the other consumers rather than reimplemented.

One behavioural difference in malformed input: the old scan tracked macros,
repeats and conditionals independently, so any ENDM closed a macro even with
a REPT still open inside it. The parser matches each terminator to a block it
can actually close, leaving the inner one unterminated. Both are defensible;
the new one is consistent with what the other consumers now see.

Verified beyond the 608 tests by diffing CLI output over 20 real sources
before and after, holding the parser version constant: byte for byte
identical.

Requires m68k-parser ^1.7.0 for blockRole, which is not published yet.

events.title: Let the keyboard pane float free of the layout
events.message:
Let the keyboard pane float free of the layout

The keyboard sits under the screen in the main column, which is a poor place
for something far wider than it is tall — and its scale is set by the width it
is given, so where it sits decides how big it is. Drag its title bar and it
tears out where it stands and follows the pointer; the title bar also carries a
toggle to send it back. A floating pane resizes from its bottom-right corner,
horizontally: the height is a consequence of the width, so there is no second
axis to drag.

Position and width persist per pane, and a pane whose stored position falls
outside a window that has since shrunk is pulled back into view on mount and on
resize. Floating is a per-pane opt-in — only the keyboards ask for it, and
sidebar panes keep the HTML5 drag-and-drop reordering they had.

events.title: Keyboards were DPR times too big on a high-DPI screen
events.message:
Keyboards were DPR times too big on a high-DPI screen

The display-scale setting counts physical pixels — one emulator pixel maps to
exactly that many, which is what keeps the picture pixel-perfect — so both
renderers divide by the DPR when they size the canvas's CSS box. The variable
the on-screen keyboards size themselves from carried the raw setting instead,
and CSS is what lays them out. The two only agree at 1x: on a Retina Mac the
canvas halved and the keyboards did not, so every cap and legend came out twice
the size relative to the screen, and the scene's own width clamp then pinned
the keyboard to the pane. Windows at 125% had the same fault at a quarter the
size, small enough to pass for right.

--display-scale now carries scale / dpr. The DPR signal moves out of Screen.tsx
into state, since two places need it and it has to re-run the CSS variable when
the window moves between displays; Screen.tsx reads the same signal it always
did. A test pins the invariant the regression broke: the CSS scale handed to
the keyboards is the one the canvas measures itself in.

events.title: Report vasm diagnostics for include files
events.message:
Report vasm diagnostics for include files

An include is excluded from assembly by default, because assembling one on
its own reports errors that exist only out of context: it depends on whatever
pulls it in. The effect was that `.i` files got no vasm diagnostics at all.

vasm names the file each message belongs to, and the include trace that
reached it, so one run describes the same error from the point of view of
every file in the chain. That was being discarded: the filename was captured
by the pattern and never read, and every message was re-pointed to the
outermost file, which is right only when that is the file being reported on.

parseVasmOutput now parses messages into their location and trace, and places
each one against a given file: at its own line when that file has the
problem, at the include statement when the file is further up the chain, and
not at all when the message belongs elsewhere. Without a target it uses the
outermost position, which is what it always did.

Saving an include therefore assembles a program that includes it and reports
what belongs to it. Saving a program is unchanged: an error in one of its
includes still appears on the include statement, with the path to the problem
in the message.

Only one program is assembled, the first that includes the file, so saving a
widely shared header does not assemble every part of a demo. Which one is
arbitrary where several qualify, and a file no program includes is still not
assembled.

events.title: Discover entry points, and offer the nearest definition first
events.message:
Discover entry points, and offer the nearest definition first

getEntryPoints reads the include graph for files that are assembled rather
than included: roots that pull in at least one other file. The second
condition matters, since a workspace holds plenty of files nothing includes -
vendored headers, unused data - and those are orphans rather than programs.
getEntryPointsFor names the programs a given file belongs to, which for a
shared header is all of them.

There is no formal marker for an entry point in assembly, so this is a
reading of the include graph rather than a fact about the project. Measured
against local projects it lines up: chonk and desire-sitm give two each,
plasma three, and tte-vaporous one per demo part.

Definitions are now returned nearest first, by steps through the include
graph, rather than in whatever order files happened to be indexed. Where a
name is defined more than once in a unit the closest one is the one a reader
most likely means, and the order was previously arbitrary.

Per-unit vasm diagnostics is the obvious next use and is not done here. vasm
does name the file each message belongs to, but the output is currently
attributed wholesale to the file that was assembled, with an included file's
errors deliberately re-pointed to the include statement. Assembling an entry
point on behalf of an include would mean publishing diagnostics to files
other than the one saved, and clearing them again, which is a larger change
than it looks.

events.title: Index the workspace on startup
events.message:
Index the workspace on startup

Symbol resolution was only as complete as the set of files that happened to
be loaded, which was whatever had been opened plus what those included. Find
references and rename therefore missed uses in files the editor had not been
shown, and results changed as tabs were opened.

The workspace is now indexed in the background once the connection is up.
Indexing keeps symbols and include edges and discards syntax trees, which is
what makes covering a whole workspace affordable: 923 files in 838ms, against
the couple of hundred megabytes retaining their parses would have cost.

Build output and dependency directories are skipped. A build directory
usually holds a copy of every source, which would otherwise show up as a
second definition of every symbol; in one local project that is 25 of 89
files. `m68k.exclude` adds further patterns.

Indexing runs after initialize rather than during it, so the first request is
not held up. Requests arriving while it is still going see what has been
indexed so far, which is no worse than the lazily populated store they saw
before.

Scoping is unaffected: with both entry points of a two-part workspace now
indexed, which is exactly the condition that used to leak, a label private to
one still resolves and renames only within its own unit, while a symbol in a
shared include is found in every part - including parts that were never
opened, which is the point.

events.title: Separate indexed files from open ones in the store
events.message:
Separate indexed files from open ones in the store

Groundwork for indexing the whole workspace. Resolution needs every file's
symbols and include edges, but only the file a request names needs its syntax
tree, and keeping trees for everything is what makes a full index too
expensive: measured over a 970 file project, retaining parse output costs
245MB against 15MB for symbols and includes alone.

IndexedDocument holds what crosses file boundaries. ProcessedDocument extends
it with the document, its parse and its block structure, and is what an open
file gets. The store holds either, and isProcessed distinguishes them.

Every site that needed the tree turned out to be working on the document the
request names, which is open by definition, so each is a guard rather than a
change in behaviour. The exception was hover, which read the declaration line
out of the defining file's text: that file is usually not the open one, so
the line is now captured when the symbol is recorded. This also fixes hover
for a definition in a file that happens not to be loaded.

Nothing indexes the workspace yet; included files are indexed instead of
processed, which is the only behavioural change here.

events.title: Scope symbol lookup to the assembly unit
events.message:
Scope symbol lookup to the assembly unit

getDependencies walked the include graph in both directions at once, so from
any file it reached everything sharing any include. Two entry points that
both include a hardware definitions file were treated as one namespace.

The effect on rename was destructive rather than merely noisy. Renaming a
label in one entry point edited the call sites of the same-named label in an
unrelated one, but not its definition - getDefinitions returned early from
the current document while getReferences walked the whole component - so the
other file was left calling a label that no longer existed.

An assembler splices includes into the file that pulls them in, so the unit
of naming is that tree, not the workspace. getUnitFiles finds the trees a
document belongs to by looking at what includes it, and the rest of each tree
by looking at what those files include. Only the document itself is followed
upwards: climbing up from a file reached on the way down is what crossed from
one tree into another.

Inclusion being textual, the scope has to run downwards as well as up. A
symbol defined in a file can be referenced by a file it includes, which an
existing test covers, so this is not simply the reverse of the old direction.

Also scopes incdir to the files a document can see. Pooling them across the
whole store let an incdir in one part of a workspace change how an unrelated
part resolved its includes.

Behaviour, checked over stdio as well as in tests: a label private to one
entry point no longer leaks into a sibling and rename touches only its own
file, while a symbol in a shared include still finds its uses in every unit
that includes it, and rename updates all of them.

Workspace symbol search is left alone. It is a search across the workspace
rather than a resolution question.

events.message:
Memotech MTX keyboard addition

The MTX500, MTX512 and RS128 share one deck, so there is one face and only the
badge's model name changes with the model. Everything sits on a 1u pitch and
no cap is under it: the typing block staggers 0.5u / 0.25u / 0.5u behind 1.5u
modifiers, the number, Q and A rows finish flush at 15u with BS, LINE FEED and
RET, and the numeric keypad and two-column function block stand off to the
right in their own recessed wells, their four rows on the main block's row
lines. The MEMOTECH rule runs across the top.

Every cap and both its legends come from MTX BASIC's own key tables — one entry
per matrix cell at 0x1729 unshifted and 0x177A shifted — which settles the caps
the host key map never named: LINE FEED is [3,6], the keypad's 8/EOL is [1,7]
and its 9/BRK is [0,8], and ENT/CLS is [7,7]. The two unlabelled caps flanking
the space bar are the one guess: the ROM gives the spare cells on their sense
line no character at all, so they are presented as further space bars.

events.title: Parse float literals
events.message:
Parse float literals

`dc.s`, `dc.d`, `dc.x`, `dc.p` and `fequ` take floating point values in
vasm's mot syntax, but a decimal point ended the number: `dc.s 1.5` came back
as 1 with the fraction dropped, and `fequ 3.14` as 3. A silently wrong value
is worse than a reported error, since nothing downstream can tell.

A dot between two runs of digits now reads as a float, with an exponent if
one follows. Digits are required on both sides, so `1.w` stays a word-sized
absolute address and a leading dot still begins a local label. A bare `1e3`
is left as a decimal followed by a symbol rather than guessed at, and there
is no use of exponent notation anywhere in the corpus to suggest otherwise.

NumberFormat gains "float". Whether a float is meaningful where it appears
is left to the caller: `dc.b 1.5` parses as a float but is not valid data for
a byte, which is a linting question rather than a parsing one.

The corpus has exactly one real occurrence, `COUNT 6.666666666666667`, which
previously fell back to a raw macro argument because the expression stopped
short of the text.

Version left alone: bumping it here is what pushed the last two releases past
1.5.0 and 1.7.0.

Einstein 256 TEXT overlay sat one character left of the text

MOS 2.1 sets the V9938's R18 display adjust to 0x0A, which shifts the whole
picture six source pixels right — a full character cell in the 6-pixel MOS
font. The renderer honours it, as the hardware does; the overlay and the cell
blanking did not, because both positioned themselves against the border origin
alone. So the transcribed text read correctly but sat a character to the left
of the glyphs it was covering.

The V9938 now exposes the adjust it is already applying, and the Einstein's
field box adds it. Blanking takes its x from that same box, so the two cannot
drift apart again.

events.title: Einstein 256 TEXT overlay sat over the wrong box
events.message:
Einstein 256 TEXT overlay sat over the wrong box

The overlay stretches the transcribed grid across the descriptor's active area,
which holds for every machine whose text fills it. The 256's does not: MOS 2.1
runs GRAPHIC 2, so a 42x24 grid of 12x8 buffer cells is 504x192 centred in a
512x212 window. The overlay was starting ten lines high and stretching 212/192
too tall, so it drifted further off the text with every row down the screen.

A transcribe driver can now report the field its grid actually occupies, in
buffer pixels, and the overlay sits over that when given; machines whose text
fills the active area say nothing and are unaffected. The Einstein reports the
same box blankCells paints into, so the two cannot drift apart.

events.message:
Expose blockRole for classifying a single line

m68k-lint needs to know whether a line is block structure without deriving
the whole tree: a rule matching a run of instructions must not span one,
since the arms of a conditional are alternatives, a repeat body runs a
different number of times than the code around it, and a macro body is not
executed where it is written.

blockRole answers the question directly, which keeps the tables inside the
parser rather than exporting them for callers to match against themselves.

events.title: Take block structure from the parser
events.message:
Take block structure from the parser

m68k-parser 1.6.0 derives macro, repeat and conditional nesting, so the two
places that worked it out here no longer need to: folding walks the block
tree instead of scanning directives with its own stack, and a macro
definition's extent comes from its block rather than a forward search for
`endm`. The opener and terminator tables go with them, since they belong
next to the parser that reads the directives.

The structure is computed once per document alongside the parse and kept on
ProcessedDocument, rather than per request.

Folding also gets more correct as a side effect. It used to treat any
terminator as closing the innermost open block, so `macro / ifeq / endm`
closed the conditional; the parser matches each terminator to a block it can
actually close, leaves the inner one unterminated, and closes the macro.

New diagnostics come with it: unterminated blocks and terminators that match
nothing were invisible before. Measured over 3,598 local sources, 15,838
blocks produce exactly one report, and it is a real bug - a macro that opens
IFLT and reaches ENDM without an ENDC.

Requires m68k-parser ^1.6.0, which is not published yet, so `npm ci` will
fail until it is.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Add a block structure layer
events.message:
Add a block structure layer

Lines are parsed independently, which is what keeps the parser usable on
half-written and macro-templated code, but it leaves every caller to recover
nesting for itself. m68k-lsp derives it twice, for folding ranges and for the
extent of a macro definition, and m68k-lint has its own module for it.

parseBlocks walks a ParsedFile once and pairs each opener with its
terminator, returning macro, repeat and conditional blocks with their
children, the arms of each conditional, and the name of each macro. blockAt
and enclosingBlocks look up what contains a line. Indices are positions in
ParsedFile.lines rather than one-based Location.line, which the doc comments
say explicitly, since mixing the two has been a recurring source of
off-by-one bugs.

Kept as a separate entry point rather than a second parse mode. There is one
line parser, so a fix cannot land in one mode and not the other, callers who
do not need nesting pay nothing, and a file that does not balance still
parses - which matters in an editor, where an unterminated block is the
normal state while typing rather than an error.

This also makes a class of real errors detectable that nothing reported
before: unterminated blocks, terminators matching nothing, and crossed
nesting such as `macro / ifeq / endm`, where the inner block is reported and
the outer one still closes.

Checked over 3,598 local m68k sources: 15,838 blocks, and exactly one file
reports an error - a macro that opens IFLT and reaches ENDM without an ENDC,
which is a genuine bug in that source.

events.title: Disassemble Knight Lore from a map someone had already drawn
events.message:
Disassemble Knight Lore from a map someone had already drawn

The other builds discover which bytes are instructions by playing the game and
recording what runs. That approach stalled here: the title screen reads the
keyboard hardware directly rather than through the ROM, and the mapped code
never got past it -- 140 addresses out of 30699 bytes.

It did not need discovering. tcdev disassembled and annotated Knight Lore in
2017 and Michael R. Cook converted that to SkoolKit form in 2019, and the map
is right: assembling their disassembly and diffing $6108-$D8F2 against the
snapshot matches on 30697 of 30699 bytes. The two that differ are the operand
of LD HL,$F100 at $D6B8, where the snapshot is right and SkoolKit's own
skool2bin is wrong -- it clamps an operand pointing past the end of the binary
it is writing.

So the map comes from there, extracted with skool2ctl -w abs: block
boundaries, the code/data split, sub-block lengths and labels, and nothing
else. Neither work carries a licence, so none of their prose is reproduced;
the commentary in knightlore_annotations.ctl and knightlore.ref is written
from the code in this build. Same posture as pobtastic's Atic Atac names --
use the facts, credit the person, write your own words.

Borrowed facts still get checked. 40696 bytes reassemble byte for byte, and
the snapshot the build writes is compared with the snapshot it read: identical
in all 49179 bytes. That second check is not redundant. The round trip only
sees the game block and is blind to the registers, and this snapshot is taken
mid-frame rather than at a cold start, so a machine resumed without its IX, IY
and alternates does not carry on playing. It caught both: the registers were
being dropped, and SP was two out, because the .sna header holds SP after PC
has been pushed while write_sna() wants the value from before.

Two build checks come out of getting this wrong first:

- check_alignment() -- an instruction comment is written "$ADDR,N" where N is
  a byte count, and SkoolKit does not complain when N stops mid-instruction.
  It resumes decoding from wherever the count ran out and carries on. Writing
  $B028,6 over a seven-byte run invented an LD B,$47, and everything above
  $B02F moved. The round trip caught it 9000 lines away, as an sjasmplus error
  about writing past 65536.
- check_coverage() -- the map's blocks must run in order from $6108, because a
  hole becomes zeros in the output rather than an error.

Two things about the game came out of writing the annotations. The object
table is forty records of thirty-two bytes at $5C08, which is LAST-K: Knight
Lore puts its own data straight over the ROM's system variables, because it
never calls the ROM once running and reads the keyboard itself at $B5F7. And
all 103 sprites share one format -- a width, a height, then a mask byte and a
bitmap byte per cell -- proved by arithmetic rather than by eye, since for
every one of them the gap to the next label is exactly
2 + 2 * (width AND $7F) * height.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: Keep macro template names out of the symbol table
events.message:
Keep macro template names out of the symbol table

m68k-parser 1.5.2 marks a symbol or label whose name embeds a placeholder,
so `.loop\@` and `BLTEN_\1` are recognised as templates resolved per macro
expansion rather than names that exist as written.

Definitions previously did this by looking for a backslash in the name, which
is now the parser's job to report. References did not do it at all, so every
use of an interpolated name was recorded as a reference to a symbol that
could never be defined, and turned up in find-references.

Requires m68k-parser ^1.5.2, which is not published yet, so `npm ci` will
fail until it is.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: grahambates

events.title: Represent macro arguments and interpolated names honestly
events.message:
Represent macro arguments and interpolated names honestly

Three related changes, all additive to the AST.

Macro arguments that are not expressions
----------------------------------------
Arguments are substituted textually, so they need not be valid operands.
`BITDEF MEM,24BITDMA,9` passes `24BITDMA`, which cannot be an identifier
because it starts with a digit; it was silently truncated to the number 24
with the rest dropped.

A new MacroArgumentNode keeps the raw text, used only where the expression
stopped short of the argument's end. Arguments that parse in full keep their
structure, so `MyMacro d0,d1` still gives registers. 36 arguments across the
corpus take this path, including a float literal that was truncating to its
integer part.

Interpolated names
------------------
`BLTEN_\1`, `.loop\@` and `PUSHM_\@` were reported as ordinary symbols and
labels, so the tree claimed a symbol existed where the name is really a
template resolved at expansion. SymbolNode and LabelNode now carry
`interpolated` for these, which is a fact about the name rather than
something each consumer should rediscover by looking for backslashes. 832
symbols and 956 labels in the corpus are marked.

Macro parameter locations inside expressions
--------------------------------------------
A parameter used inside an expression, as in `CopOffs+\1`, had a location one
character short, because the tokenizer strips the leading backslash from the
token value and the length was taken from it. Slicing the source at the node
gave `\` rather than `\1`, which would misplace an editor highlight.

Found because the under-coverage check above misfired on it, sending four
perfectly good expressions down the raw-text path.

events.title: Read a C style comment after an operand as a comment
events.message:
Read a C style comment after an operand as a comment

`ASHIFTSHIFT = 12  /* bits to right align */` was parsed with `12 /* bits`
as the operand and `to right align */` as the comment, because `/` reads as
division and continues the operand across the whitespace. The comment text
was wrong in the tree, which matters wherever it is surfaced - the language
server shows it as documentation on hover.

Motorola syntax ends the operand field at whitespace and treats the rest of
the line as a comment, which is how these comments work in the NDK headers
in the first place. Whitespace followed by `/*` now ends the operand, while
a spaced-out division such as `12 / 4` still parses as an expression, since
requiring the asterisk is what separates the two.

Found by instrumenting the parser to report tokens left over after a
complete expression and running it over 3,598 local m68k sources: this was
130 of the 175 hits.

events.title: Tatung Einstein 256 keyboard addition
events.message:
Tatung Einstein 256 keyboard addition

A second Einstein deck, picked by model the way the CPC picks between its
three. The 256 is a squarer, charcoal machine: the four left-hand modifiers
share a margin and grow rather than stepping (ESC 0.75u, CTRL 1.25u, ALPHA
LOCK 1.5u, SHIFT 2u) while the typing block staggers by the usual
0.5u/0.25u/0.5u and every row finishes flush; the function keys are their own
1.25u strip under the printed BASIC legend card; ENTER is an L across two
rows; and the cursor keys are four wedges on a detached pad out past the deck.
The POWER lamp, the ALPHA LOCK lamp and the cursor well come with it.

The cursor pad needed its wiring settled. MOS 2.1 decodes shifted [1,5] and
[2,5] to the same codes as unshifted, so the TC-01's trick of reaching the
upper legend through SHIFT gives down and right again, not up and left.
Sweeping every cell and modifier against the real ROM found left on [0,1] —
the cell MAME marks unused, and which the TC-01 has no key for — and no single
cell for up at all, so up goes through CONTROL+K, the only route to 0x0B in
either MOS. Host arrow keys follow the same per-model chords.

Caps now press a chord rather than one cell, since neither deck's cursor keys
are one switch apiece, and both faces share one layout, one geometry module and
one controller.
