A1200 report (fast Vampire, so not a CPU problem): "a flash of an unload/load
of textures as it needs to redraw the sky/floor", worse on a stock AGA machine.

load_backdrop opens BACK.CTL, NewPtr's 160 KB, reads 160 KB and frees it —
every call — to extract ONE 88x88 image and a 32-entry palette. That whole-file
read is the flash. It is the same bug the WALL loader already had fixed (the
2026-07-13 "GLIB pool flip", which stopped cw_load_slot pulling a whole ~296 KB
library to copy a few pieces out); load_backdrop was simply never given the
same treatment.

Measured on an AGA walk in amiberry, HEIRS from the SAVGAMB fixture, 10 steps
plus 3 turn-and-steps: 7 loads for 2 DISTINCT ids. Five of seven re-read the
file to rebuild a byte-identical result. Memoising the id takes the same drive
to 2 real loads and 5 cache hits.

★ THE PALETTE RE-INSTALL HAD TO SURVIVE. The wall-reload path deliberately
calls load_backdrop(g_back_set) with an UNCHANGED id, to re-lay the backdrop
band after an event picture wiped the CLUT — so an early return on an id match
would have traded this flash for wrong colours. The cache skips the DISK READ
and keeps the install, replaying it from `bpal`, which was already a static.

Verified by re-running the identical drive and diffing the frames: the only
difference is a text line in the MESSAGE PANE at (440,372)-(469,386), which is
run-to-run variance in the log. The 3D view, the backdrop and the chrome are
pixel-identical, and the entry path exercises the clut-clobbered re-install.

A negative worth recording so it is not re-tested: the first suspect was
g_clut_clobbered forcing load_wall_groups + load_backdrop + a chrome repaint
per step. It does not — instrumented with FRUA_BAR28, it fires ONCE at entry
and never during the walk (confirmed the party actually moved: cell 13,8, view
rendered, frames differ).

New FRUA_BACKPROF reports each load's id and tick cost plus cache hits; it is
pure output, so it stays.

HALF THE PROBLEM REMAINS: a FIRST visit to a zone still reads 160 KB, so a
first-time flash is still possible on slow media. Narrowing that to the
sub-GLIB the way cw_setglib_load does for walls is the next step.

events.title: music: a design's own soundtrack now converts and plays (ADR-0011 for MUSIC.SLB)
events.message:
music: a design's own soundtrack now converts and plays (ADR-0011 for MUSIC.SLB)

A fan module ships its own music and the port threw it away, in three separate
places. Measured against the module corpus (5 of 11 modules carry XMI):

1. THE ENGINE COULD NEVER FIND IT. jt986 built the bare literal "music.slb",
   so the bank could only ever resolve in the install root — the same omission
   ua_open_art fixed for whole-file art reads, and this is the same fix:
   design-first, root-fallback. It matters because a DOS module keeps its .XMI
   INSIDE <design>.DSN (curse does exactly that), so without this the module
   played the BASE GAME's music, which looks like working audio and is the
   wrong soundtrack. A design shipping no bank falls straight through to the
   root and loads the identical bytes, so unmodified designs are unchanged.

2. THE CONVERTER'S FILENAME MATCH REJECTED REAL MODULES. It required exactly
   `??DQ?.XMI` (9 chars), which missed:
     curse  Dqk1.xmi..Dqk9.xmi   8 chars, no driver pair -> 8 songs, converted
                                 to NOTHING
     g39    RODQ1.XMI only       a PARTIAL set; requiring all of Q1..Q3 threw
                                 away the one song the module has
   Now the DQK family (bare and Q-numbered) is recognised and a partial set
   converts what exists, the rest becoming empty songs exactly as the Mac-only
   slots 2..6 already are, so jt985's range check still passes. All five
   modules with music now convert; before, two did not.

3. A MODULE COULD HIJACK THE BASE GAME'S BANK. find_xmi_set walks recursively
   and the DRIVER decides, so a design shipping the arrangement the retail set
   lacks would win the ROOT bank. stage_dos now passes --skip-designs for the
   root and gives each design its own bank.

Regression control: the retail DOS set still selects Tandy and produces a bank
BYTE-IDENTICAL to the previously staged MUSIC.SLB.

The matcher tests are a separate file on purpose — test_xmi2slb.py skips
without the copyrighted DOS corpus, so on CI the selection logic had no
coverage at all. Selection is pure filename logic, so these run everywhere,
including a sensitivity control that a directory with no XMI still returns
nothing (widening a matcher must not make it match anything).

Still to do, and NOT done here: the conversion is host-side Python, so an
on-device Amiga install (uainst) still gets no music — that needs xmi2slb
ported into the installer. Also curse ships 8 songs and only Q1..Q3 map to Mac
slots, so 6 of them go unused; mapping them would need to know the module's
intent, so it is left rather than guessed.

events.title: Remove the performance rule category
events.message:
Remove the performance rule category

It had no rules and nothing belonged in it. Branch-to-branch collapsing and
redundant memory reloads are ordinary optimization substitutions; the cost of a
misaligned access is a note on a correctness rule; "expensive instruction in a
loop" is an optimization advisory.

An empty category was not free. It appeared in RuleCategory, the CLI --only and
--disable-category lists, the JSON schema, the config loader, and the
impact-measurement conditionals in lint.ts and the audit, so `--only
performance` succeeded and silently matched nothing.

Both entry points now reject it explicitly rather than ignoring it:

  m68k-lint: --only: unknown value 'performance'.
  Expected one of: correctness, suspicious, optimization, portability, style

Breaking for any config setting categories.performance, though setting it never
did anything. Tests cover both the rejection and the surviving categories.

events.title: ecs: the backend state dump — the CPU side of #19 is CLEAN, end to end
events.message:
ecs: the backend state dump — the CPU side of #19 is CLEAN, end to end

-DFRUA_ECSDUMP writes PROGDIR:ECSDMPnn.BIN at the end of each present and
tools/ecsdump.py reads it. Everything lands in GAME coordinates, so the
comparison needs no alignment — which is the entire point, after three
alignment methods disagreed (dx 21/28/22, dy 10/23/12) and made every earlier
"N% of pixels differ" figure worthless.

The dump carries BOTH ENDS of the quantiser plus the screen itself: clut and
chunky (the input, i.e. exactly what AGA displays), band_pal and band_remap
(the 32-colour cut), and the front bitplanes with s_front (what display DMA
actually fetches).

Forgotten Realms title, ECSDMP05 — 130 distinct indices, which is exactly what
artview --compose 1,4 reports, so it is provably the same screen:

  chunky vs SSI's art    1 of 64000 pixels differ, by d=6
  cut    vs chunky       5 of 64000 exceed d=120, at x=154..158 y=61,
                         mid-screen highlights, not a left edge
  planes vs cut          0 of 64000
  (earlier) copper words vs band_pal   800/800 agree

AND THE SCREEN STILL SHOWS THE DASHES — same run, same frame. So every value
the CPU computes is right and the corruption appears at DISPLAY time, which no
memory dump can see. That puts #19 in the #167 copper-timing family and
excludes a seventh cause: the cut, end to end.

Two traps handled rather than shipped:

  * The planes hold SLOTS (0..31), not chunky indices (0..255). Comparing
    against the index reported 99.4-99.97% of every frame as broken — a
    spectacular-looking result that was purely my own error. The first version
    of the test encoded the same mistake, so it passed. Both are fixed and
    there is now a named regression test for it.
  * The zeros are not vacuous: the plane checker prints its denominator, a
    round-trip test pins the decoder, and an injected 6-pixel stale run is
    caught and grouped. A "0 mismatches" from a checker that never ran has
    cost this project several rounds already.

Also recorded in TODO 19: do NOT try to measure the artefact rows from a
screenshot. Tried again, failed again — the capture is scaled, the detector
locks onto the border edge at x 7..13, and the row-mod-8 histogram comes back
uniform (12 across all eight residues), which is noise that would read as a
finding if taken at face value.

events.title: ci: Pillow was never in requirements.txt, so the compose test failed on CI only
events.message:
ci: Pillow was never in requirements.txt, so the compose test failed on CI only

The last two pushes emailed a red build. Cause is mine, not the audio work:
tests/test_artview.py's compose check actually RENDERS, so it imports Pillow —
which was present in the local tools/.venv and absent from tools/requirements.txt,
the only thing CI installs. The test therefore passed here and raised
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'PIL' there, every time.

Reproduced CI exactly in a throwaway venv built from requirements.txt alone,
and confirmed the fix is causal rather than incidental: with Pillow the test
RUNS and passes (not skips); uninstall Pillow in that same venv and it fails
again; reinstall and it passes.

The module docstring claimed "PIL is only imported inside artview.render_entry,
so none of this needs it". That was true when written and stopped being true
the moment the compose test was added — the sort of stale comment that sends
the next reader looking in the wrong place, so it now says which test needs
Pillow and why.

Note the other CI skips are NOT this bug: CI reports ~70 skipped against 6 here
because the copyrighted data/ corpus is git-ignored and cannot exist on a
runner. Those tests are correctly skipped there, not silently broken.

events.title: amiga: AHI backend with a Paula fallback, and centre the Paula mix (ADR-0021)
events.message:
amiga: AHI backend with a Paula fallback, and centre the Paula mix (ADR-0021)

Paula hard-pans its channels — 0/3 left, 1/2 right — and the port drove only
AUD0, so the whole engine mix left the machine in the LEFT speaker. Found on
real hardware (A1200 + Apollo V4 IceDrake through a capture card): L-R =
+18.1 dB, reproduced to a tenth of a dB by two independent capture paths, so
the imbalance was the port and not the capture.

  * Paula now plays the ring on AUD0 AND AUD1, started by ONE dmacon write
    with identical LC/LEN/PER — mono centred, which is the faithful rendering
    of a mono source. A separate enable would leave up to a full ring (160 ms)
    of offset and sound like an echo rather than a centre image.
  * plat_sound_init prefers ahi.device and falls back to Paula when it is
    absent or will not open. On an Apollo/Vampire the AHI driver reaches the
    SAGA audio core ("Arne"), which has no published register map, so AHI is
    the only route to it — and it is portable anyway.
  * The general mix path ducks instead of clamping: voices give up 6 dB while
    something rides on top. A deliberate divergence from the Mac, commented so
    it is a one-line revert.
  * devices/ahi.h vendored at third_party/ahi/ (AHI developer archive, Martin
    Blom; the Bebbo toolchain ships no AHI headers).

BOTH PATHS NOW PRODUCE CENTRED AUDIO, which makes the hardware test ambiguous
by construction: "the sound is centred" would confirm nothing about AHI, since
the fixed Paula path does the same. So plat_sound_init says which backend it
took —

    snd: AHI backend up (ahi.device)
    snd: no AHI - Paula fallback (AUD0+AUD1 centred)

Verified in amiberry (no ahi.device on the mount, so this exercises the
fallback, which is the case that could have hung): boots to the menu, logs the
Paula line, 947 020-only instructions in the release binary under
-m m68k:68020 (0 without the flag — the documented objdump trap). 493 tests
pass. The AHI path itself still has never executed anywhere.

events.title: Drop the MOVEQ rule; sharpen the assembler-overlap test
events.message:
Drop the MOVEQ rule; sharpen the assembler-overlap test

vasm already warns on `moveq #$ff,d0`:

  warning 2028: using signed operand as unsigned: 255 (valid: -128..127),
  -1 to fix

That is a better diagnostic than this linter would give, since it names the
valid range and the fix. So the governing test is "does the assembler already
diagnose this", not "would it reject this" - a warning counts.

Three other proposals carry the same unverified risk: divide-by-zero-immediate,
odd-address-word-access and movem-predecrement-base-in-list. Added
docs/assembler-overlap.asm so they can be checked against a real assembler
before any of them is built. move-from-sr-privileged is safe from the test:
assemblers do not model supervisor state.

Prettier has no parser for assembly, so *.asm/*.s/*.i are now ignored
explicitly rather than by luck of extension matching.

events.title: Revise the rule roadmap after review
events.message:
Revise the rule roadmap after review

Three corrections, all narrowing scope:

The proposed byte-stack rule cannot exist: optimization/stack-word-shift-eight
emits `move.b d0,-(sp)` as its own suggestion, so the linter would have flagged
its own output. The A7 byte trick is a deliberate shift idiom the project
already recommends. Only the genuinely unbalanced case survives, and it falls
out of stack-depth tracking for free.

Instruction- and addressing-mode-availability rules are the assembler's job.
Sharpened the governing test to "would the assembler reject this?", which
leaves portability meaning the more valuable class: code that assembles cleanly
everywhere but behaves differently at runtime. That also removes the need for a
CPU capability table; a small isAtLeast() helper covers what remains.

Ordering: rules run in registration order, so diagnostics came back grouped

events.title: agnus: cancel a carried bitplane fetch when the vertical flop is closed
events.message:
agnus: cancel a carried bitplane fetch when the vertical flop is closed

The bitplane sequencer honours DDFSTOP (or the hard stop) only at the
next 8-colour-clock fetch-unit boundary, and the unit that starts there
still runs as the last fetch unit. A hires window opened at DDFSTRT $3C
with DDFSTOP $DC therefore has its last unit at $DC..$E3, one clock past
the 227-clock PAL line: BPRUN is still set when the line ends and the
run is carried into the next line, where the unit finishes before
DDFSTRT can match again. Inside the vertical window that tail is hidden
past DIWSTOP.H and only the per-line word accounting shows it, but Agnus
drops BPRUN with the vertical flop's reset on DIWSTOP.V, so the line
after the last display line fetches nothing.

ddf_seq_build_line only refreshed state.bpv at the line start and left a
carried bprun running, so that closed line still fetched and the
renderer painted the whole row from memory past the plane. vAmiga clears
bprun and cnt there; do the same. The walk itself is unchanged: like
vAmiga's computeBplEvents it carries cnt across the wrap and rebuilds
the counter from the new line's clock parity, and the carried unit's
plane word falls to the refresh cycle, so a one-plane $3C/$DC line
consumes 41 of its 42 words. Regression example: the AROS boot screen,
whose amigavideo driver programs exactly this window since the
2026-09-05 ROM refresh, showed a dashed teal line under its 256-line
display.

New golden probe timing-test/ddfprobe-vspill: two hires bands, one with
the overrunning DDFSTOP and one with the standard $3C/$D4 stop, a solid
bar in each row's first word so the per-line accounting is visible, and
marker rows after each plane. Without the fix it lit the line after the
overrunning band; with it the frame matches vAmiga byte-for-byte, the
overrunning band's one-word-per-row bar drift included. A bus-level unit
test walks the same window across lines 198..200 and asserts the run is
carried inside the window and dropped on the DIWSTOP.V line. Every other
golden is pixel-identical.

events.title: Make every optimization rule measurable, or explicitly exempt
events.message:
Make every optimization rule measurable, or explicitly exempt

docs/rule-impact-audit.md requires a rule the 68000 counter cannot measure
to carry an explicit exemption, but three rules were slipping through as
"unmeasured" while the CLI still exited 0.

`redundant-zero-displacement` emitted a bare operand fragment, "(a0)", as
its suggestion replacement. Every other rule emits a full line, and that
is the contract impact measurement assumes: it measured the whole source
line as "before" against the fragment as "after". It only avoided
reporting nonsense because 68kcounter yields zero bytes for a fragment and
the zero-byte guard discarded the result. It now rewrites the operand
within the full line, and measures as the 2-byte saving ASP68K claims.

The two tail-call rules are unmeasurable by construction: JSR+RTS -> JMP
changes stack depth, so they deliberately emit no replacement text for a
human to review. They are now exempt rather than registered as measurable.

The CLI audit exit code now counts "unmeasured" as a failure, matching the
test and the documented policy.

Audit: 106 cases, 0 regressions, 0 unmeasured, 0 missing cases.
Full suite: 204 passing.

events.title: Triage the revived rule tests
events.message:
Triage the revived rule tests

All 161 rule tests now pass. The failures fell into four groups, none of
which were rule regressions:

Fixtures that did not express their stated intent. Tests named "when
flags are dead" ended with `move.l dX,dY`, but MOVE preserves X, so the X
flag still escaped through the trailing RTS and the rules correctly
returned "conditional" instead of "safe". Same for the known-register
shift rules, whose count register was never killed before the RTS, so it
was "unknown" rather than dead and the rules declined to fire. The audit
registry already got this right; the unit fixtures never did.

Stale expectations. `bset-to-tas` became opt-in, so its test has to
enable it; `MOVE #n,An` is normalized to MOVEA, so the suggestion is
`movea.w`, and the rule's description now agrees with what it emits.

One real analysis gap. `dataRegisterBitsUseAfter` propagated its bit mask
but never transformed it, and SWAP has no size so the walker bailed to
"unknown". SWAP relocates the tracked bits rather than consuming them, so
follow the rotated mask. A DIVU.W remainder read via `swap dn` /
`move.l dn,...` is now correctly seen as a use, and the rule stops
suggesting a shift that would discard it.

Underneath that, nearly every fixture was written in column-zero form.
m68k-parser applies real assembler column rules, so `move.l #42,d3`
parsed as a label named `move` and the rules matched nothing.

- Split tsconfig: `lint` typechecks tests, `build` still excludes them so

- Add `src/test/helpers.ts` with `lint`/`ids`/`fixtureContext`, sharing one

- Fix the stale `result.diagnostics` call sites.
- Fix the audit normalizer: its docstring claimed colon-terminated labels
  survive indentation, but an indented `.loop:` parses as neither a label
  nor a mnemonic, so branch targets silently vanished. Column-zero label
  definitions are now left in place.

161 rule tests now execute; 143 pass. The remaining 18 are genuine
expectation triage, handled separately.

events.title: ecs: the copper agrees with the cut — sixth cause excluded for #19
events.message:
ecs: the copper agrees with the cut — sixth cause excluded for #19

ecs_cop_verify re-derives every copper COLOR word from s_band_pal in the 4-bit
encoding and compares it against the word the copper actually reads, at the end
of every present. 800 words (25 bands x 32 slots), 0 mismatched, twice.

The probe reports its CHECKED COUNT next to the mismatch count on purpose, so a
zero cannot be mistaken for 'never ran'. That specific confusion has produced
false passes here repeatedly — a missing objdump, a missing binary, a converter
pointed at a missing file — and it produced one earlier in this same
investigation.

artview gains --compose: a title screen on screen is a BASE plus an OVERLAY,
because l19d4 loads the library twice, so a reference built from the base alone
reports the entire overlay as a difference and reads as corruption. The palette
accumulates across entries, matching the engine's successive installs.

Six causes are now excluded for #19: draw-time planar writers, both palette
caches, stale previous-screen content, the remap, SSI's art, and the copper
words. Recorded honestly: the per-pixel screenshot-to-art comparison was NOT
achieved — three alignment methods disagreed (dx 21/28/22, dy 10/23/12), so no
percentage from it is trustworthy and none is quoted.

Next step removes the screenshot from the loop: dump the backend's own chunky
surface, band palettes and remaps at the end of a title render and compare
offline against artview --compose, both sides in game coordinates.

492 tests pass (10 for artview, mutation-checked).

events.title: tools: artview.py renders the art offline — and it says the art is CLEAN

Built to settle one question the emulator cannot: when a screen looks wrong on
a 16/32-colour machine, is the mark in SSI's data or did the port put it there?

extending them to keep the pixel POSITIONS the colour-counting versions throw
away: PackBits, transparency-RLE (0 ends the row, >=128 skips 257-b, index 0
transparent), raw 8bpp, mode-9 composites placed by dx/dy, and the jt993
palette-window law. Mono pieces are skipped, not guessed — there is no pen
offline. --info prints the container tree, --item/--all render.

frame and the red gradient the marks sit in — renders smooth and clean at 256
colours. The left-edge marks are NOT in the art. That kills candidate (b) and

events.title: ecs: characterise the left-edge corruption and rule out four causes (#19)
events.message:
ecs: characterise the left-edge corruption and rule out four causes (#19)

Not fixed. Recording what it is and what it is not, so the next attempt does
not re-derive any of it.

What it is, measured on the Forgotten Realms title in amiberry at exact pixels:
thin HORIZONTAL runs of beige/white/orange, 3-60 px long, at the left of the
picture, inside smooth dark-red gradient that should hold no such colour. The
same screen on AGA is clean — same engine, same chunky surface — so the fault
is in the ECS conversion, not the drawing.

Ruled out, each by a one-variable A/B:

  - draw-time planar writers: PLANAR=0 renders the frame PIXEL-IDENTICAL
    (5c5c4e5d both ways), so this is upstream of plane writing
  - both palette caches: clutcache=off palcache=off + deleted PALCACHE.ECS,
    identical hashes
  - stale previous-screen content: 3% of candidate pixels match the preceding
    screen, and those are border pixels identical between screens anyway;
    shifted-lookup control 0%
  - a catastrophic remap: the new FRUA_ECSERR probe reports the worst
    used-colour-to-slot distance per band; worst is grey -> slightly lighter
    grey (idx 19 #838387 -> #a8a8a8), never red -> beige

Adds FRUA_ECSERR (worst per-band remap error, with the wanted and assigned
RGB) and notes an exact-pixel AGA config for matched-geometry comparison —
the stock openua.uae blends and drowns the artefact in a naive diff.

Two candidates remain: the copper palette install for non-boundary rows, or
the marks being in SSI's art with AGA's 256 colours hiding what a 32-colour
cut exposes. The latter is offline and cheap and should be tried first; it
needs a real art renderer, since TITLE.TLB does not decode with perband's
piece decoders.

All four targets build; 483 tests pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: slaapliedje

events.title: ecs: present again after the palette lands — the SSI logo now displays (#18)
events.message:
ecs: present again after the palette lands — the SSI logo now displays (#18)

A500 report: 'the SSI / Micromagic logo screen no longer even displays... it's
there on the AGA version.' That split was the clue — same engine code, same
art, one works.

The title's palette is installed AFTER the present that shows it:

    tsq:   jt117 SHOW, mode = 2
    ecsp:  present, dirty=0                 converts under the OLD palette
    ecsp:  set_palette first=16 count=240   the title's palette, after

On a hardware-palette screen that is harmless — the pixels are already placed
and the late CLUT write recolours them, which is why AGA was always fine. On a
quantiser the pixels were converted through the previous palette and no later
write can fix them; at boot that previous palette is the black startup one, so
the screen renders black and the title never appears. It also explains why THIS
screen was missing while later ones merely looked wrong: each title was being
shown in its predecessor's colours.

Quantisers now take one more present after the palette bracket closes, so the
cut runs against the complete CLUT. The backend already declines the premature
present, which is #16's defer doing useful work. HW-palette backends keep the
Mac's single present.

ecs_set_palette also marks the bands dirty for ANY palette write while a
composition bracket is open, not just count >= 32. Size is the wrong test
there: a title whose art declares fewer than 32 colours was filed as colour
cycling and never re-cut.

★ This also corrects a FALSE POSITIVE in #16. As first written, the cut-defer
swallowed jt117 — the one present each title gets, since the composition holds
the rest — so the sentinel counts read 0 because no cut happened, not because
the cut was clean, while the whole title sequence rendered black (60/60 frames)
and the metric said 'fixed'. A metric can go quiet because the work stopped.
The re-verification now requires the titles to actually render as well.

Verified: the SSI/MicroMagic screen renders on ECS and matches the AGA
reference; 4 titles composed -> 4 renders (1:1, was 0); sentinel pixels and
magenta band slots both still 0. All four targets build; 483 tests pass.

Adds FRUA_TITLESEQ (per-title compose/show/art-load tracing and ECS
present/render branch decisions), which is what made this measurable.

zynaps atari: in-game controls — ESC to the menu, F10 to TOS

Two deliberate divergences, shim-only, always-on (not cheat-gated), the
differential untouched (make test 4751).
- ESC (0x01) while PHASE_PLAYING -> the main menu, re-using the game's OWN
  back-to-front-end path (frame_loop_once returning FRAME_EXIT_TITLE, the
  all-lives-lost exit). Round trip proven twice in Hatari.
- F10 (0x44) -> TOS, re-using the shim's teardown (restore vectors/PSG/
  rez/palette/base with read-backs, then Pterm). CLEAN in a level; at the
  pure attract screen the main line is parked inside the verified
  attract_wait_for_start, which has no shim checkpoint, so the F10 flag
  latches and fires once a game starts (documented, not a flaky unwind).
- Mechanism: a second unconditional door tap zy_note_control_key beside
  the trainer's; in the ACIA interrupt it only SETS volatile flags, acted
  on the main line in play_one_game after frame_loop_once returns (never
  unwind from the interrupt). Census: no cmpi.b #$01/#$44 anywhere in the

boot_front_end_prologue between games, so an ESC auto-repeat edge would
bounce the next game after one frame — fixed by clearing g_quit_to_menu on

events.title: zynaps trainer: audible feedback — a per-key blip and a louder arm fanfare
events.message:
zynaps trainer: audible feedback — a per-key blip and a louder arm fanfare

The typed sequence works on iron, but the arm sound was inaudible: stream
35 opens `fa 03 e8 01 e9 01 ea 01` — all three tone periods = 1, a
near-ultrasonic whistle (−10.7 dBFS on a meter, thin to the ear). Measured
from out/audio/manifest.tsv.

- Arm fanfare 35 -> 23 (CHEAT_SFX_ARMED 0x23 -> 0x17): stream 23 opens
  `fa 03 e8 11 ...`, an audible mid pitch, −10.8 dBFS, 2.0 s — also `fa 03`
  and also an orphan the shipped game never plays, so the resurrected-cut-
  content spirit holds.
- Per-key blip: CHEAT_SFX_KEY 0x1d (stream 29, 0.90 s) plays on each
  ACCEPTED, non-completing letter (Z, Y — and a fresh Z that restarts),
  so the sequence is heard landing key by key; the completing N gives the
  fanfare, not a blip.
- The split honors the interrupt rule: the ACIA door raises g_blip_pending
  (a byte, like g_seq_complete); zy_cheats_tick drains it in the VBL as an
  `else if` to the arm branch, so a blip and the fanfare never sound in one
  tick and sound_start is never called from the keyboard interrupt.

Smoke: cheats reports "1 fanfare on stream 0x177a4 (= stream 23's head),
7 blips"; an independent blip-count replay and STREAM-ID PINS
(CHEAT_ARM_STREAM=23 / CHEAT_BLIP_STREAM=29) — the self-referential
fanfare read-back would stay green if the id reverted to 35, so the pin is
what catches it. Negatives (Z,Y,Z,N and Z,Y) refuse and leave no fanfare.
key_blips added to the record, 0 asserted in every judged mode (dormancy).

events.title: zynaps trainer: arm by TYPING Z, Y, N in order, not a simultaneous hold
events.message:
zynaps trainer: arm by TYPING Z, Y, N in order, not a simultaneous hold

The simultaneous Z+Y+N hold did nothing on a real STE: three keys sharing
rows/columns can ghost on the IKBD's undiode-isolated matrix and never all
report, which Hatari's event injection bypasses (so smoke.py cheats passed
while iron failed). A typed sequence touches one matrix cell at a time and
cannot ghost.

zynaps_cheats.c: a cursor over [Z, Y, N] plus a sticky g_seq_complete
latch replace g_held[]/g_hold_vbls/CHEAT_ARM_HOLD_VBLS/the_whole_combo_is_
held. The ACIA door advances the cursor on a combo-letter make while the
arming window is open — the expected next letter advances, a wrong letter

events.title: Add an MCP server over saved profile captures
events.message:
Add an MCP server over saved profile captures

`puae-debugger mcp` exposes profile_check and profile_dump to an MCP client,
so a model can analyse a .puaeprofile without a person relaying terminal
output. A subcommand of the existing binary for the same reasons `profile` is:
shared bin entry, bundle and installation.

    claude mcp add puae -- npx puae-debugger mcp

The stdio JSON-RPC transport is hand-rolled rather than taking
@modelcontextprotocol/sdk. The surface actually needed is three requests and a
notification, fully specified, while the SDK would pull express, hono, zod, ajv
and jose into a package with ten runtime dependencies for a server that only
ever speaks stdio — and this project already hand-rolls its DAP server and its
PUAE RPC dispatcher on the same reasoning.

Protocol routing is separated from the stdio plumbing so it can be tested
directly rather than through a subprocess. Two behaviours worth noting, both
covered: notifications are never answered (replying to one is a violation some
clients treat as fatal), and a tool that fails on its input returns a normal
result carrying isError rather than a JSON-RPC error, so the model sees the
message and can correct itself.

The tool descriptions carry the ordering advice that the profiling skill leads
with — run check before trusting dump — because a capture's per-function
percentages read as entirely plausible even when the frame total they are a
share of is impossible. That is how three profiler bugs went unnoticed, so a
test asserts the instruction stays in the description.

Rendering moves to src/profileReport.ts, shared with the CLI, so a number
discussed in a terminal and one discussed over MCP are formatted identically.

Emulator-backed tools (capture, screenshot, memory) are not here yet. The
groundwork exists: setupRpcDispatcher runs against the wasm under plain Node,
which is how puae-wasm/test/*.mjs drive it, so a headless PuaeRpcClient needs
no browser.

events.title: Make the stall analysis work on a real 68000 capture
events.message:
Make the stall analysis work on a real 68000 capture

Three fixes, all found by running it against one.

The measured-below-datasheet guard was exact, which rejected a correct
capture. theoreticalTiming deliberately takes the SLOWEST of an instruction's
timings, so every untaken branch inflates the datasheet side slightly; a real
68000 frame with an almost-idle bus came in at 0.997x and was refused. The gap
the guard exists to catch is far wider — a 68020 capture measured 0.73x — so it
now allows a 10% shortfall, which separates the two with room either side.

Stalls were computed from ProfileManifest.disassembly, which holds frame 0's
only. Every frame therefore reported frame 0's figures, which was plainly wrong
on a capture whose bus load alternates between frames. It now uses each frame's
own reweighted disassembly, and the analysis moves onto FrameAnalysis so
`dump --frame N --stalls` reports frame N.

model.datasheet was only set where raw disassembly exists — frame 0 — so the
profiler's stall column appeared on frame 0 and nowhere else, including the
blitter-heavy frames where it matters. Applicability is derived from a frame's
own aggregate and cannot be inherited, so it is now judged wherever a
reweighted disassembly is attached.

The result validates the premise independently of the DMA census that
corroborates it. On the same capture, frame 0 (bus idle 55.8%, no blitter)
measures -0.3% stall — no contention to suffer — while frame 1 (blitter 35.9%)
measures 24.6%, essentially all of it on TransformVisibleCityBuildings at
24.7%. That is the routine running against the blitter, and the number says
rescheduling it would buy more than optimising its CPU code.

events.title: The player's bullet was starving every collision in the pass
events.message:
The player's bullet was starving every collision in the pass

DrCollide's inner scan began at slot 7 -- the player's bullet -- which
has no droid-table entry: DrFindSlot only hands out 1..SPR_POOL_LAST
and DroidsInit's clear is the only write that ever touches
drSlotOwner+7, so that entry is 0 for the life of the game.

Both arms of DrCollided dead-end on a zero owner, and the loop services
one pair a pass and jumps out the moment it finds one. So whenever the
bullet fell inside the outer slot's box it won the pair and the routine
returned having done nothing at all -- no player bump, no droid-droid
reverse -- and _x_none was never reached, so drCollHit stayed latched
into the next pass too. A bullet spawns on top of the player, so that
cost 1-2 passes of every shot plus every pass it flew near a droid.

Scan from SPR_POOL_LAST instead. Skipping the slot rather than aborting
on it is what the C64 does in substance: its sprite 0 is the player's
shot and carries a real mode-3 record, so that pair reaches
DoCollision2 and the table acts on it, where ours has already been
serviced by DrBulletHit before the loop runs.

Found by playtester Sydney, 2026-09-03: "droids passed through me and
each other, particularly when moving fast". A fast pair -- the player
at top speed against a 302 or an 834, the only two droids with drSpeed
8 -- is only inside the box for two or three passes, so a pass eaten by
the bullet loses the collision outright, where a slow approach has
passes to spare. NOT tunnelling through the box, which was the first
reading and is ruled out in BUGS.md #20.

One immediate operand; bank 4 ends &BFF3 before and after.

events.title: ecs: defer the CUT while the palette is still arriving (#16 titles)
events.message:
ecs: defer the CUT while the palette is still arriving (#16 titles)

The A500 title corruption: the art is cut against a CLUT still holding the
art's magenta defer sentinel, so the quantiser spends 10 of every band's 32
slots on a placeholder — a fifth of the budget, which is why the screen reads
as 'colours all inverted' rather than merely speckled.

The engine already marks the window. l19d4 brackets each title's composition in
qd_palette_blackout(), and a hardware-palette backend answers by pushing black
so the half-built screen is never seen. That call RETURNED BEFORE TOUCHING ITS
COUNTER on any other backend, so a quantiser could not ask the one question the
bracket answers.

Keep the counter for every backend (only the black push is hardware-specific)
and publish it as dsp_palette_incomplete(). The state lives in
platform/planar.c — shared by the Atari and Amiga builds, since neither
backend file is linked by the other — and the shim sets it, so the layer rule
holds: compat calls down into platform, never up.

ECS then defers its cut across the bracket, keeping the last complete frame on
screen; the engine's own install at the end of the bracket sets s_dirty and
that present cuts against a whole CLUT. A quantiser cannot blackout instead —
its planes hold slots, not indices — and its problem is worse than a visible
flash: a cut taken mid-bracket is BAKED IN and no later palette write undoes
it.

Measured on the same fixture and instrumentation as the root-cause run:
chunky pixels on sentinel slots 975 -> 0, band-palette magenta slots 10 -> 0,
at every cut. The defer fires for 4 presents.

Bounded at 24 presents, because #8 is what an unbounded wait costs; the bound
is on presents, not wall-clock, so it does not vary with machine speed. An
overrun loses the title, not the game. video.cfg titledefer=off is the A/B arm.

All four targets build; 483 tests pass. Emulator-measured.

events.message:
installer: put something useful in the Amiga install console

A1200 field report (2026-09-03), after verifying the AGA installer works: 'the
extra window that pops up with the installer version in it could be used for
the Unlimited Adventures screen, or maybe some of the readme information /
license and required files list'.

That window is ours — IconX opens it from the WINDOW= tooltype on Install.info
— and when the AmigaOS Installer is present the launcher left it empty behind
the Installer's GUI. Now it prints what a first-time installer actually needs
while that GUI is up: what this is and its version, what you need before
starting (engine disk, your data disks, ~7 MB free, and the measured Kickstart
minimum for the variant), what the installer is about to ask, and that RETURN
takes every default.

It also states the thing that matters legally and is easy to get wrong: the
ENGINE is GPL-2.0 with a source pointer, and the GAME DATA is not included and
not ours to give — the data disks come from the user's own copy of FRUA.

Costs nothing at run time and adds no files to a full floppy.

AmigaDOS specifics, both of which bite silently: '*' is the ESCAPE character in
a quoted string, so the bullets are '-' (verified 0 asterisks in the generated
script); and the window is CON:0/20/640/180, which topaz 8 fills at 80x22, so
the banner is kept to 63 columns and 19 lines. Verified by reading Install back
out of BOTH built ADFs, with the ECS variant correctly getting 'Kickstart 2.0
or later (ECS/OCS; 1.3 will NOT work)'. The engine binary is byte-identical
after the rebuild.

events.title: Show datasheet stall per instruction in the profiler
events.message:
Show datasheet stall per instruction in the profiler

The 68kcounter comparison was reachable only from the export CLI. It is most
useful where you are already looking at the code, so the Disassembly view now
carries it: a per-instruction column showing cycles that execution spent
blocked rather than working, with the measured/datasheet/bus-access breakdown
on hover.

Computed host-side in attachDisassembly, next to where file/line is already
re-derived, and deliberately NOT stored in the .puaeprofile. The document holds
the raw capture rather than conclusions drawn from it — that is what lets an
older file pick up later improvements on load — and a stored timing figure
would be frozen against future corrections. It is recomputed from the
instruction text, which the document does store.

That also keeps the dependency out of the webview: profilerViewer.js is
unchanged at 5.7M with no 68kcounter in it, receiving computed values in the
model. Only the extension bundle grows, 940K -> 1.1M.

The applicability decision moves into theoreticalTimings.datasheetApplicability
so the CLI report and the UI cannot disagree about whether the comparison is
meaningful. Where it says no, the column is absent rather than showing a figure
that would be fiction — both captures on hand are 68020 and correctly show
nothing.

Also fixes DBcc going untimed: the counter register sits between mnemonic and
target ("dbf.w d7,-16(pc)"), which the branch-rewrite regex didn't allow. Since
a DBcc loop is about the most common shape in hand-written Amiga code, that was
every untimed instruction across both captures — coverage goes 98% -> 100%.

events.title: Add `dump --stalls`: measured cost vs 68000 datasheet timings
events.message:
Add `dump --stalls`: measured cost vs 68000 datasheet timings

A profile can say an instruction cost 40 color clocks but not whether that's
because it does a lot of work or because the CPU sat waiting while the blitter
and bitplane DMA had the bus. Those call for opposite fixes, and nothing in the
capture distinguished them.

68kcounter gives the datasheet cost assuming the CPU never waits, so the excess
over it is contention. `dump --stalls` reports that per function alongside the
bus accesses those executions demand — what the contention is competing for. A
high stall% says "blocked, look at the bus"; a low one says "genuinely this
expensive, look at the algorithm".

Two conversions the comparison depends on, both easy to get silently wrong:
68kcounter reports CPU clock cycles where timeDeltas are color clocks (half),
and a disassembler renders branch targets as pc-relative displacements, which
aren't source syntax and parse as no instruction at all — dropping every
branch, in exactly the tight loops this is most wanted for. Where an
instruction has several timings the slowest is taken, so the figure being
subtracted is conservative and a taken branch can't manufacture stall.

It refuses rather than misleads, via two guards. 68kcounter models the 68000
only, so a capture containing sub-color-clock samples (the 020+ cycle-exact
path) is rejected. That alone wasn't enough: a 68020 capture predating the
cycleDelta fix stores no zeros to give itself away, and the first run against
one produced a nonsensical -137.7% stall. So the second guard is that
contention can only ever add cycles — measured coming in below datasheet proves
the code isn't running 68000 timings, whatever the samples look like. Both
captures on hand now correctly refuse; the arithmetic and both guards are
covered by unit tests, since neither is a positive case.

Suggested by the library's author.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: Calibrate check's thresholds against measured data
events.message:
Calibrate check's thresholds against measured data

Two of the thresholds were picked by eye when the checks were first written.
Both now have numbers behind them.

WIDTH_DIVERGENCE_PP keeps its value but gains the justification: sweeping
columns.ts's CODE_MATCH_WINDOW put a healthy layout at 0.2pp worst-case and a
deliberately mis-tuned one at 6.8pp, so 3pp sits well clear of noise while
still catching the failure the check exists for.

LOW_ANCHOR_RATE was measuring the wrong thing. Anchored-against-samples is
capped by instruction-cache behaviour nobody controls — a real 68020 frame has
10,028 fetch cells for 31,078 samples — so it read "low" on healthy captures
and fired on all four frames of a good one. It now counts against the fetch
cells actually available: of the positions the grid could confirm, how many did
we use? The same frame went from 7.9% (blind forward search) to 59.4%
(cycle-predicted), so half is a fair line, and a healthy capture is quiet again
while genuinely struggling frames (6-16%) still report.

Also records the measured getProfileRegs transfer cost next to the register cap
it justifies: ~94 ms at the 64k cap versus 26 ms at the old 16k one, against a
30 s timeout — so that cap is bounded by memory and document size, not
transfer. Comment only; no behaviour change, binary unaffected.

events.title: Predict the fetch-cell search position from the cycle clock
events.message:
Predict the fetch-cell search position from the cycle clock

buildSampleSlots searched blindly forward from the last match within a fixed
window, which strands the cursor behind the raster the moment anything runs
longer than that window without emitting a fetch cell — and then fails
permanently, since every later sample looks unmatchable too. A cached spin loop
does exactly this. On a real 68020 capture matching died at sample 1,907 of
31,078 and never recovered: 2.5% of samples anchored to an observed position,
the rest riding on extrapolation.

A grid slot is one color clock and timeDeltas are color clocks, so cycles
elapsed since the last confirmed match convert straight into slots travelled.
The search now looks around that predicted position rather than wherever the
cursor was left, so an unmatchable stretch no longer strands it.

That also turns the window into a tolerance on how far the grid may disagree
with the cycle clock, rather than a search budget — and it has to be tight.
Widening it starts matching the wrong lap of a loop: the same PC, a different
iteration. A wrong match is worse than no match, pinning a sample to a position
it never occupied and desynchronising everything after it. Swept against the
width-vs-cycles invariant, 512 matched FEWER samples than 128 (3452 vs 5959)
and pushed worst divergence to 6.8pp; 128 sits at the plateau at 0.2pp. The
table is in the comment.

Measured on frame 0 of a real capture: samples anchored 791 -> 5959 (2.5% ->
19.2%, against a 32% ceiling set by how many fetch cells exist at all), and the
instruction the Disassembly view shows at a known fetch cell is now right 58.2%
of the time versus 23.9%. Slot error p50/p90 unchanged at 2/5.

events.title: Fix the clock fallback using CPU cycles where color clocks are meant
events.message:
Fix the clock fallback using CPU cycles where color clocks are meant

IProfileModel.cyclesPerMicroSecond is the divisor for every display-unit
conversion (µs, rasterlines, % of frame), and the values it divides —
timeDeltas — are color clocks: the emulator reports costs as
get_cycles()/CYCLE_UNIT, one DMA-grid slot is one color clock, and a PAL frame
is DMA_HPOS*DMA_VPOS = 71051 of them.

The measured path was right: frameCycles/frameUs lands on ~3.55 color clocks
per µs. The fallback used when the emulator reports no frame length was
7.09379 — the CPU clock, which is master/4 against the color clock's master/8,
so exactly twice too large. On that path a full frame read as 10016 µs / 50.1%
of a frame / 156.5 rasterlines instead of 19951 / 99.8% / 311.7. The doc
comments on the field and on display.ts's Timing both described it as the CPU
clock too, which is presumably how the constant got there.

Adds PAL_COLOR_CLOCKS_PER_US / NTSC_COLOR_CLOCKS_PER_US next to the DMA
geometry they derive from, and picks between them by isPAL rather than
assuming PAL, so an NTSC capture with no reported frame length is right too.

Only the fallback path changes behaviour; captures that report a frame length
were already correct and are untouched. The scattered 7.09379 literals in
synthetic test fixtures go too — the value is an arbitrary scale factor there,
but leaving it labelled as the PAL clock invites it being copied back.

events.title: Report the matcher's real anchored-sample count, not a width proxy
events.message:
Report the matcher's real anchored-sample count, not a width proxy

profileAnalysis inferred "how many samples anchored to a real instruction
fetch" by counting columns at least one slot wide. That can't tell an anchored
column from an interpolated one that merely happens to be a slot wide, and
since zero-cost samples collapse to zero width it systematically overstated
anchoring — on a real capture it reported ~13243 where the matcher had
actually anchored 791 of 31078 samples (2.5%).

buildSampleSlots is now exported and its own `matched` count used directly.
Re-running it repeats a linear pass buildColumns already did, which is
irrelevant for an offline report and buys an exact figure. The "~" prefix goes
with it, the number no longer being an estimate.

Also updates LAST_FRAME_OVERRUN_TOLERANCE's comment: current captures land on
the frame length, so it now only tolerates files captured before that fix.

Every capture's last frame overran by ~680 color clocks (~3 scanlines, a

going to stop at, and unlike every earlier frame — bounded on both sides by
inter-frame markers — nothing marked where the last frame really ended, so
recording ran on into a tail that belonged to no requested frame.

wasm_profile_on_frame_boundary already knew when this happened: it's the
boundary reached once every requested frame has been marked off, where it
previously did nothing. It now stops recording there.

Two things follow from having an exact end:

- wasm_profile_finish measures frameCycles to that boundary rather than to
  whenever retro_run() happened to return, so the reported figure is the frame
  length instead of overstating it by the tail. It now comes back as exactly
  71051 (227 x 313) on PAL rather than 71733.

- the last sample's cycleDelta can be finalized properly instead of being left
  at the "1 = unknown" placeholder, since its cost is the time from its hook to
  the boundary, truncated at the frame edge. Inter-frame markers still drop
  theirs — one fabricated color clock per frame, well below anything
  measurable.

Verified across five capture start phases, one and two frames, whole and
narrow address ranges, running vs paused, and 68000 vs 68020 cycle-exact:
every frame now lands within 5 cycles of 71051, where the last frame
previously sat at 71728-71731. samples == inRange still holds exactly, and
test:wasm passes.

events.title: Fix "Follow" landing on the wrong instruction in the Disassembly view
events.message:
Fix "Follow" landing on the wrong instruction in the Disassembly view

Regression from the flame-graph alignment fix. Once column positions became
cycle-weighted, instructions the 68020 measures at zero color clocks (its
lumped accounting defers cycles onto whichever instruction next touches
memory) collapsed onto the same x as the neighbour that carried the lump: 55%
of columns in a real capture are now zero-width.

The shared cursor is an integer DMA slot, so those samples became
unaddressable. Every one of those 17,213 columns round-tripped
(columnIndexToSlot -> columnIndexAtX) to a *different* PC, which broke
everything that navigates by picking a sample and letting the CPU tab
re-derive it: jump to next execution, "View in context", the register panel's
jump-to-write, the step buttons, and the editor's source-line jump.
Single-stepping skipped 27% of instructions and could stick entirely.

No slot-based mapping can fix this — two samples at the same x are
indistinguishable by construction. So the cursor now carries the sample index
alongside the slot. Navigation that knows its target passes it through;
scrubbing the flame graph passes none and leaves the slot authoritative, and
every arbitrary-slot setter goes through one selectSlot helper so a stale
index cannot outlive the slot it came from.

Jump accuracy 89.3% -> 100%, stepping exact by construction. Scrubbing still
resolves only to slot granularity (44.6% of samples) — inherent, and the
reason step/jump exist.

events.title: Add `profile dump`/`profile check` CLI for .puaeprofile captures
events.message:
Add `profile dump`/`profile check` CLI for .puaeprofile captures

Investigating a suspect capture has meant hand-reimplementing the container
parse and sample decode in throwaway JS each time — laborious, and free to
drift from what the extension actually does. This adds an offline CLI that
goes through the real path (loadProfile -> buildFramesFromCaptures ->
buildColumns), so a report cannot disagree with the viewer.

`dump` is the read side: per-frame cost tables (self cycles, flame-graph
width, DMA bus census) plus a manifest summary, with --json/--frame/--functions
for programmatic use.

`check` is the more useful half. Raw per-function numbers are easy to
rationalise — a busy-wait at 76% of a frame looks plausible until you notice
the frame's samples sum to 157% of the color clocks a PAL frame physically
contains. Each check encodes one such invariant, and each corresponds to a bug
that shipped: frame-over-budget (the cycleDelta floor), width-vs-cycles
(flame-graph runs spread by sample index), registers-truncated and frame-short
(the profile/register buffer caps). It exits non-zero on an error-level
finding, so it also works as a gate.

Run against the captures from the recent profiler work, `check` reproduces the
whole three-bug investigation in one command.

Wired as a subcommand of the existing puae-debugger binary, dispatched before
any DAP/HTTP/emulator machinery loads. Also narrows the blanket `.claude`
ignore so project skills are tracked while local state stays untracked.

events.title: debugger: classify posted-write drain waits by their own arbitration; list CPUWAIT in help
events.message:
debugger: classify posted-write drain waits by their own arbitration; list CPUWAIT in help

Review follow-ups for the CPU wait attribution.

A posted 020+ chip write drains through the ordinary arbitration, in
which a busy nice blitter keeps every access cycle: the blitter-slowdown
yield that frees a synchronous grant after three misses does not apply
to the drain. Classifying the drain's waits from the CPU's view therefore
reported the slot as free (port turnaround) from the fourth miss on while
the blitter still held it. The classifier now takes the arbitration view
the waiting access is subject to: the CPU's view for a synchronous grant
(fence and yield included), the ordinary view for a drain. A 020 test
posts a write against a four-word source-only blit and checks every
drained clock stays the blitter's.

The scanline strip in the CPU wait view overlays the denied slots on the
dimmed owner pattern, as the raster does, instead of dropping the
owners.

CPUWAIT joins the console's HELP inspect list, with a test covering the
help entry, the no-trace message, and the traced-frame summary.

events.title: debugger: attribute CPU chip-bus waits in the Frame Analyzer and profile export
events.message:
debugger: attribute CPU chip-bus waits in the Frame Analyzer and profile export

The bus trace recorded who won each colour clock but not that the CPU was
waiting for it, so a coder could see the DMA pattern of a frame but not
which of those slots cost the 68000 time, nor which instruction paid.

Every colour clock the CPU asks for the chip bus and is denied is now
attributed, from the CPU's own view of the arbitration, to the class that
held it: fixed DMA (refresh, bitplane, sprite, disk, audio), the Copper's
access clock, the blitter with BLTPRI clear (the nice hold before the
slowdown counter yields), the blitter with BLTPRI set including its
warm-up fence (where the slot's recorded owner is idle because the
blitter's own cycle needs no bus), and the 020+ chip port's two-clock
turnaround, which is a wait on the CPU's own bus unit rather than a
denial. The sample carries the pending access kind and the instruction's
start PC. It is taken only while the frame analyzer is armed, on the cold
bus-observer path, so the timeline is untouched: the new bus tests pin
the same colour-clock cost as the unarmed scenarios, and two 40-second
control-protocol runs of a demo, one profiled from boot, stop at the same
clock with identical screen digests.

FrameBusTrace gains a per-slot wait grid parallel to the owner grid,
totals by class and by access kind, and a capped PC histogram that is
only read out sorted. The Frame Analyzer's Beam tab gains a "CPU wait"
checkbox (key W) that flips the raster, scanline strip, legend and
counters column to the wait view (denied slots in the denier's colour,
everything else dimmed; waited share, breakdown, top stalled PCs), plus
an always-drawn per-line stall gutter beside the raster. The console
gains CPUWAIT, profile.jsonl gains a cpu record and a cpu_wait grid
under slots, and profile.json lists the wait classes.

Opcode prefetches count under the read kind: the 68k core issues them as
plain word reads, so the fetch kind only covers immediate and extension
words read outside the prefetch queue. Documented as such.

events.title: Two leftovers from hexwab's inline-wrap patch: a dead store and a byte
events.message:
Two leftovers from hexwab's inline-wrap patch: a dead store and a byte

Both were left out of ecefec5 rather than folded in silently, and hexwab
has asked for them (issue #1).

RedrawAll's ra_row stored bufp+1 before the BPL and .ra_nowrap stores it
again unconditionally, so the first could never be observed. bufp is zero
page, so it is 2 bytes and 3 cycles, not 3 and 3 -- 48 cycles a redraw
across the 16 rows.

sTmp's low byte died with the same patch: SetCRTCStart shifts the low half
in A now, so only the high byte is live. EQUW -> EQUB, and the three
references move off sTmp+1.

  bank 4       $BFF5 -> $BFF3   2 B
  code image   $2FE8 -> $2FE7   1 B

Verified rather than inspected, since both touch address arithmetic:

  - Buffer oracle. Deck at scrollS = 48, line = 1, all three draw call
    sites NOPed, view settled, then a forced RedrawAll over the
    incrementally-scrolled buffer: 0 of 10,240 bytes differ. Both arms of
    ra_row's wrap run in that one test -- 16 rows at any scrollS > 0 span
    the end of the strip.
  - SetCRTCStart separately, because the buffer oracle is blind to it: a
    wrong start address moves the picture, not the buffer. crtcHi/crtcLo
    read back $0B06, which is ($5800 + 48) / 8.

events.title: akiko: gate transmitter-ready on the drive buffer having room
events.message:
akiko: gate transmitter-ready on the drive buffer having room

A PIO producer polls DRIVEXMIT before each command byte. With the drive's
receive buffer full, the PIO port dropped the byte but could re-assert the
latch straight away, since the ready condition only looked at the drive
being idle: the producer was told a byte was accepted when it had been
lost. Transmitter-ready now also requires room in the buffer, at the PIO
port, at the response-drain re-arm, and after a command that sends no
reply; a byte written while the latch is clear is an overrun and stays
dropped. Regression test covers the full-buffer case through the drain.

Also tightens the peripherals doc sentence that stated the checksum-error
outcome twice.

events.title: toccata: clear play/capture-active bits independently in write_reg9
events.message:
toccata: clear play/capture-active bits independently in write_reg9

write_reg9 only cleared self.active (and so play_active()) via
codec_stop() when both PEN and CEN dropped to zero together. A driver
that disables playback while leaving capture enabled (e.g. 0x03 ->
0x02) never took that path, so play_active() stayed stuck true and
the mixer fallback added in the previous commit would keep emitting
the final sample forever -- the same bug, reached a different way.

Clear each direction's bit in `active` independently as its own
enable bit clears, so play_active() reflects PEN alone regardless of
CEN's state. Flagged by Copilot's PR review.

events.title: akiko: keep the TX DMA draining the command ring during a lead-in dump
events.message:
akiko: keep the TX DMA draining the command ring during a lead-in dump

The TX DMA fetch was gated on the drive being idle (no command in its
turnaround, no reply undelivered), so while the drive streamed a TOC dump
the guest's command ring was consumed one byte per delivered packet.
Kickstart's cd.device queues a 3-byte LED packet for every TOC entry it
receives and an unpause right behind the request, which on a disc with
more than about 25 tracks laps the 256-byte ring; the lapped bytes then
parse as garbage after the dump, and the held unpause -- whose buffer the
deferral kept appending later bytes to -- fails its checksum as well. A
39-track disc (Pinball Illusions CD32) produced four checksum-error
replies at boot that the real drive never sends.

Model the drive side of the link explicitly: Akiko's DMA engine now
drains the ring into the drive's receive buffer (tx_fifo) regardless of
the drive's state, and the drive parses one command at a time out of that
buffer, still only between dumps, so the calibrated dump-exclusive hold
and the cold-boot timing are unchanged. PIO command bytes go through the
same buffer. command_deferred_for_toc is gone; STATE_VERSION 78.

Adds a regression test that replays Kickstart's LED-per-entry traffic on
a 42-point TOC and checks that the ring never lags by more than a packet,
that every LED packet and the unpause come out intact and in order, and
that the unpause is answered only after the last TOC entry.

events.title: toccata: silence the mixer fallback once the codec stops
events.message:
toccata: silence the mixer fallback once the codec stops

peek_last_sample() is the resampler's fallback in advance_mixer for
whenever the mixer's cadence outruns the codec's own causally-paced
production. advance_codec stops running entirely once play_active() is
false, so after codec_stop() the mixer took this fallback on every
tick and peek_last_sample() kept returning the last decoded DAC value
forever -- a permanent DC offset in the stem/mix instead of silence.

Gate the fallback on play_active() so it still holds the last sample
across a genuine underrun during active playback, but returns silence
once the codec is stopped.

- The Debug Console's raw `!method` escape refuses the run-control
  verbs (continue, run_until, the steps, reverse_*, pause, shutdown): a
  raw `continue` blocked the adapter's only loop until a stop nothing
  the client could still send would cause, and a raw step moved the

- A data breakpoint watches the words from its aligned start through

  hit test uses half-open ranges, so an adjacent word no longer counts.
- A PC breakpoint whose address another of the session's breakpoints
  holds is shared only when the conditions agree (refused with a

  breakpoint to the sharer instead of deleting it under it.
- Hit conditions keep the operator: `> 3` stops on the fourth hit,

- Array-form launch `args` are quoted for the AmigaDOS command line

- An explicit terminate, or disconnect with terminateDebuggee, shuts

events.title: debugger: add a Debug Adapter Protocol server, copperline-ctl --dap
events.message:
debugger: add a Debug Adapter Protocol server, copperline-ctl --dap

VS Code, nvim-dap and other DAP clients can debug a program in the
emulator with source-level breakpoints and stepping, registers, locals
and globals, memory, the custom chipset, reverse execution and a Debug
Console, without a GDB in between. The adapter is a control-protocol
client like the MCP mode: `launch` starts copperline --control-gui (or
--control for headless) --run PROG and rides the one-shot load stop to
relocate the program's debug information by segments.list, binds the
breakpoints set before the load, and runs to the entry point; `attach`
joins a session started with --control-info.

Stepping repeats step / step_over / step_out until the source line
changes, steps out of code without lines, and falls back to temporary
breakpoints on the function's other lines for a line that outgrows 64
single steps. Step Back repeats reverse_step the same way; the adapter
takes a reverse_anchor snapshot at every run stop, since the boot
volume --run stages is a host directory mount whose traffic a replay
from an older snapshot cannot reproduce, and pins --rtc-time to the
launch time so the guest clock replays too. Conditions are the
machine's own register/immediate/word compares; data breakpoints are
memory watches; exception filters are catch breakpoints. Serial output
(where KPrintF goes) is the Debug Console's stdout, and `!method {json}`
sends a raw control-protocol request.

tools/vscode-copperline is a declarative VS Code extension (plus a
40-line activator pointing at copperline-ctl) contributing the
`copperline` debug type; docs/debugger/dap.md documents the adapter,
its launch arguments and what each toolchain's debug information gives.
tests/dap_stdio.rs drives the adapter over stdio against the bundled
AROS ROM and the guest/dap-test probe, ignored like the other
process-spawning tests.
events.author: LinuxJedi

events.title: debuginfo: read symbols, LINE hunks and DWARF from Amiga executables
events.message:
debuginfo: read symbols, LINE hunks and DWARF from Amiga executables

A host-side reader for a guest program's debug information, behind the
new `dap` feature: the hunk table, HUNK_SYMBOL tables, vasm -linedebug
LINE debug hunks, and DWARF through gimli/object, either from the
trailing debug hunk amiga-gcc 6.5 -g writes or from an ELF the program
was converted from with elf2hunk. Line rows, functions with parameters
and locals (single-operation locations), globals, the common type DIEs
and .debug_frame come out addressed as hunk + offset, and DebugInfo
relocates them by the segment list the guest reports. unwind.rs walks
the stack by CFI where the DWARF covers the PC and otherwise by the
console STACK command's return-address scan.

The amiga linker resolves every cross-section reference inside the debug
hunk (abbreviation offset, stmt_list, strp, the FDEs' CIE pointers) as
an offset in the link address space, where the block follows the text,
data and bss hunks laid back to back from 0. Rather than rewrite the
DWARF, each section is handed to gimli behind that much padding, with
the bias measured from the first unit header's abbreviation offset.

Only amiga-gcc 6.5 with binutils 2.39 keeps the DWARF in hunk output;
the current amiga-gcc images (6.5 with binutils 2.46, and 13/15/16) drop
it, so the C fixture in guest/dap-test builds with the host-installed
toolchain, while the vasm fixture uses the shared docker image. Both
committed binaries are read by the unit tests.
events.author: LinuxJedi

events.title: control: report segments, anchor the reverse ring, stop at the --run load
events.message:
control: report segments, anchor the reverse ring, stop at the --run load

Three additions to the control protocol for a debugger client:

- `segments.list` returns the hunk segments of the program the scheduled
  process is running (the walk the console SEGMENTS command and the GDB
  stub's qOffsets already share) plus the programs an armed loadseg catch
  has recorded, so a client can relocate symbols at a `loadseg` stop.
- `reverse_anchor` snapshots the machine into the reverse-debug ring at
  the current position. Host-side state a restore cannot roll back (a
  directory mount's file handles, a disk image) makes a replay from an
  older frame boundary diverge: a reverse_step after a breakpoint in a
  `--run` session landed in ROM in another task. Replaying from a
  snapshot taken at the stop is exact.
- `--run PROG` with `--control` / `--control-gui` arms the one-shot
  loadseg stop `--gdb` has (control::Config::stop_on_load). The headless
  server installs it before the first resume; the windowed driver
  installs it before the first frame, so a client attaching after the
  warp boot cannot miss the load, and a stop that fired with no client
  attached is delivered as event.stopped on connect.

Bridge::send takes &self (the writer behind a mutex, ids atomic) so one
thread can block in wait() for an outstanding resume while another
sends pause; LaunchSpec gains windowed/noaudio so a bridge can start a
--control-gui session. MCP launches are unchanged.

events.title: Layer 9 DECISION 20: an energy bar, one pixel a point
events.message:
Layer 9 DECISION 20: an energy bar, one pixel a point

The C64 shows energy by flashing the player's sprite below eight and in
no other way, which is a threshold alarm and not a gauge: between 64 and
8 -- where a player decides whether to take a fight -- it says nothing.
Stew asked for a readout and KC took a single bar under the logo.

It costs the original's artwork nothing, because it goes where the
original draws nothing at all. panelframe's bottom-middle cells carry ink
on scanline 5 alone, so scanlines 0-4 of panel row 3 are blank INSIDE the
box; the bar takes scanline 2, centred in that band. No glyph moved and
no cell of the C64's status line was overdrawn. The colour was spare too
-- palPanel had logical 1 unused, so PN_PHYS_BAR is a fourth ink and the
paper, the logo, the score and the frame are where they were.

CB_ENERGY_FULL is $40 and a MODE 1 byte is four pixels, so a full bar is
sixteen bytes and the byte count IS the energy shifted right twice. No
scale factor, no multiply, and a four-entry table for the part-lit byte.
Centring on the nine-cell logo leaves 4 px either side, which puts the
left end on a byte boundary -- nothing is shifted or masked. Units are 8
bytes apart, so the draw is one STA abs,X with X stepping 8, gated on a
shadow byte like the score's.

pmEnergy is the fourth scalar in the bank-6 bridge, for the same reason
as the other three: drEnergy is entry 0 of the droid table, in bank 4,
and panel.asm cannot see it.

Verified against the buffer, not the screenshot: PnMirror's LDA drEnergy
patched to an immediate and the sixteen bytes read back at $527A+8n --
0 empty, 6 -> 0F 0C, 27 -> six 0F then 0E, 33 -> eight 0F then 08, 64 ->
sixteen 0F with the next address still 00. Scanline 5 read $FF and
scanlines 0/1/3/4 read $00 throughout, so the box's bottom edge is
untouched. Game over shows no bar (death leaves energy at zero) and the
briefing cannot show a stale one (PanelInit runs before PnBriefing).

Bank 6 -75 B (673 free), code image -7 B (24 free, code_end $2FE8).

events.title: akiko: deliver subcode frames with a Q position during CD-DA play
events.message:
akiko: deliver subcode frames with a Q position during CD-DA play

The drive's pickup decodes P-W subcode for every frame it plays, and
Akiko DMAs each 96-byte frame into the misc page's subcode area and
raises the subcode interrupt. Copperline only did that from the data
read path, with a zeroed payload; an audio play streamed sectors into
the mixer without any subcode. The Kickstart 3.1 cd.device runs its
CD_ADDFRAMEINT servers and refreshes the CD_QCODE position from that
interrupt, so a title that starts a CD_PLAYTRACK and waits for its
first frame interrupt never got one (regression example: Liberation's
CD32 intro busy-waits on its frame-interrupt counter at 34s while the
audio keeps playing).

Deliver one subcode frame per streamed CD-DA sector through the same
sequence the read path uses (alternating 128-byte halves, $FFFF $0000
end marker, offset register advanced by 100, CDINT_SUBCODE), and fill
the Q channel from the TOC for both paths: an ADR 1 position packet
with control, track, index (index 0 counting down through a pregap),
track-relative and absolute MSF in BCD, and the inverted CRC-16-CCITT,
bit-interleaved with Q in bit 6. The SubQ drive command reports the
same position while a play runs or is paused, in WinUAE's cd_qcode
layout, instead of the all-zero packet. CdTrack::sector_count now has
a user, so its dead_code allowance goes.

No serialized struct changes; the state format stays at 77.

fix(tms9918a): inhibit 5S while F is still set and unread

Confirmed via the datasheet: the fifth-sprite status flag only updates
while F (the frame interrupt flag) is clear. An unread F from a
previous frame previously let 5S keep updating regardless, so a game
that fell behind on polling status could still see fresh 5S reports
it should not have gotten until it acknowledged F.

events.title: fix(vdp): update the VRAM address low byte on the first control byte
events.message:
fix(vdp): update the VRAM address low byte on the first control byte

Both the TMS9918A and V9938 control-port writers latched the first
byte without touching the address register at all, only combining
both bytes once the second byte arrived. Real hardware updates the
address registers low byte immediately on the first write. A data
port access sandwiched between the two control bytes (the second
never sent) previously used the fully stale address instead of the
new low byte combined with the old high byte.

events.title: fix(v9938): reset the palette write latch on R16, not R15
events.message:
fix(v9938): reset the palette write latch on R16, not R15

registerWrite() cleared paletteSecond when R15 (status register select)
was written -- unrelated to the palette port. R16 is the actual palette
index pointer, and writing it is what real hardware documents as
resetting the two-byte write latch so a fresh writePalette() sequence
starts clean.

Two failure modes from the swap: writing R15 mid-sequence wrongly
discarded a pending first byte, and writing R16 (e.g. to retarget the
index before a write) failed to reset the latch, so a stray leftover
first byte from before could combine with the next write into the
wrong entry.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: fix(v9938): show the R7 backdrop, not pens[0], for colour index 0 (TP=0)

fix(v9938): show the R7 backdrop, not pens[0], for colour index 0 (TP=0)

The bitmap path (Graphic4/6/7 via palettePen(), Graphic7 inline) already
did this correctly; the character modes didn't. Text 1/2's R7 fg/bg and
R12 blink fg/bg, Graphics 1's colour-table fg/bg, and Graphics 2/3's
colour-table fg/bg all indexed pens[] directly, so a colour-0 foreground
or blink colour rendered black instead of the programmed backdrop.

Routed all four through palettePen(), which already had the right TP
(R8 bit 5) logic. Also extended the same fix to GRAPHIC 5, which had
been explicitly excluded from palettePen()'s backdrop substitution
(hence its dropped  parameter, now unused) because it packs
two 2-bit backdrop colours per R7 byte (even/odd X) rather than one
4-bit one — added a dedicated graphic5Pen() that picks the right half
by pixel position, matching fillBackdrop's existing even/odd split.

events.title: fix(v9938): assert S2 HR (bit 5) instead of never setting it
events.message:
fix(v9938): assert S2 HR (bit 5) instead of never setting it

Real hardware toggles HR once per scanline (high during horizontal
blanking); this core has no sub-line T-state granularity to time that
precisely. It never set the bit at all, so any software polling HR
for a 0->1 edge would hang forever.

Synthesise a toggling pattern from the S2 read cadence instead — the
same technique already used for WD179x's INDEX pulse — so a polling
loop always eventually sees both states. Scoped to S2 reads only, so
the existing bit-masked S2 assertions elsewhere in the command-processor
tests (none of which check bit 5) are unaffected.

events.title: Layer 12 DECISION 6: the lift screen stipples cleared decks
events.message:
Layer 12 DECISION 6: the lift screen stipples cleared decks

Parked on 2026-08-31 because the marking walk would not fit bank 7 --
by about twenty bytes -- and nothing on ram-pass.md's reserve list
frees bank 7. That finding still stands: bank 7 measured 90 B free
today, TIGHTER than the 100-105 recorded in August, and neither of
hexwab's patches touched it.

What unparked it is the second option in that entry's own list, "put
the walk somewhere else". In August bank 6 had 7 B free and bank 5 had
6, so there was nowhere. hexwab's SCANSTEP deferred carry took bank 6
to 931 B and the code image from 3 B to 82. LvClearedMark is therefore
in console.asm, bank 6, and main RAM orchestrates the hop:

  LiftViewEnter  LvEnter4(4) -> LvStart7(7) -> LvClearedMark(6) -> LvStart7b(7)
  ConsoleTick    ConShipEnter4(4) -> LvShip7(7) -> LvClearedMark(6) -> LvRepaintAll(7)

Both bank-7 entries now stop short of LvRepaintAll, because the mark
has to reach the colour shadow between its being built and its being
painted. LvTick7 needs no second mark -- it repaints from the shadow.

THE STACK PAGE WAS NOT USED and stays an untouched reserve. It was the
August plan, but ram-pass.md lists the lift's deck-selection screen
among the paths its 128-byte measurement never exercised, and that is
the one screen this runs on. DECK_DONE is in the code image instead.

Two bank-7 dependencies had to be broken. The colour shadow is main
RAM so the walk can write it, but the deck rectangles are bank 7's:
export_sideview.py now also emits src/data/svdecks6.asm, the same four
tables under lvcDeck* names from the same listing in the same run, so
the copies cannot drift. sideview.asm came back byte-identical.
xsLineLo/Hi were not needed at all -- ten adds of 40, once a cleared
deck, on a screen drawn once.

  bank 6      931 B -> 748 B    (walk, 64 B of tables, 3 B scratch)
  bank 7       90 B ->  25 B    (the stipple in LvCellPaint)
  code image   82 B ->  31 B    (trampolines, DECK_DONE, its clear)
  bank 4       19 B ->  11 B    (exactly the 8 B August costed)

Verified in jsbeeb: CTRL+C on deck 5 sets DECK_DONE[5] and nothing
else; the walk marks 18 of deck 5's 18 cells and 18 in the whole
shadow, so nothing outside it; 16 of those paint chequered with the
halves aligned; the two that do not are char $A6, outside $80-$8F,
which has no lit partner and is left solid by design. A cleared deck
that is also the SELECTED deck paints solid, so clear one deck and
CTRL+] to another to see the effect at all.
