events.title: engine: bound the event-tail hold by WORK, not wall-clock (#8)
events.message:
engine: bound the event-tail hold by WORK, not wall-clock (#8)

Reported from the Mega STe + ATW800/2: closing a picture event shows the pic
"unloading", draining out of the view square before the view redraws. The TODO
guessed this was a missing hold and proposed adding one. It is the opposite —
the hold has been there since #161 and has never once worked.

port_event_tail_expire bounded the hold at 30 ticks, reasoned as generous
against "a wipe and a repair inside one step render" and shipped with the note
that a slow machine exceeding it "simply gets the pre-#161 flash back".
Instrumenting the tail says every machine exceeds it, and not marginally:

  tail in        tick 14515
  tail out       tick 14549   jt23+jt935+jt937+jt938 = 34 ticks, 5 presents
  L63c0 release  tick 14569   90 presents swallowed

The honest window is 54-66 ticks over two events, nearly twice the bound, on a
Falcon030 in an emulator under fast-forward. So the expiry fired on every event
ever dispatched, and l63c0's release — the designed one, the one that discards
the intermediates and lands the tail as a single frame — never ran. On a fast
machine that costs a blink nobody noticed for a month. On a slow-present card
the expiry lands mid-tail and the rest of the teardown goes out one present at
a time, which is the reported drain.

Time cannot separate the two states this has to tell apart: "busy rebuilding
the frame" and "stuck, the engine has run on without me" both look like elapsed
ticks, and the legitimate case is already ~1s on the FASTEST target. That is
not a badly tuned constant, it is the wrong axis.

Presents swallowed is the right one, because it does not vary with machine
speed — the same code path issues the same presents at 7MHz and 50MHz, so one
cap holds on every target with no per-machine table. qd_hold_swallowed() counts
what the ref-counted hold ate (never the frame bracket, which has no engine
owner that can fail to release it); the honest window measures 71-92, so 512
clears the longest five-slot message several times over while a runaway, which
presents without bound because presenting is what it does, still trips it. The
wall-clock bound survives at 900 ticks as a last resort that is never expected
to fire.

Primary protection stays STRUCTURAL, which is what the two shipped freezes
taught: the walk-step gate in port_event_tail_hold, plus explicit drops
wherever the engine waits for the player. Added the one that defeated
enumeration twice — jt511's combat entry, the rider-and-ogres shape — so it is
caught there rather than hundreds of presents later by the net.

Measured A/B, same fixture, same key timing, HEIRS 13,8 tavern-brawl event:

  HEAD   444 bracket -> 9102 text -> 3895+3900 full -> 19759 step
         = 5 separate partial states presented
  fixed  3895+3900 = 2 presents, the two flip pages of ONE frame

At ~0.5s per present on the Nova card that is ~2.5s of visible teardown gone.

Also adds FRUA_SLOWPRESENT, the harness that made this reproducible at all.
Nothing we emulate is natively as slow as the ATW's VME writes, so bugs that
only appear at that cost cannot be found by running an emulator — the reason
this one needed a hardware report. -DFRUA_SLOWPRESENT=<ticks> burns that cost
per present and turns any machine into an ATW-class one for timing purposes;
at 30 it reproduces the drain on a Falcon. Diagnostic only, off by default.

Falcon/TT, ST/STE, Amiga AGA and Amiga ECS all build; 483 tests pass. Live
drive on the clean 020 build: the 13,8 picture event fires, pages, closes, and
the new view redraws with the command bar intact.

Not yet confirmed on the hardware that reported it — that is owed at the next
pass, along with the rest of 0.9.20.

events.title: Pause is CTRL+P and mute is CTRL+Q, paid for out of four longhand pagings
events.message:
Pause is CTRL+P and mute is CTRL+Q, paid for out of four longhand pagings

KC asked for the modifier. It needs no machinery at all: keydown takes an
INKEY byte and EORs it into an internal key number, so CTRL is just
KEY_CTRL = &FE (INKEY -2, internal 1), and because keydown asks the
matrix about one key at a time a modifier is a second query with no
ghosting to design around.

CTRL gates the TRIGGERS ONLY. DoPause tests KEY_P four times -- the
trigger, two release waits and the held loop -- and only the trigger is
gated: you are already holding CTRL by the time you want out. KC: "unpause
with just P is fine." The mute has one site and it is a trigger, so
CTRL+Q throughout. At both sites CTRL-up branches to the SAME exit as
key-up, which is what keeps pausePrev and volQPrev honest -- a
half-pressed combo resets them exactly as letting go of the key does.

WHERE THE 14 BYTES CAME FROM, main RAM having had 6: none of
docs/ram-pass.md's reserves fit. sprsplit and SCANSTEP buy banks 5 and 6,
and door.asm is the only main-RAM one but is gated on freeing ~650 B of
bank 4 first. So it was paid for locally, from four sites writing
PAGEBANK out longhand where RAM pass 5 had already established the trade
of an 8-byte expansion for a 3-byte JSR: CbBulletFrame's two pagings
become JSR PgSpr / JSR PgData (-10 B), and sprite.asm's two effect-slot
pagings become a new PgSprSlot (-4 B) -- which needed a new helper
because those two set sprBank as well, which is exactly why neither
existing Pg* fitted and both had written the four stores out by hand.

Net zero: code_end was &2FFA before and is &2FFA after. Both are
transition or once-per-effect-slot code, so the 12 cycles a call cost
nothing.

Verified in jsbeeb by reading paused and sndVolume rather than by looking
at the screen: bare P held leaves paused 0, adding CTRL sets it, plain P
clears it; bare Q leaves sndVolume 15, adding CTRL drops it to 0, holding
the combo does not re-toggle, and CTRL+Q again restores 15.

docs/layer-11e-sound.md §12 carries it as DECISION 16 with the ledger,
§9 and §10 point at it, and the key lists in README and PLAN are updated.

events.title: Show the roast, and stop hiding the graphics that have no colours of their own
events.message:
Show the roast, and stop hiding the graphics that have no colours of their own

Three colour fixes, all of them cases where a rule that was right for one kind
of thing was wrong for another.

$FF cells are drawn bright white on black rather than black. $FF means leave
this cell alone, so on a page with no room behind it there is no colour to
take; black made "not coloured here" look identical to "nothing there", and
lost four graphics outright -- the cave door frame, the wall shield and two
others whose every cell is $FF showed as empty rectangles. The partly
transparent ones read properly now too: the locked cave door has white
stonework, red bars and a yellow keyhole.

The health indicator is named and yellow. Following the life-force countdown's
"redraw the roast" to $8B8A leads to $C48D and $C543, which are graphics $B5
and $B4: the whole roast chicken and the carcass picked down to the bones, 48
by 30 each, counted down as the life force drains. Their attribute pointer is
the null table at $AEEA, and running the routine shows why -- it draws 78 bytes
of pixels and never touches the attribute file, because it draws into cells the
panel has already coloured. So their colour is in no table anywhere, and $46 is
set explicitly with a note saying it is what the game shows rather than
something derived.

And the food takes its commonest colour. Sprite colours came from INITIAL_STATE
only where every record for a code agreed, which is right for monsters -- placed
once each -- and wrong for the things there are many of. A food is red in one
room and yellow in another, so all eight fell through to white. Now the
commonest placement wins, ties to the lower attribute so the build stays
reproducible, and the page says that is what it is showing.

events.title: Colour the graphics from the game's own attribute tables
events.message:
Colour the graphics from the game's own attribute tables

The pieces the rooms are furnished with have colours, and they are in the game
already. Finding them took the sprite pointer table apart properly.

It is not one table of 239 entries indexed from three biased bases, which is
what was written here. It is three tables end to end: 161 sprite pointers to
$A5FF, then 39 furniture graphics from $A600, then 39 from $A64E that are not
pictures at all but those same pieces' attribute tables, one colour per
character cell in the same width-and-height format. The bases work because the
tables follow each other, which is the reverse of the explanation given, and
161 + 39 + 39 = 239 was there to be noticed.

So codes $C9 to $EF were never graphics. They are the colour tables, and they
had been rendered as pictures -- the little 32x3 bars. They are labelled
ATTRS_xx now and draw nothing.

What this buys:

- The furniture is drawn in its own colours, a row per code.
- The four locked doors are four doors again. They share one graphic at $A69C
  and differ only in colour: $43 $42 red, $44 green, $45 cyan, $46 yellow.
- $FF is handled. It is not a colour -- the real values are $00, $07 and $42 to
  $47 -- it means leave this cell alone, so the pixels are drawn and the cell
  keeps whatever the room painted there. That is how a doorway is drawn in the
  colour of the wall it is cut into. Those cells are black here, since there is
  no room to take a colour from, and the table says which graphics are affected;
  four of them are nothing but $FF.

The status panel is cropped to its eight columns and coloured by running
PAINT_PANEL after DRAW_PANEL with a room colour of $42, the commonest in
ROOM_TABLE, rather than left in a placeholder attribute.

events.title: Add a graphics page, and find the title screen on the tape
events.message:
Add a graphics page, and find the title screen on the tape

A page for everything drawn that is not a creature: the 56 wide graphics the
rooms are furnished with, in a table with picture, codes, name, size and
address; the two character sets; the status panel; and the title screen.

Building it corrected another name. $B03A and $B32A were written up as the
title screen's character set and picture, "8 rows of 24". Drawing them shows
the parchment scroll with TIME and SCORE on it and the compass at its foot --
the status panel, 8 columns by 24 rows, at x=192, which is exactly the columns
PAINT_PANEL colours. The dimensions were transposed and the name invented, and
192 bytes is 192 bytes either way, so nothing contradicted it. Renamed
PANEL_TILES, PANEL_LAYOUT and DRAW_PANEL.

The title screen is on the tape. The game's memory holds no title picture at
all: it is a plain screen$ block, the second thing in the .tap, 6912 bytes
loaded straight to $4000 and shown while the 30K behind it loads. The build now
walks the tape's block lengths, matches the header that declares 6912 bytes at
$4000, and writes it out -- the one graphic here that no game code ever draws,
and the only one in colour.

That is what made the wrong name plausible for so long, and it is worth having
written down: there is a title screen, so something had to be drawing it. Only
the 30K was being disassembled, which turned "it must be in here somewhere"
into a deduction instead of an assumption about the boundary of what was being
looked at.

Also picks a font grid width that wastes fewest cells, since a UDG array fills
its last row with whatever bytes follow the font, and captures the panel at the
point its routine leaves the game's address space -- it does not end in a clean
RET, being normally entered with more on the stack.

events.title: Animate what actually animates, and stop animating what does not
events.message:
Animate what actually animates, and stop animating what does not

Two fixes, opposite directions, both settled by the game's data rather than by
eye.

The sword, the axe, the spawning monster and the burst were not animating at
all. #FRAMES refuses a frame larger than the first, and these change shape as
they go -- a spinning sword is sixteen rows upright and twelve on the diagonal.
An animation is a loop and can be entered anywhere, so it is now rotated to
start on a frame at least as large as every other, and the smaller frames are
offset to sit in the middle of it rather than the corner. Where no frame
dominates in both directions there is nothing to rotate to, and the cycle keeps
its stills.

The eight foods and the fifteen collectables were animating, and should not:
they are sets of different objects, not frames of one. INITIAL_STATE settles
it. A record's +$00 is the picture it starts as, so an animation places only
its first frame -- the mummy puts $70 in one room and never mentions $71 to $73
-- while a collection places every member, ten of each of the eight foods, all
eight codes. Two or more codes of a run appearing there means it is a set.

That is the third time a run of consecutive codes under one handler has been
taken for frames when it was not: sixteen codes that were four headings, two
that were halves of one icon, and now eight that were eight different things.
The three cases are now told apart by the repeated table entry of a walk cycle,
by placement in INITIAL_STATE, and by an explicit `; joined` directive for the
one that is not derivable.

33 animations, none of them wrong as far as the data can say.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: Import NEWDESK.INF/DESKTOP.INF, if EMUDESK.INF doesn't exist
events.message:
Import NEWDESK.INF/DESKTOP.INF, if EMUDESK.INF doesn't exist

This is intended for better support of existing ST and STE software,
especially where disks must be treated as read-only. If EMUDESK.INF is
not found it will attempt to load NEWDESK.INF, then DESKTOP.INF and parse
them to the extent that they are compatible.

Notably, medium (or other) resolution can be selected at boot. Desktop
icons are translated to EmuTOS ones. Windows are opened, though it's
not possible to make scrolled contents match identically.

Keyboard shortcuts #K are ignored (possibly they could be translated
to EmuTOS actions with some effort). NEWDESK.INF icon key shortcuts are
also ignored.

This does not add any ability to save either format, it is mostly intended
to help old disks start up in a more friendly and immediately usable
state.

It can be enabled/disabled as CONF_WITH_DESKTOP_INF_FALLBACK which by
default is enabled only if CONF_ATARI_HARDWARE is present.

Resolves #74.

The renderer-side envelope line says what crop a frame offers; this

events.title: Name the player's headings, and stop animating the icons
events.message:
Name the player's headings, and stop animating the icons

Two things told rather than derived, both from the person who knows the game.

The three characters' sixteen codes are four headings of four frames running
left, right, up, down. Nothing in the data says which set faces which way --
the four are drawn by hand rather than mirrored, and comparing them byte for
byte finds no pair that is the reverse of another -- so the order is recorded
as told and applied to the knight, the wizard and the serf only. The creatures
keep their headings unnamed rather than assumed to match.

And three runs are not animations at all. A sprite is only ever sixteen pixels
wide, so a wider icon is two drawn side by side: the cursor keys, the keyboard
and the joystick on the control-selection screen are each one picture in two
halves. Animated, they flicked between the halves of a single icon. They are
now shown joined, with the halves beside them, and declared in the annotations
as `; joined $48-$49` rather than inferred from the wording of a name.

Three bogus animations gone, 30 down to 27.

events.title: autocrop: keep the chrome band pinned while a menu or panel is open
events.message:
autocrop: keep the chrome band pinned while a menu or panel is open

Opening a menu used to suspend autocrop to the classic letterbox so
the overlay could not be cropped away, but that also moved the status
bar from its bottom-anchored band to the letterbox's centred position
and back on every menu click. The layout now stays two-quad while the
mode is on: an open overlay (and a session with no content yet) widens
the display quad to the full display region instead of suspending, so
menus and panels stay entirely visible, and the band never moves. Only
a pass that owns the whole display rect (bezel, CRT preset, RTG) still
falls back to the classic layout, along with programmable scans.

events.title: review: show fractional warp-boot seconds as configured
events.message:
review: show fractional warp-boot seconds as configured

The Warp boot labels rounded through {:.0}, so a warp_until of 12.5
displayed as a different-looking timestamp and sub-half-second values as
0s, while config validation accepts arbitrary positive seconds. A
format_secs helper (format_mhz's shape) keeps whole seconds terse and
fractional values exact, on both the Until state and the idle-threshold
row; the round-trip test now pins the 12.5 label.

events.title: autocrop: crop to fetched rows, keep the chrome band at its classic size
events.message:
autocrop: crop to fetched rows, keep the chrome band at its classic size

Autocrop showed no visible change on real content because the content
envelope followed the programmed display window alone, and Kickstart
and most games leave the vertical window at the full 256 lines (VSTOP
below 0x80 gains the wraparound high bit) around a 200-line picture --
the envelope matched the TV aperture and the crop was a no-op. The
envelope now counts only display-window rows that carry fetched
bitplane data, so it tightens to the picture: measured with the new
COPPERLINE_DIAG_AUTOCROP knob, the Gods intro reports rows 32..232
(exactly its picture between the black window bands) and the Kickstart
insert-disk screen its true 200 lines. A frame with no captures at all
(the RAM re-fetch compatibility path) still counts every window row.

The chrome band also stops eating the gains: sized at the surface
width fit it grew past 300 rows on a 5K fullscreen, cancelling what
the crop won. It now keeps exactly the size and horizontal placement
the classic letterbox gives it, bottom-anchored, so toggling autocrop
resizes the picture and never the bar.

Toggling autocrop on under a bezel or CRT preset says it is suspended
in the OSD instead of silently changing nothing.

events.title: Animate the sprites by heading, and colour them the way the game does
events.message:
Animate the sprites by heading, and colour them the way the game does

The sprites page was a flat wall of images with one wrong animation per
creature. Four fixes, two of them findings about the game rather than
presentation.

A creature's run of codes is not one sequence. Sixteen codes are four headings
of four frames, and each heading is a cycle whose fourth frame's table entry
points at the second frame's picture rather than a copy of it -- a four-frame
walk drawn three times. Animating all sixteen together spins through every
direction at once, which is what it had been doing. The split is detected on
that repeated entry, so a run that does not fit the pattern stays as one row.

Colour comes from the game as well. An actor record's +$05 is its attribute and
the objects and monsters in INITIAL_STATE are eight bytes each, so the colour of
anything placed at the start reads straight off: the mummy white, Frankenstein
red, the devil magenta, Dracula green, bright ink on black. Applied only where
every record for a code agrees, so the player -- whose colour comes from the
character chosen -- keeps the default.

The layout is now a #UDGTABLE per creature, columns Frame 1..N plus Animated,
one row per heading, 30 animations where there were 21. The animation is the
last column because #FRAMES needs its frames to exist by then, and the drawing
macro sits in the cell rather than above the table, which is what had been
emitting sixteen stray images before every one of them.

The intro still described the simulator pass deleted in the previous commit,
and still said codes above $A1 draw only fragments of a few pixels -- the
mis-sized furniture error once more. Both corrected.

Not done: naming the four headings. They are four directions, but the groups
are not mirror images of each other, so each is drawn by hand and there is no
structural tell as to which is which. The table says "4 headings of 4 frames"
and stops there rather than guessing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: launcher: Warp boot rows on the A/V & Emu Emulation page
events.message:
launcher: Warp boot rows on the A/V & Emu Emulation page

Two rows under Warp speed, matching the page's cycle style:

- Warp boot: Off <-> Storage idle (the boot warps until the floppy/HDD
  LEDs have been quiet for the idle threshold). A warp_until loaded from
  a config file shows as its own 'Until Ns' state; the modes are
  mutually exclusive, so one press clears it and lands on Off.
- Warp boot idle: preset stepper over 5s-120s. The upper presets exist
  because the threshold must outlast the boot's longest storage-quiet
  stretch (a big-RAM machine's MMU table build keeps the disk idle for
  seconds).

The Emulation category also gains a UI-preview render alongside its
Audio/Video/Display siblings, so the page can be eyeballed with
COPPERLINE_UI_PREVIEW=1. Row cycling and the round trip through
RawConfig are covered in the launcher tests, including the
warp_until-clearing press.

events.title: Draw the sprites from the game's bytes, the right way up
events.message:
Draw the sprites from the game's bytes, the right way up

Comparing against pobtastic's Atic Atac disassembly at
skoolkit.arcadegeek.co.uk, which reached the game first and presents its
graphics far better than this did. Adopts its approach and, in doing so,
retracts three claims made here.

Pictures are now #UDGARRAY over the game's own bytes rather than PNGs rendered
in a simulator and pasted in, so an image and the DEFBs beside it cannot drift
apart. 193 graphics blocks, 155 sprite stills, and 21 #FRAMES animations at the
pace the game plays them -- a step every fourth frame -- so the creatures walk.
The simulator sprite pass is deleted. Porting notes: SkoolKit 9.x takes the UDG
specifications after a semicolon and 10.x in brackets, and the macros need
wrapping in #HTML or skool2asm refuses them.

Three corrections, in increasing order of how wrong they were.

The rows are stored bottom up. Every picture needed flipping vertically, which
is what the flip=2 in their macro is for and why its crop carries an odd
y-offset -- the padding moves to the top. Dropped both as noise; all 369 images
came out upside down.

The two graphics formats are not split by address. Codes above $A1 are the
pieces rooms are furnished with, drawn by different code, and they carry a
width as well as a row count. This had them as sprites: nine or eleven bytes
instead of a hundred and thirty.

So there are no 556 bytes of unreferenced artwork. Those were the tails of the
furniture. Dead space drops from 1000 bytes to 444 -- 251 of padding, 164 for
the two unused staircase orientations, 29 for the two routines nothing calls.

And four names were wrong: $AE-$B1, $B2, $B9 and $BC were called doors. Drawn
at their real size they are a cave door, a grandfather clock, a framed picture,
a trapdoor and a rug. Nine-byte fragments are easy to misname. Their 30
furniture names are taken with credit in the annotations and on the Trivia page.

The lesson, recorded in docs/game-examples.md: feeding all 239 codes to
DRAW_ONE_SPRITE measures what that routine reads, not what the game reads. A
measurement repeated 239 times is not 239 pieces of evidence when the same
wrong instrument took them all, and the residue it left was named rather than
explained.

Still 100% of 30208 bytes, 401 spans with no overlaps, byte-for-byte.

events.title: Read all 151 room table entries, and find the trapdoor fall
events.message:
Read all 151 room table entries, and find the trapdoor fall

ROOM_TABLE has 151 entries, not 149. Scanning range(ROOM_COUNT) looked
obviously right -- the game has 149 rooms -- and hid the last two. Entry 150 is
shape $0C, the twelve nested rectangles drawn while the player falls through a
trapdoor: a room as far as the drawing code is concerned, but not one anybody
walks into.

The cost of the off-by-one was a wrong claim rather than a wrong byte. Shape
$0C was written up as unused artwork and counted as reclaimable dead space,
when in fact the game draws it every time you hit a trapdoor. It is named
"Trapdoor fall" now and appears on the Room types page, which goes from ten
outlines to eleven.

Three tables of nearly the same length are in play at once and none should be
derived from another, so they are separate constants: ROOM_TABLE_ENTRIES (151),
ROOM_LIST_ENTRIES (150, ending where the first list begins at $76A9 -- the fall
has no contents) and ROOM_COUNT (149, the rooms the player walks around).

Also stops the generator claiming an unused shape is "never drawn", which is
the assertion this corrects. Nothing in ROOM_TABLE pointing at a shape is not
the same as nothing drawing it. Two shapes really are unused: $05 to $08 are
one staircase in four orientations sharing a single edge list, and the game
uses $05 for five rooms and $08 for one while leaving $06 and $07 complete and
untouched.

A bound that is too small produces no error, no gap and no failed check -- it
just narrows what you are looking at, and everything downstream agrees with it.
That is now written down beside the tiling notes.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: Check what the Atic Atac disassembly claims, not just that it reassembles
events.message:
Check what the Atic Atac disassembly claims, not just that it reassembles

The round-trip check is blind to structure. A table sliced into pieces, a block
whose sub-blocks stop short of its span, two blocks claiming the same bytes --
all still reassemble byte-for-byte, because the bytes are there and in order.
The only symptom is that the disassembly quietly describes less than it did.
That is how a span returned as (start, length) rather than (start, end) undid
about 7% of the coverage with the build staying green.

check_structure() now runs before the control files are merged and fails on
overlapping spans, a sub-block that does not start where the last one ended,
or a block whose sub-blocks do not sum to its span. A good build prints one
line: 412 spans, no overlaps, every sub-block accounted for. A Span alias and
a note at _SPAN_RE say which way round the pair goes.

It found a real one. Sprites $54 and $58 overlap: $C219 is eighteen rows, but
$C23A -- another sprite's first byte -- falls four bytes inside it, and the
read traces confirm the game reads both ranges in full. SkoolKit had been
resolving that by cutting the first block short, leaving GFX_54 described as
eighteen rows above a listing of sixteen. The generator now stops a block where
the next one starts and explains the sharing, so the two agree.

Also:

- render_sprites() refuses to finish if the pages link a sprite image nothing
  drew. graphics_blocks decides a graphic is blank from its bytes, the renderer
  decides by running the game; a disagreement would only surface as a broken
  image in a browser.
- The snapshot is parsed once. game_memory() caches and returns a tuple so the
  shared copy cannot be written to; machine_memory() hands out a fresh mutable
  64K with the ROM in place for anything that runs code. Ten call sites became
  those two, and nine dead imports went with them.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: jonsole

events.title: Document every byte of Atic Atac, and catch a typo in the game
events.message:
Document every byte of Atic Atac, and catch a typo in the game

Takes the disassembly from 36% to 100%: 30208 of 30208 bytes, 631 named
entries, still reassembling byte-for-byte.

The big tables are generated rather than hand-written. build_aticatac.py
reads the sprite pointer table, the room-contents index and the shape table
out of the snapshot and emits a control file of 194 sprite graphics, 150 room
lists and 20 outline tables, each labelled and sub-blocked so one record --
or one row of pixels -- lands on a line.

Extents are measured, not inferred. Running the game's own drawing code for
every sprite code on a fresh machine, with a memory wrapper logging reads,
shows all 235 that draw read exactly 1 + 2 * rowcount bytes contiguously from
the address the table holds. So the format is one header byte and rows of two
bytes, and that is a measurement rather than a guess.

What the data turned out to be:

- $600D is the whole runtime area written out in full and moved into place
  with one LDIR -- 115 objects, five monsters, 274 doors.
- Doors are 16 bytes, not 8: one record holding both sides. 272 of the 274
  are named by two different rooms, which is why DOOR_OTHER_SIDE flips bit 3
  of an address instead of adding anything.
- Three room shapes ($06, $07, $0C) are complete and used by no room, found
  because their vertex tables sat in gaps the used shapes left behind.
- The victory message is misspelt. The bytes read CONGRATULATION then $D4,
  which is "T" with the end marker set; drawing the screen confirms the game
  says CONGRATULATIONT. Its sequence is never reached by random play, which
  is why a code map built from playthroughs left it classified as data.

Also fixes a bug in the build script that the round-trip check cannot catch:
declared_spans() returns (start, end), and the new generators were returning
(start, length), so their spans matched nothing and every generated table got
sliced back up. A mis-split block still reassembles byte-for-byte, so this was
invisible until coverage was measured -- it was costing about 7%.

events.title: The intro's data is compressed, and it hands the machine back properly
events.message:
The intro's data is compressed, and it hands the machine back properly

tools/make_intro_data.py builds two ZX0 streams from pdloader's binaries:
PINTDAT, the whole 16K sideways image with samples, song and lookup
tables at the offsets init_metadata expects (16,384 -> 4,195), and
PINTSCR, the picture (20,480 -> 1,256). 33,912 bytes of loose files
became 5,451, eleven catalogue entries became two, and the disc image
went 85,760 -> 56,064: about 5 s off every boot. src/zx0depack.asm is
INCLUDEd rather than copied so there is still one decoder, the bank
stream depacks straight into the bank, and his 16K copy loop is gone.

WHERE A STREAM MAY LAND IS THE WHOLE DIFFICULTY. Not inside &3000-&7FFF
for the screen -- ZX0 decodes forwards and at 16:1 the writer is 19K
ahead of the reader by the end. And not at &0400 either, which is where
it went first: 1,256 bytes from there reach &08E7, through &0800-&08FF,
the MOS's SOUND WORKSPACE, whose 100 Hz interrupt still owns the machine
at load time. One byte written into the stream mid-decode sent the
depacker off a wrong offset -- a band of garbage across the credits with
correct picture either side, 542 wrong bytes between &6A50 and &754C,
found by diffing the depacked screen against pdloader/screen rather than
by looking at it. &1100 is the home.

PORT 6: the intro puts the VIAs back. init_hardware retunes both and
nothing restored them, and TiBootPal takes the cold-boot palette and the
LFSR seed from User VIA T1C-L expecting the MOS's free-running counter.
We handed it over in continuous mode with a &00FF latch -- 0-255,
reloading every 257us, phase-locked to a deterministic boot -- so it
landed on the same value every time. The same save closes a latent one:
InstallIrq captures the System VIA's ACR and T1 latches to give back at
UninstallIrq, so the game-over seam would have handed the MOS our timer
setup rather than the MOS's own.

AND THE GAME BUG UNDERNEATH, which the entropy fault was hiding, and
which is the 2026-08-28 white-briefing bug in a second place: SetPalPlay
reads disrFlash and forces logical 0 white when it is non-zero, and
disrFlash is in lowbss -- uninitialised OS leftovers at boot. ts_loads
cleared it, but TiShow paints the FIRST title before ts_loads runs and
TiBootPal ends in SetTextPal which ends in SetPalPlay. TitleSeq clears it
at its top now. jsbeeb hid it by powering up with RAM zeroed, exactly as
lowbss.asm's own header warns; the intro is what made the leftovers real,
because it unpacks its advance tables over &0400-&1BFF, so it is now the
configuration to test an lowbss change against.

Verified in jsbeeb: the depacked screen is byte-identical to
pdloader/screen, the player runs at full rate out of the depacked bank
(937 SN76489 writes in 40,000 cycles against 938 before), and the whole
chain boots to the briefing on banks 4-7 and on 0,1,2,3. The title now
comes up on a deck palette with the logo embossed, not white on white.

events.title: scarybeasts' intro replaces ours, and -Release is the build for other people
events.message:
scarybeasts' intro replaces ours, and -Release is the build for other people

pdloader/ is his drop, vendored VERBATIM so his next version is a clean
diff: our picture and our lightning -- both came back byte-identical --
over a three-channel sample player, ~15.6 kHz a channel written straight
at the SN76489's attenuation registers, samples in one sideways bank.
It takes the machine (*TAPE, VIA IRQs off), plays until a keypress, then
silences the chip, restores what it saved and chains to PARA. v1's
src/pintro.asm is deleted; export_intro.py stays as the artwork's source.

Four changes to his file, each marked `\ PORT:` and listed in its header:
the bank comes from PARSWR rather than being 4; it chains to PARA; it
closes !BOOT's exec file before *TAPE takes the filing system apart under
it; and it keeps PARSWR's handover safe across its own run.

THAT LAST ONE IS NOT COSMETIC. init_player unpacks the advance tables to
&0400 and they are advance_tables_len x 256, not x 64 -- four bytes
written per packed byte, as his own comment says -- so they cover
&0400-&1BFF and &0A00 is in the middle of them. Left in place the
handover was overwritten with an AND #3 value, the game missed the magic
byte and fell back to banks 4,5,6,7: right by coincidence on a machine
that has 4-7, and a crash after every bank file appears to load on one
that does not. KC's has sideways RAM in 0,1,2,3. Layer 13b existed to
stop 4-7 being special and the first thing built on it depended on 4-7
again; docs/intro.md now carries the rule, which is to test the
relocated case through the whole chain rather than either half of it.

-Release is -Intro plus every DEBUG_ flag off. The switch is a beebasm
command-line symbol because beebasm has no IFDEF and refuses a symbol
defined twice, so main.asm cannot carry a default and EVERY build passes
RELEASE -- the symbol dump in CLAUDE.md included. main.asm's DEV is what
XFERWIN/DECK/KILL read, and ASSERT DEBUG_ANY = 0 catches a readout left
on by hand (verified by turning DEBUG_INVULN on and watching it refuse).

make_disc.py's --intro splice now carries all twelve intro files and
lays them after PARSWR, which has to run first: the intro needs a bank
number from it. 24 files on the release disc, of DFS's 31.

Verified in jsbeeb: cold boot of the release disc through intro, title,
briefing and play; the game's own sound driver healthy afterwards; the
handover intact through the intro with the banks forced to 0,1,2,3; and
the default build unchanged at 12 files with its debug line still there.

events.title: The four banks are probed at boot, not assumed to be 4-7
events.message:
The four banks are probed at boot, not assumed to be 4-7

PARSWR runs from !BOOT before PARA: stnicc-beeb's three-stage probe,
aliasing-proof by construction, over every bank the MOS found no ROM in
-- so a live utility ROM or a sideways-RAM filing system is neither
written nor chosen. It takes the highest four, prints them, and leaves
them at &0A00 for .start.

Two departures from the stnicc code, both in the file header: the ROM
type filter above, and saving each bank's original byte with THAT bank
selected -- stage 1 there reads it with the bank the inner loop left, so
it saves bank 0's sixteen times.

Solidisk boards are detected and refused rather than driven, because the
game's own SWRAM writes go through ROMSEL alone; the latched probe runs
only once the plain one has already come up short, so an ordinary
machine never touches the User VIA. A bare *RUN PARA finds no magic byte
and keeps the assembled 4,5,6,7, so debugging is unchanged.

SWRAM_DATA and friends are indices into swBank now and PAGEBANK reads
it: +1 byte and +2 cycles a site, ~150 cycles a pass against ~39,000
spare. PAGESPRBANK stops deriving SPR2 by adding one -- the two are
adjacent in the table, and the hardware promises nothing. The low
overlay could not afford the byte, so its eight raw PAGEBANKs became
JSR Pg*, which pays for itself several times over.

Verified in jsbeeb on banks 4-7 and, by forcing the handover, on 0-3:
briefing, its exit reload, deck, panel and the blitter across both shift
groups. A Master reports its own 4-7. Both refusal messages tested.

events.title: PARAFNT ships compressed too, unpacking in place below the title
events.message:
PARAFNT ships compressed too, unpacking in place below the title

Six sectors off every ts_loads -- boot, every title, and the briefing
exit -- and the last of the files worth compressing except PARTITL.

THE LANDING ADDRESS IS MEASURED, NOT REASONED. PARAFNT unpacks to
&3000, so its stream cannot use DEPK_STREAM: from &3200 the output
starts 512 B behind and gains 0.446 B per output byte, overtaking the
reader after ~1,148 of 3,503 bytes. ZX0's in-place rule is that the
stream must END where the output ends, but the gap it needs is a
property of THIS stream and not of the ratio -- a literal run copies 1:1
plus its flag bits, so the writer can gain locally however good the
average. make_disc.py's new in_place_delta() walks the decode and tracks
max(write_index - bytes consumed). For today's font that is 1,566, and
the worst point is at the very end (out=3500 of 3503, in=1935 of 1940)
because ZX0's closing matches consume almost no input. So &361E is the
minimum and FNT_STREAM = &3700 takes it with 226 B of margin.

&3700 also keeps the whole stream (&3700-&3E93) BELOW &4000: outside the
title's framebuffer, so the seam needs no display blanking, with its
tail in SPR_SAVE, which is staging scratch at that moment.

AND THE CHECK RUNS EVERY BUILD. make_disc.py recomputes the delta from
the actual compressed bytes and refuses to write a disc if FNT_STREAM
has stopped being safe, naming the address it would need -- so a
briefing.txt or font edit that compresses worse fails the build instead
of corrupting the boot. It prints the margin it found.

UnpackFont cost SIX BYTES, because all four addresses in play
(DEPK_STREAM, SWRAM_BASE, FNT_STREAM, FONT_ADDR) are page-aligned: it
loads the two high bytes and drops into UnpackBankIn's tail, which sets
both lows from one zero. That mattered -- the code image had nothing
left at all after the resident depacker.

Paid for by moving DoorTdp (56 B) into bank 4, which is a better home
than main RAM was: ALL THREE CALLERS ARE BANK 4 ALREADY -- screen.asm's
MapChar and scroll.asm's band and column paths -- so every call used to
leave bank 4 and come straight back. Now they are local.

  disc files      12 -> 11        total sectors  210 -> 177
  image       49,920 -> 45,824 B
  code image free  0 -> 48 B      bank 4 free    231 -> 175 B

Verified in jsbeeb: boots, the briefing renders from the compressed
PARMAN, and the 001 screen and panel render from the in-place-unpacked
PARAFNT -- the font is what would break first and most visibly.

PARTITL is the last one worth doing (13 -> 7 sectors) and has the same
shape of problem, but it is code that RUNS at &3000 and the 999 page is
displayed while it loads on the game-over path, so its landing area
wants checking against what is on screen as well as against the delta.
PARBRF and PARALOW save one sector each and are not worth it.

  cannot receive the invalid combination either.

  OSD, return) instead of falling through into a second toggle -- on a

events.title: One resident depacker: PARDEPK is gone and PARMAN ships compressed
events.message:
One resident depacker: PARDEPK is gone and PARMAN ships compressed

KC: "we're not doing a raw sector reader. find a way to get a single
resident depacker and compress the additional files."

THE WAY WAS THAT THE DEPACKER WAS ALREADY IN MEMORY TWICE.
zx0depack.asm's macro was instantiated in bank 4 for BuildLevel, and the
PARDEPK overlay carried a second copy for the loader -- a 273-byte
routine occupying 546 bytes, and loaded from disc twice per session, at
boot and again on the briefing exit. Bank code may call main RAM freely,
so one copy in the code image serves both: BuildLevel's JSR Zx0Unpack
resolves across the bank boundary now, and PARDEPK is deleted outright.
One fewer disc file everywhere, and with nothing landing on &3000 at the
briefing exit the way is open for ts_loads to stop reloading PARAFNT.

The ledger:

  depacker macro moved in / out      main RAM +257   bank 4 -257
  UnpackBankIn (sets its own ptrs)            + 25
  BootBanks + its three load strings          + 90
  loaddepk string, no longer needed           - 14
  DoorCopyDef moved out to balance            - 51          + 51
  result   code_end = &3000 exactly, 0 B free (was 296)
           bank 4 231 B free (was 25)

DoorCopyDef was the right 51 bytes because it ALREADY could not run
without SWRAM_DATA paged: it reads tdpLo/tdpHi and the tile definition
through them, and those are screen.asm's, in bank 4. Being in bank 4
adds no precondition it did not already have, and its one caller
(door.asm's dp_new) is main-RAM play-path code where SWRAM_DATA rests.
It sits beside the pointers it reads, and door.asm keeps a header
saying where it went and why.

PARMAN ships ZX0 now, 5,016 B / 20 sectors -> 2,730 B / 11. BrTimeout
calls UnpackBankIn where it used to call PageCopyAt page by page. It was
the free one: it already lands at DEPK_STREAM and unpacks to bank 5, so
nothing had to move.

Measured: boot to TitleSeq 10.96 s -> 10.73 s, which is PARDEPK's
0.181 s and little else -- boot is dominated by the four big bank
streams. The briefing seams take the rest: PARMAN's nine sectors are
worth ~0.5 s inbound and the dropped PARDEPK ~0.18 s outbound.

Verified in jsbeeb: boots, the briefing text renders from the compressed
stream, a deck draws -- which is BuildLevel decompressing its tile map
through the cross-boundary call -- and the view scrolls.

Also corrects layer-11f section 3d, which this work disproved: the
earlier reading blamed per-file overhead on the strength of PARDEPK
costing 0.902 s. The same file at boot measures 0.181 s, so that 0.72 s
was the first disc access after the drive had been idle, not the file.

PARAFNT is NOT done and is written up in loader-compression.md: it
cannot land at DEPK_STREAM because the writer overtakes the reader after
~1,148 of 3,503 bytes. The fix is ZX0's in-place trick -- land the
stream so it ends where the output ends, ~&3700, which also puts it
below &4000 and so outside the displayed title -- but that address comes
from the average ratio and ZX0 expands locally on literal runs, so the
real delta must be walked out of the stream and asserted in
make_disc.py.

events.title: warp boot: warp any configuration's boot until storage settles or a timestamp
events.message:
warp boot: warp any configuration's boot until storage settles or a timestamp

--run warp-launches: unpaced with muted audio until the guest loads the
program. This generalizes that to configurations that boot from their own
media (a Workbench install, a hard-disk setup like AmigaVision, a CD):

- --warp-boot / [emulation] warp_boot: warp from power-on until the boot
  storage -- the floppy and hard-disk activity the front-panel LEDs show
  -- has been idle for [emulation] warp_boot_idle emulated seconds
  (default 10), then resume real-time pacing and audio. Overshoot is
  free (the extra idle seconds pass at warp speed), but the threshold
  must outlast the boot's longest storage-quiet stretch: a big-RAM
  machine's SetPatch MMU table build keeps the disk idle for seconds
  while the CPU walks every page of fitted RAM. CD audio deliberately
  does not count as activity (CD data traffic rides the HDD LED), so a
  menu's background CD-DA cannot hold the warp; a boot whose storage
  never settles gives up after 600 emulated seconds.
- --warp-until SECS / [emulation] warp_until: the deterministic variant,
  warp until an absolute emulated timestamp.

The gate (src/warpboot.rs) mirrors the warp launch's shape: a pure state
machine over emulated time polled once per retired frame, engaged at
power-on, one-shot per session, cancelled by the manual warp toggle,
audio muted only while genuinely unpaced (a machine with a bridged
physical drive still runs the gate at normal speed). The storage-idle
condition reads front_panel_status(), whose HDD LED is a non-draining
timestamp latch, so the gate and the status bar share the signal without
stealing each other's events. Headless captures are already unpaced end
to end and drop the gate; combining with --run (whose own gate ends at a
sharper condition) or combining the two modes is a configuration error.

events.title: Re-measure the briefing's loads: 5.7 s round trip, not the estimated 1.1 s
events.message:
Re-measure the briefing's loads: 5.7 s round trip, not the estimated 1.1 s

KC asked why the front end loads from disc between the title and the
briefing, and then for the four exit loads to be re-measured. Layer 11f
section 3d costed them on 2026-08-21 by estimate; measured, those
estimates are about three times optimistic.

Timed in jsbeeb with execute breakpoints on the four JSR &FFF7 sites and
read_registers' elapsed_cycles -- cycles_run is the REQUESTED count when
a breakpoint fires and must not be used as a delta (the harness note in
memory). Sizes from the SSD catalogue.

  PARDEPK    368 B,  2 sectors   0.902 s
  PARASPR  3,098 B, 13 sectors   0.699 s
  UnpackBankIn                   0.755 s
  PARAFNT  3,503 B, 14 sectors   1.067 s
  PARALOW    927 B,  4 sectors   0.279 s
  exit seam total                3.702 s, 2.947 s of it disc

Against the section's "7,512 B and about 1.1 s", and its PARASPR line of
"2,833 B ~ 0.4 s". The inbound seam was never costed at all: PARMAN is
5,016 B / 20 sectors and loads in 1.942 s, so the briefing round trip is
5.69 s of loading and unpacking.

THE PER-FILE OVERHEAD IS THE STORY, NOT THE BYTE COUNT. PARDEPK is 368
bytes and takes longer than PARASPR's 3,098. The marginal rate is
roughly 0.1 s a sector -- five times what a contiguous sector costs at
300 rpm, so DFS is losing revolutions -- on top of a per-file overhead
of a few hundred ms that varies with head position. Eliminating a file
pays even when the file is tiny, which is what makes section 3d's three
eliminations worth 2.248 s: 1.454 s against today's 3.702 s.

Two errors in the section found on the way:

- PARMAN IS NOT COMPRESSED, though DECISION 5 says it is. make_disc.py
  ZX0s the four bank files only; PARMAN ships raw and BrTimeout copies
  it up with PageCopyAt, not UnpackBankIn.
- And it cannot simply be switched on. ZX0 takes PARMAN to 2,730 B / 11
  sectors (54%), worth perhaps 0.9 s -- but PARDEPK is dead by then,
  PARTITL having been loaded over it, and getting a depacker back costs
  a measured 0.902 s. Net zero. It only becomes a win if a depacker is
  RESIDENT, and then it wins at both seams at once: ~0.9 s inbound and
  PARDEPK's 0.902 s outbound, for 368 B of somewhere permanent. That is
  the shape of the real fix and it is not what F6 describes -- and it is
  also the prerequisite F6 already needs, since UnpackBankIn now lives
  inside PARDEPK.

Docs only; no code change.

events.title: The target's droid icon goes when the transfer verdict is called
events.message:
The target's droid icon goes when the transfer verdict is called

KC, as polish: the enemy droid icon should disappear, leaving only the
player's, once the verdict has been called to win or lose -- not draw.
It is the original's own behaviour, one instruction into a routine that
is easy to read past.

FinishTransfer2's second instruction is LDA #$80 : STA $D015. The
listing annotates that address as byte_0_D014+1, but $D015 is the VIC's
SPRITE ENABLE register: $80 leaves sprite 7 on and everything else off,
and sprite 7 is the PLAYER's icon ($E12B) while the target's is
droidSprNum+$48. So every decided transfer ends with the loser's icon
gone and the player's still there.

And only a decided one. FinishTransfer2 is reached from all three arms
of FinishTransfer1 -- won, lost, burnt out -- but a tie never gets
there: WinningColor $F8 is a short circuit and Capture's _1 loop replays
the subgame without calling FinishTransfer1 at all. The port's shape
matches, so the erase goes at xpl_endphase, the join of the won and lost
arms; the tie arm returns above it and XfReplayTick redraws both icons
with the new board.

It cost no drawing code. XfIconPix ANDs every byte with xiMask, so
XfIcon with a pen of 0 paints the icon in logical 0 -- the board's own
background in those spans, and the reason xfericon.asm's header can say
the blank rows "stay blank". X is xiCol, the column that icon was last
drawn at: XfIcons draws the player first and the target second, so the
leftover is the target's, and following it rather than recomputing means
a change to the side-swap rule cannot desynchronise the erase from the
draw. Recomputing does not work anyway -- XI_LCOL/XI_RCOL are assigned
in xfericon.asm, which assembles after this file, and beebasm resolves
constants in file order.

Verified in jsbeeb, forcing a transfer by poking xferDroid (the byte
dc_notransfer writes) and winning with DEBUG_XFERWIN: board up with
yellow 001 left and black 298 right, then on "Complete" the 001 is still
there and the 298 is gone. The lost arm falls into the same label and
the tie returns above it, so both are code-evident rather than
separately shown.

Ten bytes, in front of plandata.asm's ALIGN, so PARXFER is unchanged.

events.title: The game-over wash is a second, not three and a half, and boils faster
events.message:
The game-over wash is a second, not three and a half, and boils faster

KC: "the game over static screen goes on for way too long. the C64
version is only a second or so, if that."

88 WAS THE WRONG LOOP'S NUMBER. $3802's LDA #$58 seeds the hold on the
GAME OVER / 999 page at _5, AFTER the wash has burnt out -- and the port
already has that one, as infoscr.asm's IS_HOLD. The wash is _3,
$37C1-$37D9, and it counts in frameCount: $37BB seeds it with the paint
loop's leftover dest+1 = $4C = 76 and INC/BMI runs until bit 7 sets at
128, so the body runs 128 - 76 = 52 iterations, always. The port had
been giving the wash the page's counter.

The conversion is IS_HOLD's own [DECISION 3], unchanged. That note costs
the 999 page's iteration -- DelayScore(32), two nested busy loops -- at
about 41,000 cycles, 0.04 s, which is why 72 of them port to 72 passes
at 25 Hz. The wash's DelayScore takes Y = $10, exactly half, so one wash
iteration is ~20,500 cycles ~ 0.02 s: half a port pass. 52 half-passes =
GO_HOLD 26 = 1.04 s, against the C64's 52 x 0.0208 = 1.08 s.

AND THE ROAR'S RE-POST GOES WITH IT. GoWashTick re-posted fx $F every
time the boil wrapped, on a comment claiming "near the C64's
every-76-frames refire" -- there is no refire: $37BD/$37BF posts it
once, before _3, and the loop never touches sndFx1 again. It was audible
twice over, because goBoil leaves GoWashStart at $FF and the first tick
wrapped it to 0, restarting the roar one pass after GoWashStart had just
posted it. One post covers the wash regardless: effect 15 is a single
192-tick segment, 3.8 s at the 50 Hz sound tick.

Then KC: "increase the row-per-pass rate". GO_ROWS is that dial, now 4 --
the screen turns over every four passes, six and a half times across the
wash, as near the C64's every-cell-every-iteration as repainting gets.
The frame lock is the ceiling and it binds here in a way it does not
elsewhere, because overTick counts PASSES: a pass that overruns two
fields would stretch the 1.04 s straight back out. Budget is a two-field
pass at 2 MHz = 80,000 cycles; GoWashRow is 40 cells of XfRand plus a
16-byte copy at ~19 cycles a byte, ~13,600 a row, so four rows ~54,000
fits and eight would not. GoWashStart's 16-row paint is exempt: one-off
at entry, and the lock is a floor there.

Verified in jsbeeb on a real ESCAPE game over, at GO_ROWS 4: overTick
falls 11 -> 1 across exactly 20 frames -- ten passes, two fields each,
no overrun, the wash still 52 fields wall-clock -- and overPhase drops
to 0 with the 999 page drawing behind it. KC on the result: "much
better".

Bank 7 unchanged in size; the deltas ride plandata.asm's ALIGN pad.

events.title: Leaving the lift for another deck shows THAT deck's palette, not the old one
events.message:
Leaving the lift for another deck shows THAT deck's palette, not the old one

KC: changing deck in the lift selection screen showed the previous
deck's palette on the way out, then snapped to the new one as the deck
was drawn.

LvEnter4 saves palPlay into xfPalSave on the way in and installs
palLift; LvExit4 put the save back. That save is the deck being LEFT,
and on a changed selection the new deck's colours did not arrive until
RedrawAll's SetPalette at the far end of LoadDeck -- a charset build, a
level decode and a full redraw later, with the rupture applying the
wrong table three times a field throughout. The wrong-deck flash was
the whole load, not a frame of it.

The changed arm no longer restores anything: it sets deck, liftPlace
and lvLoad and tail-calls SetPalette, same bank, so the new deck's
palette is live before LoadDeck starts. The save slot is abandoned --
it is a slot, not live state, and the transfer game fills it afresh.
The unchanged arm still restores, and must: that palette IS this deck's,
cleared-floor override and all.

deckClear goes with it. It still holds the PREVIOUS deck's answer until
DroidsInit runs inside the load, and clearing a deck and taking the lift
onward is the ordinary way to play -- so without this the new deck came
up blue for the whole load (level.asm's cleared-floor arm) and one wrong
palette would have replaced another. A deck is presumed not cleared
until DroidsInit says otherwise, which it does either way, later in the
same load.

This is not layer-11d DECISION 4's SetPalette creeping back into
LoadDeck: that one had to go because an information screen is up across
LoadDeck at GameStart and the deck's colours overrode the text
background InfoCall had just chosen. No screen is ever up on this route,
so the call belongs to the lift.

Verified in jsbeeb on a real lift ride -- the player placed on lift 13
(deck 6, tile 8/7) by LiftPlace's own arithmetic, so CheckWalls derived
the reference cell 33/29 naturally and fire entered the lift for real.
Deck 6's floor is yellow and deck 5's white, so palPlay[0] tells it:
&03 (lift blue) -> &00 (deck 5 white) on the commit frame, held through
the load, with deck 6's &04 never appearing. The unchanged-selection
exit still restores &00.

Bank 4 tail 33 -> 25 B.

events.title: The 001 screen sounds as the C64's does: fx6 back, its $B withdrawn
events.message:
The 001 screen sounds as the C64's does: fx6 back, its $B withdrawn

KC asked whether the sounds on the 001 screen matched the original.
They did not, in both directions.

NewShipInfo -- the C64's 001 screen -- posts NO sound of its own: it
draws and waits for fire. What plays over it is $126B's effect 6, the
new-game sweep, posted as the last thing StartGame does before JMP
_entership and still running when the screen goes up. The port had
never posted effect 6 anywhere: 11e round ten parked it to kill the
game-start smear and promised it back "with the 001 screen (11d)", and
11d returned $B and lost track of it, so its record shipped in bank 4
playing nothing. And $B is $1282's alone -- the _shipclean path before
ShowShipClear, which the port already does as isSndFor's entry 4.

GameStart posts 6 now, at $126B's place, and the 001's isSndFor entry
is IS_FX_NONE: a zero request, which stk_req already drops, so no
branch is needed. Both could not stay -- $B lands a fraction of a
second later on the same voice and would cut 6 off before it is heard.

That put the last untreated sub-floor effect back on the chip: 40% of
fx6's ticks measured as the flat 1023 clamp, the buzz its siblings were
cured of. Its instrument 8 is shared with fx14 and fx20, both right as
tones, so it takes FX_PERIODIC's clone. As periodic bass it plays the
whole 64.8-210.5 Hz sweep. Built both ways onto two discs and A/B'd;
KC: "the periodic version has more character". The exporter's sub-floor
review list is now down to fx17, which is on it only because the list
counts sub-floor share and not whether a cure was applied -- fx17 mutes
rather than clamps, which was its cure.

The clone allocator reshuffled slots as designed: fx6's clone took free
slot 1, pushing fx16's to 12, fx23's to 13 and the chatter's to 14, and
every record was retargeted. Exactly the case FX_LEVEL's key-by-effect
rule exists for.

Verified from the chip. On the 001 screen: CH3 noise=3 vol=3 with its
own tone channel silenced and the pitch on CH2 sweeping N 84 -> 55 ->
reset to 120, the full 37-120 span. Dismissing it hands over to fx7 at
234.5 Hz, inside its 150-291 Hz range and above fx6's 210 Hz ceiling.

Bank 4 tail 44 -> 33 B (5 B of code, 6 B of cloned instrument).

events.title: The briefing is not white on a cold boot: disrFlash is zeroed first
events.message:
The briefing is not white on a cold boot: disrFlash is zeroed first

KC: "sometimes the frontend picks a level with a white background
palette and the text is not visible in the briefing scroller." The
palette was right and the deck pick was innocent.

FontCell paints paper in logical 0 and ink in logical 3, and logical 3
is physical 7 for every deck, so the scroller is legible exactly as
long as logical 0 is not white. TiBootPal already applies SetTextPal,
not SetPalette, and deckTextPal's logical 0 is only ever physical 1, 4
or 5 across all sixteen decks -- the white floors (0, 5, 9) are in
deckPalette, which the front end never reads. Measured, not assumed:
forcing the boot deck to 0 gives a red scroller, and a game over and
back round gives a magenta one. Masking decks out would fix nothing.

The cause is disrFlash. SetPalPlay reads it on every fire 1 and, when
non-zero, overrides logical 0's four ULA entries to white -- the
disruptor flash, an override rather than saved state for the reason
CbDisruptor's header gives. It lives in lowbss, which is SKIPped and
never shipped or zeroed, so at a cold boot it holds whatever the OS
left in the soft-character area at &0C90-&0CFF. GameStart clears it
($10DB) but that is a whole game away: the title, the high-score entry
and the entire briefing run under the IRQ first. Non-zero garbage means
a white briefing, once, on the first boot of a session.

Nothing caught it because jsbeeb powers up with RAM zeroed. Reproduced
by seeding &0CF5 before a SHIFT+BREAK autoboot -- the byte survives
BREAK, which is the real-hardware case: white block on the old build,
legible on the new one.

ts_loads now stores 0 to disrFlash immediately before InstallIrq. There
rather than in the boot path alone because ts_loads is every route to
the front end and none of them can be inside a burst -- GoTitle and
BrDispatch have torn the game down before they arrive. The other three
disruptor bytes need nothing: only CbDisruptor reads them and GameStart
clears them first. lowbss.asm's header carries the standing rule now.

The disruptor itself is unaffected, checked in play: disruptorCnt 2 and
disrFlash 1 during a burst, both back to 0 after it.

events.title: video: own scaler pass, uncapped integer scaling, display-window autocrop
events.message:
video: own scaler pass, uncapped integer scaling, display-window autocrop

Replace the pixels crate's built-in scaling renderer with the emulator
window's own pass (window/scaler.rs; tool windows keep the built-in
Fill). The built-in renderer draws the texture only at whole multiples
of itself, welding the displayed integer multiple to the supersample
cap, so fullscreen integer scaling stopped at 4x the canvas however
much room a large display had. The new pass takes the destination rect
and filter as inputs, so the planned multiple is drawn whatever the
texture factor is. Point sampling stays exact past the cap because the
present copy replicates each canvas pixel into an S-wide texel block:
every texel a sample can land on inside a canvas pixel holds the same
colour, and sample centres can never fall on a canvas-pixel boundary.
The smooth filter is the same texel-snapped sharp bilinear the Fill
renderer used. PresentLayout is the single source for the pass's
draws, the cursor mapping and the overlay anchors.

Add [display] autocrop (default off; menu and launcher toggles): crop
the window presentation to the display window the hardware programs,
so a display driving fewer lines than the full scan fills more of a
wide screen, with the whole-number fit retaken against the crop. The
envelope comes from the renderer's own per-line display-window bounds
(mid-frame rewrites and carried-open flops already folded in), rides
the same shifts and row/column maps the present copy applies, and is
smoothed by a latch that grows instantly, holds through border-only
frames, and shrinks only after the smaller window has held steady.
The status bar and instrument panels keep their size in a band along
the window bottom. Presentation-only: captures keep their aperture,
and the crop suspends itself under open overlays, the bezel and CRT
presets, RTG scanout and programmable scans.

3196 unit tests (18 new: GPU pass, layout, latch, both coordinate
mappings, renderer envelope, config), 44 golden probes byte-exact
(the renderer change is pixel-neutral), clippy and fmt clean.

events.title: timing-test: accelprobe, a 020-060 accelerator probe with real A4000 columns
events.message:
timing-test: accelprobe, a 020-060 accelerator probe with real A4000 columns

A 32-row bootable probe for accelerator CPUs measured against the CIA
E-clock: exception round trips (supervisor stack in chip vs fast RAM),
call/MOVEM/CPUSHL costs, chip-window and per-fast-region read/write
rates, and a composite that replicates, primitive by primitive, the
per-4K-page sequence of the SetPatch/mmu.library boot-time MMU table
build. The probe walks the exec MemList at boot, so one binary adapts to
whichever CPU card and RAM mix is fitted and reports each region's base
address; the composite walks the largest fast region (signature
ACCE1B02). CPU identification is by live MOVEC PCR/ITT0 probes with
fault recovery, and each family gets a defined cache state.

The header records Copperline predicted columns for the A4000 machine
shapes (tt-a4000-060/-040/-030.toml) and REAL columns captured on a real
A4000: a 50 MHz BFG9060, a 25 MHz A3640 (MAPROM on), and a 25 MHz 68030
board, all via serial, with per-row verdicts. Highlights: the 040's
plain execution is over-billed ~2-2.5x by the scaled approximation while
its buses are under-billed; the real 030's core rows land on the real
A1200's 68020 figures; fast RAM is three distinct speed classes on real
silicon; the A3640/BFG9060 CPU-slot bridge prices a chip move.l read at
2.5-3.4us; and the MMU boot walk costs 17.6us/page (040) / 12.2us/page
(060) over Zorro III RAM against 11.0/5.1 emulated.

vpos in the probe's frame sync is debounced (two agreeing samples):
assembling vpos from separate VPOSR/VHPOSR reads can straddle the line
255->256 boundary and read a bogus 0, which a fast CPU's poll loop hits
reliably; the main disk's 280 threshold dodges this by construction.

events.title: James Pond 2: Codename RoboCod (CD32, 1993) — measurements of the pressed disc
events.message:
James Pond 2: Codename RoboCod (CD32, 1993) — measurements of the pressed disc

Nineteenth disc in the CD32/CDTV documentation set. Millennium Interactive,
mastered 1993-08-17, preparer `Dean Ashton` — a sixth name in that field, and
the first whose owner is identifiable from the disc in his own words.

What the disc turns out to be:

  * a 128.000000 MiB hole (65,536 sectors, 2^16, verified zero) in front of
    the files, 65.55 % of the declared volume — the third round hole in the
    set after 50 MiB and 100 MiB, and with the CDXL padding, trailing run and
    overrun the data track is 69.75 % zero;
  * and the hole is not why the track is big: 93.90 % of the file bytes are
    CDXL video, 2,631 frames in three streams. Two of the four ranked
    hypotheses are true at once;
  * the boot script is a shell-level main loop offering Cartoon / FI5H /
    RoboCod, plus 44 lines of signed development diary whose three date claims
    the filesystem confirms (Sunday 15 Aug 1993, Friday 13th, 1:30am 14.07.93);
  * a three-language manual with no characters in it: 115 IFF ILBM pages,
    one shared palette, one page identical across languages, a Deluxe Paint
    DPPS chunk on 17 of them and none in German;
  * all seven Red Book tracks reachable from an 86-record level table, with
    bit 7 of the music id choosing Red Book or Paula, and the TOC never read;
  * five bitplanes with a 24-bit LOCT palette, an unreachable message in which
    the programmer apologises for the plane count and says he left no debug
    symbols — both claims verified;
  * nothing packed, with a mechanism: all three hunks are CHIP, 1,185,496 of
    a 2 MB budget, so there is no room for a decrunch buffer;
  * the size band's floor moves again, to 1,033,508 on disc / 1,258,076
    resident.

Ships measurements, the stored output of every run, and the code that
reproduces them. No image, no extracted file, no decoded picture.

events.title: review: a mid-frame tie over an open flop keeps its fetched rows visible
events.message:
review: a mid-frame tie over an open flop keeps its fetched rows visible

The tie-as-closed level reading only holds where the flop never opened:
rewriting DIWSTRT.V == DIWSTOP.V mid-frame over a flop an earlier
DIWSTRT match already set changes nothing until the beam reaches the
shared comparator line, where reset wins. Rows scanned in between keep
fetching and displaying, and the unconditional tie-as-closed gate
blanked them.

Take the flop's own history as the vertical authority wherever it
exists: in the renderer, a row whose DMA capture recorded a fetch means
the Agnus flop was open there, so captured rows override the level test
at every consumer (paint bounds and anchors, the planned-line and
manual-BPL pixel gates, the closed-interval border mask); the level
test decides only rows where nothing was fetched, which keeps the
whole-frame-closed case (vdiwprobe-empty) intact. On the bus side the
live collision replay now takes the current line's flop instead of a
per-pixel level test; only the future-line lookahead still falls back
to the level approximation, where a tie misread errs toward an early
blitter wakeup and a recompute.

New golden probe timing-test/vdiwprobe-tieopen pins the case: a tie
armed at line 112 over a window open since line 80 keeps the stripe
band lit through line 150 and stays border from the shared comparator
line 151 down. Verified to flip with the override reverted;
vAmiga-verified (identical band rows 80..150 and stripe columns).

events.title: Eighteenth disc: Alfred Chicken (Twilight / Mindscape, CD32, 1993)
events.message:
Eighteenth disc: Alfred Chicken (Twilight / Mindscape, CD32, 1993)

The first disc in this set read from physical media rather than from an image
file, which is what makes it worth its own repository beyond the game.

Three things a file could not have settled:

  * the 0000000000000 CATALOG that four discs in the set carry is on the disc,
    read from subchannel Q with MCVAL set. It is the mastering, not a dumper
    losing a real EAN, so four checklist rows stand;
  * the 32..232-sector overrun past the declared volume is cut into the glass
    master. The volume declares 691 sectors, the disc physically holds 918 of
    valid MODE1 -- each verified on sync, header address and EDC -- and the
    extra 227 stop exactly where track 2's pregap begins. The data run is
    padded up to the following track;
  * MODE1/2048, which every cue in this set asserts and no disc had ever been
    checked for, is verified by descrambling raw sectors and reading the mode
    byte on all 902, not sampled.

Plus per-track ISRC (absent on all ten), pre-emphasis and channel-count bits,
and real pregaps: nine audio tracks perfectly contiguous, one 150-sector pregap
on the whole disc.

The image took two independent read paths because neither could read all of it,
and they agree byte for byte on their 675-sector overlap -- a cross-check no
single dumper can perform. The drive was caught returning wrong data on the
first transfer after a seek; the descrambled MODE1 header lets every sector
prove its own identity, so the tool checks and retries.

Measurements: 918-sector data track against 92,445 audio sectors, so 99.02 % of
the pressed disc is audio. 1,261,776 B on disc breaks Guardian's floor by
43.9 % after seventeen discs; expansion 1.297x is the lowest of eleven. RNC
ProPack method 1, 11 streams, CRC-validated 11 of 11, nesting depth 0. Preparer
Abersoft -- the second company in that field -- with a 32-sector run, and since
Mindscape's other disc is D J Pocock with 232, the field follows the work and
not the label. Tile geometry 16x16x4 derived three independent ways. No C2P, no
Akiko, no save system, no IFF, and no text at all: a fifth string model, with
the game's own title existing only as a 320x184 picture.

And intro, built from source checked out fourteen months before alfred, ships a
working Amiga hardware debugger: 47 register description strings lifted from
Commodore's hardware/custom.i, and copdis, a copper list disassembler.

Predictions scored 19 right, 7 wrong, 1 vacuous, in docs/13.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: fix: an empty vertical display window (DIWSTRT.V == DIWSTOP.V) never opens
events.message:
fix: an empty vertical display window (DIWSTRT.V == DIWSTOP.V) never opens

The vertical DIW flop's set and reset comparators both match when
DIWSTRT.V equals DIWSTOP.V and reset wins the tie, so the window never
opens; AGA software parks both comparators on a line below the visible
area via DIWHIGH to blank the bitplanes for a frame while it redraws its
buffers, keeping a BRDRSPRT sprite backdrop on screen (Nexus 7 blanks
its scene transitions this way, vstart = vstop = 301).

The bus-side flop already resolved the tie as closed (bitplane DMA never
ran), but the renderer's register-derived level approximation wrapped
stop <= start by +0x100 including the tie, reading the empty window as a
full wrap-around one. A frame whose window never opens captures no DMA
rows at all, which routes every row onto the synthesized no-capture
re-fetch path where that gate is the only thing blanking the frame - so
such frames painted mid-redraw buffer contents the hardware never
fetched (the Nexus 7 corrupted-ball scene transitions).

Read the tie as closed in both display_window_contains_line and the
bus-level display_window_contains_vpos fallback; the stop < start wrap
is unchanged.

New golden probe timing-test/vdiwprobe-empty pins the whole-frame case:
stripes armed behind an empty window with BRDRSPRT sprite bars, no
bitplane pixel may display. Verified to flip with the fix reverted and
vAmiga-5-verified bijectively exact. vdiwprobe-flop's tie band pins the
mid-frame case but its frame fetches other bands, so the DMA-capture
authority masked the synthesized-path gap.

events.title: Myth — History in the Making (CD32): full structural teardown
events.message:
Myth — History in the Making (CD32): full structural teardown

The CD32 release is the 1992 three-floppy release pressed whole: three of the
five files are 901,120 bytes each — one 880 KiB Amiga floppy disk, exactly —
with an 18,656-byte shim that emulates a floppy drive out of CD sectors.

94.86 % of the declared volume is a hole of exactly 50.000000 MiB, leaving a
2.72 MB game (3.73 MB resident, expansion 1.369x, the lowest of ten measured).

Compression is Bytekiller under the magic `DAVE`, the programmer's first name;
23 streams, all validated three ways, nesting depth 0. The loader has four
media back ends, zero relocations, a hand-written LoadSeg and an Akiko CD
driver. The preparer field names a company — Rob Northen Computing, author of
RNC ProPack — on a master that does not use it. And the PVD's 1992-12-21 is
falsified by the disc's own .TM block, which is copyright 1993.

events.title: launcher: the boot order takes in the Lide board, and pages
events.message:
launcher: the boot order takes in the Lide board, and pages

Every drive that can boot belongs on one list. The Lide board's four kept
their priorities on their own page, which meant two places to look and two
orders to reconcile; they move to the Boot Priority page, after the IDE
bays and the SCSI units, which is also the order the cascade default ranks
them in. They appear on the same terms a SCSI unit does -- once a slot
carries a disk.

That reaches thirteen drives on a fully fitted machine, more than the panel
has rows for. Past a page's worth the list runs onto a second, reached by a
Next Page button beside Back; its own Back returns to the first. The
priority-range note goes at the same point, since it sat under a row the
drives now need.

A greyed row's reason starts where a value starts, rather than out past the
stepper's first arrow, so "A2091 only" lines up with the bundled-ROM text
above it.

events.title: ARM64 JIT: demote trap blocks by opcode class, not wholesale.
events.message:
ARM64 JIT: demote trap blocks by opcode class, not wholesale.

Whole-block interpreter demotion for RAM blocks containing any
trap-capable opcode (added to preserve trap PC under the CPU tester)
costs 3-17x on division-heavy user code: every block containing
DIVU/DIVS/DIVL/CHK ran fully interpreted.

Keep whole-block interpretation only for structural/supervisor trap
opcodes (ILLEGAL, RTE, STOP, SR and system control moves, MMU/cache
control, TRAPcc). Arithmetic trap opcodes that are hot in user code
stay compiled; the opcode itself runs through the per-opcode fallback,
which syncs the 68k PC before the interpreter handler call. With
cputester=true every trap-bearing block still demotes, matching
previous behavior for the internal tester.

Ported from Amiberry #2305 (verified there on Pi 5: cputest DIVU.W
10983/10983 pass, SysInfo ~1500->2100 MIPS, AIBB InstTest up several
times; full integer CPUTESTER suite passes).
events.author: midwan

events.title: Make CHK2/CMP2 N/V flag probes wrap-safe (signed overflow UB).
events.message:
Make CHK2/CMP2 N/V flag probes wrap-safe (signed overflow UB).

setchk2undefinedflags() tests the sign of subtractions that can
overflow. As signed int that is undefined behavior: gcc/clang optimize
the overflow-only comparisons away, MSVC keeps the two's-complement
wrap. GCC/clang-built hosts (od-unix, macOS, ARM64 with clang) get
wrong N/V flags and fail CPUTESTER CHK2.*; MSVC builds pass.

Emulate the wrap explicitly so every compiler produces the same flags.
Verified on GCC aarch64 (Amiberry): CHK2.B/W/L CPUTESTER JITLM now
passes 5006/5256/5066 with zero CCR mismatches.

events.title: Load tapes, hear them, and see what is on them
events.message:
Load tapes, hear them, and see what is on them

The tape subsystem and a viewer for it. A tape resolves to a one-bit EAR
level as a pure pull -- ear_at(hc) answers only when the CPU reads port
0xFE, so the clock loop is untouched -- with .tap and .tzx parsed into
blocks rather than expanded into the ~800,000 pulses a real image holds.
Standard-speed blocks can be satisfied instantly by trapping the ROM's
LD-BYTES; anything turbo falls back to real pulses on its own.

The viewer is a tree in the debug sidebar, docked with Call Stack and
Breakpoints, listing the tape block by block: headers with their
filenames decoded, the data blocks that inherit those names, and the
tone and pause blocks a .tzx can carry. The block playing is marked, the
loaded ones dimmed, and a clock icon flags any block whose timings will
make fast load decline it -- which is the answer to "why is this one
taking 90 seconds". Seek hangs off each row's hover button rather than
its click command: the rows expand, and a click that both expanded a row
and moved the tape would make reading the detail destructive.

The block list rides on every tape reply over both protocols, so one
poll answers "what is on this tape" and "where has it got to", and MCP's
tape_control with no arguments is a contents listing. It is cached
behind a generation counter rather than republished per yield -- the
list is parse-time data, and the run loop services the tape ~1700 times
a second.

Riding along, because they interleave in the same files and separating
them would mean splitting hunks inside engine.cpp and main.cpp:

- The beeper and audio output (beeper.cpp, audio_*.cpp), the mirror
  image of the tape: a latched write integrated lazily, where the tape
  is a lazily-resolved read. Which is what makes a real-speed load
  audible.
- Symbol annotation in the bus trace (symbol_resolver in rom_source,
  TraceOptions::resolve_symbol), which dap.cpp, mcp_server.cpp and
  main.cpp all reference.
- The game disassembly build scripts the README documents.

Copyrighted game snapshots are now ignored by name, with the freely
distributable Z80 exercisers listed back in.
