events.title: The wrap fallback drew its digits white, because it never sees colPix
events.message:
The wrap fallback drew its digits white, because it never sees colPix

KC spotted it straight away: black rotor, white number, intermittently.

SprDrawSlot has two paths. A sprite that clears the up-front wrap test
runs the compiled program and takes its pixels from colPix. A sprite
that does not — about one in five — runs the per-row fallback, and in
that loop the digit block never opens: all eight rows go through
SprFetchRow and are blitted interpreted from drSprData, which is stored
at logical 3. Nothing recoloured them. The rotor stayed black because
its rows are still compiled unless they individually straddle, and
usually none do — which is exactly why the number was the visible half.

SprFetchRow's mask loop already holds the byte in X, so the recolour is
three instructions in the same loop, on a path whose own comment says
correctness matters and speed does not.

Reproduced on demand rather than waited for: patching LDA sprNoWrap to
LDA #0 at the fast-path test forces every sprite down the fallback.
Same deck, same droid, same frame — before, a black rotor around a
white 329; after, all black, with the player still white as a control.

Effect sprites are untouched: SprEfDraw builds and blits its own rows
and never calls SprFetchRow.

events.title: diag: the slot churn is mostly the CUT, not the labelling — #146 retargets to #139
events.message:
diag: the slot churn is mostly the CUT, not the labelling — #146 retargets to #139

#146 was opened on a measurement (57.2% of used indices change slot per re-band)
and an assumption (B3.2's stable-slot alignment is weak). The assumption is mostly
wrong, and the counter that settles it is small enough to keep.

A permutation can only RELABEL — it cannot preserve a colour the new median cut no
longer produces. So split every move: does the index's NEW slot hold the same
colour its OLD slot did (labelling could have kept it) or a different one (the cut
moved, and no labelling could)? Over six re-bands of a fixture walk, 124 moves:

    moved, IDENTICAL colour available    22   18%   avoidable by better labelling
    moved to a NEAR colour (<=1 gun)     52   42%   cut shifted slightly
    moved, CUT changed the colour        50   40%   unfixable by permutation

So 40% are beyond any alignment, and the existing greedy is nearer its ceiling
than "57% churn" suggested. It is not naive: it builds a tab[new][old]
correspondence over USED indices, reserves slot 0 for the border by colour, takes
the strongest correspondences greedily, then falls back to nearest colour. An
exact 16x16 assignment would recover the 18% — worth having, but see below.

★ AND THE PAYOFF I OPENED #146 FOR DOES NOT ARRIVE THAT WAY. The force-full skip
(3f39203f) fires only when ZERO used indices move. Going from 55 moves to 45 does
not reach that threshold; only a STABLE CUT does. Better alignment buys fewer
stale planes and fewer #141 freckle opportunities — real, but not the 297 t200
rebuild I was chasing.

So #146 retargets to #139 (offline pre-quantise): fix the palette at build time and
re-bands stop renumbering at all, which collapses the force-full, the freckles and
B5's staleness fallbacks together.

Counter is FRUA_STPROF-only; a shipping build carries none of it.

make test 471 passed; ST 68000, ST STPROF, Atari 020, Amiga AGA and Amiga ECS clean.

Refs #146, #142, #141, #139.

events.title: The player flashes below energy 8, which is the only energy cue there is
events.message:
The player flashes below energy 8, which is the only energy cue there is

$3DEE tests the player's energy against 8 and, under it, indexes
LowNrgColor_t with frameCount AND 7 — or LowNrgXferCol_t in transfer
mode. Both are eight entries and both are a symmetric pulse out of the
base colour and back, ending on white: greys down to black in normal
mode, yellow-orange-red in transfer.

This matters more here than it does on the C64. Layer 9 decision 4
dropped the port's own energy bar because the original has none, which
left the flash as the whole of the readout — and layer-9-hud.md
decision 5 then said the flash could not be built, because a compiled
blitter bakes its colours in. That is no longer true, and this is the
first thing the colour indirection buys back.

[DECISION, KC 2026-08-19] Take the RATE, not the ramp. Eight inks
collapse onto three and two already mean "enemy" and "player", so the
tables cannot survive: rank-quantising them leaves the transfer cycle
barely flashing, every colour in it being mid luminance. So it is the
base colour for four fields and black for four — bit 2 of the same
8-field cycle the C64 counts — which reads at speed as the flash it is
meant to be. Rejected alternatives are recorded with their numbers.

Worth knowing before it looks like a bug: a 001 you fall back to after
dying gets energy 7 from BlowInto001 ($1591), under the threshold, so
it flashes continuously until it finds a recharge pad. A fresh game
starts at $40 and does not. Both are the original's.

Verified in jsbeeb by poking drEnergy: at 5 the player alternates FF
and 0F on a four-field duty, and at 64, with maxEnergy raised to match,
it holds FF across the boundary.

events.title: The player is white, and something else in transfer mode
events.message:
The player is white, and something else in transfer mode

$3DE5 runs at the tail of the C64's rotor-animation pass and writes
sprite 7's colour register every frame. Two arms: moveMode not 0 gets
$F1, white ($3E06), and moveMode 0 gets clr6_xfer ($3E21). MM_TRANSFER
is 0 here too, so the test ports across unchanged, and the port's
SprAnimateAll is the same place in the same order — the last thing
before the draw.

clr6_xfer is SLOT 6 of the deck's 12-byte colour record, the record
Layer 1 already took deckBg from as slot 0. It is never written by any
routine, which is what gives it away. Ripped across the seven schemes
it is orange, yellow, dark grey, red, blue, light blue and cyan — a
different colour on every deck, like the floor.

We cannot have that colour, and cannot even approximate it by the
usual route. Pushing clr6_xfer through each deck's own colourMap sends
it to logical 0 on decks 13 and 14 — the background, an invisible
player — and to logical 1, the enemy droids' black, on six more. So
transfer mode takes logical 2, the deck's highlight: the only ink left
that can be confused with neither, and per-deck like the original's.
The alternative and its numbers are in docs/layer-7-combat.md.

Verified in jsbeeb: L to Transfer puts moveMode 0 and sprColour+0 = F0,
the panel reads Transfer and the droid draws in the deck's highlight;
back to Mobile and it is FF and white again.

events.title: Enemy droids are black, which is what the C64 has always drawn
events.message:
Enemy droids are black, which is what the C64 has always drawn

dMd0_droid's _new arm ($18FA) writes $F0 into SpriteColor — C64 colour
0 — the moment a droid is given a hardware sprite, with SpriteMC clear,
and nothing changes it while that droid lives. Only the player is ever
another colour. The port drew every sprite in logical 3, white, because
that is what the compiled artwork happened to be stored as.

So drs_place, our dMd0 slot arm, sets sprColour to SPR_COL_BLACK. It is
set every pass rather than once at allocation: a slot that has been
round the pool as a bullet or an explosion comes back with the right
colour without anyone having to remember to put it back. The player
cannot reach this code — DroidsUpdate's loop starts at entry 1.

Verified in jsbeeb on deck with a 5xx in view: sprColour reads FF FF FF
FF FF FF 0F FF, and breaking on SprSetColour with that droid in hand
gives colPix = 01 02 03 04 06 07 08 09 0C 0E 0F — the white set with
the high nibble gone, which is logical 1. On screen the droid is black
against the deck and the player is still white.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: kieranhj

events.title: Give the compiled sprite a colour it can be told at run time
events.message:
Give the compiled sprite a colour it can be told at run time

The C64 puts every sprite's colour in a register of its own. We draw
from generated code, and a generated immediate is the same colour every
time it runs — which is why the low-energy flash was written off in
layer-9-hud.md as something a compiled blitter cannot do.

It can. export_droids.py writes the artwork at DROID_COLOUR = 3, so an
opaque pixel sets bit 7-n AND bit 3-n and every pixel byte the compiler
emits is P | P<<4 for a 4-bit opacity pattern P. Choosing a colour is
choosing a nibble: &0F leaves logical 1, &F0 logical 2, &FF logical 3.
Across 24 types, 8 phases and 4 shifts only ELEVEN patterns occur, so
the code reaches its pixels through eleven zero page bytes and
SprSetColour rewrites them when the colour changes.

ORA zp is 3 cycles against ORA #'s 2 and the same two bytes, so the
1,038 converted sites cost one cycle each and not one byte of bank —
banks 5 and 6 end exactly where they did. Around 75 opaque bytes go
into a sprite, so ~600 cycles on a full eight-slot pass, plus ~200 per
colour change; sprColCur keeps that to twice a pass once the sources
are wired up. Main RAM pays 61 bytes, 148 free down to 87.

Behaviour is unchanged, and by construction: every slot starts at
SPR_COL_WHITE, and colPix is then sprColPat masked with &FF, which is
sprColPat itself — the same eleven bytes the immediates used to hold.
Confirmed in jsbeeb rather than argued: breaking on SprSetColour with
the player in hand and reading &05-&0F gives 11 22 33 44 66 77 88 99 CC
EE FF, exactly the immediates the previous build baked in. The opcode
stream differs only where it should — 750 ORA # to ORA zp, 288 LDA # to
LDA zp, and 18 new instructions for SprSetColour and its two callers.

A cross-build play-buffer diff is NOT available as a check here: the
title's dwell seeds drSeed, and a build of a different size reaches the
title at a different cycle, so the two pick different decks and there
is nothing to compare. Pin the seed first if that check is ever wanted.

events.title: build the needle geometrically, center the ring, and hide it when stopped
events.message:
build the needle geometrically, center the ring, and hide it when stopped

Three faults Duane spotted, all in the same small piece of art.

**The ring was not centered.** Its pattern was eight wide but the shape sits in
columns 0-6 with the last blank, which is how the sprite byte holds it -- so the
ring drew half a pixel left of its node's center while the needle sat exactly on
it, and the two were never concentric. Most visible due north and due south, as
reported. Trimmed to seven, so both patterns are 7x7 about their own middles.

**The diagonals were wrong**, because the needle was a hand-drawn plus with a
tail bolted on, and a plus does not rotate. It is now constructed: the stem runs
inward from the rim toward the middle, and a short bar crosses it perpendicular
at the outer end. One construction, eight directions, and the diagonals fall out
of it correctly rather than needing their own drawings.

**And it stayed up after the expedition stopped.** The original simply leaves
sprite 0's bitmap empty when not moving. A step here is instantaneous, so the
needle is shown on each step and taken away again shortly after the last one.

makes it simply the negated direction.

events.title: one marker for both modes, a cross for the bearing, and a much denser sea
events.message:
one marker for both modes, a cross for the bearing, and a much denser sea

Three corrections, all from Duane playing the original and from reading the
sprites while the party was ashore.

**There is no landing party sprite, and there never was.** Ashore, sprite 1 has
the same pointer ($2D) and the same seven bytes as at sea: the expedition is one
ring either way, and only the bearing beside it changes. So the invented party
figure is gone -- it was solving a problem that did not exist -- and the two
modes now share a marker. That also explains why no party sprite ever turned up
in $5529 or anywhere else: there is nothing to find.

**The ring is chunkier than it was drawn.** Both sprites are hardware-expanded in
x and y ($D01D = $D017 = 03), so an 8x7 shape with two-pixel-thick edges draws at
16x14 -- about one map tile across. The previous version was 11x11 with
single-pixel edges and read thin and spindly. The shape here follows that
measured geometry rather than being copied byte for byte, which for a hollow
diamond outline amounts to the same drawing.

**The bearing is a cross, not a square.** Sprite 0's shapes are three or four
bytes forming a small cross, drawn in $D027 = $2 red against the ring's $D028 =
$1 white, and it sits on the rim toward the heading rather than out past it.

**And the sea was six times too empty.** Measured on a live frame: 12 specks
among 70 water glyphs, about 0.17 a glyph. A tile is four glyphs, so roughly 0.7
specks per tile -- most tiles carry one. The previous version stippled one tile in
eight. Each of 48 appearances now draws up to one speck per quadrant at the
measured rate, and which appearance a tile uses is still a pure function of its
map position, so the stipple stays fixed to the world.

96 tests pass.

So a tile's speck is now a pure function of its map position and nothing else --
about one tile in eight carries one, which is what 17 of 144 glyphs measured --
and the tile definitions are plain rather than animated. The sea is painted on
the world instead of on the screen. Verified the opposite way this time: zero
pixels change in the sea over three seconds while stationary.

events.title: stipple the sea, hollow out the compass, and put a bearing pip on it
events.message:
stipple the sea, hollow out the compass, and put a bearing pip on it

Three things the captures described and the viewer was not yet doing.

**The compass is two things, not one.** The original overlays two sprites: a
static ring -- a diamond OUTLINE with a hole in it -- and a bearing that is a pip
rather than an arrow, three or four bytes rewritten in place at whichever point
of the rose is being steered toward, and left empty while stopped. The viewer had
a solid diamond and no bearing at all. It now draws the ring hollow, puts the pip
on it in the direction of the last step, and hides the pip until the expedition
moves. The colors come from the sprite registers rather than from taste: $D027 =
$2 for sprite 0, the pip, and $D028 = $1 for sprite 1, the ring -- so a white ring
with a red pip riding on it, which is the difference Duane spotted.

**The sea is stippled, and it moves.** There is no wave art to load: the tile
buffers the $5529 table points at hold a uniform $55, every bit-pair 01, which is
solid $D022. A wave is one pixel-pair zeroed inside an otherwise-uniform water
byte so it draws in $D021 -- measured $54, $51 and $45 against $55, and $D021 in
the map region is yellow, 176 pixels of it against 8,800 of water on a captured
frame. On that frame 17 of 144 glyphs carried exactly one speck and 127 were
bare, and diffing both charset buffers across a voyage showed those bytes moving.

So water now gets eight variants, each an animated SKTileDefinition whose cycle
is bare except for a single frame, with the speck in a different place and the
cycle at a different phase per variant. That keeps the sea mostly empty and
twinkling rather than blinking in unison, and SpriteKit runs the animation so
nothing is redrawn per frame. Which variant a tile uses is a pure function of its
position, so the pattern does not shuffle when the view is rebuilt.

**The party is a figure now** rather than a colored block -- still invented, and
still flagged as such. $5529 has no entry for a landing party and the sprite was
never captured: the quest that would have shown it ran out of food first.

All of these are drawn from patterns in source rather than extracted, because the
sprite bitmaps live in RAM at runtime with no known source on disk. They follow
the structure that was measured; they are not the original's pixels.

96 tests pass.

events.title: Reorder the level-draw zero page so eleven bytes come free
events.message:
Reorder the level-draw zero page so eleven bytes come free

The sprite colour work needs eleven zero page bytes and &00-&8F has no
gaps. It does not need them to be globally dead, though: the colour
table only has to survive inside SprDrawAll, so anything the blitter
and the IRQ do not touch will do.

&00-&0F splits cleanly on that test. bandDo, colFirst, colCount and
sDelta cross a sprite draw — SprSplitOK reads bandDo and colCount, and
ReframeView clears the pair after SprDrawAll has run. The other eleven
are consumed no later than the end of DoRedraws, which the main loop
runs before SprDrawAll. So the five move to &00-&04 and the eleven to
&05-&0F, where the table can alias them as one contiguous run.

Nothing but the addresses changes. Reducing both listings to a stream
of opcode bytes gives 20,238 instructions, identical; the 164 lines
that differ at all are zero page operands inside &00-&0F.

events.title: write down what the position hunt found, and what it ruled out
events.message:
write down what the position hunt found, and what it ruled out

Two sessions of memory archaeology have narrowed where the expedition's position
lives without closing it, and the negative results are worth as much as the
positive ones because they stop the next attempt repeating them.

Ruled out: the position is not a coordinate that counts. The whole 64 KB was
diffed across twenty confirmed single-tile westward moves and then ten
northward, and no byte and no 16-bit pair moves by the step count or by any
consistent multiple on both axes. $0032 survives one axis and dies on the other
-- +10 on twenty west, still going north -- but 135->145 cannot be a column in a
128-byte row. The four bytes at $E22E-$E234 move in lockstep, so they are one
quantity mirrored rather than coordinates.

The likely reason: the map is streamed in pages. $8C = 145 and $256C = 96 held
constant across moves, so what they describe is quantized to a page rather than
to a step, which is consistent with the game reading map regions off the disk as
it scrolls, and explains the complete absence of anything per-step.

What does work is matching terrain, and it is the technique to build on. The
buffer at $B600 holds one tile per byte -- not nibble-packed the way the disk
is -- and a 40-tile run of it is unique enough to find in the decoded 256x400
world by plain string search. That fixed a position at (134,145) with no memory
archaeology at all.

But $B600 is not the display buffer, and this is the correction that matters:
the visible 6x6 window, classified off the composed charset, matches nowhere in
that page, and the page's row breaks only fit a 48-tile stride relative to one
anchor rather than absolutely. So every origin calculation made against it was
against the wrong region. $B600 is probably what is streamed ahead of the ship.
Finding the buffer the view is actually composed from is the next step, and
$3107/$58B8 are where to read for it.

Also recorded because it cost real time: joystick input does not reach the game
through vice-mcp, tapped or held, on either port.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: record what the running game showed: waves, sprites, and a position that hides
events.message:
record what the running game showed: waves, sprites, and a position that hides

Duane got a real quest running on the historical map, which made three of the
open questions answerable and one of them harder.

**The waves are solved as a mechanism, and need no more capture.** The sea is
flat: the buffers the $5529 table points at ($94B0 deep/shallow, $94D8 medium)
hold a uniform $55 -- every bit-pair 01, solid light blue -- and $94D8is often
all zeros. There is no wave art anywhere to extract, confirmed twice: both
buffers are all zeros in the decrypted program image, and $94B0 read as uniform
$55 on a live frame. A wave is instead one pixel-pair zeroed inside an otherwise
uniform water byte, stamped into the *composed charset*: $54, $51 and $45
against a $55 background, pair index 3, 2 and 1 set to 00. On one frame 17 of
the 144 terrain glyphs carried exactly one speck and the other 127 were pure
$55. And they animate -- diffing both charset buffers across twenty moves shows
those same bytes toggling all over the surface. What is left is the placement
rule, which is a reading job in the composition step rather than a capture job.

**The marker question is closed** and already fixed in the viewer: two overlaid
hardware sprites at sea carrying a compass rose, and the $3 ship tile is a map
tile -- which is what the historical disk's fourteen cells of terrain $3 are.
Whether the sprite pointers cycle with heading is still open; they hold steady
while stationary, and Duane reports the heading only shows under way.

**The start position got harder, and that is the useful part.** The expedition's
map position is not a plain coordinate anywhere in $0000-$BFFF. Diffed all 48 KB
across twenty confirmed westward moves: not one byte changed by 20, by 10, or by
any consistent amount, and no 16-bit pair moved by a plausible step. $86/$87,
which $58B8 reads map bytes through, held at $B600 throughout. Two candidates
from a narrower 4 KB diff were disproved by the wider one. The suspicion worth
chasing is that the position is held as a disk track/sector plus offset rather
than as x/y, since the game streams map regions off the map disk as it scrolls.

Also recorded, because it cost a lot of time: joystick input does not reach the
game through vice-mcp, tapped or held, on either port. Movement has to be driven
by hand, which is exactly what boot_demo.py built the demo path to avoid.

events.title: perf: skip the force-full when a re-band moved no USED index
events.message:
perf: skip the force-full when a re-band moved no USED index

#142, after the profile put st_present at 51% re-band during the walk and the
re-band's own split at FORCE-FULL 297 t200 / quant 93 / used_idx 82.

★ FIRST, WHAT THE FILE ALREADY SAID. The obvious fix — rebuild only the rows
holding a value whose slot moved — was TRIED AND REMOVED (2026-07-26, during #61).
Its dirty map is computed once per re-band against the remap ONE page was last
drawn with, and the pages alternate, so the map is wrong for the other page: the
"brown chrome". Reading that comment before proposing it saved re-inventing a
known-bad design.

★ AND THE MEASUREMENT SAYS IT COULD NOT PAY ANYWAY. The b4audit counters over 19
re-bands of a fixture walk: 57.2% of USED indices change slot per re-band (range
0-86%). At that churn effectively every row holds a moved index, so a dirty-row
map skips nothing. The force-full is genuinely necessary — usually.

Usually, not always: one re-band moved 0 of 59 used indices, B3.2's stable-slot
alignment succeeding completely. There every plane on screen still encodes the
right colour and the 297 t200 rebuild is pure waste. So skip it in that case —
all-or-nothing and page-independent, which is why it does not inherit the removed
smart-skip's bug. s_remap_gen is left alone too, so B5's copy path (2b1acdd7)
survives a change that changed nothing rather than dropping to the conversion.

Unused indices may still have moved: harmless, since no pixel carries one and
anything drawn afterwards is stamped through the new remap.

MEASURED: fires on 1 of 14 re-bands; AE = 0 against the arm that matches the
256-colour Falcon. Small and exact — roughly one re-band in fifteen, ~2-3% of
in-present on this sample. Booked as that, not as more.

★ THE REAL LEVER IS THE 57.2% ITSELF. B3.2 exists to keep colours on their slots
and is achieving ~43%. Every point gained there shrinks the force-full AND the
#141 freckle class together, because both come from the remap moving under
already-stamped planes. That is a quantiser problem, not a present-path one.

★ AND A HARNESS DISCIPLINE, WRONG THREE TIMES TODAY IN THREE DIFFERENT WAYS: an
AE comparison is only meaningful when both frames are in the SAME game state. The
pre-command-bar reference (#141), a twelve-step drift, and here a twenty-step
drift each produced an authoritative-looking number that meant nothing. Screenshot
for AE at the settle, THEN drive for counters.

make test 471 passed; ST 68000, ST STPROF, Atari 020, Amiga AGA and Amiga ECS clean.

Refs #142, #141.

events.title: show the compass at sea, and the ship only where it is actually moored
events.message:
show the compass at sea, and the ship only where it is actually moored

The marker was exactly backwards, and the running game settled it. Captured from
the exploration screen: at sea the expedition is a pair of overlaid **hardware
sprites** -- $D015 = 03, both at the same position, colors $2 and $1 -- carrying
a small diamond. That is the compass rose showing heading, which is why Duane
noticed it turns into something else on land. It is also what the 24 pixels of a
fifth color, outside the four the terrain multicolor uses, were in the earlier
static capture.

The ship tile from $5529 entry $3 is a *map* tile, not a marker. That explains
something already sitting in WorldMap's own notes: the historical map disk
carries fourteen cells of terrain value $3 and a generated world carries none.
Those fourteen are moored ships.

So the marker is never the ship and the ship is never the marker. The moored
ship is drawn at the ship's own position while the party is ashore, and the
marker is a compass at sea or the party on land.

The shapes are drawn rather than extracted. The sprite data lives in RAM at
runtime and has not been traced to anything on disk, so the diamond is a square
turned forty-five degrees of our own making, not the original's pixels. The
landing party is invented outright -- $5529 has no entry for one, and its sprite
was not captured.

The marker is also no longer rescaled to hold a constant size on screen. Both
forms sit on a particular tile, and a marker that keeps its own size swims free
of the ground it is standing on as the aperture changes.

events.title: paint the screen the colors the original actually uses, measured off a live frame

paint the screen the colors the original actually uses, measured off a live frame

Duane got the game running under VICE and reported the text colors were wrong
and the bottom lines missing. Both true. These are now sampled from a live
exploration frame rather than assumed:

  date, message and the two status lines   $07 yellow
  panel labels                             $0E light blue
  panel values                             $07 yellow

Everything is yellow except the panel labels. The earlier white came from
reading an older captured frame that was in a different screen state.

Reading *color RAM* would have given black for every one of those rows, and the
reason is worth keeping: the charset is inverted, so a glyph's ink is its zero
bits -- the letters take $D021 and the background takes color RAM. The raster
split at $2250 then rewrites $D021 down the screen, which is how a single
color-RAM value produces several different text colors. That is a second,
independent confirmation of the EOR $FF finding from the font work.

The two lines under the viewport now switch with where the expedition is, as the
original switches them: SPEED and DEPTH at sea, PACE and TERRAIN ashore. Speed
and pace hold dashes for the same reason the four panels do -- nothing stands
behind them yet. Depth and terrain are real, because the map knows both.

Position, explored percentage and tile style moved off the screen and into the
window title. The original has exactly two lines there and they are worth
spending on the world rather than on the renderer.

events.title: land the expedition, walk it around, and let it row back to the ship
events.message:
land the expedition, walk it around, and let it row back to the ship

Chunk four: the coast stops being a wall. The rules are in SevenCitiesCore as
`Expedition`, not in the scene, because landing and walking are game rules and
this project's whole method is to make rules testable rather than clickable.
WorldScene now draws whatever `Expedition` says and contributes none of its own.

The two rules that are not simply "stay on your own terrain" are the ones that
make the harness work, and both are deliberate:

  - Aboard, stepping at land is not refused -- it IS the landing. The ship moors
    on the water it is already floating on and the party walks ashore. There is
    no separate "land" command, exactly as there is none in the original.
  - Ashore, stepping at the ship's own tile re-boards it. Every other water tile
    is refused, so the ship is the only way back off the continent.

Rivers are land here, via `Terrain.isLand`, which is what the manual means by
calling them the fast route inland.

`Outcome` carries a *reason* rather than a sentence -- `.blocked(.partyCannotSwim)`,
not "THE EXPEDITION CANNOT WALK ON WATER" -- because the wording belongs to the
screen and the rule belongs to the core. The message line now carries the
expedition's status the way the original does ("THE EXPEDITION IS ON LAND."),
which is what that line is for; the world's name moved to the window title,
where the original effectively keeps it too.

Nine tests, including the round trip: sail to the coast, land, walk inland, walk

events.title: stop the ship sliding across the world, and write down the missing waves
events.message:
stop the ship sliding across the world, and write down the missing waves

Two causes behind the jerkiness and ghosting while moving, both fixed here.

The camera and the ship disagreed. The ship's position was set outright while
the camera was handed an 0.08s move(to:), so for an eighth of a second the ship
slid across the world instead of the world sliding under the ship. That is the
ghosting, and it is worst exactly where the tiles are biggest -- the classic
aperture -- because the same tween has to cover more pixels. Both now move in
one step. Snapping is also what the original does: it scrolls the map by whole
tiles and never between them.

The fog repainted all 102,400 cells on every step, which cost more than the move
that triggered it. But a step can only change the alpha of cells that fell in or
out of the sight radius -- a block around where the eye was and one around where
it now is -- and everything else is already painted correctly. Only those two
windows are touched now. `full` still forces the whole map, which is needed the
first time and after the fog has been hidden, since while hidden the state keeps
advancing and the two windows would no longer describe everything that changed.

TODO gains three things, all of which want the game running under VICE and
nothing else, so they belong in one sitting:

  - **The ocean has no waves, and it is not an animation problem.** Water's
    patterns point at RAM (`$94B0`, `$94D8`), below `TerrainTiles`' `< $9000`
    cutoff, so there is nothing in `game` to read and all three depths extract
    as `animated: true` with a single flat fill. The viewer therefore draws the
    sea as a solid blue field where the original has white specks across it.
    That is a gap visible *at rest*, before animation enters into it, and it is
    the most conspicuous thing still wrong with the exploration view. The
    bitmaps are sitting in RAM; reading those two buffers off a running game is
    the whole job, and it also settles whether the three depths differ in
    pattern or only in color.

  - **Where Spain puts you.** `shipStart` reasons rather than measures. The real
    number that matters is how much ocean stands between the start and landfall,
    since that decides whether the opening minute is discovery or tedium.

  - **Whether the expedition marker is a hardware sprite.** The captured
    exploration screen holds 24 pixels of a color outside the screen's four-color
    terrain palette, dead center of the 12x12 grid. A fifth color there is what a
    VIC-II sprite gives you. If it is one, animating the ship and the party is a
    pointer cycle rather than something to invent.

87 tests pass.

events.title: put the expedition in the game's own ship, and keep it on the water
events.message:
put the expedition in the game's own ship, and keep it on the water

The yellow debug circle is gone. The expedition is drawn with the original's
ship, which cost no new art at all: `$5529` entry `$3` points at pattern
`$5833`, one of the thirteen static patterns extract.sh already lifts off the
program disk. It is drawn at exactly one map tile and, unlike the marker it
replaces, is deliberately NOT rescaled to hold a constant size on screen -- a
marker should stay readable at any zoom, but a ship is a thing sitting on a
particular patch of water and has to shrink and grow with it.

Every way to steer is live at once, and none of them has to be chosen:

  - arrows, for the four cardinals
  - the numpad, which is the eight directions laid out as they point
  - Q W E / A S D / Z X C
  - vi's Y U I / H J K L / B N M

The two letter clusters do not share a single key, so the vi set can be
available for people who prefer it without being the default -- which is how the
same keys are offered in the roguelike this borrows the idea from. S is south
rather than a stand-still: there is no turn economy here for a rest key to mean
anything in, and WASD is what the muscle memory expects.

The ship keeps to water. Landing and walking are the next chunk, so for now the
coast is a wall rather than a beach, and the refusal says so on the line the
original announces discoveries on. WorldScene gained `onMessage` for that, with
an empty string meaning "nothing to announce" so the owner can put the world's
name back rather than leaving the line blank.

`shipStart` puts the expedition at sea off the eastern edge at mid-latitude,
three tiles clear of the first water, because the original sails you west out of
a Spain that is off the map entirely. `suggestedStart` finds land and is what
the free-roaming viewer wanted; a ship needs the opposite.

**`shipStart` is reasoned, not measured**, and the doc comment says so. The
original's start is almost certainly a fixed constant, and reading it off the
running game would settle both the latitude and how much ocean stands between
you and landfall -- which is the number that decides whether the opening minute
is interesting or tedious. Recorded in TODO rather than guessed at twice.

87 tests pass; none of this touches the generator.

events.title: remember where the expedition has been, and offer the original's window instead
events.message:
remember where the expedition has been, and offer the original's window instead

Two apertures, and the explored mask that one of them needs. Game > Aperture
switches between them; Classic is the default because it is the faithful one.

Classic is the original's window: six map tiles square, no fog, and no black.
That distinction took a wrong turn to find and is worth recording. The first
version of this shipped a "Fog of War" toggle described as the purist's setting,
which was backwards -- switching the fog off left the wide window showing
everything in it, which reveals far MORE than the C64 ever did. The original's
constraint was never darkness. It is the size of the hole: every one of its
thirty-six tiles is drawn, nothing is remembered on screen, and what you cannot
see is simply outside the frame. So the toggle now switches the aperture rather
than the drawing, and because the classic grid is fixed the integer scale is
free to rise -- the whole screen is drawn about half again as large as the wide
one manages, which is the point of having it rather than it being a smaller
version of the other.

FogOfWar is game state, not a rendering trick, and the discovery screen is what
proves it: LAND, RIVERS, NATIVES, MINES and SPECIAL are reported there as
percentages *found*, and none of those is computable without a per-cell record
of where you have been. So it carries exploredCount and exploredFraction beside
the three visibility states. Chebyshev rather than Euclidean, because the
original's aperture is a square window and not a circle of sight: radius 3 is
its 6x6 window recentered on the expedition, so nothing is ever revealed that
the C64 would not have revealed. Nothing occludes anything in open ocean, so
there is no shadowcasting and none is wanted.

The drawing is one 256x400 texture, a pixel per cell, stretched over the world
and linearly filtered. That filtering is the whole mechanism: dimming has to
feather ACROSS cell edges rather than step at them, or the explored frontier
reads as a staircase of hard squares. A per-cell overlay of flat quads cannot be
interpolated -- each quad is its own texture and filteringMode samples within a
texture, not between them -- which is the same reason buildOverviewMap draws the
world as one small image rather than as tiles.

Four faults found by running it, all worth keeping:

  - The fog drew mirrored, so the lit circle sat two hundred rows from the
    expedition and everything you could see was black. buildOverviewMap flips
    vertically because it DRAWS THROUGH a CGContext, whose coordinates are
    bottom-up. This writes bytes into the backing buffer, and a bitmap buffer's
    first row is the image's top row. Flipping as well was one flip too many.

  - Explorer's default zoom was 3.0, at which the window shows about five and a
    half tiles -- entirely inside the seven-tile lit block. Every visible cell
    was genuinely `.visible`, so nothing was ever dimmed and the fog looked
    broken while working perfectly. An aperture tighter than its own sight
    radius cannot show fog by construction. Now 1.0.

  - Releasing the classic lock left the classic zoom behind, so switching back
    to the wide aperture inherited a 2x zoom and looked unfogged for the reason
    above. The zoom is restored on the lock-to-unlock transition only, so a
    window resize does not fight the user's own zooming.

  - updateFog held exclusive access to fogPixels while building the texture from
    it, which traps at runtime ("Fatal access conflict detected"). The image is
    now made inside the closure and everything else outside it.

The status under the viewport is two short lines now, because the classic
aperture is a NARROWER screen than the wide one and the old forty-character line
ran off both edges of it. Zoom came out of it: it means nothing while the
aperture is pinned, and the two lines the original has there are better spent on
the world than on the renderer.

Seven tests, including the one the plan called for: sail a straight line and
every column well clear of the ends is explored for exactly rows -3 to +3 and no
more. 87 tests pass in all.

TODO gains the discovery screen, since it is what this state is ultimately for.

events.title: perf: st_present is RE-BAND bound — and the used_idx scan is store-bound (negative result)
events.message:
perf: st_present is RE-BAND bound — and the used_idx scan is store-bound (negative result)

#142's next item after the tile hit path and the clock. Profiled with the
backend's own FRUA_STPROF breakdown, walk phase separated from boot by diffing
consecutive dumps (the counters are cumulative, and mixing the phases is what
made #125's divide conclusion wrong).

WALK PHASE, per present:  in-present 69.4 t200, of which
    band (re-quantise)  35.3   51%
    pass1                9.4   14%
    vpcomp               1.6
    copy                 0.4
and per re-band (~2 per 16 presents):
    FORCE-FULL rebuild  297 t200
    quant_banded         93
    used_idx scan        82

So st_present is dominated by RE-BANDING, not by conversion or by the composite.
`rows converted` is ~0 during the walk, which means the obvious target from the
cycle profile — planar_c2p_span_stlow at 132.8M — is the wrong half.

★ NEGATIVE RESULT, RECORDED IN THE CODE. The used_idx scan carries a #63 note
calling it "a SECOND full-frame pass ... priced before it is removed", and it ran
a byte at a time through a LONG index. Reading it long-wise — one fetch feeding
four table stores, the same substitution that took the row compare from 93
cycles/byte to ~30 — changed the marginal cost per re-band by NOTHING: 82.0 t200
before, 82.0 after, over 9 re-bands each way. Reverted.

The reasoning did not transfer because #63's win was on a COMPARE (loads only)
while this is a SCATTER-STORE: 64,000 byte writes into a 256-entry table, one bus
cycle apiece. The loads were never the cost. A future attempt has to remove
STORES, and the two candidates are now written where it will be found — including
that the "obvious" halving (scan only the rows quant_banded samples) is a
SEMANTIC change rather than an optimisation, since scanning every row makes
s_used_idx a superset of what the quant actually saw.

★ AND AN EARLIER READING OF MY OWN WAS WRONG: I first scored this as -16% by
comparing cumulative averages across runs with different re-band counts. The
marginal figure is what is comparable, and it is flat.

The real target is FORCE-FULL at 297 t200 — the whole-frame rebuild a remap
change forces, which is the same fact behind the B5 regression fixed in 2b1acdd7
— and behind that, why a steady walk re-bands at all. Both are structural and
shared with #141/#139.

make test 471 passed; ST 68000, Atari 020, Amiga AGA and Amiga ECS clean.

Refs #142, #141.

events.title: draw the exploration screen in the game's own font and frame
events.message:
draw the exploration screen in the game's own font and frame

The map used to sit in a bare window with a translucent AppKit HUD over it.
It now sits inside the original's screen: black ground, the game's charset, the
dithered yellow frame, the four status panels, and two status lines underneath.
Checked against a VICE capture from the user's own disk and against the C64
screenshot on Wikipedia, which agree with each other.

The load-bearing question going in was whether the frame could be obtained at
all, since the exploration charset is assembled at runtime and appears nowhere
on either disk. It can, and the answer turned out to be better than expected:

  - The font is static data on disk 1, at offset 4713 of the raw stream of
    tracks 1 to 10 at twenty sectors a track. tools/extract_font.py had already
    found it. Ninety-six glyphs in ASCII order from space, which is why the
    game's text tables index it as character = ASCII - $20. It is the game's own
    charset and not the Commodore ROM's, so the whole styled screen costs no
    font license, and like the tiles it comes off the user's disk and is never
    committed.

  - The running game holds the inverse of it: what lands at $A000 is this data
    EOR $FF, measured exact for 94 of 96 glyphs. Nothing here reproduces that,
    because nothing here is a VIC-II. A set bit is ink.

  - The viewport frame is the five glyphs immediately after the font, charset
    codes $60-$64, and it is far plainer than it looks. $60 and $61 are AA bytes
    top to bottom -- 10101010 -- and $62/$63 are the same dither in half a cell
    so the border's ink hugs the viewport rather than facing away from it.
    Alternating yellow and black pixels at 320 across is what the eye turns into
    an olive band. There is no cornerpiece anywhere in the block.

  - Four of the ninety-six are blank on disk: space, correctly, and ?, n and o,
    which the running game has and this has not traced. Text containing those
    three will come out with holes. Recorded in GameFont rather than papered
    over.

The colors are measured off the capture, not inferred from VIC registers:
background $00 black, frame $07 yellow, date and message $01 white, panel
labels and values $0E light blue.

GameShellView is not a VIC-II and does not try to be. The original's screen is
a fixed 40x25 of characters at 320x200; this one grows its aperture with the
window, which is the whole point of choosing fog of war over a six-tile
porthole. Scale is integer only, because anything else resamples an 8x8 glyph
and the charset stops being the charset. What it keeps is the palette, the
charset, the layout and the frame.

The panels hold dashes. They are present rather than omitted deliberately:
gold, food and crew get hooked up behind these exact slots as later chunks, and
leaving the slots out now would mean laying the screen out twice.

Two faults found by running it, both worth recording. The viewport callback was
wired after the shell was first given a size, so the only layout pass that runs
on a window nobody resizes reported to nobody and the map view kept the frame
it was born with. And the map view was a sibling of the shell rather than a
child -- the shell is flipped and the container is not, so the viewport rect
crossed a coordinate boundary and the map drew low by the difference. It is now
a child of the shell, where there is one coordinate space and no conversion to
forget.

All 80 tests pass unchanged; none of this touches the generator.

events.title: diag: count the viewport composite balance — planes 3 presents in 4
events.message:
diag: count the viewport composite balance — planes 3 presents in 4

2b1acdd7 made the composite fall back to the c2p conversion whenever the remap
moved since the planes were stamped. That fixed the freckles, but it left an
open question the fix itself could not answer: if the guard fires on most
presents, B5's copy path is largely notional and the planar composite is paying
for a plane buffer and draw-time stamping to STILL run the conversion.

Measured over a fixture boot plus twenty walk steps:

    vp COPY presents = 6      vp c2p fallbacks = 2

3:1 for the copy path, with the fallbacks clustered at boot/entry where the
palette is still settling. The design holds.

★ IT ALSO QUALIFIES A CLAIM IN b4849085. I wrote there that "the chunky->planar
conversion no longer runs for the viewport". Correctly stated: it does not run
when the remap is CURRENT — most presents, not all. (And before 2b1acdd7 it did
not run even when it should have, which was the bug.)

SMALL SAMPLE, said plainly: 8 composites. Enough to rule out "fallbacks
dominate", not enough to pin a steady-state ratio. A sustained walk on a stable
palette should skew further toward copies, since that is exactly when the remap
stops moving.

★ AND THE COUNTER LOGS ON THE FIRST CALL, with the reason in the code. "No
output" and "a reading of zero" are the same text, and a threshold sized for a
long profile drive then read on a short fixture drive has produced silence I
misread as data FIVE times in this work — the lazy-pass skip/draw pair, the #125
divide dump, and this counter three times over. One extra line removes the
ambiguity permanently.

events.title: FontCell had to be main RAM, not the code image
events.message:
FontCell had to be main RAM, not the code image

82 bytes of &1100-&3000 — the one region that is genuinely full, and
the one Layer 11e's sound driver has to live in because the IRQ reads
no sideways bank. FontCell only ever needed to be reachable from both
banks, and the room the 1bpp font freed is main RAM too, so it moves
into the PARAFNT file next to the font it decodes. The code image goes
back to 148 bytes.

FONTCODE_BYTES is declared up front beside FONT_BYTES, because beebasm
resolves constants in file order and PN_TABS needs the size, and it is
ASSERTed against the assembled length — which is what caught the first
guess of 83. Nothing calls FontCell before PARAFNT loads: FillPanel
does not touch the font and the title carries its own glyphs.

Verified in jsbeeb with the decoder running from &3CD6: the panel is
0 diffs of 2,560 against the build from BEFORE the font was packed at
all, the droid database's text is byte-identical to the previous
build, and the transfer's panel line renders descenders correctly.

The rest of TASK 8 is costed and declined in the layer notes: sharing
the two-cell wrapper would buy ~200 bytes across banks 6 and 7, which
was worth having when they held 47 and 282 bytes and is not now they
hold 1,609 and 4,410.

events.title: start every session on a new game screen, and build worlds off the main thread
events.message:
start every session on a new game screen, and build worlds off the main thread

The viewer used to open straight into a map and offer the two worlds as menu
items. That is the wrong shape for what this is becoming: a session starts by
choosing a world, so the choice is now a screen you land on, and Game > New
Game (Cmd-N) goes back to it from either world.

The reason it could not simply be a menu item is that "Generate New World" ran
the World Maker on the main thread. Measured in a debug build, a whole world is
1.2 to 2.2 seconds, which is long enough that the window froze solid and gave no
sign it was working. Generation now runs on a detached task with a progress bar
in front of it, and the old blocking path is deleted rather than left beside the
new one — two ways to do the same thing, one of which freezes the window, is
worse than one.

WorldMaker gained a Progress struct and an optional progress handler, threaded
through world(config:seed:), randomWorld(), world(of:rng:), firstBand and
secondBand. Each band reports after each of its nine phases and the land-mass
stage is step 1, so nineteen steps in all. No shared counter was needed: each
band's step range is a fixed constant, which meant no parameter had to become
inout and no call site had to change. All 80 tests pass unchanged, which is the
check that matters here — the instrumentation must not perturb a single
generated world, and it does not.

The bar counts phases rather than weighting them by measured time. The split
between stages swings hard from run to run: across three runs the second band
came in at 131ms twice and 886ms once. Weights fitted to that would lurch and
stall, where a phase count moves unevenly in time but is never wrong about where
the run actually is. Progress is hopped to the main actor to be drawn and
unstructured tasks carry no ordering guarantee between them, so the view refuses
any step that is not ahead of the last one — except across a retry, where
randomWorld throws a stuck world away and the count legitimately restarts.

The New Game screen is deliberately plain AppKit. The C64-styled shell is the
next chunk and depends on frame glyphs that have to come off the user's own disk
first; holding this flow hostage to that would have meant nothing runnable until
both were done. Expect it to be restyled.

Two smaller consequences. Importing disk images now rebuilds the New Game screen
when that is what is on screen, because an import changes whether the classic
map can be offered at all. And reload()'s old fallback — generate a world in
place when historical.map is missing — is gone, since the screen only offers the
classic map when the file is actually there; if it vanishes between the choice
and the load, the only thing left to do is go back to the screen.

events.title: model the raster interrupt's entropy stir, and repair four latent hangs
events.message:
model the raster interrupt's entropy stir, and repair four latent hangs

The World Maker was failing to produce a map for 18.8% of its input space.
That number was real, the framing around it was wrong twice over, and both
corrections are worth having in the log.

$2406, inside the raster IRQ handler at $23FC, is LDA $D41B / ADC $CD / STA $CD:
live SID oscillator noise added into the LFSR's high byte on every interrupt,
tens of times a second. It is why no world was ever reproducible on real
hardware, and why most of the rejection samplers cannot hang there -- one with
no answer from the current register is handed new bits within a frame and walks
out. tools/wm_deterministic.py NOPs that instruction so a seed reproduces and
the port can be graded at all, and the port had silently inherited the choice.
Nearly all of the 18.8% was the cost of that determinism rather than anything
Ozark did.

So the stir is modelled now, and it is a property of the generator rather than
a global: WorldMakerRNG.stirInterval, zero for a frozen register.
WorldMaker.randomWorld() is the game's own behaviour -- seeded from the machine,
stirred throughout, and it takes no seed argument because on hardware there is
no such thing as a seed. world(config:seed:) stays frozen and is what every test
and fixture uses, which is the same relationship wm_deterministic.py already has
with the original. The viewer uses randomWorld() and its retry loop is gone.

The second correction is that "the original never fails" -- the obvious
conclusion from the above -- is false. Run the 6502 with its stir intact across
ninety worlds, the nine snapshots times ten noise streams, and two never finish:
1.2 billion instructions and 240,000 stirs apiece, against a largest known-good
run of 353 million. Entropy cannot rescue them because what fails is the map
rather than the register. The loops test the terrain, so a fresh draw only picks
a different losing candidate out of the same losing set.

Four such sites, each found by sampling a stalled process rather than by
reading, and each repaired where it hangs:

  $380D  no row of a mountain range is clear of lake marks within eleven cells,
         and $38A6/$3450 retry from a new row for ever. Gives up on the range
         after 1024 rows; the span is about 208, so that is five times over
         having tried them all. The landmass loses one river.
  $38CD, $3A83, $3CEB  a river that can neither finish nor unwind to nothing
         proposes and unwinds for ever. Abandoned after 50,000 turns; the
         longest river the original draws writes 1,941 cells.
  $3268  $3232 clamps $53 to $FF -- checked against the listing rather than
         assumed, BCC $3234 / LDA #$FF, so the port was faithful -- and
         CPX $53 / BCC is then a test no column can win. Stops after one lap,
         which has visited every column in the row anyway.
  $4373  no row in the band carries a thirty-cell run of land. After 1024 throws
         against a row space of about 256 it takes $2473, the restart the
         original already has, and a different mask gets built.

Every one of those fires only where the original would have hung, so no world
that completes is altered. All 80 tests pass unchanged, byte-exact fixture
included.

$2473 itself now restarts the phase the way the original does instead of
throwing. Throwing surfaced the restart honestly while the phase was being read
and is simply wrong behaviour: it turned 4.3% of the input space into a failure
the original does not have.

Where the rates land: deterministic world(config:seed:) 18.8% to 0.87%, stirred
single attempt to about 0.5%, and randomWorld() -- which keeps a retry as a
backstop -- zero failures in 60,000 worlds. The backstop stays because "four
sites found" is not "four sites exist"; each round of hunting turned up another
with diminishing returns, and discarding a world costs fifty milliseconds while
a hang does not.

NOTES.md records the whole arc, including both wrong turns and the two
measurements that produced confident wrong numbers -- a step budget that could
not tell a hang from a slow world, and a draw-count comparison against an
unverified window.

events.title: The string table existed twice because neither reader could see the other
events.message:
The string table existed twice because neither reader could see the other

1,542 bytes in bank 6 for the console main screen and 1,542 more in
bank 7 for the droid database, one bank visible at a time. But neither
reader cares where the table is: ConTok and DbTokFind both patch a
self-modifying absolute with its base and then scan for bit 7, and an
absolute reaches main RAM from either bank. So one copy goes in the
room the 1bpp font freed, carried by PARAFNT after the border cells,
and both banks get their 1,542 back.

Bank 6 goes from 67 bytes to 1,609 and stops being the tight bank;
bank 7 reaches 4,410. export_strings.py no longer emits the second
copy and src/data/strings7.asm is deleted.

Verified in jsbeeb: the table loads at &36D0 with the source's own
bytes; the droid database — the reader whose base address changed —
prints "Unit type 001" and "Influence Device" correctly; and the
console main screen is byte-identical to the previous build on the
same deck bar the rotor-and-digits image, which is bank 6's own
artwork and state-dependent.

BUGS.md #9 gains an observation from the verification: the same
column-shaped failure appeared at unit 22, not unit 0, after a
diagonal — so the column at fault may be whichever was newly exposed.

events.title: The font was shipping a converted copy of bytes it could ship verbatim
events.message:
The font was shipping a converted copy of bytes it could ship verbatim

PARAFNT held 3,488 bytes of MODE 1 artwork in which half of every byte
was redundant. The text is two colour, so a MODE 1 byte holding it is
n<<4 | n — four pixels in eight bits. Pair a cell's byte i with its byte
i+8, the same scanline's left and right halves, and the result is
(left<<4) | right, which IS the C64's own byte. So this removes an
encoding rather than adding one: export_font.py emits glyph_rows now and
asserts the round-trip for all 103 glyphs and 12 border cells.

1,744 bytes, and &3730-&3E00 is free — enough for constrings, which
exists twice at 1,731 bytes and is what TASK 7 deletes.

Four renderers in two banks read the font and packing breaks the loop
they share, so FontCell in main RAM replaces all four copies and each

events.title: The offset tables were 192 bytes of the only region that is full
events.message:
The offset tables were 192 bytes of the only region that is full

rowMul and unitMul held nothing but n*640 and n*8, and they held it
inside &1100-&3000, which is the one part of the machine with no room.
They are addresses in the free page at &5400 now, written at startup by
BuildMulTabs, and main RAM goes from 30 bytes free to 148 — enough for
Layer 11c's loop, which has been blocked on 39 of them.

They stay in main RAM because SetCell reads them with the sprite bank
paged in, which is what bufcore.asm is for. The call sits with
BuildCharPtrs and SprBuildMask because &5400 is under both the staging
overlay and the title's framebuffer.

&5400 looked free and was not: PnClear clears HI(PANEL_BYTES) pages and
then LO(PANEL_BYTES) bytes, but LO(4*640) is zero and the tail's
CPY #0 with Y already zero only matches after Y wraps — so it cleared a
whole extra page every PanelInit. Assembled away by a guard on the
constant, which also gives bank 6 seven bytes back.

Verified in jsbeeb: all 192 bytes byte-exact and never written again
(silent write breakpoint), nothing reading the rest of the page (silent
read breakpoint), and the buffer 0 diffs of 10,240 against a forced
RedrawAll stationary, horizontal, and both diagonals. One unexplained

events.title: render: FIX a B5 regression — baked viewport planes survive a remap change
events.message:
render: FIX a B5 regression — baked viewport planes survive a remap change

MY BUG, introduced this afternoon in b4849085 and live on main across three
commits. The viewport planes bake SLOT NUMBERS. When st_reband re-quantises or
st_patch_new_ink re-points an index, those slot numbers come to mean DIFFERENT
colours — and st_vp_composite_copy re-copied the already-stamped planes instead of
re-deriving them, painting grey stone walls in whatever the slots became: cyan and
red freckles. Before B5 nothing had to track this, because the composite
converted from the chunky scratch through the CURRENT remap on every present, so
a palette change corrected itself. The copy path has no such self-correction.

Proven on ONE binary via the vpplanar=off knob: the chunky arm gives clean walls
matching the 256-colour Falcon build; the planar arm freckles, 8,584 pixels
differing. Fixed arm is now AE = 0 against the chunky arm.

THE FIX: s_remap_gen is bumped wherever the remap moves (after quant_banded,
after st_patch_new_ink), recorded into s_vp_gen when the planes are committed, and
compared before the copy path is trusted. A stale generation falls back to the
c2p conversion. Both markers are logged, because a generation check that never
fires is indistinguishable from one that works.

★ AND THE LAZY CHUNKY PASS (#145, 1697425b) IS RETIRED, for correctness rather
than measurement. That fallback reads the chunky scratch, so it must be FRESH on
any present that finds the planes stale — and st_patch_new_ink moves the remap
from INSIDE the present, after the render, which no prediction can see. #145 was a
real optimisation resting on an assumption that B5's own baked planes invalidated.
It costs the ~310M cycles back; the 479M hit-path win (8ccfd174) is untouched, so
the walk is still far ahead of this morning.

★ FOUR WRONG HYPOTHESES BEFORE THIS ONE: a stale remap (the task title's guess),
a missing neutral in the chosen 16, st_patch_new_ink rewriting slot RGBs (it does
not — it re-points indices to the nearest EXISTING slot), and then, writing the
fix, I set VPP_KEEP_CHUNKY to 0 and dropped the lazy term, which disabled the
chunky pass entirely and turned the viewport SOLID BLACK. What broke the cycle was
the 256-colour Falcon build as ground truth: it shows red/cyan HUD text is
AUTHORED (so the "good" ST reference was the degraded frame — I had the polarity
backwards) and clean grey walls (so the freckles were real).

★ THE CHECKS ALL REPORTED SUCCESS WHILE THE SCREEN WAS BLACK. "STALE -> c2p"
fired, both composite paths were exercised, the fallback demonstrably worked — and
nothing was drawn. Only an implausible AE sent me to look at the image.

★ AND THE GATE THAT SHOULD HAVE CAUGHT THE ORIGINAL REGRESSION COULD NOT. The AE
reference used in #144/#142 is a PRE-COMMAND-BAR frame, and the palette only moves
once the command bar's inks arrive, so the bug was outside what the gate could
see. A walk AE gate must wait for the command bar (70 s settle), and must compare
against a frame confirmed against the Falcon.

diag: FRUA_PALTRACE — #141 is the 16-colour budget, not a stale remap

★ IT IS NOT INTERMITTENT — THE HARNESS WAS. Eight boots of the slot-B walk
fixture: AE = 0 six times, AE = 61,848 twice, and the two bad frames are
BYTE-IDENTICAL to each other, which is not what random corruption looks like.
Diffing the traces shows the runs agree for 50 events exactly and the "bad" ones
then simply continue — three small palette writes, a re-band, then ~80
`setpal first=97 count=6` (palette cycling). They did not diverge, they
PROGRESSED: to the complete walk screen WITH the command bar, while the clean runs
were photographed before the bar was drawn. A 70 s settle reproduces it every
time, so the repro is deterministic now.

★ WHICH MEANS THE AE REFERENCE FRAME USED THROUGHOUT #144 AND #142 IS AN
INCOMPLETE STATE. st-dungeon-skipfill.png has an empty command-bar box, so every
AE = 0 in that work compared one pre-command-bar frame with another. Those
changes were all in the 3D viewport and the gate did cover that, so their
conclusions stand — but it never exercised the HUD/command-bar palette path,
which is precisely where this bug lives. A walk AE gate has to wait for the
command bar or it silently tests less than it appears to.

★ AND THE CAUSE IS ONE NUMBER. Distinct CLUT indices per re-band across a boot:
7, 84, 59, 59, 129, 129, 182, 182, 32, 32, 16, 20, 64, 66. The complete walk frame
asks for 64-66 colours against ST_NCOL = 16 — and the re-band that speckles runs
with vp_active=1 chunky_ok=1, i.e. the viewport IS folded into the quant source
correctly. Nothing is stale. The command bar's inks join the competition for
QUANT_KEEP's six exact slots, the wall colours lose, and the median cut puts greys
on red/cyan.

Grey -> red/cyan is a HUE error, not an approximation, so it narrows to either the
16 chosen colours carrying no neutral or the nearest-match metric mis-picking.
Both are #138/#139 (offline pre-quantise) rather than a remap repair.

FRUA_PALTRACE traces every event that can move the remap — palette installs with
first/count, new-ink patch accept/decline, re-band run/skip with the viewport

events.title: The wash was one flat colour because XfRand's low bits are always zero
events.message:
The wash was one flat colour because XfRand's low bits are always zero

KC, from the first play: the game-over wash only showed in the left-hand
column of the play area. It looked like a drawing bug and it was a
random-number bug.

XfRand called itself "the same maximal 8-bit LFSR (taps $B4)". $B4 is
not a primitive tap for a left-shifting Galois LFSR -- the feedback has
to reach bit 0, and $B4 = %10110100 has its low TWO bits clear. So bit 0
of every output is zero for ever, bit 1 is zero from the second step on,
and the period is 65 rather than 255. GoWashRow's AND #3 therefore
returned 0 almost always and every cell came out pattern 0. The
left-hand column survived because GoWashTick stirs the seed once a pass,
which puts the low bits back for exactly one cell before the shift
clears them again.

One byte: $B4 -> $1D, droid.asm's own polynomial, which is primitive.
Two seeds on one polynomial are two independent sequences, which is all
XfRand ever needed from being separate.

It was not only the wash. Three of the four other callers mask with
AND #$F, which could only produce six of sixteen values -- so
XfPutRandom's CMP #3 : BEQ at $551 had never been taken in any transfer
game ever played on this port, its CMP #5 was a coarse near-even split
instead of 5-in-16, and XfGetMove's CPU target row could only be 1, 5, 9
or 13. The board and the opponent were both less varied than the
original's, invisibly, since Layer 10.

Verified: the wash now covers the whole play area with a mix of all four
densities and the game still restarts after the hold. Written up as
BUGS.md #14, with the simulation of both polynomials.

events.title: perf: memoise plat_ticks — __udivsi3 212.3M -> 87.4M cycles (-59%)
events.message:
perf: memoise plat_ticks — __udivsi3 212.3M -> 87.4M cycles (-59%)

#142's next item after the tile hit path. The 68000 has no 32-bit divide, and
#125's --wrap histogram says where they come from: 63% of every software division
in the program is plat_ticks — 121,168 of 191,501 over a boot plus a walk. The
200 Hz source advances 200 times a second while TickCount is asked far more
often, so nearly all of those divides recompute an answer that has not changed.
Cache the last (h200 -> tick) pair; the divide now happens once per 5 ms tick.

    __udivsi3   212,288,132 -> 87,370,516   (-59%)
    plat_ticks   96,248,568 -> 85,724,576

★ THE CACHE IS RACE-FREE BY CONSTRUCTION, NOT BY LUCK. plat_ticks is also called
from the sound VBL (jt1091 -> jt1149 -> TickCount), and a two-word cache written
by an interrupt is exactly what tears on a 16-bit bus — a long store is two bus
cycles. The interrupt path does not touch the cache: it computes directly, as it
already had to, because Supexec is a TRAP and trapping inside an interrupt
handler is fatal here (g_plat_in_super exists for that reason). That leaves the
main path as sole reader AND writer, and it cannot race with itself.

NOT a multiply-shift: exact /10 over the counter's range needs a 64-bit
intermediate, and the same histogram shows __udivdi3 costing FOUR __udivsi3 calls
apiece — worse than what it replaces.

★ #125's CAVEAT DOES NOT CARRY OVER, AND THAT HAD TO BE MEASURED. It warned that
a caller count cannot tell a hot path from a busy wait, since WaitNextEvent spins
on GetNextEvent + TickCount. True of the BOOT: 2,962 calls, all 2,962 timing out,
35,192 spin iterations. Not true of the WALK, which is the phase that matters
here — 63,736 divides, 27,248 TickCount calls, only 8,977 spin iterations, so
~14% of walk divides are the wait and the rest are real work. #125's dump fires
at "menu: modal up" only, so boot.c now dumps every 8 renders too (FRUA_DIVPROF)
and the walk figure is a later dump minus the boot one.

Remaining divide sites, for whoever picks this up: dc_map 22,620 (two sites),
qd_planar_bridge_rect 19,211, __udivdi3 3,903 (a 64-bit divide, 4x the cost),
jt1134 3,314.

★ AN INTERMITTENT FAULT SURFACED HERE AND IS NOT THIS COMMIT'S. One AE run came
back 61,752 with a SPECKLED viewport and red/cyan HUD text — the RGB-nearest
fallback signature. It is not reproducible: the same binary gives AE = 0. So the
memoised clock is exonerated, but the fault is real and it matches #141's
signature (speckled, stale remap suspected), now seen in the WALK rather than a
title screen. s_rb_stale did NOT fire, so it is not the lazy-chunky staleness I
first assumed. Recorded on #141.

★ AND IT CORRECTS SOMETHING I ASSERTED IN e697fe99: that the chunky arm
reproducing an older screenshot at AE = 0 "establishes the fixture is
deterministic". It is mostly reproducible, not deterministic — roughly one run in
six differs. Every AE = 0 in this work is a single sample of that, which is
evidence against gross breakage but does NOT rule out a fault appearing one run
in six.

make test 471 passed; ST 68000, Atari 020, Amiga AGA and Amiga ECS clean.

Refs #142, #141.

chunky->planar BRIDGE for the viewport is gone and the engine stamps planes:

and 10.4% of all cycles in the window, screen pixel-identical (AE = 0). The

The chunky viewport pass has one remaining reader — st_reband copies s_vp_scratch
over a shadow of s_chunky so the 16-colour palette is derived from the walls and
sky, not just the HUD — and e697fe99 measured what deleting it outright costs:
AE = 45,472 against AE = 0, wall indices falling to the RGB-nearest fallback.

But that reader is RARE. A re-band happens at scene transitions; the palette
dirty flag is set BEFORE the render. So ask the backend whether a re-quantise is
coming and draw the chunky viewport only on those frames.

  dsp_reband_pending()          is a re-band due at the next present?
  dsp_viewport_chunky_valid(v)  tell the backend whether the scratch is fresh

★ ASKING BEATS RE-RENDERING ON DEMAND. The obvious alternative — st_reband calls
back into the engine for a fresh chunky viewport — runs a full render from INSIDE
present, re-entering l6148/jt199 and the A5 clip save/restore mid-frame. On an
engine whose globals are A5-relative that is a reentrancy hazard for a saving the
prediction gets anyway.

★ THE PREDICTION OVER-PREDICTS ON PURPOSE. s_dirty is not the re-band condition:
present also skips when the CLUT already matches the banded one. So `pending`
fires more often than a re-band does. That costs an unnecessary chunky pass; the
opposite error costs a palette derived from LAST frame's walls. Wrong in the
cheap direction by construction.

★ AND A WRONG PREDICTION IS COUNTED, NOT SILENT. If a re-band ever lands on a
frame the engine skipped, s_rb_stale increments and DBG.LOG says so once. Without
it the failure mode is a subtly wrong shade nobody traces back here — and the
FRUA_VPPLANAR verifier cannot see it, since the verifier only runs where the
chunky path is alive.

MEASURED over a fixture walk:

    renders 8    skipped 6    drawn 2    rebands seen 2    reband-on-stale 0

`rebands seen = 2` is what makes `stale = 0` evidence rather than a tautology —
the check ran and found the scratch fresh both times. The two draws are the scene
entry, where the palette is being established.

Profile (same drive, same window) against the two arms of e697fe99:

    l309c_tile          639.7M -> 482.0M   (never-draw floor 483.8M)
    render_3d_faithful  313.7M -> 159.0M   (floor 159.0M)

It lands on the floor because the profiled window is steady walking with no
palette change, so nearly every render skips; the draws cluster at transitions
outside the window. Both measurements agree. AE = 0 at the fixture state, and the
composite is still COPY (B5).

★ FOUR RUNS PRODUCED NO COUNTER OUTPUT BEFORE THESE NUMBERS EXISTED, and each
time the silence was a threshold above the render count, not a zero. "No output"
and "a reading of zero" are the same text. The log now fires on the first call
during investigation; what ships logs every 256th render, because dbg_log goes
through Cconws and paints into screen memory on this machine — a per-frame line
corrupts the display AND skews the timing it exists to measure.

LIMITS: eight renders, two re-bands, one route. If a palette install lands
BETWEEN the render and the present, that frame was skipped and the re-band
quantises stale walls; it did not happen here, and s_rb_stale is what would catch
it — on hardware too, since it ships compiled in.

make test 471 passed; ST 68000, ST diag, Atari 020, Amiga AGA and Amiga ECS clean.

Closes #145. Refs #144.

events.title: render: split the planar writers from the verifier — and find what the chunky pass still feeds
events.message:
render: split the planar writers from the verifier — and find what the chunky pass still feeds

#144's plan was to delete the chunky viewport pass once the planes were proven.
The planes ARE proven (b4849085: the composite copies them, 844,096 pixels, zero
mismatches) and the deletion is still WRONG. Two readers stood behind those
writes. One is fixed here; the other is a subsystem's worth of work and the
deletion is demoted to an opt-in flag until it exists.

WHAT SHIPS: FRUA_VPP_WRITE compiles the planar writers in any ST/STe planar
build, FRUA_VPPLANAR additionally keeps the chunky path as a REFERENCE and runs
the verifier. So the viewport is composited from the engine's planes in the
shipping binary, with no chunky->planar conversion — and the screen is
PIXEL-IDENTICAL to the pre-change build, AE = 0 through the slot-B walk fixture.
Amiga is excluded until its backend registers dsp_viewport_planes: the hook would
return NULL and nothing would stamp, but the caches are ~56 KB of BSS an A1200's
chip RAM should not carry for nothing.

★ READER ONE, FIXED: THE BACKDROP'S OWN SOURCE. bfc40e9f built the planar strips
by reading the scaled image back out of vtgt, justified at the time as the SAFER
choice — "the mirror cannot disagree with the picture through a scaling
difference of my own making". True, and it quietly made the planar path depend on
the chunky path it was meant to replace. Deleting the chunky pass took the source
with it: the walls survived (tile cache) and the sky and floor came back BLACK.
The scale maps are hoisted to file scope and the planar rebuild now scales
g_back_img itself, so the tables still keep #132's divides rare and the
dependency is gone. Correct either way, so it lands regardless.

★ READER TWO, NOT FIXED: THE QUANTISER. st_reband copies s_vp_scratch over a
shadow of s_chunky before quantising, so the 16-colour palette is derived from
the walls and sky and not just the HUD — display_ste.c says so, and says exactly
what breaks without it: the wall indices fall to the RGB-nearest fallback and
come back in HUD greys. That is what the planes-only build renders.

It does NOT transfer to the planar side. The planes hold SLOT numbers, already
collapsed through the current remap, while the quantiser needs the original CLUT
indices WITH populations in order to choose that remap. Recovering them from the
planes is circular. The way out is to hand the backend the viewport's index
HISTOGRAM instead of its pixels: a cached tile's index counts are fixed when it
is converted, so a frame's histogram is O(distinct) per blit rather than
O(pixels). Subsystem, not tweak — hence -DFRUA_VPP_NOCHUNKY, which builds and is
known to render wrong, so it cannot rot before someone takes that on.

★ MEASURED ON ONE BINARY. A new video.cfg key (vpplanar=off, same reader as
display_nova's novalut) selects the arms without a rebuild — two builds differ in
layout and codegen, which is how a performance claim quietly becomes a claim
about the compiler:

    chunky + c2p arm      AE =      0   pixel-identical to the pre-change build
    planes-only arm       AE = 45,472
    shipping default      AE =      0   planes out, chunky kept, conversion gone

The chunky arm reproducing an older build's screenshot exactly also establishes
the fixture is deterministic, so 45,472 is signal and not boot noise.

★ AND THE VERIFIER COULD NOT HAVE CAUGHT EITHER OF THEM. It only ever runs in a
build where the chunky path is alive — that is what it compares against — so
"uncovered = 0, MISSED = 0, MISMATCH = 0" were all true and all irrelevant to
what breaks when the reference is removed. Green meant "the two paths agree while
both run", never "the planar path stands alone". A screenshot caught the black
backdrop; the backend's own comment named the palette. Worth remembering the next
time a counter says a migration is finished.

I also owe a correction: I described the remaining step as "delete the chunky
writes and l309c_tile's 19.9% collapses into the 11.6% already being paid". Too
clean. Part of that pass is feeding the palette derivation, and that part has to
be REPLACED, not removed.

make test 471 passed; ST 68000, ST diag, ST no-chunky, Atari 020, Amiga AGA and
Amiga ECS all build clean.

Refs #144, #138.
