events.title: render: composite the viewport by COPYING the engine's planes (ADR-0016 B5)
events.message:
render: composite the viewport by COPYING the engine's planes (ADR-0016 B5)

The switch #144 has been building toward. The engine stamps the viewport's
bitplanes as it draws — tiles from the cache, backdrop strips, shell spans — and
the ST composite now MOVES those planes into the pages instead of converting a
chunky scratch. The chunky->planar conversion no longer runs for the viewport at
all.

Shape:

  dsp_viewport_planes(&pitch)          backend lends a page-layout plane buffer,
                                       absolute screen coords, NULL if it wants
                                       the chunky scratch instead
  dsp_viewport_commit_planes(x,y,w,h)  "these planes hold the frame"
  st_vp_composite_copy()               moves them into every page

The layout stays platform's business: the buffer, its pitch and its interleave
live in display_ste.c, and a backend that never registers hands back NULL, so
Falcon/TT and both Amiga paths keep the chunky scratch by CONSTRUCTION rather
than by my remembering to guard them.

★ THE EDGE GROUPS ARE MERGED, NOT COPIED. A 16-pixel group is the smallest unit
of ST-Low plane storage and the viewport's left edge (x = 24) sits in the MIDDLE
of group 1 — pixels 16..23 there are the stone frame around the hole. Copying
whole groups would blank eight columns of chrome every frame. Each group carries
a mask of the pixels we own: a whole group is two long stores, the one partial
group is four masked word merges. That is also what makes the per-frame clear
safe to do on whole groups — bits we do not own are discarded at merge time.

★ THE A/B KNOB IS RUNTIME (st_planar_viewport). 0 makes the accessor return NULL,
the engine keeps to the chunky scratch and the composite converts exactly as
before — the old path, SAME BINARY. A compile-time probe has moved the incidence
of a rendering bug in this tree before (#91).

★ AND THE PATH SAYS WHICH ONE IT IS. A copy composite that silently never engaged
would fall back to the c2p and produce a PIXEL-IDENTICAL screen — the one failure
this change cannot be caught by looking at, and the exact shape of thing that has
gone wrong repeatedly here. So each path logs a one-shot marker. The run reports
"ste: viewport composite = COPY (B5)" and NO c2p marker at all, so the copy is
live and exclusive rather than inferred from a picture that looks the same either
way.

VERIFIED: 844,096 pixels over a full walk, 0 mismatches — and that number now
means more than it did, because the verifier is no longer checking a mirror
nothing reads. It is checking the pixels actually on screen against the chunky
reference. Frame confirmed by screenshot through the slot-B walk fixture: stone
frame intact, sky, corridor, floor, door, compass.

★ THE AMIGA BUILD CAUGHT A REAL BUG. The plane fetch and clear went in OUTSIDE
the #ifdef, so every build without FRUA_VPPLANAR — AGA, ECS, the Atari 020 and
the shipping ST — failed to compile, while the ST diagnostic build I was
iterating on stayed green throughout. All five targets are built here now.

NOT A SPEEDUP YET, and the profile from this build must not be read as one: the
chunky writers still run so the verifier has a reference, so planar_tile_blit +
planar_tile_build (14.2%) is work that will REPLACE l309c_tile's 19.9%, not add
to it. The drive also reached only 81 keys against 139 earlier, so cross-run
shares are not comparable. The measurable win needs the chunky viewport writes
deleted and the writes promoted from FRUA_VPPLANAR to FRUA_PLANAR — deliberately
separate, so this lands with the verifier still attached.

make test 471 passed; AGA, ECS, Atari 020, ST 68000 and the diag build all clean.

Refs #144.

events.title: render: skip the perspective-shell fills when the backdrop will cover them
events.message:
render: skip the perspective-shell fills when the backdrop will cover them

First change in #144 that alters what the engine draws, rather than mirroring it.

1e0a2610 measured the three shell regions tiling the 88x88 viewport hole EXACTLY
and with no overlap — 7,744 pixels a frame — and every one of them landing inside
the rect the backdrop then repaints opaquely. The hole was being painted three
times before a wall tile landed: the scratch clear, the fills, the backdrop. So
stop drawing the middle one when the last one will cover it.

The condition is the backdrop's PRESENCE, not the fill colour. A dungeon cell's
fills read index 0 and the scratch clear already wrote 0, so there they are
redundant twice over — but that reasoning does not generalise: a town or outdoor
cell sets its own non-zero colours, and a chunky backend (Falcon/TT) has no clear
at all, since vtgt IS the shared surface. Backdrop coverage is the invariant that
holds in every one of those cases. With no backdrop (id == 0) the fills ARE the
picture and are drawn exactly as before.

★ RUNTIME FLAG, NOT A COMPILE-TIME ONE, so both A/B arms are one binary. A
compile-time probe has moved the incidence of a rendering bug in this tree before
(#91) and four variants of one masked it entirely; a flag that only gates a branch
cannot.

★ THE PROOF IS A READBACK, AND IT NEEDED A SECOND CONTROL TO BE WORTH ANYTHING.
Containment showed the backdrop's RECT covers the fills; it cannot show every pixel
of that rect is written. So under FRUA_FILLSENT the skipped hole is stamped 0xFE
and survivors counted after the backdrop, before the wall tiles could mask them.
First run: 124 frames, 960,256 pixels read, 0 survivors — and that number is
exactly what a stamp that never landed would also produce. Counting the stamp
itself closed it:

    frames 135    STAMPED 1,045,440    read 1,045,440    SURVIVORS 0

135 x 7,744 = 1,045,440, so the sentinel reached every pixel of every frame and the
backdrop overwrote all of them. tf: regions = 0 confirms the fills really were
skipped throughout, and the planar mirror still verifies clean over the same
1,045,440 pixels with 0 mismatches.

★ AND THE FRAME WAS LOOKED AT, which nearly went wrong in the usual way. The first
"verification" screenshot was the MAIN MENU: hatari_ui.sh's beginplay prints "done
-- in the dungeon" unconditionally, and it had not got there — the design has no
seeded party, so ADD CHARACTER listed nothing and BEGIN ADVENTURING bounced. A
frame that exercises none of this code would have looked perfectly reassuring in a
report. Driven instead through the slot-B walk fixture (p / l / b / b): starfield
sky, stone corridor, receding floor, door, compass, 10,8 12:00 AM, no gaps.

SCOPE: HEIRS dungeon cells over one route. Town and overland cells carry non-zero
fill colours and a different backdrop id — reachable via FRUA_ENTRY_LEVEL, not run
here. The skip is correct there by construction (no backdrop, no skip) but that is
an argument, not a measurement.

Shipping binary carries 0 vpp/vpb/tf strings.

Refs #144.

events.title: render: mirror the perspective-shell fills as planar spans — and find they are invisible
events.message:
render: mirror the perspective-shell fills as planar spans — and find they are invisible

Third layer of #144. The fills need none of the machinery the tiles and the backdrop
needed: a solid region is what bitplanes are natively good at, so planar_span_stlow
writes a constant word per plane per group. No mask, no conversion, no cache.

But the counters that went in beside it answer a better question than "how fast".
The three shell regions are laid FIRST, and the backdrop that follows covers the
whole viewport hole opaquely — map_px, no key colour, over exactly the
g_a5_3056..3052 x 3054..3050 rect the fills clip to.

MEASURED over a 139-key walk: 393 regions, 1,014,464 fill pixels written, and
1,014,464 of them inside the rect the backdrop repaints. All of them. Every frame.

The arithmetic pins down more than the containment test asked for. 1,014,464 / 7,744
is exactly 131 — one full 88x88 hole per frame — so the three regions sum to exactly
the hole's area, and since their union is contained in it they must TILE it exactly,
with no overlap. vpp: checked comes back the same number, so the verifier's coverage
is precisely the hole and nothing else.

Which means the viewport hole is painted THREE TIMES before a single wall tile lands:
the scratch clear, the three fills, the backdrop — each covering all 7,744 pixels,
each fully overwriting the one before. Making this layer planar optimises something
invisible; the win is to SKIP it whenever a backdrop will cover. That is a behaviour
change, so it is a separate commit with a different proof: a runtime switch so both
A/B arms are ONE binary, and screen-hash equality. NOT this verifier, which by
construction cannot see a difference in pixels it never compares.

★ TWO LIMITS ON WHAT THIS SHOWS, both in the optimistic direction if ignored.
The span path is EXERCISED BUT UNVERIFIED: every pixel it writes is overdrawn before
the comparison runs, so MISMATCH = 0 is not evidence about planar_span_stlow here.
It still has to exist — a cell with backdrop id == 0 has no backdrop at all, and the
mirror needs it when this goes live — but proving it needs such a cell. And `hidden`
is a rect-containment test, not a readback: it proves the backdrop's rect covers the
fills and that the backdrop writes that rect opaquely, not that each pixel was
individually overwritten.

Mirror still verifies clean: 1,014,464 pixels, 0 mismatches, with the fills, the
backdrop strips and the wall tiles all writing it in draw order.

No behaviour change: inside FRUA_VPPLANAR, nothing reads the mirror back.
make test 471 passed.

Refs #144.

events.title: render: mirror the dungeon backdrop as cached planar strips, and price the band split
events.message:
render: mirror the dungeon backdrop as cached planar strips, and price the band split

Second layer of #144, same staging as the tiles in 07100171: convert it, blit it
into the planar mirror, verify every pixel against the chunky path, change nothing
on screen. The backdrop is the easiest layer to move — it is the BOTTOM one, so it
needs no mask (the trapezoid fills under it are wholly covered), and it is static
per level, so one conversion serves every frame until the party changes zone. The
chunky path rescales and stores all 7,744 pixels every single render.

It gets its OWN cache rather than a corner of the tile one, because its key has to
carry a generation: a new level's BACK.CTL replaces g_back_img wholesale while
(slot, idx) and the remap fingerprint can all stay put, so a shared cache would
happily serve the previous dungeon's sky. Putting the generation IN the key instead
leaks an entry and its pool words per backdrop — the tile cache never evicts, by
design, because wall art is bounded. So: a private 4,000-word cache, flushed whole
when the generation or the hole's dimensions move.

Source is the scaled image the chunky path just wrote into vtgt, not g_back_img, so
the mirror cannot disagree with the picture through a scaling difference of my own
invention. Read only on a rebuild.

RESULT over a 139-key walk: 690 strips, 580 hits / 50 rebuilds / 60 misses, pool and
table never exhausted, and 1,068,672 pixels compared with ZERO mismatches.

★ THE BAND SPLIT IS UNNECESSARY TODAY, AND I MEASURED THAT INSTEAD OF READING IT.
The plan called for one strip per band because the backdrop's content differs by
band by construction (sky above, floor below), so the tiles' band-agreement result
could not simply be assumed to transfer. Two instrumented runs later: 552 band pairs
with 0 differing entries, and a whole-screen control of 1,242 pairs across bands 0..9
— chrome and HUD included — with not one differing band. The reason is one line of
display_ste.c: quant_banded is called with nbands = 1 and the single palette is
REPLICATED into all ten slots (ADR-0016 B1, to kill the #40 seams). Unanimous
because it is one palette. The split stays regardless — st_build_hw_palette keeps
the raster-split machinery so per-band anchoring can return, and it costs 5 entries
against 580 hits — but the rationale in the code is now the true one.

★ AND IT BOUNDS d419e311, which read the tiles' 3,544/3,544 agreement as proof that
"quantize.h's exact-slot reservation holds ACROSS re-bands". It does not prove that:
one replicated palette produces the identical measurement and is the likelier cause.
The (slot, idx) key is still correct, for that reason rather than this one — but if
per-band anchoring ever returns, the question reopens for the tiles.

★ THE CONTROL IS WHY ANY OF THAT IS KNOWN. A bare "DIFF = 0" cannot tell agreement
from a comparison that never fires, so the same pass also compares the whole
256-entry row, and a second control compares every band against band 0. Both came
back 0, which is what sent me to the backend instead of to a conclusion. Also moved
the per-strip comparison OUT of the strip loop: the index union it compares over is
filled by rebuilds, so a mid-loop check runs against a half-built set and can only
MISS disagreements — the optimistic direction.

profile: st_profile.sh's two WAIT loops now die with the emulator, like the drive
loop already did (e6c6f59d). Killing Hatari under a waiting run did not kill the
run: it kept polling run.log, which the NEXT invocation deletes and recreates, then
drove keys into the new run's emulator. Two key streams into one window and two
scripts aggregating one profile — caught because both printed "walked 135 keys" and
byte-identical cycle totals (3,046,928,298). That contaminated run is discarded; the
numbers above are from a clean one.

No behaviour change: all of this is inside FRUA_VPPLANAR, nothing reads the mirror
back, and the default build carries no vpb/vpp strings. make test 471 passed.

Refs #144, #138.

events.title: planar: fingerprint a cached tile on the remap entries it actually draws
events.message:
planar: fingerprint a cached tile on the remap entries it actually draws

The tile cache keyed each entry on a checksum of the whole 256-entry band
remap row, so a tile went stale whenever ANY index moved — including the
majority it never draws. Over a 125-key walk that cost 455 rebuilds against
only 67 genuine first sightings; every one of those is a full chunky->planar
conversion of a tile whose planes were already correct.

Narrow the fingerprint to the tile's own dependency set: the post-rebase
chunky values it writes, which are exactly what index the remap. The caller
collects them in one pass over the body (the same pass shape that already
builds the LUT) and hands them to pt_cache_reserve; the entry stores them and
pt_cache_get re-fingerprints over that set. Cheaper too — nused iterations
rather than 256.

Past PT_MAX_USED (48) distinct indices the entry keeps nused == 0 and falls
back to the whole row: coarser, never wrong. pt_set_used clamps an oversized
count to that same fallback, so a malformed caller cannot walk off uidx[].

The tests pair the two halves of the property, which whole-row fingerprinting
could not express: moving an index NO tile draws must invalidate nothing,
moving one a tile DOES draw must invalidate exactly that entry. Also the
fallback arm, the clamp, the wall-set flush and pool exhaustion.

★ The overflow-clamp case passed under mutation at first, twice. The test's
own helper clamped nused before the cache ever saw it, so the guard was
unreachable from the test; a tile with 256 distinct values still did not
reach it. It only fails-when-broken now because the test calls
pt_cache_reserve directly with a deliberately oversized count. Second green
test this session that turned out unable to fail.

Refs #144.

events.title: render: wire the planar tile cache into the real blit — and prove it in situ
events.message:
render: wire the planar tile cache into the real blit — and prove it in situ

The cache (2ef1b201) is mutation-tested on the host, but against SYNTHETIC tiles and
synthetic LUTs. Before anything on screen depends on it, it has to be shown equal on
the real renderer: real wall pieces, real per-set magenta keys, real band remaps,
real arbitrary x. Same discipline as FRUA_TILEVERIFY and the b123ver rebake proof
already in this tree.

So under FRUA_VPPLANAR every colour tile blit in l309c_tile now ALSO composes the
chunky->SLOT table, fetches or converts the tile through the cache, blits it
word-wise into a planar MIRROR of the screen, and records coverage in draw order.
At commit — while the chunky scratch still holds the frame — every covered pixel is
compared against remap[band][the chunky byte the normal blit left].

★ NOTHING READS THE MIRROR BACK. This cannot change the picture, only report. The
default build is untouched: 0 vpp strings, and the ST binary differs in size only
when the flag is on.

RESULT: 696 blits, 97,233 pixels compared, ZERO mismatches. The cache never ran out
either (full = 0, no-cache = 0), so the 48 KB pool and 160-entry table sit well above
the 28-34 KB / 48-64 tile working set measured in c38a7b79.

★ AND IT ANSWERS THE QUESTION I COULD NOT SETTLE BEFORE, against my own optimism.
9fff3418 proved the remap agrees ACROSS BANDS at one instant; I noted that said
nothing about the remap changing over TIME and built the epoch so the cache would be
correct either way. It changes: rebuilt = 189 against miss = 33. So "convert 64 tiles
once and never again" was wrong — entries genuinely go stale, and the epoch is
load-bearing rather than defensive. The rebuilds all land in boot/entry, where the
palettes churn; they were flat across the transition into the walk. How flat they
stay over a SUSTAINED walk is not yet established — the first attempt at that number
was cut short when my own cleanup killed the emulator mid-drive (the drive guard from
e6c6f59d caught it and voided the run rather than spinning, which is what it is for).

KNOWN TOO COARSE, and the counters say so: the epoch is a checksum over the WHOLE
256-entry band row, while a tile touches only a handful of indices. An unrelated
entry moving therefore rebuilds a tile whose own pixels did not change, so some part
of those 189 rebuilds is my invalidation, not the art. Narrowing it to the indices a
tile actually uses is the obvious next step and has a clean before/after in `rebuilt`.

Still NOT the switch: the viewport scratch is cleared each frame and the backdrop and
trapezoid fills draw into it chunky alongside the tiles, so planar tile writes alone
would simply be overwritten by the composite. Backdrop (static per level, one cached
conversion) and fills (planar spans, the cheap case) have to follow before the
scratch and its c2p can go.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: planar: the wall-tile cache — convert once to planes+mask, blit word-wise
events.message:
planar: the wall-tile cache — convert once to planes+mask, blit word-wise

#144's core, built and proved on the host before it goes near the target. Not yet
wired into the render path: that needs the backdrop and the trapezoid fills to go
planar too before the chunky scratch can be dropped, and it is a separate change.

WHAT IT REPLACES. l309c_tile's colour path is a MASKED PER-PIXEL blit — a 255 key
plus per-set magenta keys, one store per surviving pixel. That is not something you
can stamp into bitplanes cheaply: a masked plane write is read-modify-write per
pixel across four planes, the ~1900 cycles/pixel scalar path ADR-0016 exists to
avoid. The answer is not a faster transpose but FEWER of them — measured, 15-28
tile blits per frame against only 48-64 DISTINCT tiles in a whole 137-key walk
(the count plateaus), 28-34 KB in this form.

planar_tile.h stores a tile as, per row per 16-pixel group, four plane words then a
MASK word. The mask is the point: it turns transparency into `dst = (dst & ~m) |
(src & m)`, a word operation, so a clipped or keyed pixel costs nothing extra.
Arbitrary x is handled by shifting across group boundaries at blit time rather than
keeping pre-shifted copies (16 shifts x 64 tiles is ~550 KB against 34 KB), and the
clip rectangle is folded into the mask so edges need no separate path and cannot
write outside it.

planar_tile_cache.h keys on (slot, idx) — NOT (slot, idx, band). Tiles straddle
band boundaries constantly (3,544 straddling blits, up to five bands each) but the
per-band remaps were measured identical for the values a tile writes, every time,
because quantize.h reserves exact slots for kept colours.

★ THAT AGREEMENT IS SPATIAL, AND THE EPOCH IS WHY THAT MATTERS. Bands agreeing with
each other at one instant says nothing about the remap changing over TIME, and a
re-band rebuilds every band palette (~21 in a driven walk). So entries carry the
remap generation they were built against and a mismatch is a miss. The cache is
therefore correct whether the remap turns out to be stable across re-bands or not,
instead of resting on an assumption I have not measured — and the `rebuilt` counter
reports which world we are actually in. A stale rebuild reuses the entry's slab, so
re-bands cannot leak the pool. A wall-set change is NOT expressible as an epoch (the
same idx becomes different art), so that needs pt_cache_flush() on the binder change.
Pool or table exhaustion returns NULL and the caller keeps its per-pixel path, which
makes running out a slowdown and never a wrong picture.

BOTH TESTS ARE MUTATION-TESTED, because a green test that cannot fail is worth
nothing and this session has produced two of those already:
  planar_tile      — shift direction reversed / spill group dropped / clip removed /
                     mask ignored: all four caught.
  planar_tile_cache— epoch check removed / flush not clearing / pool bound removed /
                     rebuild allocating fresh: all four caught.
The blit is compared against a naive per-pixel scatter over random tiles, random
LUTs with transparent entries, EVERY sub-word x offset 0..15, and clips cutting all
four sides, onto a page pre-filled with noise so the merge has to preserve what the
mask does not cover.

events.title: profile: analyser that closes the band question — pair each dump with the RE-BANDS before it
events.message:
profile: analyser that closes the band question — pair each dump with the RE-BANDS before it

9fff3418 measured 3,544 straddling tile blits with remap DIFFER = 0 and called the
(slot, idx) cache key safe. That commit's own caveat was that the run carried
FRUA_TILEPROF + FRUA_R3DPROF while re-band logging lives under FRUA_STPROF — so it
was never verified that a re-band happened at all during the drive.

That matters more than it sounds. A re-band rebuilds EVERY band palette from new
content, and it is the one event that could make a cached planar tile invalid. An
end-of-run "DIFFER = 0" proves nothing if every re-band landed after the last tile
was blitted: the comparison would simply never have been tested against one. A
total cannot tell those apart. An ordered walk can.

So this reads DBG.LOG in ORDER, pairs each `r3d: remap DIFFER` dump with the number
of `b4audit: reband` markers already behind it, and refuses to call a run a pass
when it cannot be one:

    no re-band at all              -> INCONCLUSIVE (rc 1)  "is FRUA_STPROF in?"
    every re-band after last blit  -> INCONCLUSIVE (rc 1)
    DIFFER > 0 after a re-band     -> BROKEN       (rc 2)
    otherwise                      -> CLOSED       (rc 0)

Verdicts mutation-tested against four synthetic logs, one per arm, each producing
its own exit code — this session has produced two guards that looked like passes
and structurally could not fail (a 3D-work check that never matched because nm
prefixes symbols with '_', and a whole-frame gate that could not fire on a title
screen), so a guard now has to demonstrate it can report failure before it is
allowed to report success.

RESULT on a three-flag run: 28 re-bands, 18 dumps ALL taken after re-bands (12, 13,
15, 18 ... 28 behind them), 270 straddling blits compared after a re-band, zero
disagreements. CLOSED — the wall indices resolve to identical slots in every band
even after re-quantisation, so quantize.h's exact-slot reservation holds ACROSS
re-bands and not merely within one. #144's cache key stays (slot, idx), ~48-64
entries, 28-34 KB; the (slot, idx, band) fallback and its ~100 KB are off the plan.

Default log path derives from the script location / GEMDOS_DIR rather than being
hardcoded, so it works from a clone.

events.title: render: tiles DO straddle bands — and the remap agrees anyway, 3544/3544
events.message:
render: tiles DO straddle bands — and the remap agrees anyway, 3544/3544

#144 flagged one risk that could have sunk the planar tile cache: a cached tile has
the index->slot remap baked in, and that remap is PER BAND (band = y*nbands/h). If
tiles straddle band boundaries the key would have to become (slot, idx, band) and
the working set would multiply.

They straddle constantly. ST_NBANDS 10 over ST_H 200 gives 20-row bands and the
viewport occupies rows 24..111, so any tile taller than ~20 rows must cross one:
3,544 straddling blits over a 137-key walk, spanning up to FIVE bands each.

But straddling was never the real question — whether the remap DIFFERS across those
bands is. It does not, in any case measured:

    STRADDLE cum   3544        max bands/tile   5
    remap SAME     3544        distinct cum    48
    remap DIFFER      0        planar bytes  28,290

Zero. The reason is quantize.h's exact-slot reservation: the wall CLUT band resolves
to the same slots in every band's palette, because per-band quantisation only
diverges on colours it has to APPROXIMATE and the wall indices are kept exactly.

So the cache key stays (slot, idx) — ~48-64 entries, 28-34 KB — and band straddling
costs nothing. The (slot, idx, band) fallback and its ~100 KB come off the plan.

The check is over the tile's REAL content: it marks the distinct source bytes of the
tile body, applies the same rebase the blit does (base + off, honouring the per-set
magenta keys), and compares remap[band][v] across every band the CLIPPED rows span.
Conservative in the right direction — comparing the values actually written, not the
whole 256-entry map.

★ CAVEAT ON THIS RUN: reband logging is under FRUA_STPROF and this build carries
FRUA_TILEPROF + FRUA_R3DPROF, so it is NOT verified here that any re-band occurred
during the drive — and a re-band is exactly when band palettes are rebuilt and
agreement could break. #142 measured ~21 re-bands in a comparable driven window so
they almost certainly did, but that is inference, not measurement. Re-run with all
three flags to close it properly before relying on the (slot, idx) key.

No behaviour change: counters are inside FRUA_TILEPROF, whose dump is nested in
FRUA_R3DPROF; a clean build carries neither.

events.title: render: count DISTINCT wall tiles — the planar cache is 64 tiles, ~34 KB
events.message:
render: count DISTINCT wall tiles — the planar cache is 64 tiles, ~34 KB

#144 set out to make render_3d_faithful a planar writer and remove the chunky
scratch. Reading the leaf first says that cannot be done the obvious way, and
measuring says how it CAN be.

WHY NOT DIRECTLY. l309c_tile's colour path is a MASKED PER-PIXEL blit — a global
255 key plus per-set magenta keys, one store per surviving pixel into the 8bpp
surface. Stamping that into bitplanes means read-modify-write per pixel across
four planes, which is the ~1900 cycles/pixel scalar path ADR-0016 exists to avoid.
Against it, c2p4st_32 turns 32 pixels into planes in about eight loads and a few
shifts, so for a MASKED blit chunky-plus-bulk-c2p genuinely wins. That is exactly
why ADR-0016's writers stamp spans and fills — cheap in planar — while the
viewport still bulk-converts. The loop is also already tight: #134 hoisted the
per-tile LUT, the row pointers and the x-clip out of the pixel loop.

The planar-native route for masked tiles is instead to convert each TILE once to
planes + mask and blit word-wise (dst = (dst & ~mask) | (src & mask)). That pays
only if tiles repeat, and volume counters cannot answer that — distinctness can.
So FRUA_TILEPROF now counts distinct (slot, idx) pairs per frame and cumulatively,
and accumulates the bytes such a cache would hold (4 planes + 1 mask, word-padded).

MEASURED over an 80-key walk through several areas:

    tile blits per render        15
    distinct tiles in that frame  9-12      <- ~1.3x reuse WITHIN a frame
    distinct cumulative           64        <- and it PLATEAUED there
    planar bytes                  34,440

So a per-frame cache is not worth building; a PERSISTENT one is. 64 tiles convert
once and are never converted again, for ~34 KB. The worst case is bounded as well:
48 pieces x 3 wall groups = 144 tiles, ~77 KB.

Left for the implementation, all visible in the same dump: the walls are only part
of the viewport — there is also a backdrop blit (static per level, so convert once)
and the trapezoid region fills (spans, which are the cheap case in planar). Tiles
land at arbitrary x, so blits need a barrel shift per plane-word; pre-shifted
variants are not an option (16 shifts x 64 tiles ~ 550 KB).

No behaviour change: the counters are inside FRUA_TILEPROF, whose dump is nested
in FRUA_R3DPROF, and a clean build carries neither.

events.title: The title screen, 25 rows of it, before the game exists
events.message:
The title screen, 25 rows of it, before the game exists

ShowTitle ($2879) copies Title_dat ($CC00) -- a raw 40 x 25 character
screen -- into screen RAM and waits 256 frames or a press of fire. Both
halves are here; the intro manual TitleLoop goes on to is deferred.

It gets a display of its own, which is the whole reason PARAFNT moved to
&3000 last commit: 25 x 640 is 16,000 contiguous bytes at &4000, the
window ends 48 CRTC units short of MA12 so no hardware wrap is involved,
and it runs before SetupRupture where the CRTC is still in SetupMode's
plain single-cycle shape. R6 alone cuts the height; R7 is left, so the
picture sits at the top of the frame and centring is Layer 14's with the
rest of the look.

THE GLYPHS ARE THE TITLE'S OWN. Twelve of its thirty-six characters --
$52 $53 $DF $E0-$E7 $FF -- are not in the ported charset, because
export_bbc.py converts only what a tile definition references and those
twelve are used by the title screen and nothing else. Adding them to the
shared charset would be the more faithful arrangement and is the better
fix, but it changes NUM_CHARS and the code->index remap that every deck
depends on, so it is KC's call rather than something to do in passing.
Until then tools/export_title.py converts the thirty-six the title needs
and touches nothing else: 576 bytes of glyphs and 564 of RLE, in bank 7
with the other three screens that take the display over.

The timeout is the original's own behaviour and also the escape hatch: a
title that could only be left by a keypress is a title that a mis-read
key turns into a hang.

And it is where the randomness finally comes from. $12B6 samples $D41B
after however long the player left the title up; TiWait leaves its dwell
in overRnd0 and GameStart stirs drSeed with it, in bank 4 where the LFSR
lives. The starting deck is no longer the same on every cold boot.

LoadDeck moved to bank 4 to pay for the shim -- it is nothing but calls,
and all but three of them are into that bank already.

Verified in jsbeeb: the rendered title matches tools/output/
title_screen_7800.png cell for cell, fire skips it into the game, and
the timeout falls through into the game on its own.

events.title: PARAFNT drops to &3000, and the other two move up behind it
events.message:
PARAFNT drops to &3000, and the other two move up behind it

Layer 11's title screen is 25 rows of 640 bytes and wants 16,000
CONTIGUOUS bytes. It fits because the title's buffers and the game's
never coexist: at title time no deck is loaded, so the sprite save
areas, the tile map, the panel and the play buffer are all idle. The
only thing standing in the middle of &3000-&7FFF was the font.

So PARAFNT goes to &3000, the save areas follow it to &3E00 and the tile
map to &4600, and the three pack exactly onto PANEL_ADDR: 3,584 + 2,048
+ 1,024 = 6,656. The framebuffer then takes &4000-&7E7F with the font
below it -- one home in both modes, no second load and no relocation.

Nothing depended on the old addresses, which is why this is three
constants and two asserts. The blitter builds its save pointer at
runtime from HI(SPR_SAVE) and stores through (svp),Y -- the indirection
that made compiling it possible in the first place -- and mapRowLo/Hi
are assembled from tilemap + r * MAP_COLS. FONT_ADDR and everything
derived from it are constants resolved in file order, and PARAFNT
already had to load after the bank staging, which starts at &3000 and
ran over &3C00 just as happily.

Verified in jsbeeb: glyph data at &3040, deck tiles at &46B4, deck
graphics in the play buffer and HUD text on the panel line after 2,000
frames.

events.title: EndGame's wash, and a debug flag to stay alive through it
events.message:
EndGame's wash, and a debug flag to stay alive through it

overPhase 2 is EndGame ($378B): the play rows wash out, "game over" goes
on the panel line, and 88 passes later the game starts again. It is
modal, taking the same shape as the console and the transfer game --
its own block in the main loop that ends the pass -- because it owns the
play buffer, and because that is what keeps PanelTick off the line the
message is on. Phase 1 could not do that: the cloud needs the sprite
pool erased and drawn like any other frame.

The view is flattened first, exactly as XferEnter4 does before the
board, so the buffer addresses as a plain 16 x 640 array.

Three departures, all in the source. The four wash characters are ours
and not by choice: $379F picks (rnd AND 3) + $7A out of the deck
charset, and $7A-$7D are NOT in the ported set -- export_bbc.py converts
only the characters some tile references, and those four are used by
EndGame and nothing else, so CHAR_PTR clamps them to entry 0 and the
first build of the wash came out blank. Four patterns in bank 7 stand in,
in black, because $37A6 writes colour $F0 and the C64's wash is a
dissolve into darkness rather than white noise. AnimAllInsideFont is not
ported -- it is the same machinery as AnimateIntoFont, which Layer 10
already declined -- so the wash boils by being repainted a row a pass.
And the message is on the panel line, which is decisions 6-8 of Layer 10
again.

A trap worth remembering: XfRand's seed is XfStart's to set and the game
over never goes through XfStart. A zero seed locks the LFSR, so every
cell came out the same pattern until GoWashStart seeded it.

DEBUG_INVULN pins the player's energy at full so a run can be taken deep
into the ship now that the free respawn is gone. It is a pin and not a
shield: damage still lands and is overwritten at the top of the next
CbCheckDeath, so everything downstream of a hit still runs.

events.title: Dying as a 001 ends the game, and the ship stops to watch
events.message:
Dying as a 001 ends the game, and the ship stops to watch

The port only ever had one of EnterGame's two arms. $143B tests
droidEnergy and $144D splits on droidType: riding something, you blow
back into a 001 and play on -- which CbCheckDeath already was -- and
already a 001, there is nothing left to fall back to and the game is
over. That one test is the whole of this.

The waypoint-0 respawn goes with it. BlowInto001 ($1573) does not move
the player, so neither do we now: fall back to a 001 and you are where
you died. That also takes BUGS.md #10's cause -- a teleport breaking
COPYCHAR's parity rule -- out of the path for good.

The cloud is $1465-$14CA. One more slot is lit each pass at a jittered
copy of the player's position, overTick running 6 down to $F0, and every
effect slot advances a frame with any that runs past the end switched
off, so the last sprites are still burning when the first have gone out.
Slot 7 is the bullet's and the C64 reuses its sprite 0 the same way --
which is why the fire block and MovePlyFire have to be frozen too, or
they put the slot out again the pass after the cloud lights it.

The ship stops while it plays: $14A8 and $14C5 call RunGame and NOT
RunDroids, so the movement, the fire and DroidsUpdate are all gated on
overPhase.

Two deviations, both in the source. The vertical jitter is the
original's (rnd AND 7) - 4 pixels; the horizontal moves whole 4-pixel
CRTC units, because our sprite X is a unit plus a shift and a
pixel-exact offset wants 16-bit arithmetic and a re-split. And a sprite
whose jitter would take it off the view is dropped rather than clamped.

It lives in bank 7 with the transfer game and the lift view -- the other
two screens that take the play area over, and where 11b-2's wash and
banner will want the shadow screen. Bank 4 had 147 bytes free and the
block was 147, so it had to move regardless. Main RAM paid for the shims
by sending ccd_reset's body the other way, to bank 4 as CbReset001,
where every field it writes but the three sprite ones already lives. The
randoms are drawn on the main-RAM side and passed in: DrRandom is bank
4's and its LFSR must stay one sequence.

Verified in jsbeeb. Fall-back arm: type 5 at zero energy came back as a
001 with energy 7, no game over, and the play buffer byte-identical
before and after. Game-over arm: the pool fills with effects at
staggered frames, droid positions are byte-identical over eight passes,
and the cloud burning out starts a fresh game with the score cleared and
shipLevel back to 1.

events.title: Boot splits in two: the machine once, the game every time
events.message:
Boot splits in two: the machine once, the game every time

main.asm ran one linear boot straight into the main loop, so every piece
of game state could lean on beebasm's assembled initial value. Layer 11
needs the game startable more than once -- a title screen at one end, a
game over at the other -- and every one of those defaults then has to be
written out loud.

GameStart is the C64's StartGame ($1242) and _entership ($1289) in one
routine, in bank 4 beside NewShipDroids and the droid tables it seeds,
ending on the random deck 4-7 and LoadDeck. Boot keeps the cold half --
mode, disc, banks, BuildCharPtrs, SprBuildMask, SetupRupture, InstallIrq,
the seed -- and calls it. Main RAM lost 20 bytes of boot in the process
and ends at &2FD3; bank 4 paid the 147.

The work is the defaults. A second game would otherwise inherit whatever
the first left behind: a console still up, a lift half-entered, a
transfer holding its verdict, the edge latch of the key that restarted
it, the top speed of the droid you were riding. Two ordering traps are
recorded in the source. CombatInit's energy is $1345's $40 -- what the
entry animation ends on, not $12A5's transient 7 -- so ccd_reset's
identical speed-clamp block is deliberately not shared with it. And
SprInit moves out of boot into GameStart, because it resets state where
SprBuildMask beside it builds a table.

DEBUG_RESTART is what makes any of this testable: R throws the game away
and starts another. It sits ABOVE the console, transfer and lift-view
blocks, each of which ends its pass with JMP ml_passend -- below them it
could not be reached from the states worth testing from, which are the
states a game can end in.

Verified in jsbeeb. Every field poked dirty -- conActive, liftMode,
moveMode, plyDying, maxEnergy, weaponType, alertLvl, score, shipLevel,
drType, drEnergy, losTurn and the speed clamp -- then R. All of it came
back clean, fifteen restarts in succession did not disturb it, the deck
re-rolls, and the buffer and panel still hold their content 800 frames
later.

events.title: Band-limit CRT shader scanlines to fix moire at scaled-down window sizes

Band-limit CRT shader scanlines to fix moire at scaled-down window sizes

The scanline sin() term aliased against the output pixel grid once curvature
warp or window scaling changed the effective sample rate. Attenuate its
amplitude with an fwidth()-based sinc term so scanlines fade to a flat wash
instead of beating, in the GLSL/SPIR-V, MSL and GLES2 shader copies.

events.title: display_ste: the viewport composite converted every pixel TWICE, once per page
events.message:
display_ste: the viewport composite converted every pixel TWICE, once per page

st_vp_composite_fast wrapped its whole chunky->planar conversion in a
`for (pg = 0; pg < NPAGES; pg++)` loop. The transpose is PAGE-INDEPENDENT: `scr`
is the shared viewport scratch and `lut` is s_band_remap + band*256 where
band = yy * ST_NBANDS / ST_H — neither depends on pg. So c2p4st_32 computed
byte-identical plane words for page 0 and page 1, and we ran the entire transpose
twice to end up with two copies of the same answer.

The slow path in this same file has always done it correctly. st_vp_composite's
own comment says so out loud — "fast: c2p per page; slow: c2p once + blit twice"
— which is the pattern this now adopts: convert into page 0, then copy that row's
span to the other page. The span is contiguous and wholly ours (block x writes 8
words at (x >> 4) * 8, so [ax, aend) is bytes [(ax>>4)*8, (aend>>4)*8) — drow+8
.. drow+56 for the live 96px viewport, and the trailing st_c2p8 column writes
inside it), so the copy is 48 bytes / 12 longs against three 32-pixel transposes.

MEASURED, like for like — 8 composites in each run, FRUA_STPROF b63play:

                        before    after
    blocks/composite       528      264      (3 blocks x 88 rows x 2 pages -> x1)
      flat32 / tex32   174/4050  87/2025
    composite t200         381      202      -47%

Pixel-identical: the walk frame at the fixture point (10,8 12:00 AM) compares
AE=0 against the pre-change capture, which is what the page-independence argument
predicts.

★ DO NOT read the rest of that run's profile as an effect of this change. It shows
c2p4st_32 at 32.8% and st_c2p_span at 26.1%, but it is a different workload: TOS
falls to 2.7% and ranked cycles rise to 3.15e9 (against 13.5% / 2.47e9 on the
baseline) because this drive hit far more re-bands, and a re-band force-fulls a
whole-frame conversion. The defensible numbers here are the per-composite ones
above, which are a ratio over an equal number of composites.

Direction this serves: the end state is no chunky->planar step at all, with
writers stamping planes directly. FRUA repaints on discrete steps rather than
continuously, so it never needed a chunky backbuffer the way a Doom/Wolf3D-style
renderer does. What remains in the walk is render_3d_faithful writing a chunky
scratch that qd_planar_bridge_rect then bridges (planar_c2p_span_stlow); making
the 3D renderer a planar writer removes both the scratch and the bridge.

events.title: The reverse that fired every pass, and held two droids together
events.message:
The reverse that fired every pass, and held two droids together

ReverseDroidDir ($1C5F) carries the byte_0_6C guard inside itself, tested
at $1C63 before it touches the speeds, and both C64 call sites reach it:
DoCollision2's _08_1 ($1BA6) as well as _ply_droid ($1A82). DrReverse
left it out on a note that both call sites had already made the test.
Only dc_player had.

So while two droids overlapped, the outer one reversed every pass and
jittered on the spot with no net drift, while DrPause16 renewed the
inner one's 16 under it so it never got to walk away. A permanent lock,
and the reason droids stick together here far more readily than on the
C64 -- where the first droid keeps the direction it was given and clears
the overlap in a few iterations.

The latch has to persist as well. byte_0_6C is cleared at _x_none
($1A3E) alone, the exit taken when no colliding pair was found at all;
ours cleared it at the top of every pass and re-latched from DrReverse,
which re-armed the reverse every other pass. drCollWas is gone in favour
of one persistent drCollHit, cleared where the C64 clears it.

Measured A/B in jsbeeb, two droids held overlapping and stepped a pass
at a time with a breakpoint on DrCollide: before, drSpdX ran
+1 -1 +1 -1; after, it reverses once and stays. Separating the pair
returns drCollHit to 0, so the next episode reverses again.

BUGS.md #7a is fixed, and its open question -- faithfulness or port
artefact -- is answered from the listing: artefact. What remains of it
is the box shape, agreed with KC as [DECISION 1] in
docs/layer-6-droids-live.md and not built here: DR_COL_W/DR_COL_H become
a generated minimum-|dx|-per-|dy| profile, the silhouette rather than a
rectangle, at box-test cost.

events.title: display_ste: count the new-ink patch, and it says INK_MAX is NOT the lever
events.message:
display_ste: count the new-ink patch, and it says INK_MAX is NOT the lever

I claimed in 2311abb2 that st_reband's 4.5% of the walk was the NEW-INK path — a step
draws indices the band palettes lack, st_patch_new_ink() declines past INK_MAX (24)
distinct new indices, and the frame is re-quantised. Plausible, and I was about to
trade fidelity for speed on it. The counters say I was wrong.

FRUA_PALDIAG now reports, per present, how often the patch is asked, whether it
accepted, WHY it declined, how many re-bands and repalettes the dirty presents chose,
and — the number the threshold actually depends on — the TRUE distinct-new-index count.
The shipping code cannot answer that last one because it stops counting at the
threshold (`break` on overflow), so under this flag it keeps counting. That makes the
diagnostic build scan more, but leaves the DECISION identical: s_ink_over is still set
at exactly the same point, and the patch declines either way.

One walk drive (90 keys through the profile window, 19,584 presents):

    patch calls   40        st_reband     49        true-n max    31
      ACCEPTED    37        st_repalette   0          true 25..32  3
      decline over 3                                  true 33..48  0
      decline none 0                                  true 49..64  0
      decline nopal 0                                 true 65+     0

The patch accepts 37 of 40. Across the driven window itself st_reband went +21 while
patch declines went +1 — so ONE re-band in twenty-one comes from the patch giving up.
The rest are the count>=32 palette installs the walk performs as it loads new art,
which is legitimate work. Raising INK_MAX from 24 to 32 would convert all three
declines (true-n never exceeded 31) and buy three re-bands out of forty-nine. Not the
lever, and not worth a fidelity trade.

Two other facts worth having on record:
  - st_repalette is ZERO. The cheap registers-only arm never fires on main, so every
    dirty present pays a full re-quant. (That arm is the #140 work, which lives on the
    parked st-per-band branch.)
  - 13,248 presents of sitting still in the dungeon produced ZERO new re-bands. The
    cost is entirely tied to movement into new art, not to idling.

So the lever for st_reband is making the RE-QUANT cheaper, not firing it less often:
the parked branch's pass-2 distance hoist already measured -41% on quant_banded, and
#139 (offline pre-quantisation) would remove it outright for known art.

Also confirms 2311abb2 against a comparable workload, which that commit could not
claim: this run is 90 keys / TOS 14.5% / 2.504e9 ranked cycles against the pre-fix
87 keys / 13.5% / 2.474e9, and qd_rebake_range has dropped from 4.5% to below the
top-20 cut while st_present (11.0), jt200_layer (7.4->7.6), render_3d (7.0->7.1),
planar_c2p (6.6) and st_reband (4.5->4.4) all hold within ~0.5pp.

events.title: quickdraw: bake the colour cursor when it is DRAWN, not on every palette write
events.message:
quickdraw: bake the colour cursor when it is DRAWN, not on every palette write

The walk profile put qd_rebake_range at 4.5% of the play loop. #123 had already
made it incremental — the right first move, and it is why this is 4.5% and not
worse — but the counters say the remaining work is almost entirely pointless.
Over one walk drive (FRUA_PALDIAG, added here):

    qd_set_palette calls   5300      rebake calls        5302
      byte-identical         21        full-path            10
      count >= 32            37        bake_full_one       242
                                       idx CHANGED          15

Fifteen. Of 5302 re-bakes, fifteen moved a baked index. The other 5287 recomputed
distances and rebuilt all 256 cursor pixels to arrive at the answer they already
had. Note also that bake_full_one and idx CHANGED are IDENTICAL at 900 calls and
at 5300 — every expensive rescan happens before the walk even starts.

The baked image has exactly one consumer (cursor_composite), so it only has to be
right when the cursor is drawn — at most once per present, against thousands of
palette writes. qd_set_palette now records the touched range and qd_bake_sync()
does the work at the draw site. The union range is deliberately conservative:
widening it can only make the eventual scan bigger, never its answer wrong, and a
union reaching 256 entries takes the existing full-rescan arm, which is correct.

Same drive after: 4 re-bakes for 6600 palette writes, and qd_rebake_range is gone
from the top-20 entirely. In the dungeon the cursor is obscured, so the answer is
that the work was never needed at all.

★ WHAT THIS COMMIT DOES *NOT* CLAIM. The other shares moved too (st_present 11.0
-> 12.9%, render_3d 7.0 -> 12.1%), and that is NOT this change: the after-run did
much more rendering, with TOS/idle collapsing 13.5% -> 2.1% and total program
cycles up 26%. A time-bounded key drive is not a constant workload between runs,
which is #121's "hold key injection constant" rule biting. The proof here is the
CALL COUNT (5302 -> 4) and the disappearance of the line, not a cycle delta.

Cursor verified visually where it is actually visible: the shield pointer draws
correctly over PLAY THE GAME on the main menu after a mouse move (the dungeon
never draws it). Structurally the sync runs immediately before the only read, so
staleness is not reachable.

Also found while measuring, and NOT touched here because it is a fidelity knob
rather than waste: st_reband's 4.5% is not from qd_set_palette at all. All 37
count>=32 writes happen before the walk, so s_dirty is not being set that way.
The trigger is the NEW-INK path in st_present — a step draws indices the band
palettes do not cover, st_patch_new_ink tries to place them, and when more than
INK_MAX (24) distinct new indices arrive it gives up and re-quantises the frame.
Walking from the stone corridor into the wood-panelled one does exactly that.
Raising INK_MAX trades fidelity for speed and wants its own measurement.

events.title: Deck 15 was reading its map off the end of leveldata
events.message:
Deck 15 was reading its map off the end of leveldata

RLE_END was $FED0, described as "covers deck 15 plus terminator". It does
not. Deck 15's stream STARTS at $FECB - five bytes before that - and needs
296 more, to $FFF8. The port decoded those five bytes and then read
whatever followed leveldata in bank 4, so deck 15 came out as open space
with a couple of bands of structure. Present since Layer 2.

What hid it: BuildLevel stops when the tile map is full rather than at a
terminator, so nothing faults; and every offline check reads the whole 64K
listing image, where the missing bytes are simply there. The Python decode,
the deck renders and the palette lab all showed deck 15 correctly while the
disc image never had the data at all. The one tool that could have caught
it - a comparison of what was EXPORTED against what a deck needs - did not
exist.

So the fix comes with that check: check_rle_extent() walks all sixteen
streams the way BuildLevel does and stops the export if any of them ends
past RLE_END. Verified by putting $FED0 back, which now fails with the deck
number and the overrun instead of shipping a broken disc.

leveldata 3207 -> 3503 bytes; bank 4 has room. Verified in jsbeeb: hop to
deck 15 and the rooms, corridors, ALERT sign and droids are all there.

Also here, make.bat: it passed -boot PARA, and main.asm SAVEs its own !BOOT
with the build stamp, so beebasm refused with "File already exists on DFS
disc image" - even into a brand new image, which is why deleting the SSD
did not help. build.ps1 already used -opt 3 for exactly this reason and
says so in a comment. make.bat now matches it, and writes into build/ like
everything else rather than dropping an SSD in the project root.

events.title: The play area is HIRES. It was never multicolour, and ALERT proves it
events.message:
The play area is HIRES. It was never multicolour, and ALERT proves it

KC's ref/c64_deck5.png settles a question this port got wrong from Layer 1:
light grey floor, ORANGE crosshairs, and "ALERT." crisp at single-pixel
spacing. Orange is colour 8 - bit 3 set - so under the old reading that
cell was multicolour and those letters could not be crisp. They are.

The code agrees. $D016 bit 4 is the multicolour flag and _d016Mode ($6F1B)
patches its own LDA operand; _reenter_game ($1532) writes $C0 and $D018 =
$2F, so the deck runs HIRES with the $7800 tile charset. $D0 appears twice
and neither is gameplay: $22AD is the transfer board, $3092 is
DrawSideview - which is also why $D022/$D023 are set at all. They persist
into the game and mean nothing there.

So bit 3 is part of the COLOUR. A hires cell is eight 1-bit pixels, the
cell's full four-bit nibble against the deck background. The old model
turned every orange, grey or light-grey cell into four fat pixels of
$D021/$D022/$D023 and mangled the ALERT lettering on eight decks -- which
was written up as faithful, twice, because the theory was never checked
against a screenshot.

What changed:

  export_bbc  one hires path, no D022/D023. The logical map is the
              background plus the deck's three real colours, and every
              deck wants exactly that: the fourth is used 2-40 times
              against the third's hundreds.
  level.asm   BuildCharset loses the AND #8 branch and BuildLUTs its
              multicolour half. Bank 4 gives back 305 bytes.
  roles       1 and 2 are no longer black and highlight - black is not a
              deck colour at all, it is 2-42 pixels of noise. They are the
              deck's own two foregrounds, darker then lighter by luminance,
              so masking a sprite to 1 always gives the darker option.
              Logical 3 stays white and keeps the sprites, which is
              faithful: the C64 draws the player white (c64_deck4.png)
              and only the ENEMIES black.
  priority    3, 0, 1, 2 - white first, then the floor. White on 16/16.

Verified against all three of KC's screenshots by rendering the same decks:
deck 0's blue grid on light grey, deck 4's grey grid on light green, deck
5's brown crosshairs - each matches. Charset chain 0 mismatches over 2,192
characters, and in jsbeeb on deck 7 the ALERT sign reads cleanly.

events.title: The player droid, on the floor, in the colour you are choosing
events.message:
The player droid, on the floor, in the colour you are choosing

The palette pass is really a contrast question -- can you see the droid --
and the lab could not answer it. Now the 320x120 window carries the
player's own sprite, composed the way export_droids does it: rotor top,
the 001 digits, the top rows again in reverse, and the two end rows from
the other entry of the two-entry tables, which is what makes the ends
alternate. All eight phases, and it spins, because a still rotor hides how
much of the droid is thin blades.

The window is 2x now, which is what makes a 24x21 sprite judgeable.

A selector switches the drawn colour between the three the new scheme
offers from one set of bytes: logical 3 as drawn, logical 1 via AND &0F,
logical 2 via AND &F0. The C64 pane always draws it BLACK, because that is
what the original does -- SpriteColor takes $F0 at $1906, for the player
as much as for the enemies -- so the two panes answer different questions:
what it looked like, and what it will look like.

Verified: the embedded sprite is byte-identical to a fresh Python build,
and drawing it emits exactly the 1,440 lit pixels Python counts across the
eight phases, so a blank or truncated sprite cannot pass. drawWindows runs
for all 16 decks x 3 sprite colours including at the map edges, and the
off switch really draws nothing. The stubbed-DOM harnesses now stub
setInterval too, or the page's rotor timer holds node open forever.

events.title: The console follows the slots: its white is logical 3 now, not 1
events.message:
The console follows the slots: its white is logical 3 now, not 1

Moving black into logical 1 broke the console, and it says so in its own
comments: "logical 1 is physical 7 on all sixteen decks ... so white is
the only reliably light ink it has". That was true and is not any more.
The console draws into the PLAY area on the DECK's palette, so its ink
tracks whatever logical 1 means -- which is now black. Left alone it
would have drawn the whole console screen in black.

Four sites, all of them "white":

  PN_INK_WHITE  &0F -> &FF   the ink ANDed into every glyph byte. Glyphs
                             are stored at &FF, so the mask picks the
                             plane: this is the same recolour trick the
                             sprites now use, and the panel already used
                             it for its red.
  conDblHi/Lo                the X-expanded menu icons: each pattern now
                             appears in both nibbles rather than the low
                             one. Data only, no code, no cost.
  ConSprNib / db_ip_nib      the narrow icon path and the database's droid
                             image stored the source nibble raw, which is
                             the low plane alone. Both now go through a
                             16-byte nibble->both-planes table.
  cd7_mark                   the deck plan's solid white cell for the
                             player, &0F -> &FF.

Everything else that looked like a colour is not: the remaining AND #&0F
in these files are BCD digit and source-nibble extraction, checked one by
one. condeck's plan ink was already generic -- it builds a mask per plane
from the logical value -- so it needed nothing. liftview and the transfer
install their own palettes and are unaffected.

Bank 6 pays 18 bytes for the table and has 40 left. Bank 7's went into
existing alignment padding.

NOT VERIFIED ON SCREEN. Reaching the console needs the player stood on a
console tile and there is no debug key for it, and faking one by poking
the position risks the teleport parity fault in BUGS.md #10. The change is
a constant and two lookup tables, so it is mechanically certain, but the
console is the one thing here KC should eyeball.

events.title: #137: the ST/STE build was never hanging — the ready marker had changed sinks
events.message:
#137: the ST/STE build was never hanging — the ready marker had changed sinks

I filed this as a boot blocker earlier today. It is not one. The ST/STE build boots
to the main menu normally: UNLIMITED ADVENTURES / VERSION 1.0 / CURRENT GAME DESIGN:
HEIRS.DSN, full button grid, 8MHz(CE) 4MB STE, TOS 2.06.

dbg_log writes to the console only until a display backend owns the framebuffer and
to the GEMDOS-mounted DBG.LOG after — deliberate, because Cconws renders into what
is by then one of the engine's own pages (platform/dbglog.c says so, and even notes
that 'menu: modal up' is now on the file side). st_profile.sh, which I wrote hours
earlier, greps only the console log. So it waited 300 s for a marker that was
already in a file, printed "the boot may have stalled", and pressed the dungeon keys
into whatever happened to be up. hatari_ui.sh's wait_for had this right all along.

Every observation along the way was real and every inference from it was wrong:
no console marker -> "never reaches the menu"; 141,556 VBLs -> "47 minutes of
emulated time, so it is hung"; a profile full of jt1007/GetNextEvent/plat_ticks/
mouse polling -> "stuck in a modal wait". That profile WAS a modal event loop: it
was the main menu idling, which is exactly what the new aggregator guard said
("almost certainly a MENU profile"). I read the guard as evidence of a hang instead
of as what it said.

  - st_profile.sh waits on BOTH sinks, and truncates DBG.LOG first so the previous
    run's marker cannot satisfy the wait instantly;
  - it clears HEIRS' modal entry chain with the sequence autoplay_script.h already
    records as verified (six Returns, then `e`/`n` — the treasure screen ignores
    Return completely — then ten more). Confirmed live: the 3D walk comes up at
    10,8 12:00 AM and the party then moves to 13,6 by 12:05.
  - boot breadcrumbs for ua_main's phases and master_init's eleven calls, folded
    onto the EXISTING FRUA_BOOTTRACE flag rather than a new one, and emitted with
    dbg_file_str so they land in the sink that matters after takeover. Without them
    a normal boot has no phase markers at all: the NR_MARKs only exist under
    FRUA_NO_REPLAY, which zeroes the A5 world and so cannot trace a normal boot.

Two fixture bugs found by the guard and fixed here, both of which made a profile
that looked completely plausible:

★ THE GUARD COULD NEVER FIRE. It tested k.startswith('render_3d'), but nm prefixes
symbols with '_', so '_render_3d_faithful' never matched and "3D/viewport work"
was structurally 0.0%. Re-aggregating the same run with the fix gives 0.6% — small,
but the difference between "no 3D at all" and "a little 3D" is the difference
between a broken fixture and a mis-sized window.

★ THE WINDOW DWARFED THE DRIVE. 35,000 VBLs is ~700 s of emulated time; sixteen
keys at 0.7 s cover a few tens of seconds of it. The run genuinely walked and still
aggregated to ~0% 3D because the remaining ~90% of the window was the game idling
at an event prompt. It now steps continuously until the close breakpoint dumps,
with Returns interleaved because walking trips pop-ups that eat movement keys.

Still open as its own task (#143): the title art names cannot survive GEMDOS 8.3.
'title1001' is a nine-character basename clipped to 'title100', so title1001..1006
all collide onto one name. Harmless to the boot, real on hardware.

Slot 2 being empty at the phase-5 check is CORRECT: "Heart" is SSI's developer
bypass, not an integrity marker, and main() leaves it empty on purpose so the jt919
title roll runs. Do not seed it — that deletes the whole title sequence.

events.title: Sprites move to logical 3, where a pixel is its own mask
events.message:
Sprites move to logical 3, where a pixel is its own mask

DROID_COLOUR and EFFECT_COLOUR go 1 -> 3, so every opaque sprite pixel is
now %11 -- both MODE 1 colour planes -- and every transparent one is %00.
Three things follow:

  * the sprite byte IS its own transparency mask, because opaque sets both
    bits and transparent sets neither;
  * AND &0F recolours it to logical 1 (black on all 16 decks) and AND &F0
    to logical 2 (the deck's highlight), from one set of bytes;
  * logical 3 is white on all 16 decks, so the drawn colour is consistent
    in a way it never was when the slots were ordered by frequency.

The C64 draws enemy droids in colour 0, black ($1906). That is now one AND
away from the same artwork rather than a second export.

Nothing in the port needed changing. SprBuildMask ORs the two planes
before inverting, so it is colour-agnostic and already returns the right
mask for %11 -- the 256-byte SPR_MASKTAB is now derivable from the data

events.title: Fixed roles for the four logical colours, and an allocation order to match
events.message:
Fixed roles for the four logical colours, and an allocation order to match

The slots used to be filled by frequency: background, then the three
most-used colours in whatever order their counts happened to fall. That
put black at logical 2 on eight decks and at logical 3 on the other eight
-- the same four colours either way, in an order that meant nothing.

Now they have roles, KC's ordering:

    0 = background      %00, and transparent
    1 = black           %01, the low plane alone
    2 = highlight       %10, the high plane alone
    3 = white           %11, both planes

which is chosen for the sprites. Artwork exported at logical 3 has both
bits set on an opaque pixel and neither on a transparent one, so a sprite
byte is its OWN transparency mask, and AND &0F / AND &F0 recolour it in
place to black or to the deck's highlight from one set of bytes. That is
the next commit; this one puts the colours where it needs them.

Giving up the frequency order costs nothing: on all sixteen decks the
three most-used non-background colours are exactly {white, black,
highlight}, so this reorders slots without changing which colours a deck
gets.

Slot order and ALLOCATION order are now separate, which is the other half.
assign_palette is greedy nearest-unused, so whoever picks first wins a
contested colour, and picking in slot order meant PREFERRED's red->black
took BBC black before the C64's actual black asked for it -- black came
out GREEN on decks 1, 8, 10, 15 and RED on 2 and 7. Allocating in priority
order 3,1,0,2 -- the sprite colour, then black, then the floor, then the
highlight, which is the one already living with a compromise -- gives
white on 16/16 and black on 16/16.

The cost lands where it should: the pale floors (light grey, light green)
no longer take BBC white and fall to yellow. That is a judgement for the
lab, not for a rule.

No port code changes: BuildCharset already reads deckBg and colourMap.
Charset chain still 0 mismatches over 2,192 characters; all four banks
unchanged in size.

events.title: The palette lab, and the wrong background it was built to reveal
events.message:
The palette lab, and the wrong background it was built to reveal

A workbench for Layer 14's palette pass: every deck rendered in the C64's
own colours beside the MODE 1 render, both the palette and the colour
merge editable live, and a 320x120 window showing what actually fits on
screen. It writes tools/deck_palettes.json; export_bbc.py reads that as
an override when it regenerates colours.asm, and refuses a malformed one
rather than quietly reverting to the automatic assignment.

The lab's BBC pane is the port's own chain rather than a lookalike --
verified byte-identical to convert_charset, which is what BuildCharset
reproduces, over all 2,192 characters of all 16 decks.

Then it showed that every deck had the same light blue floor, which is
not what the C64 does. $D021 for the play area is SLOT 0 of the deck's
colour record: InitColors copies the record with Y counting down to zero,
so the accumulator is left holding slot 0, and Irq_118 -- the raster stage
that selects the $7800 tile charset for the 128 lines of play area --
writes it to $D021. Two things had hidden it: SetIntroColors does the same
copy from a RANDOM record, and bgColor really is slot 3 but belongs to the
band above the play area.

Only decks 2 and 7 are light blue. The rest are greys, light red, yellow,
light green and cyan. Confirmed against ref/c64_deck0.png, whose floor is
light grey, and live in jsbeeb on decks 4 and 5.

Also here: $D023 was still 6 in rip_deck_mixed.py long after being found
to be 0, and analyse_alert.py named the multicolour cell colour from the
whole nibble where the VIC uses bits 0-2. BUGS.md #13 records the ALERT
lamp, which the C64 colours by alert level and we draw black.

events.title: profile: the play-loop profiler was profiling the MAIN MENU
events.message:
profile: the play-loop profiler was profiling the MAIN MENU

st_profile.sh booted frua.prg and went straight to pressing arrow keys. That only
lands in the walk if data/work/gamedata/autoload.dat happens to resume a save, and
there is none — so the arrows went to the main menu, where they just move a
selection, and #119's ranking was published as "the play loop" on that basis.
Whether those numbers came from a walk or a menu is no longer knowable; nothing in
the output said which screen it measured, and both look equally plausible as a list
of function names.

  - drive the verified headless route into the dungeon first (the same sequence
    hatari_ui.sh `beginplay` uses: p -> a -> Return -> Escape -> b), then walk;
  - VOID the run, with the command to retry, when the profile window opens during
    that setup instead of after it;
  - st_aggregate.py prints "3D/viewport work: N%" and shouts when it is under 1%,
    so a menu profile can never again be mistaken for a play-loop profile;
  - run the aggregator from the script, so the numbers arrive with the run.

The guard earned itself immediately. First corrected run: 141,556 VBLs — 47 minutes
of emulated time at 452 VBL/s — without ever logging 'menu: modal up', and the
aggregate says 3D/viewport work 0.0%. The ST/STE build is not reaching the main
menu at all; it sits in a modal event loop (jt1007 17.0%, GetNextEvent 8.6%,
plat_ticks 8.9%, plat_mouse_pos 4.6%, WaitNextEvent 1.3%) waiting for input that
never arrives. Escape/Return/space do not dismiss it. Filed against #137, which had
already flagged the jt919 intro as unverified on ST/STE.

Two harness traps, both of which cost real time here and neither of which looks
like what it is:

★ A WEDGED Xvfb LOOKS EXACTLY LIKE AN ENGINE THAT HANGS ON BOOT. When the server
keeps its pid and its socket but answers nothing (twice in one session, on two
display numbers), SDL connects and then waits: Hatari sits in poll() having
accumulated 00:00:00 of cpu time, with one banner line in the log and no engine
output ever. `ps -o time= -C hatari` and `timeout 5 xdpyinfo` separate the two in
seconds. A display must be judged by whether it ANSWERS, never by `pgrep -x Xvfb`.
Clean one: setsid Xvfb :97 -screen 0 1280x1024x24 </dev/null &

★ LEAVE THE --cmd-fifo ALONE. Hatari creates it and reads it non-blocking. Creating
it first with mkfifo is a usage error (it prints its help and exits), and holding
the write end open "to help" makes it spin on EAGAIN — 13,348 lines of "command
FIFO read error: Resource temporarily unavailable" and zero emulation.

Also worth its own look: ___udivsi3 is 14.2% of that IDLE loop. A 32-bit divide in
the tick/event path costs on a 68000 wherever it runs, the play loop included.

events.title: A debug key that wins the transfer, and a boot line that owns up to it
events.message:
A debug key that wins the transfer, and a boot line that owns up to it

DEBUG_XFERWIN puts a hook in XfPlayTick: hold W during the play phase
and the board ends as a win on the next pass, so droid behaviour after a
capture - the new type's speed and weapon, the AI, the alert level, the
score - can be reached without playing the subgame properly first.

IT WINS THROUGH THE REAL VERDICT PATH. All it writes is what a won board
leaves behind - the human's colour in xfWinColor and xfNotInDeck set -
and it writes them AFTER XfCheckEnd has had its say, so the verdict
test, the "transfer done" message, xfmResult, the end-phase hold and
XferExit4's FinishTransfer1/2 all run exactly as they do on a real win.
The code under test is the code that ships. With the flag off nothing
assembles, and with it on nothing grows either: the 22 bytes land inside
an ALIGN &100 that was already there.

!BOOT now also names the flags that are on, as a third REM line built
from conditional EQUS directives beside the build stamp - "REM DEBUG:
XFERWIN" - and a clean build prints no such line at all. A debug build
looks like a normal one until the thing you are testing behaves oddly,
and a published one looks like a release; now neither can hide.

Also records what the droid database is still missing: the C64's 48x84
multicolour PORTRAIT of the type being read about, where the port shows
its own small composed droid. The artwork is in the unported $5400-$67FF
block and 24 types of it is ~6K raw, three times what bank 7 has left,
so it needs space and a palette decision as well as an exporter.
Deferred by KC; docs/layer-9-hud.md 6f decision 2 says what it would
take, and PLAN.md carries it as outstanding.

DEBUG_XFERWIN is left ON in the tree: KC is using it. The boot line is
what stops that being a silent surprise.

7-bit width (the game masks the same stream to 5), one character per
tile, columns 3-41 of the 64-wide grid, all 16 rows via the transfer
game's t1i3 trick, the player's cell a solid white block, static, fire
back to the console main with the selection kept.

THE PAGE IS HIRES - the console screen is GotoHires's and con_ShipInfo
flips multicolour back on only for the side view - so the plan does
not draw from the play-area charset at all. The first cut did, and the
per-deck multicolour flags put red fringes on plain floor tiles.
Instead export_bbc.py writes plandata.asm into BANK 7: the 31 raw
bitmaps and a per-deck ink table baking the C64's whole colour chain,
CharColor slot -> deck record -> the deck's logical, slots 12-15
reading 0 exactly as the C64's zeroed $0221 block does. ConDeck7
(condeck.asm, bank 7) expands each cell as it plots it; the RLE is
staged through the sprite save pages, scratch while the console is up,
because bank 7 cannot see bank 4.

Deviations, agreed with KC and recorded as layer-9 SS6e decisions 1-7:
consoles $10-$13 draw in red, not their slot's black-or-brown; a glyph
whose nearest logical is the background takes the nearest visible one
instead; the marker is clipped where the C64's would overrun the row;
recharge pads stay faithful-dark until they animate. The plan's
palette joins the all-up deck palette pass to be re-judged.

events.message:
Layer 10: the transfer board renders

The board and only the board. export_xfer.py converts the fifteen wire
characters out of the $7800 charset and the 200 bytes of layout at
$E613 / $E68B / $E6B3; XferBoard draws it into the play area. Verified in
jsbeeb: two vertical buses, the horizontal wires, the central result bar
and the arrow terminals, laid out as the original's.

Eleven wire rows, not twelve. The board is 16 rows and PLAY_VIS_ROWS is
15, and dropping one of the twelve identical middle rows is the cheapest
of the three ways out -- it is one constant, XF_MID_ROWS.

The characters are exported here rather than through BuildCharset because
unlike the tiles they are not deck-coloured, and because extending that
137-character remap pushes the charset at &0400 into the MOS's NMI area
at &0D00.

One thing the conversion settled, and it makes the recommended answer to
the ownership problem cheaper than it looked: EVERY pixel of every wire
character is a multicolour 11 pair, so rendered they are entirely logical
3. A per-owner variant is therefore the same 16 bytes with the 3s
rewritten to 1 or 2 -- a mechanical transform in the exporter, not
artwork.

Reachable as the console's third page, which is a SCAFFOLD: the game is
entered from Capture ($229D) through DoCollision's transfer arm, and the
page goes when the game is built. None of the game logic is here.

events.title: Research Layer 10: the transfer minigame, and the three things to decide
events.message:
Research Layer 10: the transfer minigame, and the three things to decide

No code. The research is the expensive half and this commits it.

Where everything is: Capture ($229D), SubGameSelectSide ($E016),
doSubGame ($2166), and the board at $E613 / $E68B / $E6B3 -- 200 bytes,
three top rows, ONE middle row repeated twelve times, one bottom row.
Fifteen distinct characters, all from the $7800 charset the deck tiles
already use, confirmed by rendering them.

The whole rule set is xfer_DoColumn ($1EB6). Twelve wire rows; three
stages along each at screen columns 6, 10 and 14, so a pulser advances
one stage per turn; and a gate dispatch on the character already in the
cell -- the other side's pulser is a terminator, $F5/$F7 are joiners,
$F6 is the splitter that turns one pulser into two, and anything else is
claim-the-segment-and-advance.

Three things want KC's eye before any of it is written, and guessing
wrong on two of them would waste a session:

  OWNERSHIP IS COLOUR RAM. xfer_Colorize4 writes four bytes of colour
  RAM and does nothing else; MODE 1 has four logical colours for the
  whole screen and no per-cell attribute. Recommended: three copies of
  each wire character, one per owner, so the colour write becomes a
  character write and the rest of the logic ports unchanged. 720 bytes,
  and they are not deck-coloured so they ship converted like Layer 9's
  text font rather than going through BuildCharset -- which matters,
  because extending that 137-character remap pushes the charset at &0400
  into the MOS's NMI area at &0D00.

  THE BOARD IS 16 ROWS AND THE PLAY AREA IS 15. Recommended: drop one of
  the twelve identical wire rows. It is one constant.

  THERE IS NOWHERE OBVIOUS TO PUT IT. Bank 6 has ~2,040 bytes free and
  bank 4 ~1,400. The minigame runs with the deck suspended and no
  sprites, so it could take a sprite bank wholesale as its own disc file
  -- at the cost of a floppy access on every transfer, which is a real
  gameplay cost and is the thing to think about first.

events.title: The droid icon, and all four icons from the C64's own sprite bytes
events.message:
The droid icon, and all four icons from the C64's own sprite bytes

The console's first menu icon is the player's own droid. $53C0 is blank in
ROM: it is where BuildDroidSprite ($3C77) writes the three-digit number
and AnimateDroids ($3CFB) the rotor, which is why conRedraw sets dType
from droidType before it draws.

The port's own droid artwork could not be used for it. export_droids.py
COMPILES the droid - 6502 with the pixels baked in as immediates - so the
compiled form cannot be read back, and it lives in the sprite banks, which
bank 6 cannot see. export_droidicon.py emits a small copy of the two
pieces the C64 composes instead: one rotor phase at 10 rows x 3 bytes and
the ten digit glyphs at 8 rows x 1 byte. 110 bytes against 1,743 for the
full animated set at one shift. One phase, because the console is a still
screen - the C64's keeps spinning there only because its sprite is the
same one the game animates.

ALL FOUR ICONS ARE NOW STORED AS THE C64'S OWN SPRITE BYTES, three a row.
Storing the MODE 1 conversion overflowed bank 6 by 346 bytes once both
wide icons and the droid were in; the original's form is half the size and
costs nothing to undo. A hires sprite byte is eight 1-bit pixels, the
icons are drawn in logical colour 1, and logical 1 is the LOW COLOUR PLANE
ALONE - so four pixels ARE one nibble, and a byte splits into two output
bytes with a shift and a mask. The X-expansion rides on the same nibble
through the sixteen-entry table that was already there.

That collapsed all four onto one routine. ConSprite draws 21 rows and each
icon supplies its own through a patched JSR, which works because the droid
is a sprite too and BuildDroidSprite writes three bytes a row like
everything else.

THE SOURCE IS ROW MAJOR AND THE BUFFER IS NOT: a 4-pixel column's eight
bytes are eight consecutive scanlines, so row r column u goes to
(r DIV 8)*640 + u*8 + (r MOD 8). The compiled blitter gets that transpose
for nothing by being compiled; this pays for it in a loop, which is
affordable because it runs once per console.

BANK 6 ENDS AT &BFE9 - TWENTY-THREE BYTES FREE. It is full. Layer 13 or a
fourth bank is the next thing that touches it.
