events.title: wonderboy: boot sector is a resident virus, not the Copylock
events.message:
wonderboy: boot sector is a resident virus, not the Copylock

Disassembled disk 1's factory boot sector (freshly dumped, checksum
0x1234, the sector the TOSEC preservation copy lost). Premise refuted
on every axis, independently re-verified: no SR write, no trace/illegal
vectors, no $ff86/88/fa hardware access, body entropy 5.68 bits/byte
(plaintext) — none of the Rob Northen trace-vector-decoder markers. It
is a self-replicating boot-sector virus: 430 bytes resident at $140,
hooks hdv_bpb, rewrites every floppy's boot sector, mouse-reverse
payload every 5th infection. Returns to TOS — the game boots normally
from AUTO/SWB.PRG, which is why it went unnoticed.

The Copylock lives in SWB.PRG's encrypted body, consistent with the
existing note on disk_check_signature ($5e3e): boot+2 must be $face,
reached only from the encrypted body, and no surviving boot sector
satisfies it. The black-screen hang is that Copylock issuing raw READ
TRACK against an hxcfe STX with no track image — not the boot sector.

Corollary: SAGROTAN did not overwrite the TOSEC boot sector at random —
it disinfected an infected disk. Both surviving disk-1 boot sectors are
post-infection; the genuine $face master is preserved nowhere here.
Acceptance test for any future dump: word at boot+2 == $face.

Note: projects/wonderboy/notes/bootsector.md (full annotated disasm,
READ-TRACK-by-elimination, no game-side key handoff).

events.title: stop the World Maker hanging on the seeds that never finish
events.message:
stop the World Maker hanging on the seeds that never finish

The World Maker does not always produce a world. Swept over its whole input
space -- every seed from 1 to 65,535 in all three configurations, 196,605
worlds -- 37,000 of them produce no map: 28,508 that never terminate and 8,492
that hit $2473's restart, which the port throws rather than loops. That is
18.8%, not a corner case. The viewer draws a fresh seed on every "Generate
World", so roughly one click in five would have hung the app forever.

TODO.md called this insurance against something that "terminates on every seed
and configuration measured". Nine seed and configuration pairs had been
measured. Nine is not a sample.

What is here:

WorldMakerRNG counts draws and carries a ceiling. Every unbounded rejection
sampler in the pipeline gives up when the count passes it -- $0FF8 redrawing
until its throw lands on land, $22B4 until the byte falls in range, $4373 until
an even row falls inside a band, $4A37 until a village fits. None of those can
spin without drawing, so one counter on the generator sees all of them,
including any nobody has enumerated. WorldMaker.world(config:seed:) throws
WorldMakerRNG.Stuck; there is no partial result worth keeping, because the
loops give up where they stand and everything after them is drawn from a
generator that is out of step.

Counting draws was not enough, and that is the finding worth keeping. A whole
second class of loop spins without ever touching the generator, so no counter
on it can see them: $194E and $1961 (the flood fill's row scans), $17F2 and
$1816 (the isthmus), $3268 (the treeline), $369F (the river carry) and $4021
(the land runs) all step a wrapping column with no stop of their own, and
$16D1's unwind can walk the undo ring forever. Each of those now bounds itself
at the point where it would be repeating work it has already done -- one lap of
a wrapping column, one pass of the ring -- and reports through declareStuck().

$16EC is a real hole in the original rather than a transcription slip. Its
ring-full guard compares the slot counter $46 against the slot the search
started from, which $2507 computes as $46 + 1 as a byte. The ring holds 201
entries, so $46 runs 0 to 200; a search beginning on the last slot looks for
slot 201, a value the counter never takes, and the unwind circles the ring
without ever recognizing that it has come all the way round.

The ceiling cannot decide what a seed generates, and that is measured rather
than argued. The whole space was swept twice, at twenty million draws and at
the fifty million shipped here, and the two runs agree exactly: the same 37,000
failures split the same six ways, and the same worst finishing world at
13,175,820 draws (seed $5D28, configuration 1). A third run with the ceiling at
two billion -- off, for all purposes -- agrees as well. Not one world anywhere
was rescued or cut off by where the ceiling sits. What extra room does cost is
time, since a run going nowhere spends its whole budget before anything
notices: two billion took eight times as long to give up for identical answers.
Fifty million is margin against the long tail without the wait.

The viewer now tries eight seeds a click instead of beeping on the first
failure, which at 18.8% puts an empty click at about one in two million.

All 80 tests pass, and pass unchanged, which is the check that matters: the
watchdog altered no map.

The method is in NOTES.md and is the reusable part. Three of these sites were
found by running the sweep, waiting for it to stall, and sampling the stalled
process -- the call graph names the routine outright, in minutes each, where
reading would have taken hours. The third was invisible from the caller,
because the loop that never returned sat one frame below the guard meant to
stop it. Reasoning about which loops could spin produced a list that was right
about the samplers and missed the wrapping scans entirely; a fix that does not
make the sweep get further is not a fix.

events.title: Measure the flicker instead of inferring it
events.message:
Measure the flicker instead of inferring it

The raster-ordered updating item had never been instrumented. ruptState
says where the beam is — state 2 means the play area is on screen — so
four histograms bumped either side of the two pool calls answer it for
about 20 bytes and no cycles worth counting.

Over 128 passes: the restore runs inside the off-display window every
single time, and the draw is still running with the beam over it on 120
of them. That is the flicker, and it is not a race that sometimes goes
wrong — it is the normal case.

It also rules out the cheap fix. The window is 184 scanlines, 11,776
cycles, and the draw half alone is about 24,000, so no scheduling of the
existing work fits inside it. What remains is ordering the pool against
the beam, which means restoring and drawing a sprite as one unit, which
breaks the restore-all-then-draw-all invariant for the same reason
round-robin did. The overlap problem has to be solved first.

The instrumentation is not kept: main RAM has 116 bytes left. The method
is written down in docs/layer-5-blitter.md and takes ten minutes to redo.

events.title: Layer 6: mode dispatch, line of sight, and collision
events.message:
Layer 6: mode dispatch, line of sight, and collision

DroidRun now dispatches on the mode in the top bits of the type, as
DroidModeJump does; bullets and explosions arrive in Layer 7 and until
then a type claiming to be one is simply not run.

DrLineOfSight is LineOfVisibility ($24AE) with CalcDeltaAdd's scaling
trick intact — double the delta pair while both fit in a byte, then add
the originals — so the long axis steps about one character and there is
no division. The original walks a pointer into a 16K character map and
compares pointers to know when it has arrived; we have no such map, so
the coordinates are held apart and the walk ends when the dominant axis
reaches its target, which is the same test written differently. A droid
behind a wall keeps its sprite slot and is not drawn, which is what the
C64 does with SpriteEna. That needed slot OWNERSHIP separated from
sprActive: drSlotOwner is what DrFindSlot now scans.

DrCollide replaces the one thing with no faithful port available. The
C64 reads $D01E, the VIC's pixel-exact sprite collision latch; a
software blitter knows what it wrote, not what it overlapped, so this is
a box test — and deliberately a box smaller than the sprite, because
most of a droid's corners are the rotor's transparent gaps. One pair a
pass, as DoCollision does. Droid v droid reverses the first and pauses
the second; player v droid pauses and reverses the droid and bounces the
player, with the bounce clamped to CAM_TOPSPD because our band redraw
brings in one character row a pass and the C64's doubling would skip one.

DrLineOfSight does NOT preserve X — the scaling loop uses it, the way
CalcDeltaAdd does. Missing that made the caller write sprActive through
an index read out of the wrong array: slots nobody owned were switched
on with no position in them, and the player vanished behind three slots
of rubbish.

Verified: 0 of 10240 against a forced RedrawAll with the draw disabled,
and a droid walking into the player is paused for 16 iterations while the
player is nudged clear.

events.title: Top speed 8, so the camera's 4 px step divides it
events.message:
Top speed 8, so the camera's 4 px step divides it

At a top speed of 7 the world must average 7 px a pass, and the CRTC
scrolls in 4 px units once per 2 fields — so the camera can only ever
move 0, 4 or 8, and it settles into 8, 8, 8, 4. That periodic 4 px
hiccup is the jerk. The average is forced by arithmetic, so no deadzone
or camera policy can remove it; only a top speed the 4 px step divides.

CAM_TOPSPD (main.asm) is that number, and 8 makes the step uniform.
It is the one movement constant in the port not taken from the C64 —
14 % fast, bought deliberately for a scroll that does not stutter, and
it lands exactly on the one-row-per-pass ceiling the ASSERT guards.
Verified in jsbeeb: xSpd clamps at &0800, ySpd at &F800, picture clean
at full speed on both axes.

Four settings were built and played; the table is in the layer doc.
Two are worth knowing about:

  CAM_TOPSPD = 4     lands within 15 % of the 1985 release's 117 px/s,
                     but PLY_ACCEL is not scaled with it, so the ramp
                     is 0.20 s against the original's 0.52 s. Right
                     terminal velocity, wrong ramp.
  PLY_ITER_FRAMES=3  the only setting that reproduces 1985 properly,
                     speed AND ramp, because it scales velocity by 2/3
                     and acceleration by 4/9 together. Lost on feel:
                     4.67 does not divide 4 either.

Also records two camera schemes that were costed and rejected, both of
which look right on paper:

  A fixed-rate lazy camera cannot keep up — 3 px/pass deficit against a
  140 px margin, and the decks are far too long to hide it. The longest
  horizontal open run is 1088 px (decks 3, 10, 11), measured by decoding
  levels.asm + tiledefs.asm; the table is in the doc.

  Splitting the CRTC step across the pass's two fields corrupts the
  picture. 15 rows of 80 units are 9600 contiguous bytes of a 10240-byte
  ring, so rows are ADJACENT: moving the displayed start back one unit
  splices rather than translates, taking each row's left column from the
  row above's right column — the leading edge just redrawn. It was built,
  and a still screenshot looked clean; exaggerating the lag to 20 units
  in jsbeeb showed the re-frame. Same wrap geometry as 39315d0.

Corrects the layer doc's speed table, which still carried the
FRAME_LOCK = 1 era's 52/44/3.5 per-frame figures, and the matching
stale comment in ApplyMove.

events.title: Fix the sprite smear at the strip wrap: the interpreted row fell into the wrong tail
events.message:
Fix the sprite smear at the strip wrap: the interpreted row fell into the wrong tail

sd_slow ends by putting bufp back to the row's first column, so it has
NOT advanced a scanline - and it ran straight into sd_nextnw, the tail
for rows that walked themselves. Every row after the first wrapping one
was drawn on top of it. sr_slow had the same fall-through. The fix is one
JMP sd_next and one JMP sr_next.

The two tails arrived when the compiled rows took over their own walking,
and the comment above them says in as many words that "blank rows and the
interpreted paths do not" advance - which is precisely the case then left
falling into the wrong one.

This is BUGS.md #5, open since 2026-08-14 and misdiagnosed twice. A row
only takes the interpreted path when its seven columns straddle the end
of the circular strip, which depends on scrollS - so it fires at
particular scroll offsets, which for a given route are the same map
positions every time. That is why it looked like a doorway bug: doors are
where you stop and look.

WHY NO TEST CAUGHT IT: the restore mirrored the fault exactly, collapsing
the same rows onto the same scanlines it had drawn them at, so the
background came back correctly and the buffer diff against RedrawAll -
which runs with the DRAW DISABLED - reported 0 differences. The fault was
only ever in the drawn sprite. Every oracle we had was blind to it.

Reproduced deterministically: player at unit 37, line 0, scrollS = &17B0
puts seven of the sprite's 21 rows across the wrap. Before, the droid is
a one-row streak; after, at the identical position, it draws in full.

KC found the thread: pixels erasable at both &5800 and just below &8000
means rows landing across the wrap, which is the interpreted path.

events.title: quantize: reserve exact palette slots for each band's flat AREA colours
events.message:
quantize: reserve exact palette slots for each band's flat AREA colours

The median cut in quant_banded is PRESENCE-weighted — a colour counts once
however many pixels it covers, because the population isn't known at
set_palette time. So a flat panel filling half a band was averaged into a box
with its neighbours and came back a different colour. Two consequences, and
the second is why per-band palettes are currently switched off:

  - Fidelity. Measured on captured HEIRS frames at the ST's 16-colour budget
    (tools/quantsim.py), mean squared RGB error: 3D walk view 446 -> 207,
    BigPic event 828 -> 429, the UNLIMITED ADVENTURES title 1713 -> 466.
  - SEAMS. A flat colour spanning bands was averaged against DIFFERENT
    neighbours in each one, so it came back as different shades either side of
    a boundary — the striping (#40) that drove ADR-0016 B1 to abandon per-band
    palettes for a single global one. On the same frames a plain per-band cut
    costs 685 seam pixels; with this it costs 100.

So before cutting, each band now reserves up to QUANT_KEEP (6) slots for the
colours covering at least QUANT_KEEP_PCT (3%) of it and reproduces them
EXACTLY. A colour that big is a flat area — chrome, a panel, a backdrop — and
exactness is both what it wants and what makes it identical across bands.
Two CLUT indices that snap to the same hardware colour share one slot.

Restructured the presence histogram into a per-band population histogram taken
band by band, which touches the same pixels, drops the 10 KB `used` static, and
costs 512 bytes of counters. Slot selection is at most QUANT_KEEP max-scans
over 256 rather than a sort.

tests/test_quantize.py grows flat_area_test, which reproduces the #40 seam: a
panel colour with neighbours spread far ABOVE it in one band and far BELOW in
the other, four slots available. MUTATION-CHECKED — with QUANT_KEEP forced to 0
it fails with "the flat panel is 200,120,72 in band 0 but 184,88,40 in band 1",
so it is pinning the behaviour and not recomputing it.

Backends still pass nbands=1, so this lands the fidelity win with NO change to
the band machinery; flipping st_reband/ecs_reband to real per-band palettes is
the next step and is what the seam guarantee above unblocks.

events.title: tools: add quantsim.py — try ST/ECS palette strategies offline
events.message:
tools: add quantsim.py — try ST/ECS palette strategies offline

The palette reduction lives on an 8MHz 68000 behind a ~170s emulator boot, and
"does this look better?" is not a question a unit test answers. quantsim.py
takes a FALCON or AGA screenshot (chunky 8bpp = the 256-colour ground truth the
banded backends approximate) and renders it three ways on the host — one global
palette, per-band palettes, and per-band plus an error-weighted checkerboard
dither — reporting mean-squared RGB error and writing PNGs to compare.

The dither is selective for free: a colour whose nearest palette entry is exact
never dithers, so chrome and glyph text stay crisp while gradient art blends.
That answers the objection recorded in docs/ecs-st-quantizer-plan.md fork #3.
Expect +dither to raise the reported MSE — ordered dithering trades pointwise
error for perceptual accuracy; the numbers are there to keep band-vs-global
honest, the PNGs are what you judge the dither on.

Measured on real HEIRS frames, mean-squared RGB error at the ST's budget:

    frame            global-16   band-16   band-16+dither
    3D walk view         448       162          187
    BigPic event         585       190          221
    UA title             403       278          319

which is the evidence that st_reband's nbands=1 (one global 16-colour palette
for the whole frame, ten identical band loads) is leaving most of the fidelity
on the table. Also worth recording: a whole 3D-walk frame contains only 63
distinct colours, and a BigPic event 196 — FRUA uses its 256 entries as a lazy
palette, not as a colour budget.

Host analysis tooling; embeds no FRUA data.

events.title: quantize: the absent-colour fallback must keep hue, not just brightness
events.message:
quantize: the absent-colour fallback must keep hue, not just brightness

Fixes the intermittent CYAN STONE WALLS on the ST/STE and Amiga ECS.

quant_banded builds each band's palette from a presence histogram of the
frame, then needs a mapping for CLUT entries that were NOT present, so that
content drawn after the reduce (the composited cursor, a changed 3D view)
does not fall to black. That fallback bucketed by LUMINANCE alone.

Luma throws away hue, so any two colours of equal brightness are
interchangeable to it — and FRUA has a textbook collision under the engine's
own 2:5:1 weights:

    party-roster cyan  (0,200,200)   -> luma 150
    mid-grey stone     (150,150,150) -> luma 150

A wall shade that missed the histogram therefore fell back to whichever
reduced entry was nearest in brightness, and when that was the roster cyan,
stone walls rendered cyan. It only happened sometimes because the histogram
samples every OTHER row (y += 2), so whether a given wall index counts as
"present" depends on which rows its pixels landed on.

Bucket in 3-D instead: a 4x8x4 RGB grid (green gets double resolution — it
carries most of the luminance), each cell resolved to the nearest reduced
entry under the same 2:5:1 weights, now applied per channel instead of
collapsed. Cost goes from n*32 to n*128 scalar distance evaluations per band,
still far below the n*256 per-colour linear search whose ~1.3M cycles per
re-band at 8MHz was the original reason for bucketing at all.

tests/test_quantize.py grows hue_fallback_test, which constructs exactly that
collision: grey150 is in the CLUT but absent from the image, its luma distance
to cyan is ZERO and to either surviving grey is 30, so a luma bucket MUST pick
cyan. MUTATION-CHECKED — reverting quantize.h to the luma bucket makes the new
test fail, so it is pinning the behaviour and not recomputing it.

events.message:
1 px step D: the droid is drawn where it actually is

player.asm and droidtest.asm split the screen X at the bottom two bits -
they are the shift, what is above them is the 4 px unit. Cheaper than the
2 px version it replaces, which needed a shift and a mask to separate the
same two fields. Three steps of groundwork for two lines of change.

The port now positions droids exactly as the C64 does, per pixel, instead
of at the even pixel below.

Verified at each shift. Restore against a SPACE-forced RedrawAll at shift
3: 0 of 10240. The digit block reconstructed byte-exactly from the glyph
data at shifts 0, 1, 2 and 3 - 22 spill bytes for 001 at 3 px, and none
at 1 px, which is right: 7 px shifted one still fits its cell. Movement:
plyX 100/101/103/104 gives (unit 37, shift 0), (37,1), (37,3), (38,0) -
one pixel at a time, carrying correctly across the unit boundary.

MEASURED, deferred from step B and now meaningful: SprDrawAll with seven
sprites goes 24,821 -> 24,943 cycles a pass, +122 or 0.49%, against
79,872 in a pass. PAGESPRBANK is 18 cycles once per drawn slot, 7 x 18 =
126 predicted, so the measurement and the arithmetic agree to four
cycles.

The first attempt at that measurement was invalid and looked alarming.
The patch meant to move the T1 bracket off DoRedraws silently failed - an
em dash that did not match the file's encoding - so the build had TWO
brackets, dbgAcc summed two routines and dbgN counted twice a pass. That
read as one field per pass instead of two, i.e. the game running at
double speed. It was not: the release builds move plyX 612 -> 901 in the
same two seconds before and after. The layer 5 doc said "one call site at
a time"; it now also says how two fail, which is not a hang but a
plausible number.

BUGS.md #6's leading hypothesis is refuted while we are here: the rotor
debris survives freezing the rotor phase, so it is not the phase
advancing between draw and restore. It also varied 0/6/24/39 with the
player's POSITION within one build, which is what to vary when
reproducing it. The digit block was byte-exact in every one of those
runs.

events.title: hook the viewer up to the real World Maker, and delete the placeholder
events.message:
hook the viewer up to the real World Maker, and delete the placeholder

"Generate World" now runs the ported pipeline, and `--dump ... generated
--gen <seed>` renders one headlessly. WorldGenerator is gone — it was
always a stand-in so the viewer had something to explore, and it has been
stood in for.

The configuration is drawn the way $2146 draws it, a byte over ninety,
and offered alongside the seed rather than folded into it. That is not
tidiness: the port's seed is the generator's state *after* $2146 has
already chosen, so they are genuinely two inputs and pretending otherwise
would be a lie about what a seed means.

Two things came out of actually looking at the output rather than
trusting the digests, which is the whole reason to look.

DumpMode could not render a generated world at all — it asks for a
CGImage per cell and OriginalTiles rebuilds the texture from pixels every
call, so a 256x400 dump was a hundred thousand rasterisations and minutes
of wall clock. Now memoised. The first attempt at that memo keyed on
ObjectIdentifier, which is only unique while the object is alive; these
are released as soon as the image is taken, addresses got reused, and the
whole map rendered as ocean. The key is terrain plus (x % 4, y % 4),
which is exactly what Tile.pixels(x:y:) selects on.

And the maps look right, which is the check no digest can make: two
continents for configuration 0, one paired continent with its isthmus for
1, one and six islands for 2. Forest dense at both poles and thin across
the middle. Mountain ranges on the western coasts. Rivers from the
interior to the sea, lakes with outflows, villages inland. Every one of
those is something the reverse engineering predicted from the 6502 before
anything was drawn.

The test suite drops from 35 seconds to 12 with the placeholder's tests
gone; its river-mask test survives, repointed at the real generator,
because $329C has since settled what it was guessing about.

events.title: engine: run the engine's own jt919 title sequence (music + the UA frame)
events.message:
engine: run the engine's own jt919 title sequence (music + the UA frame)

The port drew the SSI / AD&D / Forgotten Realms / Unlimited Adventures /
credits screens from port_show_intro() — ~300 hand-written lines that
re-parsed TITLE.CTL and re-composited each screen. The engine's own path,
jt919 -> l19d4("title", 2..6), was dead code. Two bugs fell out of that:

  - NO TITLE MUSIC. jt919 opens with jt52(32), "play song 0". The real Mac
    plays ~57 s of it across those screens (measured 2026-08-14 under Mini
    vMac, which unlike BasiliskII emulates the raw 22254.5 Hz buffer the
    legacy Sound Driver writes). We played silence.
  - NO STONE FRAME on the Unlimited Adventures screen — the one screen every
    original version frames and ours did not. l19d4 has an explicit special
    case for it: mode == 5 -> jt103(1, 1, 38, 22). Its art really is
    unframed; SSI draws the rect instead. TITLE.CTL agrees — set 5 is two
    type-2 pieces 38 cells wide and 100+77 = 177 rows tall, i.e. exactly
    that rect. port_show_intro special-cased set 5 the other way ("blit its
    pieces opaque, no backdrop"), so it got neither.

jt919 was dead because src/main.c seeded string-table slot 2 with "Heart".
That is not an integrity marker, it is SSI's DEVELOPER BYPASS: ua_main runs
the title roll only when slot 2 does NOT equal it, and dumps FC statistics
at exit when it does. The Mac runs jt919, so its slot 2 is not "Heart"
either. Slot 3 ("Boots") is the real marker and still suppresses jt931.

Also seeds the engine clip rect full-screen once, at display-init time.
The Mac's display init leaves -3054/-3050/-3056/-3052 describing the whole
screen; ours did not and the A5 pool replays them as zero, so every blit
before the first screen sets its own clip was rejected. jt81 already
carried a local copy of this seed for that reason; jt919 paints earlier
still, and without it the title roll played its music over a black screen.
jt81's guarded copy now finds the rect already set.

port_show_intro() stays behind FRUA_PORT_INTRO (off) as an A/B until the
ST, Amiga AGA/ECS and Nova backends are checked; then it goes.

Verified on Falcon/Hatari: 61.4 s of song 0 from a stock boot (`driver.sh`
+ tools/avi_audio.py reported "0 burst(s) ... NONE" before), all five
screens render, the UA screen is framed, and the menu comes up unchanged.
Boot to "menu: modal up" goes 10s -> 21s under fast-forward, ~61 s at real
speed — the Mac's own pacing, and any key skips a screen.

events.title: 1 px step C: four compiled shifts across two sprite banks
events.message:
1 px step C: four compiled shifts across two sprite banks

shift_row generalises from a hard-coded 2 px to any of 0-3 - a MODE 1
pixel is bits 7-n and 3-n, so the nibbles move together: keep &EE >> 1
with &11 << 3, or &CC/&33 at 2, or &88/&77 at 3. Shifts 0 and 1 px go to
droids.asm in bank 5, 2 and 3 px to droids2.asm in bank 6, loaded by a
third *LOAD staged through &3000 like the others.

TWO BANKS SHARING ONE SET OF LABELS is the part worth reading twice.
beebasm labels are global, so the same table cannot be declared in both
files - and duplicating the contents is exactly what is wanted, since
each bank dispatches to its own code. The resolution is layout: each file
is a fixed table section FIRST, whose size does not depend on which
shifts the bank holds, then that bank's code. So the tables land at the
same addresses in both, the blitter names bank 5's, and it reads bank 6's
when bank 6 is paged. drBlkSave6 is in that section too - code, but
called by name. The second file's labels are prefixed x, and main.asm
asserts all nineteen addresses agree, because a mismatch would send the
blitter into compiled sprite rows with no run-time diagnostic at all.

Table indices are bit 0 of the shift, not the shift: bit 1 chose the
bank. Four shifts of sequence table would be 320 entries and sprSeqBase
is a byte, so this is not just tidier, it is the only thing that fits.

The fallback now shifts one pixel at a time, sprShiftW passes of one
loop, masks derived afterwards rather than during - a partly-shifted
byte's mask is meaningless. Slower than a per-shift routine and the right
trade at one row in fifty.

The player and the test droids move from shift 1 to shift 2, so the
picture is bit-for-bit unchanged while half the pool draws out of bank 6.
The odd shifts are compiled and loaded, waiting for step D.

  bank 5  12,374 used / 4,010 free    bank 6  12,697 / 3,687
  code    &1100-&267E                 disc    +12.4K for PARSPR2

Verified: 0 of 10240 against a SPACE-forced RedrawAll after scrolling;
the digit block reconstructed byte-exactly for five slots - three at
shift 0 in bank 5, two at shift 2 in bank 6 with 2 and 9 spill bytes;
and the rewritten fallback shift against the compiled path with every
row forced through it, 0 of 10240.

Target machine is now 3 x 16K sideways RAM - a B+ 128 or a B with a
32/64K board. Recorded in PLAN.md's decisions and CLAUDE.md.

events.title: 1 px step B: the pool pages per slot, not per pass
events.message:
1 px step B: the pool pages per slot, not per pass

Which bank a sprite needs is a property of the sprite once the four
compiled shifts are split across two, so SprDrawAll and SprRestoreAll
stop paging SWRAM_SPR in around the whole loop and each slot pages its
own. Still one bank, so the value is constant and this step changes
nothing observable - which is the point of doing it separately.

PAGESPRBANK takes the shift in A and pages SWRAM_SPR + (shift >> 1). The
draw pages in SprSetSlot right after it reads sprShift, before the
drDigit read below it, which is in the bank. The restore pages in
SprRestoreSlot from sprShiftS - the DRAW's shift, because that is where
the compiled restore for that sprite lives, and sprShiftS already existed
for exactly this class of reason. Both loops still leave SWRAM_DATA in on
the way out.

measured on the T1 harness yet: a before/after only means something once
both banks exist, so it waits for step D rather than being claimed here.

scroll, and - since SprFetchRow's return-page changed from a constant to

Move the level draw into bank 4, beside the data it reads

Main RAM had 39 bytes free below &3000 and the droid layers had not
started. The fix was to move CODE rather than data: screen.asm,
scroll.asm and level.asm assemble into SWRAM bank 4 now, next to the
tile definitions, deck RLE and charset source they read. It costs no

and from SprCalcAddr. SetCell's rowMul/unitMul tables come with it. A
JSR the other way with bank 5 in would land in compiled sprite rows and
nothing would diagnose it, so the rule is stated at length and repeated
where the includes are.

events.title: assemble the second band — the whole World Maker now reproduces the original
events.message:
assemble the second band — the whole World Maker now reproduces the original

Both bands, and the generator ends exactly where the original's ends,
which is the strictest single check available: every draw of every phase
of both bands, in order. WorldMaker.world(of:) is the pipeline.

The seam works the way the disk makes it work. $0C9B unpacks all four
hundred rows and writes them out as it goes; $0F0C reads a band back at
the top of every $0E20 and $0F47 writes it out at the bottom. So by the
time the second band is read, the sixteen rows it shares with the first
have already been overwritten by the first band's *finished* terrain, not
the raw mask. Nothing else in the port can produce those rows.

The bug that stood between the two bands was an operand again. $32FC and
$33F0 hold the persistence and the erase allowance, and $38BB calls $32CC
*before* $38C3 and $38C8 patch them — so a $380D river runs with whatever
the last one left. Band 0's last river finishes, $38F3 leaves $B4 behind,
and band 0's $3961 and $3EAD inherit it, and so does band 1's first
$380D. Band 0 never needs the carried value, which is why it came out
exact with the persistence hard-coded and band 1 diverged on the fifth
write of its first river.

Fourth time an immediate operand has turned out to be a variable, after
$443F, $3662 and $4B83. NOTES.md now says it as a rule: in this program
an immediate is a variable until proven otherwise.

events.message:
finish the village strip walk — the survey's threshold is not a constant

All 121 villages the strip walk places now match the original's first
121, cell for cell. The remaining six of the band's 127 come from $49F2,
which is not ported yet.

The last bug was a good one. $4B82 disassembles as CMP #$1A and reads
like a fixed one-in-ten chance, and it is neither: $0E71 writes $1A into
$4B83 — the CMP's own operand — once per band, and $4BED adds **five** to
it every time the survey's hunt finds somewhere to file. So the survey
starts willing and gets steadily harder to satisfy as it fills the map
in. Eight fires over the first band take the threshold from 26 to 66.

That is why the port never ran the hunt at all: reading the operand as a
constant means every draw of 26 or more skips, and by the time the map
has any density most draws do. The interpreter said A was 27 with the
carry *clear*, which is impossible against an operand of 26, and that is
what pointed at the operand rather than at the branch.

Third piece of self-modifying code in this phase to matter — after
$443F's RTS and $3662 — and the second where the operand rather than the
opcode is the moving part.

events.title: Give the shifted glyphs back the column they were losing
events.message:
Give the shifted glyphs back the column they were losing

A digit is 7 pixels wide in an 8 pixel cell, so two bytes hold it
unshifted - but the exporter truncated a row to two bytes BEFORE
shifting it, and shift_row drops the carry out of the last byte it is
given. The 2 px shift therefore threw the rightmost pixel column away,
taking a column out of the right edge of every glyph but 1 at odd 2 px
positions: five of the eight rows for a 0, which is the right-hand
stroke minus its caps. Reported from play on the player's own 001.

The assert that was supposed to catch exactly this could never fire.
It read `len(row) < 3 or row[2] == 0` against rows the same truncation
had just made two bytes long. drYcol2's zero uses were read as evidence
that no glyph spills, when they were evidence that the spill had already
been deleted.

Keeping the third byte means the three positions overlap under a shift,
which is the thing the save-folded-into-the-draw step assumed away. A
glyph still saves only its own two columns; SprDigitBlock now draws the
positions 2, 1, 0, so the owner of each shared column saves it clean
before the spill arrives, and the spill merges into what the owner drew.
Column 6 has no owner and is saved by drBlkSave6 - generated into the
sprite bank, not written in sprite.asm, because main RAM is the binding
constraint and the bank is not. SprBlkRest restores seven columns again.

Costs 7 bytes of main RAM, ~35 of bank 5 and ~200 cycles a sprite.

Verified in jsbeeb with slots at both shifts on screen: 0 differences in
10240 against a SPACE-forced RedrawAll with the draw disabled, and with
the restore disabled every slot's eight digit rows match a byte-exact
reconstruction from the glyph data - 10 spill bytes for 001 at shift 1,
the pixels that used to be missing.

Those runs also turned up debris the restore leaves in the ROTOR rows,
at shift 0 as well as shift 1 and never in the digit block. Recorded as
BUGS.md #6 with the per-slot row mapping; not this change's doing and
not fixed here.

The rounding is the part that has to be right. $0BEE and $0C0C both

early. Configuration 2's southern band divides 920 by 263 for a remainder

the difference between villages being placed on a draw and being placed

events.title: count the ground the villages can use, and get it right for all three configs
events.message:
count the ground the villages can use, and get it right for all three configs

`VillageBudget.eligibleQuadrants` reproduces what $0C9B counts off the
finished mask: 240 northern quadrants and 246 southern for configuration
0, 84 and 361 for configuration 1, 171 and 92 for configuration 2.

The geometry came out of the numbers rather than the listing, which was
the only practical way. $0C9B shifts mask bytes out of its own
instruction stream with ASL abs,X into a rolling buffer, and reading that
directly had already produced two wrong guesses. What the counts say is
unambiguous: 1,600 quadrant evaluations for a 256 by 400 map is four
hundred sixteen-by-sixteen windows, row major, quartered — and the
north/south split lands exactly on 240/246 when a quadrant is assigned by
its own top row against 208 rather than by its window's.

Two things a port gets wrong by reading. $1060 counts **column pairs**,
not cells: the buffer holds two nibbles to a byte and CMP #$0B passes
$0B, $B0 and $BB while rejecting $00, so a quadrant scores out of
thirty-two and the threshold of twenty means twenty pairs. And the split
is the quadrant's row, not the window's.

$40FA is read and written up in NOTES.md — round-to-nearest division
throughout, a cap that keeps the two budgets summing to 255, and a
subtraction of the island counts at the end — but not ported. The one
input still unaccounted for is $A8/$A9.

events.title: measure the village counter rather than reading it
events.message:
measure the village counter rather than reading it

The unpack at $0C9B is self-modifying — it shifts mask bytes out of its
own instruction stream with ASL abs,X — and the buffer it fills is
rolling, so the geometry is hard to get right by reading. Measured
instead, off the interpreter.

The buffer is 16 rows by 16 columns at $0200, eight bytes a row and two
nibbles a byte, with a second at $0280. $1047 quarters it into four 8x8
blocks and $1060 counts the **byte pairs** that hold at least one land
nibble — CMP #$0B passes $0B, $B0 and $BB and rejects $00 — so a
quadrant scores out of 32 rather than 64, and "twenty or more land cells"
means twenty of the thirty-two column pairs.

The numbers a port has to hit, seed $1234 configuration 0: 1,600 calls to
$1060 over 200 iterations of two mask rows each, 240 northern eligible
quadrants and 246 southern, which $40FA turns into budgets of 121 and 125
with thresholds of 127 and 127. Those are in NOTES.md and TODO.md.

The counter needs nothing but the mask, so it can be ported and checked
against 240/246 before $47DF itself is touched.

events.title: find where the village budget actually comes from
events.message:
find where the village budget actually comes from

$47DF does not compute how many villages a band may have. That is done
two phases earlier, during the mask unpack, and carried in zero page —
which is why reading the phase alone leaves it unportable.

$0C9B walks the mask in 8x8 windows; $1047 splits each into four 4x4
quadrants and $1060 counts the cells that are $0B or above. A quadrant
with twenty or more land cells increments a sixteen-bit counter, $70/$71
for the northern half of the map and $72/$73 for the southern. So those
two counters are the number of village-eligible quadrants per band, and
twenty is the same threshold $48EC applies later when it comes to place
one.

$0D5D then calls $40FA, which turns the two counts into $6C/$6D, the
number of villages a band may have, $6E/$6F, the draw a quadrant has to
beat, and $82/$83. The result is complemented at $4173, so a band with
more eligible ground gets both more villages and an easier draw.

That is the whole chain, written into NOTES.md and TODO.md so the next
pass does not start at $47DF and go looking for state that is not there.

events.title: read the village phase, and answer what reads $77-$81
events.message:
read the village phase, and answer what reads $77-$81

$47DF does, and it reads them before anything else: $7A,X is the band the
site belongs to, $78,X the row and $77,X the column, and the phase walks
east from there until it finds somewhere a village will go. So the two
sites $44EF picked out during the mirror are the first two villages on
the map. That question has been open in TODO.md since $44EF was ported.

The rest of the phase is read and written down rather than ported: one
village thrown at random with the box test patched out for it alone, then
a walk over the same sixteen-by-sixteen strips $3EAD uses — downward for
the first band and upward for the second — quartering each and placing a
village in any quarter with twenty or more land cells that also wins a
draw. Villages go into high RAM as well as onto the band, at $E800.

Also corrects an overgeneralization from the last commit. Three half-open
boxes in the water engine against none in the terrain phases looked like
a house style, and then $4441 turned up in the villages scanning its box
closed on both axes. It is not a style and not a rule to generalize from;
check the two branches every time.

events.title: port $3EAD, and with it the water engine is done
events.message:
port $3EAD, and with it the water engine is done

All 1,311 writes of the rivers phase in the first band, cell for cell,
and the generator left exactly where the original leaves it. That is the
third and last entry into the water engine: $380D, $3961 and $3EAD are
now all exact, at 5,007, 259 and 1,311 writes.

$3EAD is not a third routine. It patches five bytes over $3AA5 and five
over $36A2 and NOPs two more, then runs $3961's walk and puts the bytes
back afterwards. What that changes: a finished river is followed by the
upstream pass and a cleared mouth table instead of a distant swamp; a
river shorter than ten cells is not run out to sea but taken back; and
$348D loses its "fewer than two river neighbours" refusal while keeping
its other two.

Its own contribution is where rivers start. It walks the band in
sixteen-by-sixteen strips, 208 of them, and a strip qualifies only if
every cell in it is plain land. Dry interior, not open sea — an earlier
reading in NOTES.md had that backwards and is corrected.

Two bugs, both found by diffing the generator rather than the writes.

$34D9 refuses the *sparse* case, not the crowded one: CMP #$02 / BCC
$34F1 means a river may only join another where there is enough of it to
join. The port had the test inverted, which had never mattered because
nothing before $3EAD reached that path.

And $3DE7's ten-mountain check scans its box half open on both axes. The
port counted the bottom row, found ten mountains on the flank of a range,
and skipped a swamp the original placed — after which every river was one
draw out of step. That is the third half-open box in this engine, against
none at all in the terrain phases, which is too consistent to keep calling
a slip.

events.title: finish $3961 — every write and the generator with it
events.message:
finish $3961 — every write and the generator with it

All 259 writes of the lakes phase in the first band, cell for cell, and
the generator left exactly where the original leaves it. That second part
matters as much as the first: $3EAD starts from it.

What was missing was a swamp, and the reason it was missing is worth
keeping. $3755 has no RTS. Every river finish goes through it, and it
falls through into $3D90 or $3E8B and places a swamp on its way out. So
"JSR $36CC" does not mean "file the river and come back" — it means "file
the river, put a swamp down, and come back". The port had the second
swamp, the one $3AAE asks for explicitly, and not the first.

The symptom was the tell. The rivers after the missing swamp came out in
the right cells with the wrong nibbles: only the plain-or-forest coin
flips were out of step, which is what "the port is one draw behind" looks
like. Diffing writes says where a port diverges; diffing the generator at
each write says how many draws it is out by. Recording the generator
alongside the journal for a single run found this in minutes after an
hour of reading had not.

events.title: grow the rivers back inland from their mouths
events.message:
grow the rivers back inland from their mouths

$3B75 is the last thing $3961 does: once every lake has run, it walks the
mouth table $3531 filled and tries to push each mouth further into the
land. A mouth with two or more river neighbours east and west is measured
north and south instead, and the other way round; the longer run of
unbroken land wins and has to be at least twenty-five cells. Then a river
runs that way until it has come far enough — ten cells at least,
forty-five at most, and never further than the mouth's own river was long.

Its walk is the third setup, $3661, and it is the strictest of the three:
the fan is six cells deep in all three directions and every one of them
must be land, so these rivers are short. Seven of them in the first band
and none longer than ten cells.

It is not right yet. The port reproduces 215 of the phase's 259 writes
and then drifts by a single draw — the cells it erases are the right
cells, and only the plain-or-forest coin flips are out of step, so
something between the last forward step and the erase costs a draw in one
and not the other. TODO.md carries the suspects.

The test grades the part that is finished — the marsh and the outflow,
211 writes — and says plainly that the rest is not graded. A test that
passes on a prefix is not a test.

events.title: port the lakes' outflow, and fix a satellite column that was off by one
events.message:
port the lakes' outflow, and fix a satellite column that was off by one

$3961 is the second entry into the water engine: for each lake, a
radius-7 marsh on the lake itself, then a river out of it. The marsh and
the outflow now match the original exactly — 211 writes, cell for cell —
which is everything the phase does per lake.

Two things had to be right first, and neither was.

$1D42 mirrors the satellite table the same way it mirrors the landmass
tables, `256 - column`, and the port had `255 - column`. Measured across
all three configurations: configuration 0's northern satellite goes from
column 106 before the mirror to 150 after. Nothing noticed because until
$3961 the only thing reading that table was $2D23, whose radius-10 box
marks the same cells either way when the ring around a lake is land. A
digest that matches is not proof the numbers behind it are right — only
that nothing has yet asked them a question they can get wrong. Second
time these tables have done this.

And $3999 drops a marsh on the lake before anything flows out of it,
radius 7, the largest the World Maker places. Missing it costs a draw as
well as ninety-eight cells, so the river diverged four steps in.

$3B2F also turns out to do the opposite of what it looks like: while the
walk is within ten cells of its source it *skips* the lake test rather
than failing it. The source is against a lake by construction, so the
test would refuse every step out of it.

What is left of $3961 is $3B75, the pass it makes over the river mouths
once every lake has run — the other seven, short rivers of the first
band, 48 writes.

The two trace tools now hash the same text, which they did not: one wrote
"x,y,v" and the other the repr of a tuple, so a correct port failed on a
digest for reasons that had nothing to do with it.

events.title: read the other two water entries before porting them
events.message:
read the other two water entries before porting them

$3961 is the lakes finding their outflow: hunt outward from each
satellite for the $0F mark, measure the land in four directions with
$4014, and leave by the shortest run of at least seventeen. Its walk is
$38CD again with different rules — a river crossing another writes $4
rather than unwinding, the direction fan is scored rather than taken
first come, and a step landing within ten cells of the source is refused.

$3EAD is not a third routine. It copies five bytes over $3AA5 and five
over $36A2 and NOPs two more, which swaps the direction pick inside $369F
and the finish, and makes $348D always return carry clear. Same engine,
two holes filled differently.

Writing the reading down before porting it, because the reading is the
expensive part and it is the part that gets lost.

events.title: finish the rivers, and with them $2E32
events.message:
finish the rivers, and with them $2E32

Every one of the 6,658 writes $2E32's range half makes in the first band
now matches the original — spine, spur, clearing, all ten sourced rivers
with their unwinds, their fifty-one mouths and their swamps, and the arms
— in both configurations the fixture holds. The phase is done.

The piece that was missing is what happens when the walk finds open water
ahead: it does not stop. $369F carries the river the last few cells to
the shore, stepping the one direction until the ground gives way. $3755
files both ends into the table at $E681 — the source, the mouth, and the
length written once positive and once negated, which is how a pair is
recognised as a pair, capped at $7F and accumulated into $EBCA. Then two
swamps through $3D97: one where the river met the sea, four to seven
cells to the side, and a second ten to twenty-nine rows away.

$3D97 is the swamp, and it is more careful than it looks. It throws
radius-squared-times-two cells into a box, keeping only land that is not
already swamp or a lake mark, up to 256 tries each. It refuses outright
where $1021's latitude forbids swamp, and again on a draw against three
times the distance from the middle of the map — so swamp thins toward the
poles rather than stopping at a line. And it gives up before it starts if
the box already holds ten mountains or ten swamps.

$38EE also leaves the engine set up for whoever runs next: the erase
allowance drops from ten to six and the persistence rises from $AA to
$B4, and neither is put back. That is not tidiness, it is how $3961 and
$3EAD get their parameters.

The range test now grades every stage of every landmass rather than
stopping at the first one the port could not reach. Configuration 1 is
kept for a different reason than before: it is the only case whose first
band never sources a river, so it is the only one that exercises $2F0B
first.

events.title: port $380D, the river the mountains source — 6,563 of 6,658 writes exact
events.message:
port $380D, the river the mountains source — 6,563 of 6,658 writes exact

The last stage of $2E32, and the first thing to drive the river engine.
It picks a row part way down the mountain spine, walks west to the coast
and back east past the range, checks the spot is clear of the lakes, and
hands the position to the engine.

Graded against the write trace, the whole of $2E32's range half now
reproduces the original's first 6,563 writes exactly — spine, spur,
clearing and 4,982 of the 5,007 the sourced rivers make — including all
fifty-one river mouths, in order. That covers $32CC's setup, $333C's
chooser, $33B7's aim, $3300's recorded step, $33EF's erase and $3531's
mouth finder, none of which had been exercised before this.

Two things the diff caught that reading had not.

$3450 does not end the attempt. A river that unwinds to nothing jumps
back to $380D itself, and the whole placement runs again from a new row —
the first landmass in the first band makes ten attempts before one
sticks. Treating the unwind as the end left 16 writes where there should
have been 5,007.

The lake-mark boxes at $3897 and $3506 are scanned **half open**. $38A9
and $3515 step the column and compare it against the right edge with BCC,
so the right-hand column is never looked at, and $38B3 and $351F do the
same to the bottom row. Every other box in the World Maker — the marking,
the spread, the scatter, the shading — is closed on all four sides, so
this reads as a slip rather than a design. It is worth 1,745 correct
writes before a river takes one step the original refused.

What is left of $380D is the finish. When the walk finds open water ahead
it goes to $3959, $369F, $36CC and $3E53 rather than simply stopping;
that path writes 32 cells of $0E in the first band and none of it is
ported, so the port's last river runs on past where the original ends it
and files one mouth too many. Everything before that point is exact.

events.title: add the river engine's erase and its mouth finder
events.message:
add the river engine's erase and its mouth finder

$33EF is the half of the engine that makes the rest of it safe: a river
that cannot finish is not left half-drawn, it is walked backwards along
the record and overwritten with plain and forest, one cell at a time on
the sign of a draw. Verified against the trace before writing it — the
first river $380D draws in band 0 is exactly eight steps out and eight
back, and the erase writes are the forward path in reverse.

$3531 finds the river mouth. Fifteen steps back along the record; the
cell three steps back is the candidate, the four after it must still
carry this river's own tile, and none of the fifteen may already be a
$4. Then the candidate is a mouth only if fewer than three of its four
neighbours are river or shallow, with the edges of the band counting as
if they were. What it files at $E2F1 is row, column and the river's
length, and it puts a $4 down — which is why a river mouth reads as
navigable water rather than as river.

The mouth finder was written twice. The first pass guessed at $11's
countdown and inverted the neighbour test; reading $35B1 through $3610
properly says the count is of cells in $4 to $A and that three or more
disqualifies. Guessing at a routine and moving on is the exact habit this
codebase keeps punishing.

Neither routine is exercised yet — the entries that drive them are still
to come, so this is transcription rather than anything verified. The
grading follows once $380D can run.

events.title: trace the whole pipeline's writes, and start on the water engine
events.message:
trace the whole pipeline's writes, and start on the water engine

The method that made $2E32 portable in pieces, widened to everything that
is left. Every write goes through $0FD3, and there the pointer and index
registers say exactly where; pipeline_trace.py records the sequence for
all nine phases $0E20 runs, tagged with the phase and — inside the river
phases — with the river, since $32CC and $3661 each start one.

That matters because the three phases left are not three phases. $380D,
$3961 and $3EAD are three entries into one river engine and share 776 of
their addresses; measured separately they are 1,060, 1,459 and 1,635
distinct addresses, but 1,996 in union. A port arrives at parts of all
three at once and has to be graded that way, river by river.

The capture also settles two things. $4CF2 writes nothing to the band in
either band of a whole run, so the earlier reading that it needs no port
holds. And $2C14 does write — 213 cells in the first band and 65 in the
second — so the band writer is not only a writer.

The engine records what it draws in high RAM and neither table is on the
band: $E000 holds a river's steps three bytes at a time and $E2F1 holds
the river mouths. Their contents are map data and stay in local/; the
fixture gets their digests.

RiverEngine is the forward half of the walk: the tables at $329C, which
turn out to be routing rather than data — $32AC is four (dx, dy) pairs,
$32B4 says where a turn goes, and $329C maps a pair of directions to the
nibble written, which settles that the map's 5 to A are connection masks
and not depths. The four entries it refuses are the reversals. Also
$333C's chooser, $33B7's aim, $3300's recorded step and $363B's straight
run. The erase at $33EF, the mouth finder at $3531 and the three entries
are still to come.

One correction while reading it: $33CC adds to the column without a CLC,
which looks like a carry bug worth reproducing and is not — both $33B7
and $33C8 ASL a value that is 0 to 3, so the carry is always clear there.
The same shape is genuinely live elsewhere in this engine, which is why
it was worth checking rather than assuming.

events.title: file the landmass the isthmus creates, and grade the ranges on a second configuration
events.message:
file the landmass the isthmus creates, and grade the ranges on a second configuration

$1B5F has two call sites and the port had one. $226A files a landmass after
the placement loop has grown it, which is the obvious one. $1866 files one
from inside the walker: $17C8 builds the isthmus, works out where the
partner continent's centre will be — $0C for the column, $08/$09 plus the
radius for the row — and files it there and then, before the walk that
grows it has taken a step.

So a whole continent was missing from the position tables at $0300/$033C.
It only shows in a configuration that places a pair, which is
configuration 1 and no other, and every fixture until now was
configuration 0. The mask was right the whole time in all three
configurations; it is only what the walk filed away while it ran that was
short, and nothing read those tables until $2E32 did.

The order matters too. The isthmus files before the placement containing
it finishes, so appending at the end of the loop would put the entry in
the wrong slot and the mirror at $1D42 would then transform the wrong
rows. Measured against the interpreter, all three configurations now
reproduce the original's tables exactly.

What caught it was grading a second configuration, which was nearly free —
the range fixture merges runs. Configuration 1's first band turns out to
be the one case where nothing is out of reach: its continent sits on the
last row of the band, too low for $3134 and with too short a spine for
$380D, so the band grades end to end. That verifies $2F0B, the
small-landmass drawer, which configuration 0 could not reach at all
because every instance of it there is drawn after a $380D.

The range fixture now also carries the generator state at $2AE9 and $2E32
and the band digest at $2ED2, so the range tests stand on their own
instead of borrowing phase boundaries from the terrain fixture. A stage
that writes nothing is not recorded by the trace tool, so the comparison
drops the port's empty stages rather than expecting them to line up.

events.title: port $2E32, the terrain generator, except for its river stage
events.message:
port $2E32, the terrain generator, except for its river stage

The biggest phase in the pipeline, and it comes apart into two halves that
do not depend on each other.

The first half is three sweeps of the whole band. Every plain cell pushes
shallows into the water around it ($2C3A: $4 in a cross five rows tall and
three columns wide, $5 on a draw under $64 in a plus inside that). Every
shallow becomes ocean shelf and drags up to six more cells of it out to
sea each way ($2CDB). Every plain cell becomes forest on a draw against a
threshold that moves with latitude — the first band starts at $96 and
loses one every even row, the second starts at $36 and gains one, so the
map is forested at both poles and bare across the middle. Four constants
and an LSR on the row counter.

The rows they start at are not consistent: 0 for the first band, and $10,
$0E, $10 for the second. The sixteen-row overlap is skipped by the first
and third sweeps and swept twice by the second, so two rows of the seam
get their shelves laid over again. That is in the finished map and a port
does not get to tidy it.

The second half walks the landmass tables and draws a range through each,
and the radius picks between two completely different drawers at $46.
Below it, $2F0B throws two arms of mountain into two quadrants and a third
of swamp where the latitude allows swamp at all — nothing walks, every
cell is thrown independently and rejected if it lands on water, so a small
island's mountains are a blotch. At $46 and above, $2F8C follows the west
coast down: each row it finds where the land begins, steps inland by a
drifting amount, and runs east, never past the landmass center. $306C is
what makes that a range rather than a stack of bars — after each row it
looks along the row above for mountain further east than it reached, and
closes a gap of five columns or more by halves.

$3134 then adds a second range east of the spine on a coin flip, and
$31E6 runs back down the middle turning forest into plain on a draw that
widens toward both ends of the range. Treeline, and the only thing in the
World Maker that takes terrain away rather than putting it down.

Two things had to be right or the whole thing desynchronizes quietly.
$0B16 is a scattered draw — twelve register advances summed, centered,
halved, scaled — and it is what gives the walkers a wandering line instead
of a fraying one. And $328A reads $03 off the zero page rather than the
value $0B16 returned, because the return is clamped at zero and $03 still
holds the signed step; that is the only reason a run drifts west as well
as east.

Graded: the three sweeps against the band digest and the generator state
at each checkpoint, and $2F8C, $3134 and $31E6 against the writes the
original made — 892, 212 and 490 of them. $0B16 against 400 real calls,
value and register both.

Two corrections that came from measuring, not from reading. $13E0 ends at
$141B with an RTS that $28F3 patches in at run time; the listing shows NOP
there, and the JMP $0FAE at $141C is a separate entry point rather than
$13E0's tail. Reading it as a tail leads to a flat contradiction and only
a probe settles it. And $3134's coin flip runs the other way round: the
RTS sits between the BPL and its target, so the branch is the go-ahead,
not the refusal.

What is left is $380D, and it is not really terrain code — it picks a spot
in the middle of the spine, checks it clear of the lake marks, and calls

events.title: capture the terrain generator's sweeps and its per-stage writes
events.message:
capture the terrain generator's sweeps and its per-stage writes

$2E32 is 1,750 addresses and there was no way to grade a port of it in
pieces. The pipeline fixture only had a digest at the phase's entry and at
the next phase's, so a first attempt could only be told "wrong", not which
of its several loops was wrong. Two additions fix that.

terrain_reference.py now records the band and the generator state at
$2E5B, $2E84 and $2ED2 — the three points where one of $2E32's band
sweeps hands over to the next — and at $2F04, the head of the per-landmass
loop, along with the entry it is about to draw. That makes each sweep
gradeable on its own digest.

The ranges after them cannot be graded that way at all. $2E32 draws each
landmass in four stages, a port arrives at them one at a time, and the
moment one is missing the port's band and the original's legitimately
differ — so every landmass after the first starts from somewhere the port
has never been, and a digest of either band says nothing. range_trace.py
grades on the writes instead: every cell either drawer puts down goes
through $0FD3, and there the pointer and the index registers say exactly
where ($29/$2A is the row, Y * 2 + X the column, X being the parity $0FC3
left behind). Each write is tagged with the stage that made it, so a port
of $2F8C alone can be checked against $2F8C's 892 writes.

What that leaves in the fixture is counts and SHA-256s. The write list
itself is a list of map cells and goes to local/, which is ignored;
range_diff.py reads it back and names the first cell the two disagree on.

Also captures $0B16, the scattered draw the mountain walkers steer by,
with the generator state before and after each call. It costs twelve
register advances rather than one, so a port that gets its values right
and its cost wrong desynchronizes everything downstream — worth its own
fixture rather than being inferred from a band that disagrees.

events.title: BUGS.md: record the sprite-at-a-doorway defect and the debug-state request
events.message:
BUGS.md: record the sprite-at-a-doorway defect and the debug-state request

Defect 5, reported from play on the Layer 8b build: the player sprite's
lower part is missing at a doorway on deck 4, with stray pixels beside
it that nothing clears.

The useful half is what it is NOT. Reproduced headless at the reported
spot and measured:

  - sprite draw NOPed, buffer vs a SPACE RedrawAll: 0 differences in
    10240, so the restore leaves nothing behind
  - sprite RESTORE NOPed instead, buffer vs the no-sprite buffer: 79
    bytes across strip rows 7, 8 and 9 - top rotor, digit block and
    bottom rotor all present, and the only absent scanlines are sprite
    rows 5, 14 and 20, which are blank for every droid by design
  - field counter reads 2, so the pass is not overrunning its frame
  - slot 0 is nowhere near the cull limits, and took the compiled fast
    path

So the blitter drew a complete sprite into the right place and the
restore put the background back exactly. The buffer holds what it should
and the screen does not show it. That removes the blitter, the
save/restore pair and the door redraw from suspicion.

Also recorded as a technique: sample with the RESTORE disabled, not the
draw. A dump at an arbitrary cycle count can land between SprRestoreAll
and SprDrawAll, where the buffer legitimately holds no sprite - which
reads exactly like the blitter having drawn nothing, and did cost a
wrong conclusion here before it was spotted.

The obvious reading of "buffer right, display wrong" is a raster race,
and the numbers support one - the body is ~39,100 cycles against a
~24,600 cycle window. KC has rejected that; the mechanism is still open
and the entry says so, so nobody re-derives it.

Also notes the request for a way to hand game state back. What is
actually wanted is smaller than a state dump - a position bookmark of
deck, plyX and posY is enough to poke the player back to the spot, since
everything else is reachable from the emulator once there. Blocked on
main RAM: Layer 8b left 46 bytes below &3000, so it waits on PARADAT
moving to sideways RAM. Two options costed for when the space exists.

events.title: port the landmass tables and the mirror's fixup of them
events.message:
port the landmass tables and the mirror's fixup of them

The tables at $0300 and $033C now match the original's exactly. Three things
had to be right together, and each was its own small trap.

$1B5F's filing: a continent tall enough to reach into both bands is filed
twice, and its northern entry lands at the band boundary — row $C0 — rather
than at row minus radius. $1BAF sets $23 to $C0 for the call and puts it back
afterwards, which is easy to read straight past.

$1D42's fixup: every byte goes through $1C2A and $1C3D into a scratch buffer
at $9100, and a vertical flip then swaps which buffer goes back into which
table, because a row mirrored inside 208 rows belongs to the other band. $63
and $64 are byte counts and get swapped with the tables; $0D84 divides both
by three on the way into the pipeline, which is why they read as entry counts
by the time $2E32 sees them.

And only what is filed before the mirror is fixed up. The command table's
islands are placed by the second command, after it has run, so they stay
exactly as filed. That made two of five entries look untransformed and for a
while looked like a fault in the arithmetic rather than in when it ran.

With this $2E32 has what it needs. Its own first sweep is the next unread
thing: $2C3A off every plain cell, through $2D96/$2D9E to $2CAF/$2CC0.

events.title: Explain the reversed x-position index and the scenery hit flags

Explain the reversed x-position index and the scenery hit flags

check_scenery_collisions and layout_objects share a page and neither end
of it was pinned down.

$EAFE and $EAFC are the last two words of the page layout_objects fills:
the left and right hand x-positions for the nearest road slice, pushed in
that order from $EB00 down. They vibrate in the debugger because they are
rewritten every frame, and they say where a roadside object on each side
would stand rather than that one is there. That also answers "how is
$EAFC different to $EAFE".

The ~(IY[0] * 2) that puzzled both loops is one instruction doing two
jobs: the doubling is the tables' 16-bit stride and the complement
reverses the direction of travel through them, so slot depth N reads the
word at index 127 - N. ~(2N) is always odd, which is why the reads that
follow take the high byte first and step down to the low one.

The flags at $A558 and $A574 are scenery_hit's documented A: 0 flips
right, 1 flips left, with $8C the speed cap it takes in A'. $A40E's bit 6
is clear for plain road and set for a tunnel, a fork or a dirt track.
$A3D1 clears the passed-object trigger because the car is alongside the
left hand object.

events.title: Name the depth set pairs and stretchy graphic height rules
events.message:
Name the depth set pairs and stretchy graphic height rules

The 850 "TBD" words in the stretchy graphic parts are depth set pairs: a
depth threshold in the low byte and, in the high byte, a byte offset from
the bitmap pointer at the head of the set. Offsets are multiples of 7, the
size of one bitmap descriptor in the original, so each names a bitmap by
index. Ten pairs per set, matching depthset_pair_t and DEPTHSET_MAX in
C/libraries/ChaseHQ/Data/Stages.h.

The 137 "?index" bytes that head each stretchy graphic entry are the height
rule, not an index: 2 draws at a fixed height taken from the bitmap width,
3 to 10 scale the perspective height by a fixed percentage and 1 terminates
the list. Every value in the data falls in that range, and the terminator
the skool already named is 1, which is what STRETCHY_TYPE_END is.

events.title: Fire is L, and the lift is driven by the movement keys
events.message:
Fire is L, and the lift is driven by the movement keys

Two fixes to Layer 8b's controls, both reported from playing it.

FIRE MOVES FROM RETURN TO L, INKEY -87. Verified in the emulator with a
scan of every negative INKEY code while the key was held, rather than
recalled - key codes are exactly the kind of fact CLAUDE.md says not to
write from memory.

THE LIFT IS NOW DRIVEN BY K/M, THE UP/DOWN MOVEMENT KEYS, not the cursor
keys. Binding it to the cursors was simply wrong: ChangeDeck ($2705)
steps on joyYDir, which is the joystick - the same control that walks the
droid - so in a lift, up and down are the up and down already under your
fingers. It reads far worse than an ordinary bug, too, because the only
feedback a lift has until Layer 9 draws the side view is the deck
changing: with nothing bound, stepping into a lift looks like a freeze.

The lift's edges get their own prevLU/prevLD rather than sharing
prevUp/prevDn with the debug hop, so a cursor key held on the way in
cannot swallow the first press inside. The cursor keys stay the debug
free hop outside a lift, which is worth keeping until every deck can be
reached by lift and tested that way.

Verified: on deck 1's lift at tile (26,4), L sets liftMode with liftPos

events.title: Layer 8b: lifts, and the ship becomes traversable
events.message:
Layer 8b: lifts, and the ship becomes traversable

Stand on a lift platform, press RETURN, and UP/DOWN move through the
decks that shaft serves. RETURN again steps out. Outside a lift UP/DOWN
stay the debug free hop, which is worth keeping until every deck can be
reached by lift and tested that way.

WHERE THE LIFT ACTUALLY IS took a search, because it is not written down
anywhere. liftPosX/Y are the VIEW ORIGIN in characters - DoLift ($267A)
writes ScreenPosX/Y = liftPos * 8 and FindLift compares them against the
tile-aligned origin. Scanning every offset from there and asking which
gives a consistent tile across all 30 stops:

  dx=5 dy=2  ->  tile 3 on 30/30
  dx=8 dy=2  ->  tile 21 on 21/30   (next best, and not consistent)

Tile 3's sixteen characters are all bit-7-clear - a 32x32 patch with no
wall in it, which is what a platform you stand on should look like. The
exporter applies the +5/+2 so the offset never appears at run time. That
is the third contradiction of the tile catalogue in graphics.md, which
calls tile 3 part of the "core wall set"; treat that catalogue as
unreliable throughout.

A shaft is a contiguous run of indices and the decks it serves are NOT
adjacent - shaft 0 runs decks 0, 2, 3, 14, 15 - so stepping walks the
table rather than the deck number. Index 0 and 31 carry shaft 8, which
matches no real shaft, and that one fact is the whole bounds check.

Lift mode is a FLAG, not a modal loop. DoLift spins its own loop because
nothing else has to keep running there; here the rupture, the sprite
pool and the edge redraws all do, so a loop would have to reimplement
the main loop. The flag suppresses movement and re-points UP/DOWN.

LiftFind matches on the TILE the player's reference cell is in, not on
the view origin: our play area is 15 rows to the C64's 17 and the
horizontal dead zone means the origin is no longer a fixed offset from
the player, so the origin test does not carry over.

Arrival places the player at tileCol*32, tileRow*32-48 - chosen so posY
lands on a multiple of 8, because LoadDeck forces `line` to 0 and a posY
that disagreed would jump a scanline on the next pass. That retires
CentreOnDeck as the spawn path and with it the "lands inside a wall on
some decks" defect.

IT COST THE LAST OF MAIN RAM. code_end hit &307A, 122 bytes past the
sprite save areas. doorDef (112 B) and blankTileRow (64 B) moved into
the data bank - sideways RAM is RAM, and both are only ever touched with
SWRAM_DATA paged in, which is the resting state. That leaves 54 bytes
free below &3000, so PARADAT moving out is now the binding constraint
rather than a someday one.

Verified in the emulator: riding shaft 2 from deck 1 steps liftPos
10 -> 11 and deck 1 -> 4, arriving at plyX 512 / posY 176, exactly the
recorded stop (16,7), with the platform visibly under the sprite.
Stepping down from index 13 leaves it at 13, so the sentinel holds.
LiftFind fires at the platform centre and at its first character, and
refuses one tile off.

events.title: wonderboy/atari: batch 36 — six clean monsters, and the grep-to-zero rule
events.message:
wonderboy/atari: batch 36 — six clean monsters, and the grep-to-zero rule

Slots 14-19 ($35d8..$4118, 1,940 B, all CLEAN — the family's first block
with no boundary): the escort-dropping patroller whose retry sits below
the failed-allocation branch; the turn-and-hop walker (list chosen
BEFORE the turn, where slot 14's is after — pinned per slot); the
lobbing hopper whose bclr is test and write at once; the drifter on two
GLOBAL cursors whose 1-in-8 draw seeds five records numbered 5 to 1
(the y table is HALF the x one, so the burst fires twice per horizontal
figure); the charger that saves its whole flag byte across the charge;
and the two-phase glider that PUBLISHES THE RECORD IT JUST ALLOCATED as
a sprite — an original defect, reproduced both-armed (offset $14 of the
new record, or the vector page's word on a full pool) and generalised
into docs/m68k-disassembly.md. 43 of 62 rows live; verified 249 /
30,456 B (68.8%); suite 4670 -> 4812. The plate was the cheap authority
six for six. Two inbound edges from unported rows (slot 24's bra.w into
the seed burst, slot 25 borrowing slot 18's rts) are pinned and
cross-referenced in the OWNERS' plates so batch 37 reuses instead of
re-porting.

THE GATE'S FIND: the batch's own plate-fix pass failed silently — the
ledger certified four corrections of which one landed, one landed
transposed, two never landed (a scripted replace asserting only "text
changed" met a pattern that matched nothing). The rule that fixes the
class, now in docs/methodology.md and applied here with proof: A PLATE
CORRECTION IS LANDED WHEN THE OLD PHRASE GREPS TO ZERO — assert each
replacement individually, and never let a retraction quote the
retracted phrase. The tree-wide grep immediately caught a rename miss
no new-name grep could find. Also fixed under it: slot 19 documented
as irreversibly attacking on four surfaces while the bytes (and its
own test) return it to the glide; the spawner family rule that
contradicted the durable doc written from the same defect; and the
sibling-table over-read ambiguity — reconciled from the image to five
of thirteen rows, then CLOSED with three-way discriminating cursors
(raw vs masked-same vs masked-sibling), 8/8 composite mutants caught.

Queued: slots 20-27 close the family (extents in their plates), then
pickup ($38), 39-46, 57, player last.

events.title: Let the view scroll off the map vertically, so the top row is reachable
events.message:
Let the view scroll off the map vertically, so the top row is reachable

The player's reference cell is fixed at PLY_REFY (63 px) below the view
origin, so clamping the view at the map edge stopped the player eight
character rows short of it - at each end. On deck 1 the top wall is
character rows 0-3 and the first corridor is 4-7, so the player was
pinned to the bottom scanline of that corridor and could not reach the
two doors on it. The same applies at the bottom of any deck that is a
full 16 tiles tall.

DoMove ($3849) has no clamp at all: it adds the speed to ScreenPosY with
plain 16-bit arithmetic and lets the view run off the map, which is why
the original shows blank space above the top wall. Only the wall probes
stop the player. We now do the same, bounded to PLY_VOID = 64 px either
side - enough for the reference cell to reach rows 0 and 63, and small
enough to keep mapYr inside a signed byte.

mapYr and cellY are signed from here on, so ApplyMove's posY >> 3 became
an arithmetic shift. That is not pedantry: floor division is what makes
posY AND 7 the right sub-row offset on the negative side too. ClampY's
low end is now a compare against MIN_PX_Y rather than against zero,
using the same unsigned-compare trick ca_clampneg already used.

The draw side turned out nearly free. Map rows are 0-63, so ONE
`AND #&C0` catches both a negative row and one past 63, and off the map
is simply a row of tile 0 - whose definition is 16 zero bytes:

  BandSetRow  points maprow at 64 zero bytes, so every tile on the row
              reads as tile 0
  DrawColumn  points tdp straight at tiledefs
  MapChar     returns character 0 - blank, and bit 7 clear, so the
              probes read it as walkable and only the deck's own edge
              wall stops the player

Nothing else in the band or column paths changes.

Verified: play buffer diffed byte-for-byte against RedrawAll at
mapYr = -3, after a diagonal scroll along the top edge, with
JSR SprDrawAll poked to NOPs - 0 differences in 10240. That is the check
that matters, since the incremental path reaches the blank rows through
BandSetRow and DrawColumn while RedrawAll reaches them through MapChar.
Confirmed by walking: posY reaches -24 and the player stops on the wall
with its reference cell on row 4, the top of the first corridor.
