events.title: port the World Maker's bounded draws
events.message:
port the World Maker's bounded draws

$22B4 (8-bit) and $247B (16-bit) become nextByte(from:below:) and
nextWord(from:below:) on WorldMakerRNG, with randrange_reference.py capturing
what the original returns across 4 seeds: 40 byte cases and 24 word cases.

Three things had to be right.

They are rejection samplers, and the waste matters. Each rejected candidate
still advances the LFSR, so a port that reduced one draw by modulo would produce
entirely plausible values and desynchronize every later draw in the world. The
byte fixture is therefore a sequence captured from a single seeding rather than
independent cases, so it tests that the port throws away the same candidates.

$247B consumes two advances per candidate, not one. The first supplies the low
byte; the second is drawn only for its sign, and the high byte is 1 when that
draw is below $80, else 0 (LDA $CF / BMI / INX at $24E1). Results therefore cap
at 511, which is exactly enough for the map's 400 rows and looks deliberate.

The bounds are two parameters rather than a Range. Swift's Range traps at
construction when inverted, so it cannot represent lo > hi -- which $22BA
explicitly handles by returning lo without advancing the register. Modelling
these bounds as a Range would impose an invariant the 6502 does not have and
convert a reachable path into a crash. Two of the three tests failed that way
before the signature changed; the type system was reporting a real mismatch.

events.title: measure the land-mass phase instead of reading it
events.message:
measure the land-mass phase instead of reading it

The $2286 table is not three seven-byte records of signed motion vectors. That
reading came from noticing the x7 stride and assuming the stride was the record
size. Following the actual read order -- $2158/$2165/$216B, then STX $56 and the
loop back at $227A -- shows three command sequences of 3-byte commands
terminated by $FE, where the x7 only picks which sequence to start at. Parsed
that way all three land exactly on the sentinel, which a wrong stride would not
do three times out of three.

The fields are (size class, flags, count). The $FF is read with BIT, never as a
number, which is what rules out the vector reading.

That is a falsifiable prediction, so wm_config.py tests it: patch the ten bytes
at $2146 that draw the configuration, run the phase headlessly, flood-fill the
result. All three build exactly what the table predicts -- 2+2, 1+2 and 1+6.
Configuration 1 is the telling one: its command count is 1 and it always builds
two continents, because flag bit 7 places a second landmass at a fixed offset.

Two traps found on the way, both of which produced confident wrong answers:

Forcing a value by stopping at a checkpoint and writing a register assumes the
stop happened where you think it did. It did not: $57 read back as 1 whatever
was written, because the phase is entered more than once. Worse, that broken
first pass "worked" -- three runs returned the three predicted shapes, just
permuted, which is exactly what an uncontrolled random draw looks like at n=3.
Patching the instructions that compute the value removes the timing question,
and a read-back proves it took.

Waiting on vice_ping for "paused" reports halts that never happened. Three runs
were misread as stopping at $22DB, $2385 and $236C, all inside the placement
loop, none of them a checkpoint. Poll the checkpoint's hit_count instead.
wm_trace.py still waits the old way and its snapshots deserve re-checking.

wm_landmask.py settles the buffer visually. At 32 bytes per row $5700 is
continents with coastlines; at 128 it is the same data repeated four times
across. No statistics needed, which matters on this project.

wm_deterministic.py makes the phase reproducible. Patching the seeding site at
$20CB, the raster IRQ's entropy stir at $2406 and the configuration draw at
$2146 turns it into a pure function of (seed, config): the same pair reproduces
all 12,800 bytes across separate emulator boots. $0A49 also reads hardware but
is a raster sync that always returns the same value, so it needs no patch.

wm_coverage.py answers what the port actually has to cover. Static reachability
cannot: walking from $23D3 reaches 7,924 of 8,152 instructions, because $1900's
bounds guard jumps to $2473 -> $20A3 and restarts the whole generator if the
coastline walker runs off the buffer. One such edge makes everything reachable
from everything. Measured with non-halting checkpoints, the phase executes 64 of
207 routines, and completes in about 7 seconds under warp.

Fixtures are digests, not masks. A land mask is 12,800 bytes of map produced by
Ozark Softscape's generator, and this project does not ship map data; the
existing fixtures are numeric behavior of general-purpose routines, which is a
different kind of thing. Land-cell counts and blob areas travel alongside so a
failure is diagnosable. Full masks go to local/, which is gitignored.

events.title: diag: trace the UI text CLUT slots (Nova black-hotkey report)
events.message:
diag: trace the UI text CLUT slots (Nova black-hotkey report)

Field report: on the Nova the menu hotkey letters are BLACK until the char-gen
sprite page loads, then correct for the rest of the session. The letters paint
with FIXED clut indices (11 cyan / 15 white — the l6c2a label draw), not a
nearest-match, so black means slots 11/15 held black when the menu painted.

Measured locally (STE, so the engine side is machine-independent) and it
ELIMINATES the ordering theory:
  main: clut 129 installed, entries = 256      <- the 256-entry art palette
  main: clut 129 installed, entries = 256         (documented to clobber 1/7/11/12/15)
  paltrace: UI palette install entries = 33    <- UI palette lands AFTER them
    menu_pal[11] cyan  rgb = 0x67FFFF          <- correct value
    menu_pal[15] white rgb = 0xFFFFFF
  menu: modal up
i.e. the engine writes the right cyan/white to 11/15, last, before the menu is
up. So the remaining suspect is the Nova pen mapping (nova_hw_inverse) — the one
thing in display_nova.c that can only be validated on the card.

Trace changes: log every UI-palette install (engine side, with the 11/15 RGB),
and in nova_set_palette log each write to slot 11/15 WITH the vs_color pen it is
routed to. Budget raised 80 -> 400 lines and narrowed from "all idx<16" to just
11/15, because the old bound was exhausted during boot and never reached the
char-gen install that "unlocks" the colour. One card run then distinguishes:
same rgb+pen written again at char-gen (=> mapping/timing) vs different values
(=> engine gating).

events.title: fix: Exit-From-Play freeze — jt574 must restore -27932 on every create exit
events.message:
fix: Exit-From-Play freeze — jt574 must restore -27932 on every create exit

Hardware DBG.LOG (Nova card, P->C->D->E->E) pinned it: the l07dc cleanup
`while (g_a5_27932 != 0) jt19(0,1)` spun forever (counter climbed past 188),
with 27928(party)=0 and 27932=cg_rec (the static char-gen buffer, 0x1c37c0).

Root cause in jt574 (Create Character): l3666's Done sets -27932 to the temporary
cg_rec so the stat sheet / name / review operate on it, but the restore
`-27932 = -27928` lived ONLY on the full-commit pool-add path (inside
`if (cg_pool_count < 16)`). Every cancel — sheet Exit (the user's first E),
body-icon review cancel, "Save NAME?" declined — and a full 16-char pool
returned with -27932 still dangling at cg_rec. jt19 is faithful (the Mac's
L2d8a also just rts when -27928==0), so it never clears a selection that isn't
in the party list -> the drain loop never terminates -> hard freeze. The Mac's
jt574 tail restores -27932 on every exit; the port didn't.

Fix:
- jt574: route all create-cancel returns through a cg_done label that restores
  -27932 = -27928, and move the commit-path restore out of the pool-count guard
  so it runs on every exit.
- l07dc cleanup: add a no-progress guard (if jt19 leaves -27932 unchanged, drop
  it and break) so any future dangling selection degrades to a dropped pointer
  instead of a machine-hard-freeze.

Display-independent (not Nova-specific); the FRUA_NOVA correlation was
incidental — the merge only changed which builds reach this Hall path in
testing. Instrumentation (FRUA_FREEZELOG) retained, inert in shipping, pending
a hardware confirm of the fix.

events.title: use a lossless WebP for the screenshot, at native size with alpha
events.message:
use a lossless WebP for the screenshot, at native size with alpha

Three faults in how I first added it.

Transparency was destroyed by a convert("RGB"), so the window's rounded corners
got a black background that was never in the source.

Resampling with Lanczos was wrong twice over: it blurs pixel art into gradients,
and those gradients then compress badly. Nearest at exactly half is crisp and
much smaller -- but it visibly mushes the title bar and HUD, which are
antialiased text and cannot survive any downscale. So there is no resampling at
all now; the browser can scale it for display, and it looks better on a retina
screen for it.

Lossless WebP at native size is 436 KB against 859 KB for the equivalent PNG,
and the saved file is verified bit-identical to the source crop.

events.title: restore the mountain variant formula; it was right all along
events.message:
restore the mountain variant formula; it was right all along

(x & 3) + T[x & 1] + T[y & 1], T at $58B4, is correct, and the data layout shows
it was designed that way: the mountain region is 144 bytes, exactly four $24
slots, and a tile is 32 bytes, so every slot carries precisely the four bytes of
headroom that x & 3's shift needs. T[x & 1] + T[y & 1] picks slot 0, 1 or 2.
Rendering all twelve combinations gives twelve whole, distinct peaks; ranges now
read as ridges rather than repeating one shape.

I rejected this twice and both rejections were wrong.

The first was an oracle that could not answer the question. The formula matched
only 56 of 400 tiles sampled from the community reference map, which looked
decisive -- but these notes had already established that map is an atlas render
by another author using a single fixed variant. A correct position-dependent
formula can only agree with such a render where it happens to emit that variant,
about one position in eight. 56/400 is 14%. The measurement was confirming the
formula and I read it as refuting it.

The second was a misattributed symptom. Mountains really did look sliced in the
app, but the cause was tile textures being 64 pixels in a 32-point cell, so
nearest-neighbour minification dropped pixel rows at every zoom below 2.0.
Fixing the texture size fixed the slicing, by which point the formula had been
reverted for a fault it did not cause.

Check that the oracle can answer the question, and that the symptom belongs to
the suspect.

events.title: keep the real terrain art far further out; drop linear and mipmaps
events.message:
keep the real terrain art far further out; drop linear and mipmaps

Answering a fair question: the glyphs are SpriteKit textures on a tile map and
do scale, so swapping to flat colour below 1.0 was compensating for a filtering
choice rather than a real limit, and it threw the terrain art away across the
whole range people browse at. Checked by minifying a rendered region 2:1 both
ways -- the art survives, rivers stay continuous. The overview threshold is now
0.3 instead of 1.0.

An attempt to follow the zoom with the filter went badly and is reverted.
SpriteKit exposes one filtering mode per texture, and linear plus mipmaps drops
to a lower mip level and magnifies it, so at 0.89x the map came out as fuzzy
blocks -- far worse than the aliasing it was meant to fix. Nearest with no
mipmaps holds up now that a tile texture is exactly its cell size; the original
breakage was a 64-pixel texture in a 32-point cell, not the filter.

events.title: draw the overview as one filtered image so it can interpolate
events.message:
draw the overview as one filtered image so it can interpolate

The zoomed-out view went blocky immediately and no filtering setting helped,
because there was nothing to filter. filteringMode interpolates within a
texture, and the overview was a tile map where every tile was its own
flat-coloured texture, so each stayed a hard-edged square however far out you
went. The blockiness was tile boundaries, not sampling.

It is now a single SKSpriteNode carrying one pixel per map tile -- 256x400 --
stretched over the world with linear filtering. Coastlines, river courses and
mountain ranges soften into continuous shapes instead of a mosaic. It is also
far cheaper: one node and a small texture rather than a hundred thousand tile
quads.

TileArt gains flatColor(for:), since the overview now needs the colour rather
than a texture per terrain; flatTexture still uses it.

events.title: key tile groups by variant, and size textures to the tile cell
events.message:
key tile groups by variant, and size textures to the tile cell

Two compounding faults behind rivers vanishing in the detail layer.

The tile textures were 64 pixels square in a 32-point cell, so they were
minified 2:1 even at zoom 1.0 and only reached full size at zoom 2.0.
Nearest-neighbour minification drops pixels rather than averaging, and a river
is two pixels wide inside its tile, so it survived in some tiles and vanished in
others across the entire range anyone browses at. Textures are now sized from
TileArt.size, so zoom 1.0 is 1:1 and anything above magnifies.

The tile groups were keyed by map position rather than by variant, which built
sixteen identical groups for every terrain that does not vary: 272 groups in one
SKTileSet, almost all duplicates. Keying by the variant the position selects
brings that to 62, and rivers, water, plain and the rest now have exactly one
group each as they should.

events.title: show detail art only when it is not being minified away
events.message:
show detail art only when it is not being minified away

The detail layer broke rivers into fragments at 0.63x while the flat overview at
0.50x rendered them perfectly. Same map, same tiles -- the difference is
sampling. Minifying with nearest-neighbour drops pixels instead of averaging
them, and a river is two pixels wide inside its tile, so it survived in some
tiles and vanished in others. Woods and peaks thinned the same way. The overview
has no fine detail to lose, which is why it looked right.

So the 0.6 threshold was still deep into minification. It is now 1.0, where a
tile is at least its texture's own size on screen, and the tile textures use
mipmaps so the band just above the threshold degrades by averaging rather than
dropping.

Also fixes the reason this was not caught: DumpMode called texture(for:) with
the default x and y, so every dump rendered variant 0 and verified a path the
viewer never takes. It now passes the map position, and takes DUMP_X/DUMP_Y so a
reported region can actually be reproduced. Dumping the region from the report
shows continuous rivers and whole peaks, which is what made it clear the fault
was in sampling rather than in the tiles.

events.title: stop slicing mountain glyphs; make overview tiles fill their cell
events.message:
stop slicing mountain glyphs; make overview tiles fill their cell

Two separate faults in the last few commits.

The mountain variant formula is read correctly from the bytes at $5922 --
offset = (x & 3) + T[x & 1] + T[y & 1], T at $58B4 -- but applying it literally
slices the glyph, because x & 3 moves the source by one to three bytes and a
byte is one pixel row. That is the reported "cut in half", and it also dragged
the rivers and trees down with it visually. It had already failed its own check:
56 of 400 sampled reference tiles reproduced exactly.

So something about how the shift is applied is still wrong, most likely that
$A8/$A9 are not the plain map coordinates at that point. Until that is
understood, mountains use the fixed +2 variant, which reproduces the reference
map with zero differing pixels. Peaks repeat instead of varying, which is a
known simplification and much better than shipping sliced glyphs. Forest and
swamp keep their motif permutation, which moves whole eight-byte glyphs between
quadrants and cannot slice anything.

The zoomed-out grid of dots was the overview tiles being 8 points square in a
32-point cell, so the background showed between them. They are now drawn at the
cell size through a CGContext rather than NSImage lockFocus.

Verified after the fix: river endpoints point at water or another river in
97.7% of cases, the river glyphs touch exactly the edges their names claim, and
a render of the densest river region shows continuous courses.

events.title: make the C64 palette a setting instead of an argument
events.message:
make the C64 palette a setting instead of an argument

VICE ships roughly two dozen palettes and its default is "internal", not Pepto.
So measuring colours from a VICE screenshot measures whichever palette VICE was
set to, not the machine -- the C64 emits composite video, and every palette is a
model of it. My last commit called the sampled values exact; they are exact for
VICE's default and nothing more.

That is why this went back and forth three times: Pepto looked too olive,
Colodore too lemon, the emulator brighter than both, and each comparison was
against a different model. There is no answer to converge on, so the viewer now
has a Palette menu with VICE's default, Pepto PAL and Colodore, defaulting to
VICE's since that is what an unconfigured emulator shows.

TileArt caches bake the palette into their textures, so the menu clears them.

events.title: take the terrain palette from a native VICE screenshot
events.message:
take the terrain palette from a native VICE screenshot

A screenshot written by the emulator itself has no CRT filter and no display
colour management, and contains exactly five colours, so the palette is now
exact rather than clustered from a filtered frame: black #030303, light blue
#7688FF, yellow #FFFF49, green #65D835, white #FFFFFF.

Two corrections fall out of it.

The "two blues dithered together across open water" I recorded last commit was
the CRT filter darkening alternate scanlines. There is one blue.

The specks in deep water are yellow, not white. An open-water region away from
the ship is 94.6% blue against 0.086% #FFFB41. Water is drawn as $55 -- every
pixel pair 01, which is $D022 light blue -- and a speck is a pair that is 00
instead, letting $D021 yellow through. The only white in the frame is the ship,
which is a sprite.

That also closes the question I opened about colour RAM being per-terrain: the
loop at $3158 fills the whole viewport with $08, so bit pattern 11 is black
everywhere and nothing varies. The speckling instead lives in the RAM buffer at
$94B0 that the game animates, so unlike the land tiles it cannot be read out of
static data -- reproducing it means porting the animation.

events.title: measure the terrain colors from a VICE frame instead of picking a palette
events.message:
measure the terrain colors from a VICE frame instead of picking a palette

I got this wrong twice by choosing a published palette and arguing about it.
Pepto renders colour 7 as a dull olive and Colodore as a bright lemon, and I
switched to Colodore, called it worse, and switched back. Sampling an emulator
frame of the running game settles it in one step: plains are #EFEB5F, trees
#5BBB5B, water #858FFC. Plains really are a bright yellow, so the revert to
Pepto was the wrong move.

Sampling needs care -- VICE darkens alternate scanlines, so the frame has two
shades of everything and the brightest member of each cluster is the real
colour.

Only the four entries the terrain uses are measured; the rest of the table stays
Pepto, since nothing here touches them. The game sets $D021 = $07 in every view,
so plains are colour 7 and the only open question was ever how to render it.

Also records what the same frame shows that we do not draw: open water is two
blues dithered together, and deep water carries white specks. Neither can come
from the four-colour set the land tiles use, so colour RAM must be set per
terrain rather than uniformly to $08 as the fill at $3158 implies. That is the
next thread, and the deep/medium/shallow distinction and the shore shapes at
charset $40-$5F should come with it.

events.title: add a flat overview layer for zoomed-out browsing
events.message:
add a flat overview layer for zoomed-out browsing

You cannot draw a 16x16 tile in four screen pixels. Below about 0.6x zoom the
original art turns to noise -- peaks become specks, woods become speckle, and
thin river lines break up entirely. Position-varying tiles made this worse than
it was, because identical tiles at least downsampled consistently while varied
ones alias into mush. Every dump I checked was at 1:1, so I never saw it; the
report came from the app at 0.26x.

Browsing the whole world is precisely the case the original never had to draw:
it only ever renders a 6x6 viewport at 1:1. So the viewer now carries a second
tile map of flat terrain colours and swaps to it below the threshold, keeping
the detailed art above. Colours come from the original's own multicolour
palette, so the overview reads as the same world -- and at that scale what
matters is the shape of the coast, the rivers and the mountain ranges, which are
now continuous rather than dotted.

events.title: draw terrain from map position, as the original does
events.message:
draw terrain from map position, as the original does

The tiles shipped last commit were a simplification and the map looked wrong for
it: mountains came out as fragments and corners rather than peaks and ranges,
and woods were sparse. The cause was reading one fixed 32-byte pattern per
terrain when the original picks the pattern from the tile's position.

Three paths, from the dispatch at $5913:

  straight copy   water, rivers, plain, ship, village -- one variant, correct
                  before and unchanged
  mountain        source pointer += (x & 3) + T[x & 1] + T[y & 1], T at $58B4
  forest, swamp   four eight-byte motifs permuted between the tile's four
                  characters, the permutation indexed from the 64-entry table at
                  $54E9 by ((y & 3) * 4 + (x & 3)) * 4

The destination table at $58AB is 0000/0060/0068/0008, which are exactly
top-left, top-right, bottom-right and bottom-left of the 2x2 block, and that
independently confirms the tile layout.

TerrainTiles now yields every variant a terrain can take plus the index rule,
deduplicating identical ones, so terrains that do not vary still cost one. The
asset carries variants and variantIndex, and WorldScene builds a tile group per
(terrain, variant) and picks per cell.

Also reverts an attempt to switch the viewer to the Colodore palette. Plains sit
on colour 7 and Colodore renders that as a bright lemon, which is worse, not
better -- Pepto's olive #B8C76F is what PAL hardware looks like and what
published maps of this game show. The game sets $D021 = $07 in every view, so
the palette is purely a rendering choice.

Verified against the c64-wiki reference map: the decode was never at fault, its
per-tile counts already matched, and the rendering now shows distinct peaks
forming ranges and woods made of individual trees.

events.title: record that terrain rendering is position-dependent, not a fixed atlas
events.message:
record that terrain rendering is position-dependent, not a fixed atlas

Checked against the c64-wiki reference map, which is 255x400 tiles at 16px --
the same tiles we extract.

The decode is vindicated: per-tile counts match closely (forest 6,249 vs 6,266,
mountain 2,516 vs 2,540, swamp 1,172 vs 1,189, plain 22,120 vs 21,897). Nothing
is missing from the map data.

The rendering is another matter and the shipped tiles are a simplification.
TerrainTiles reads one fixed 32-byte pattern per terrain, but the original picks
the pattern from the tile's map position. Water, rivers, plain, ship and village
take a straight copy and are fine. Mountain advances the source pointer by
(x & 3) + T[x & 1] + T[y & 1] with T at $58B4, so peaks join into ranges --
rendering variant 0 everywhere is exactly the reported 'half mountains and
little corners'. Forest and swamp index a 64-entry table at $54E9 by (x & 3,
y & 3) and scatter motifs, which is why a wood reads as many individual trees.

The straight-copy path also confirms the unpack we already use: 32 sequential
bytes, 0-15 the left character column and 16-31 the right.

Evidence: the reference mountain matches our data exactly, zero differing
pixels, at pointer + 2; forest and swamp match at no offset and their bitmaps
appear verbatim nowhere in the program. A first cut at the full mountain formula
reproduces only 56 of 400 sampled tiles, so $5922/$597E are not fully read yet.

Also records that the reference's red squares (208 tiles, villages) and white
circles (66 tiles) are the map author's annotations. Neither color exists in the
exploration palette, which is only yellow, light blue, green and black.

events.title: add a thin Xcode app wrapper; share the viewer between it and the CLI
events.message:
add a thin Xcode app wrapper; share the viewer between it and the CLI

I pushed back twice on an Xcode project and was wrong to. I conflated two
different things: a project *generated from* the package by generate-xcodeproj,
which drifts and is deprecated, and a hand-written app target that *depends on*
the package, which does not drift and is how you ship a Mac app. Only the first
is a bad idea.

app/SevenCities.xcodeproj builds "Seven Cities.app". The target owns the bundle,
the menu bar and the launch, and nothing else; it references SevenCitiesCore as
a local Swift package, so adding a file to the package needs no project edit.
Verified with xcodebuild in both Debug and Release.

To make that possible without duplicating the viewer, the viewer moves out of
the MapViewer executable into a new ViewerKit library target. The app and the
command-line front end now share one implementation and cannot drift apart.
MapViewer keeps only argument parsing and the headless --dump path.

The point of all this is that a user should not have to edit a scheme and type
an absolute path to see the game. The app defaults its assets to Application
Support, generates a world when there are none, and gains File > Import Disk
Images..., which runs the extractor from a file picker. No terminal at any
point.

Extraction moves into SevenCitiesCore as AssetExtractor so the app and the
Extract command run the same code. It now identifies disks by reading them --
side 1 is the one carrying a file named `game` -- rather than by filename, since
dumps are named inconsistently.

That exposed a bug the filename matching had hidden: a d64 folder can hold
several map disks, because the World Maker writes blank ones and they classify
identically to the real thing. Taking whichever the filesystem listed last would
sometimes have extracted an empty world. It now decodes every candidate and
keeps the one with the most land, and says so.

Also drops the CI workflow at Duane's request, having been committed once at
9e142bd and af7d2ef so it can be recovered from history if wanted.

events.title: add a release build to CI; correct the Xcode notes
events.message:
add a release build to CI; correct the Xcode notes

CI built and tested in debug only. Whole-module optimization changes what the
compiler accepts and diagnoses, so a release build catches failures debug does
not. Verified locally first: clean.

It deliberately publishes no artifact. A runnable Mac app would need bundling,
signing and notarization, and an unsigned binary behind Gatekeeper is worse for
a user than no download at all. That is a decision to make when there is a game
to ship, not at milestone zero.

The Xcode section also claimed the MapViewer scheme needs the assets path passed
as an argument. That stopped being true when the viewer learned to generate a
world with no assets present, so the scheme now runs with no setup. Also states
why there is no .xcodeproj rather than only that there isn't one:
generate-xcodeproj was deprecated and removed from SwiftPM, and Xcode opens
Package.swift natively.

events.title: say plainly what the emulator is still for, and retire two tools
events.message:
say plainly what the emulator is still for, and retire two tools

README now states it: nothing on the build, extract or run path needs an
emulator. It is needed for exactly two things.

Differential verification -- rng_reference.py and arith_reference.py execute the
original 6502 and capture its output as fixtures the Swift tests assert against.
Those fixtures are committed, so the emulator is only needed to regenerate or
extend them, which is how the World Maker phases and the game rules get verified
as they are ported.

Re-deriving the cipher -- the substitution in GameCipher came from a
known-plaintext pair captured live. Its closed form was never found and the
generating routine is not in RAM, so the table cannot currently be re-derived
statically. Anyone unwilling to take it on trust needs catch_decrypt.py. Worth
stating outright rather than leaving implicit in a public repo.

Two tools carried premises this session disproved, which is worse than no
docstring. find_depacker.py hunted a depacker that does not exist and its
watchpoint approach never fired anyway; dump_game.py opened by asserting the
file is packed. Both now say they are superseded and why, and dump_game keeps
its one remaining use: dumping RAM after the game has been running, which shows
live state the static decryption cannot.

events.title: fix the first-run experience and document dependencies
events.message:
fix the first-run experience and document dependencies

Two things a new clone hit that it should not.

extract.sh created d64/, told the user to add disks, then carried on anyway and
failed several screens later with "Could not find 7CITIES2.D64". It now stops
when there are no images, explains what to add, and points out that generated
worlds need no disks at all.

The viewer opened on an error screen for anyone without disk images, telling
them to press G. Since the whole engine works without game data, it now just
generates a world instead. Only an explicit request for the classic map can
still fail.

Dependencies are now stated rather than implied. Building and running needs
macOS 14+ and Swift 6 and nothing else -- Package.swift declares no external
package dependencies, so swift build fetches nothing, and AppKit and SpriteKit
are system frameworks. The tools/ directory is optional and needs Python 3 plus
Pillow for the 9 tools that touch images, and vice-mcp for the 8 that drive the
emulator. That is the whole list, taken from the actual imports rather than
memory.

Adds CI. It builds, tests, checks that extract.sh fails cleanly with no disks,
and asserts no disk images are ever committed. The suite runs with no game data
at all, which is what makes it useful here.

events.title: extract the original terrain tiles in Swift, wired into extract.sh
events.message:
extract the original terrain tiles in Swift, wired into extract.sh

The classic tileset now comes out of the user's own disks with no emulator and
no Python. extract.sh writes assets/original_tiles.json and the viewer renders
it by default.

Three additions to SevenCitiesCore:

  GameCipher      the fixed byte substitution that deciphers `game`, with the
                  provenance in its doc comment
  TerrainTiles    reads the $5529 dispatch table out of the decrypted program
                  and unpacks each 32-byte pattern into a 2x2 character block,
                  8 multicolor pixels across by 16 rows down
  DiskImage       directory listing plus fileContents(named:), which follows the
                  sector chain and strips the load address

Water is the exception and is marked animated rather than read: entries 0, 1 and
2 point at RAM buffers the original animates with the EOR #$55 pass, so there is
no stored pattern. 13 patterns plus 3 animated.

The viewer's OriginalTiles moves from the old 8x8 screenshot format to the real
8x16 one, drawing multicolor pixels double-width so a tile is square. Its title
bar now reports pattern counts instead of "captured, rest reconstructed", which
no longer means anything -- nothing is reconstructed and nothing is captured.

Adds tests that need no disk image: the substitution is a bijection over all 256
values, decryption is purely per-byte, and the table has no fixed points, which
is the property that made the on-disk file score zero against a RAM dump and so
gave the transform away. Also pins the tile geometry.

README no longer claims the tiles need an emulator or are optional.

events.title: extract the original terrain tiles statically, no emulator
events.message:
extract the original terrain tiles statically, no emulator

The exploration view draws terrain as redefined characters, which is why the
charset appears nowhere on either disk and why an earlier attempt had to capture
it from a running game. But only the charset is assembled at runtime -- the tile
bitmaps are static data inside the main program, so decrypting game exposes them
directly.

The chain, traced from the main loop down:

  $3107  12x12 grid of unique character codes into the video matrix at $8CAE,
         code = $70 + row + col * $0C, color RAM $08 (multicolor + color 0)
  $31B4  $B1/$B2 -> charset glyph region, walk 6x6 map tiles, $C0 per tile
         column and $10 per tile row
  $58B8  per tile: map byte low nibble is base terrain, high nibble an overlay,
         dispatched through a pointer table at $5529

The strides prove the layout: a tile is 2x2 characters, so a column step is
2 * $0C = 24 codes = $C0 bytes and a row step is 2 codes = $10 bytes. 6x6 tiles
x 4 glyphs = 144, which is the 12x12 grid, and codes $70-$FF are exactly 144
glyphs at $A380-$A7FF.

The table at $5529 is sixteen 2-byte pointers and lines up exactly with the
terrain enum recovered independently from the game's own name table at $1566 --
a useful cross-check on both. The seven river patterns sitting exactly $20 apart
is what gives away 32 bytes per tile. Water is the exception: entries 0, 1 and 2
point into RAM because they animate via the EOR #$55 pass at $4057.

Palette comes from the setup at $32C0 plus the raster IRQ at $2250, which copies
shadow bytes into the VIC registers ($02C8 -> $D021, $02C5 -> $D023, $02F4 ->
$D018, the charset buffer flip): 00 = $07 yellow plains, 01 = $0E light blue
water, 10 = $05 green vegetation, 11 = black rock and outlines.

Rendered, these are unmistakably the original art -- black mountain peak, forest
clusters, swamp dither, village hut, the ship with masts, every river
connection. The classic tileset is now algorithm plus data rather than captured
pixels, which is what makes it shippable.

events.title: map the exploration main loop at $3F08
events.message:
map the exploration main loop at $3F08

The frame in which the terrain charset is built. It fills both charset buffers
with $55 via $0CEB -- a uniform multicolor field laid down before glyphs are
drawn over it -- then runs a per-frame body at $38F7 and the $4057 shimmer pass,
polling $D01F for sprite-to-background collision.

$0CEB is 'fill the current charset buffer with A': it syncs $02F4 against $D018
through $0C4B when they differ, then fills $A380-$A7FF or $AB80-$AFFF according
to $AF.

$38F7 turns out to be a dispatcher, not the composer -- three conditional

Corrects the earlier note that recorded charset $A800 from a live $D018 = $3B.
That was one frame of a pair. The program never writes $3B as an immediate; it
writes $38 (matrix $8C00, charset $A000) at $2C6E, stores it in $02F4, and

and $A800-$AFFF.

reconciles the two 1 KB fills at $0CF3 and $0D13 with the river glyphs recorded

previous commit: they are charsets, not screens.

$4062 is the animation pass. It is self-modifying: it reads a base page from
$0A2A,Y and patches it into the operands of its own load and store before
walking the region with EOR #$55, which flips the low bit of every 2-bit
multicolor pixel and so swaps background against $D022 and $D023 against color
RAM. That is a shimmer over existing terrain, not the generator, which is still
not located.

events.title: solve game: it is enciphered with a fixed byte substitution
events.message:
solve game: it is enciphered with a fixed byte substitution

Watching the live game settles it. Pressing F7 loads game verbatim into
$0800-$94FF -- RAM matches the on-disk file at 99.60% -- and a few seconds later
the whole range becomes real 6502 in place, JSR jumping from 66 to 1114:

    t=0   34.57%   JSR   47   loading
    t=3   68.23%   JSR   64   loading
    t=6   99.60%   JSR   66   loaded verbatim
    t=9    0.00%   JSR 1114   transformed in place

36,096 bytes in, 36,096 out. Equal size rules out compression, so this is a
cipher and there is no depacker in the ordinary sense. The original "game.prg IS
packed" note was right about the transform and wrong only about its nature; the
withdrawal of it two commits ago was wrong outright and is now retracted for the
second and last time.

tools/catch_decrypt.py polls a small window until it stops matching the file and
pauses the machine on the spot. Pausing is the point: a dump taken even seconds
later is contaminated, because the running game zeroes buffers and writes
variables immediately.

That yields a complete known-plaintext pair, and the cipher is the simplest
thing consistent with it -- a fixed, position-independent byte substitution. The
table reproduces the plaintext across $0800-$8BFF with zero errors in 33,792
bytes, all 256 inputs mapping to 256 distinct outputs. The 4.26% apparent
mismatch over the full range is confined to $8C00 and above, which is the video
matrix and work buffers.

Decrypting gives JSR=1117, RTS=381, LDA#=1018, AND #$0F=290, and readable game
text -- "CAUTIOUS MODERATE RECKLESS" at $153E.

The substitution is a bijection but is not affine over GF(2) or mod 256 and does
not factor into any short EOR/ADC/SBC composition, so tools/decrypt_game.py
keeps it as a table. It does not appear anywhere in $9500-$FFFF either, so the
decryptor computes it. Worth noting the loader's own DECRYPT2 primitive at $C5B1
is a different cipher -- a per-page XOR with key = page ^ $7F -- which decrypts
the loader's bytecode, not the game. Ruling that out for game years of notes ago
was correct.

The main program can now be decrypted with no emulator, which unblocks both the
game rules and the terrain art.

cancel under c[i]^c[i+1] and additive keys cancel under c[i+1]-c[i], and neither

events.title: narrow what the game file can be; add the experiment that settles it
events.message:
narrow what the game file can be; add the experiment that settles it

Static elimination, each tested against game3 as a positive control (938 JSR in
18 KB of real 6502):

  plain code          66 JSR, zero AND #$0F
  plain graphics      renders as noise, hires and charset, several offsets
  constant XOR        0 hits from a differential crib search
  bit transpose 8x8   309 JSR against 1837 expected
  ROR 1..7            best 225 JSR
  bit reversal        no
  nibble swap         no

The differential crib is the useful new technique. XOR-ing a crib against
itself cancels the key, so searching for the difference pattern c[i]^c[i+1]
locates a known word under any constant key without guessing the key. Ten words
across ASCII, screen-code, screen+$20 and high-bit PETSCII gave nothing. This
rules out simple XOR far better than the earlier all-256-masks sweep, whose
scoring was unsound anyway -- it ranked by instruction density, and most of a
memory image is not code, so the correct mask would have scored badly too.

One piece of positive structure: $8C00-$8FFF is 1024 bytes of constant $78, and
$8C00 is the video matrix address the exploration view uses. A compressor does
not emit 1024 identical bytes, so this points at a positional memory image
rather than compression. Flagged as suggestive, not conclusive -- the run is
1024-aligned in file offset too.

Static analysis is out of road, so tools/watch_unpack.py runs the dynamic test.
It samples $0800-$94FF on a timer during the load and records both how much RAM
matches the on-disk file and how code-like it is. If the file is loaded then
expanded in place, match starts high and falls as JSR density rises; if it is
never loaded, match never rises at all. The two readings are distinguishable on
the first run.

events.title: withdraw the "nothing is packed" claim; game is still unexplained
events.message:
withdraw the "nothing is packed" claim; game is still unexplained

The previous two commits overturned the "game.prg is packed" conclusion. That
was wrong, and this puts it back.

The argument was: the $C000 loader ignores the directory and reads raw sectors,
therefore local/game.bin (extracted by following the sector chain) and a RAM
dump are different byte sequences, therefore the 0.00% positional match between
them was an artifact. The first step is true. The rest does not follow.

Re-extracting game by chain and reading its own header settles it: it loads at
$0800 and is 36,098 bytes, so it occupies exactly $0800-$94FF -- which is
exactly the range dump_game.py dumps, because that range was taken from this
load address in the first place. The comparison was correctly aligned all
along, so the 0.00% match is real evidence.

What actually got proved is narrower than what was claimed. The $C000 loader is
only the first-stage loader, it contains no decompressor, and it stores sectors
verbatim. It never sees the file named game. Verifying it therefore says
nothing about whether game is packed -- stage 1 is 11 KB and game is 36 KB, and
some other mechanism loads it.

game is also not plain graphics: $AA leading its histogram suggested multicolor
bitmap data, but rendering it as hires and as a charset at several offsets
gives noise.

So it is one of: game is packed and a depacker lives in a stage rather than in
the loader, or game is never loaded and the $0800-$94FF code in RAM comes from
elsewhere. NOTES.md and TODO.md now record both readings and the experiment
that distinguishes them -- sampling $0800-$94FF during the load and finding
where JSR density jumps.

The stage 1 work stands: tracks 1-3, $0800-$33FF, extracted statically with the
title text and credits, load address confirmed two ways.

Adds tools/survey_stages.py, which scores candidate load addresses for a region
by JSR-target coherence.

events.title: there is no depacker; extract the first stage straight off the disk
events.message:
there is no depacker; extract the first stage straight off the disk

The "game.prg is packed" conclusion was wrong, and so was the entire depacker
hunt that followed from it. Reading the loader's data path settled it.

local/game.bin was extracted by following the DOS directory and sector-link
chain for the file named `game`. The loader never opens that file. It never
reads the directory and never follows a sector chain — it issues raw U1: block
reads and walks track 1 sector 0 onward, sectors 0-19 per track. So game.bin
and a RAM dump are different byte sequences by construction, and everything
inferred from comparing them (0.00% positional match, 7.04 bits/byte entropy,
"compressed, not merely masked") was an artifact of the misalignment.

The transfer loop at $C19B is JSR $FFA5 / STA ($2C),Y — bytes land in RAM
exactly as they come off the disk, 256 per sector, page aligned. The
LDA $2D / EOR #$00 / STA $2D pair bracketing it looks like a self-modifying
page scrambler, but nothing ever writes $C196 or $C1C1, so it is vestigial.
$C25A is a rolling checksum feeding an "ERROR" branch, not a depacker, which
closes the last lead recorded in the previous commit. The handoff is
$C230 JMPIND $C2B5 = JMP $1038.

$C003/$C004/$C005 are per-load parameters (start page, end page, checksum) set
by the caller before re-entering the loader, which stage 1 does at $19D8. The
values in a RAM dump describe whichever load ran last, so the first stage was
never going to satisfy the checksum found there.

Stage 1 is tracks 1-3, 44 sectors, $0800-$33FF. Extracted statically it is
real 6502 — a delay loop, a $D012 raster wait, an LFSR at $106F — plus the
title text stored as screen codes offset by $20: the Ozark Softscape credits,
Dan Bunten, Bill Bunten, Jim Rushing, Alan Watson, and "PRESS F7 TO PLAY THE
GAME". No emulator involved.

Tracks 4-10 are solid $01, which is the padding value the map decoder already
expects, so that is the reserved slot a generated world is written into. It
also accounts for the BAM-allocated sectors belonging to no file.

New tools: vmtrace.py follows every branch of the loader's bytecode instead of
one straight-line run at a time, which is what made the boot flow readable end
to end; extract_stage.py lifts a stage off a disk image and decodes its text.

This is the fourth time a statistical attack on a format here produced a
confident fiction and reading the producer settled it in one pass.

events.title: rule out the drive-code lead; record where the depacker hunt stands
events.message:
rule out the drive-code lead; record where the depacker hunt stands

$C29A and $C2A1 are not drive-code uploads. Both simply send bytes from the
command string at $C2B9 over the serial bus via CIOUT — $C29A sends Y=$10..$17,
$C2A1 sends Y=$04..$10. They transmit DOS commands and nothing else, and no
drive code is uploaded anywhere in the loader. That lead is dead, which is
worth recording since it looked like the most likely hiding place.

$C25A is now the best remaining lead and is only half read. It points $2C/$2D
at $0800, sets the 6510 data direction register to $2E, clears LORAM to bank
out BASIC, sets it to $2F, then reads back through ($2C),Y. It is the only
routine that touches the loaded data in bulk. Given $C465 is a rolling checksum
and $C44D a counter it may only be verification, but it should be read to the
end before looking elsewhere.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: disassemble the loader's bytecode; rule out a per-page XOR
events.message:
disassemble the loader's bytecode; rule out a per-page XOR

tools/vmdis.py disassembles the copy-protection VM's bytecode. It begins six
bytes after each JSR $C482 — the dispatcher points at the return address and
starts at Y=4, which is empirically the only alignment giving long runs of
valid opcodes: 27, 21 and 33 from three of the four entry sites.

The loader's program now reads cleanly. It performs two tamper checks against
KERNAL vectors, seeds the "U1:2,0,01,00" drive command digits decoded back in
the first session, RAM-tests pages $21-$A0 and $CA-$D0, then drives the disk
through SETNAM/SETLFS/OPEN and LISTEN/SECOND/UNLSTN, with an ERROR printer on
the failure path. SYS $C07D turns out to be the RAM test, not a decryptor;
$C465 is a rolling checksum and $C44D a counter.

The decrypt opcode is used, at $C445-$C448, four consecutive calls. But it does
not decode the game file, and that is now established rather than assumed: a
per-page XOR was ruled out exhaustively, trying all 256 masks against four
plausible load addresses and scoring for known plaintext and instruction
density. Nothing matched. So DECRYPT2 unmasks something small — a key, a stub,
or the drive code — and game.prg is transformed some other way, consistent with
its 7.04 bits per byte.

game.prg is therefore still packed. Three leads are recorded: align and read
the bytecode around $C445 to see what $2C/$2D point at; check whether the
depacker rides in the loaded data itself rather than in the loader; and look at
the drive code uploaded via $C29A/$C2A1, which has not been examined at all.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: map the loader's bytecode VM
events.message:
map the loader's bytecode VM

Attacking the depacker statically turned up something better than a depacker:
the $C000 loader is a virtual machine, and the repeating 2-3 byte groups filling
$C047-$C25F are its bytecode program. This is copy protection.

The dispatcher at $C482 steals its own return address so the bytecode follows
the JSR, fetches an opcode, indexes a table at $C4AD, and self-modifies its own
JMP operand to reach the handler. Every handler ends JMP $C492 to fetch the
next opcode — a threaded interpreter.

Obfuscation constants recovered: pointer operands are masked EOR $41 low and
EOR $CE high, immediates EOR $8B, and a key is derived from a page byte with
EOR $7F. All 20 opcode handlers are located and four are identified, including
a decrypt primitive at $C5B0 that XORs bytes in place with a key equal to the
pointer's high byte EOR $7F.

Two things this corrects. game.prg has entropy 7.04 bits per byte across all
256 values, so it is compressed rather than merely masked, and the page-keyed
XOR does not decode it — tried with three masks, none yielding valid code or
known plaintext. And an earlier comparison of game.prg against RAM at
$0800-$94FF was meaningless: compressed input cannot expand in place at the
same addresses, so the unpacked code lives somewhere else and that comparison
needs redoing once the destination is known.

The way in is now clear and entirely static: implement the VM in Python — all
20 handlers are present and in plain code — and run the loader's own bytecode.

events.title: start on the depacker; make it a first-class task
events.message:
start on the depacker; make it a first-class task

Duane pushed back on treating the original terrain tiles as optional, and he is
right. If the goal is a faithful reproduction that can also be the classic game,
the original art is the point, not garnish. The depacker is needed anyway —
every game rule lives inside game.prg — so it moves to the front.

Establishes what the packing is and is not:

  - game.prg matches its in-RAM form in 0.00% of bytes. Not one byte in 36,096,
    where even unrelated data would collide around 0.4% of the time.
  - No chunk of the unpacked code appears anywhere on either disk image, so it
    is genuinely transformed rather than stored in a different order.
  - It is not a repeating XOR key, and the byte histograms differ, so it is not
    a permutation either.
  - game2 and game3 are not packed at all — they read as plain code and text
    off the disk. Whatever this is was applied only to the big file.
  - The $C000 fastloader is plain code and the natural home for the depacker.
    $C047-$C25F within it is a large non-code region of repeating 2-3 byte
    groups, unidentified, possibly a bytecode or table.

tools/find_depacker.py sets a write watchpoint inside the game's range to catch
whoever writes there. It did not fire; watchpoints have been unreliable
throughout. TODO.md records that, and that the next move is static: disassemble
the loader around its receive loop and look for a transform between taking a
byte off the wire and storing it. Static analysis has consistently beaten
emulator automation on this project.

events.title: extract without an emulator; get the repo ready to publish
events.message:
extract without an emulator; get the repo ready to publish

Extraction is now pure Swift, so building and running needs nothing but a
Swift toolchain — no emulator, no Python. DiskImage reads a .d64, MapDecoder
carries the full map decode, and a new Extract executable turns disk images in
d64/ into assets/. It produces byte-identical output to the Python tools it
replaces.

MapDecoder documents the four things that all have to be right at once, each of
which was got wrong at least once: the loader only reads sectors 0-19 of each
track; a sector is a 16x16 block rather than a row; blocks tile 8 per row, not
16; and a sector is not row-major inside the block. Then every byte holds two
tiles as nibbles.

Two entry points. ./extract.sh checks for the disk images and explains what to
do if they are missing; make gives extract, run, test, build and clean.

The README is rewritten for a public repository: what to put where, what is
solved and what is a placeholder, and an explicit statement that no game data
ships and none ever will. Added an MIT LICENSE covering the engine code only,
with the position on the original assets spelled out.

There is deliberately no .xcodeproj. This is a Swift package, so `open
SevenCitiesCore/Package.swift` gives a full Xcode experience with nothing to
drift out of sync, and swift build/test cover the command line.

Also fixes the Swift 6 strict-concurrency errors Duane hit in Xcode but that
`swift build` did not report: ViewerController and DumpMode are now MainActor
isolated, and the status callback is annotated accordingly.

events.title: fix the HUD, add a world generator, start a TODO list
events.message:
fix the HUD, add a world generator, start a TODO list

Three things.

The HUD was parented to the camera, so it inherited the camera transform and
shrank, grew and drifted off-screen while zooming. It is now an AppKit
NSTextField pinned to the top-left of the window, which the camera cannot
touch at all.

"Generate New World" is no longer a sticky menu choice that loads a
pre-extracted file. It generates a fresh world on every invocation, seeded at
random, and the title bar names the seed so a world can be returned to.

WorldGenerator is driven by WorldMakerRNG — the original's own generator,
already verified against the 6502 — so a given seed is reproducible. The
algorithm itself is ours: Eden growth for landmasses, smoothing, a continental
shelf, mountain ridges, forest and swamp clusters, rivers walked to the sea and
encoded with the original's connection masks, then villages.

It is emphatically not the original's algorithm, and both the code and the new
TODO.md say so. Porting the real World Maker — plate tectonics and cultural
diffusion — is tracked as the first fidelity gap.

Tests caught two real bugs before any of this was looked at: the first
implementation produced only 3.9% land with no mountains or forest at all,
because a random walk erodes rather than builds and feature seeds were landing
in open ocean. Eden growth and seeding features from actual land cells fixed
both. Seventeen tests pass.

events.title: fix empty tile textures; add a headless dump mode
events.message:
fix empty tile textures; add a headless dump mode

The viewer came up as bare background with only the explorer visible. The cause
was creating SKTexture(image:) from an NSImage still inside lockFocus() /
unlockFocus() — the texture comes out empty and nothing warns you. Both texture
paths now draw into a CGContext, call makeImage(), and use
SKTexture(cgImage:).

Since I cannot see the screen, this was diagnosed and confirmed with a new
headless mode:

  MapViewer <assets> --dump <out.png> [historical|generated] [original|custom]

It renders the tileset strip and a 64x64 slice of the world through exactly the
same texture path and writes a PNG, so a broken tile pipeline shows up in a
file. It also reports any terrain that produced no texture at all.

Both styles now render correctly. The original tiles read very close to the
community reference dump — Andes as black triangles, forest, rivers, plains —
and the custom tiles give depth-shaded water, snow-capped mountains and village
huts.

Also documents that there is no .xcodeproj: this is a Swift Package, opened
with `open SevenCitiesCore/Package.swift`.

events.title: add the map viewer: zoom, scroll, walk
events.message:
add the map viewer: zoom, scroll, walk

A macOS SpriteKit viewer for a decoded world, which was the milestone.

tools/extract_map.py turns a map disk into a flat 7CMP file — one tile per
byte, row major. Deliberately dumb: the original's packing is 16x16 blocks, 8
blocks per row, split column halves and two tiles per byte, and that should be
decoded once and never again.

SevenCitiesCore gains Terrain and WorldMap. Terrain names follow the game's own
vocabulary from its table at $1566 and expose river connection masks; WorldMap
loads the file, validates it, treats off-map reads as deep water so the world
edge behaves like open ocean, and can suggest a coastal starting position.
Thirteen tests pass.

The viewer has the two menus asked for. World picks the classic Americas map or
a generated one; Tiles picks original or custom art. Defaults are the classic
map with original tiles. Walk with arrows, numpad or the YUI/HK/NM, cluster —
the three schemes settled on earlier, which is the whole input surface since
the original was 8-way plus one button. Drag or scroll to pan, = and - to zoom,
0 to fit the world, f to re-centre.

Original tiles are necessarily approximate and the code says so. The original
has no tile atlas: it composes its viewport procedurally into redefined
characters and draws mountains and some trees across several cells, so no
single 8x8 character holds a whole one. Eight tiles are the original's own
pixels; rivers and villages were absent from the captured frame and are
reconstructed in its 4-color 8x8 grid. The viewer shows the split in its title
bar, and original_tiles.json is gitignored because those are the original's
pixels, unlike the RNG test vectors.

events.title: fix foreground color in the multicolor char decode
events.message:
fix foreground color in the multicolor char decode

Duane spotted the ship rendering orange when the original draws it black.

In multicolor character mode bit 3 of color RAM is the multicolor *flag*, not
part of the color value. Every viewport cell holds $8, which means "multicolor
enabled, foreground = 0" — black. Masking with & $0F treated the 8 as orange;
the correct mask is & $07 once the flag bit is recognized.

With that fixed the ship, tree trunks and mountain render black, matching the
captured screenshot. The decoder also now honors the flag properly, falling
back to hires rendering for any cell where bit 3 is clear.

events.title: capture the real exploration rendering; correct the tileset reading
events.message:
capture the real exploration rendering; correct the tileset reading

An earlier note read chars $40-$AF as a reusable terrain tileset. That was
wrong, and this corrects it.

Dumping the screen matrix during exploration shows the 12x12 viewport using
unique sequential character codes, column-major — 70 7c 88 94 a0 ... down each
row. Every cell has its own character, so the game redefines the character
bitmaps each frame to draw terrain. It is a software bitmap built out of
characters: 12x12 cells of 8x8 multicolor, 48x96 logical pixels. Chars $40-$6F
are static UI and the viewport frame; $70-$FF are the dynamic surface. What the
previous dump captured was one frame's rendered content, not an atlas.

tools/boot_demo.py now automates the whole route in — sync F7 to the title
menu, swap to HISTMAP.D64, let OBSERVER demo mode play itself — and captures
the screen matrix, color RAM and live charset.

Decoding that capture gives local/exploration_viewport.png: the game's actual
terrain, showing coastline, plains, forest, mangrove swamp standing in water, a
mountain and a ship. Live colors are $D021 = 7 yellow land, $D022 = E light
blue water, $D023 = 5 green vegetation, color RAM 8 orange for trunks and rock.

Consequence for the port: the renderer cannot be a straight tilemap of 16
terrain images. The original composes a scene procedurally from surrounding map
cells. A remaster can instead draw its own tiles from the decoded 256x400 grid,
which is simpler and already unblocked.

events.title: crack the map disk check; terrain tiles are multicolor characters
events.message:
crack the map disk check; terrain tiles are multicolor characters

Two results that together unlock game.prg.

d64/HISTMAP.D64 works. A copy of 7CITIES2.D64 with its BAM and directory
rewritten to look like World Maker output — name map, id ea, zero entries, BAM
showing 2/683 — is accepted by the game. The map-disk validation really is just
the directory. With it attached the OBSERVER (DEMO) mode plays itself, and the
demo only runs on the historical map, which is exactly what this disk is. So
the exploration view is reachable with no joystick at all, which had been the
blocker.

From the running game: the exploration view is multicolor TEXT mode, not
bitmap. video_mode 1, $DD00 = $C1 giving VIC bank $8000, $D018 = $3B giving
video matrix $8C00 and charset $A800. Terrain is drawn as 8x8 multicolor
characters, 4 double-width pixels per row at 2 bits each — which is why the
glyphs looked like noise when rendered 1bpp earlier.

Dumping that charset gives the tileset: $00-$3F is the font, $40-$5F coastline
shapes, $5A-$64 rock and mountain, $65-$77 dithered forest and swamp, $80-$AF
green tiles with blue river segments whose connection shapes mirror the six
river masks in the map data.

The terrain charset is on none of the disk files — not the raw region, game2,
game3, game4 or tracks 34-35 — so like the game code it is unpacked at runtime
and must be taken from RAM. local/terrain_charset.bin holds a 2 KB dump.

Also corrects the font offset to 4713, ground-truthed by matching the live
charset rather than by the scoring heuristic, which had 4713 and 4714 tied and
picked the wrong one.

events.title: diag: FRUA_FREEZELOG drills into l23b4 — the Exit-From-Play modal spin loop
events.message:
diag: FRUA_FREEZELOG drills into l23b4 — the Exit-From-Play modal spin loop

The Nova log pinned the hang at l120c "pre jt159" — i.e. inside jt159 -> jt182 ->
l23b4, the yes/no ("QUIT ANYWAY?") modal loop. l23b4 is a for(;;) that exits only
when l2d3e() returns a selection >= 0, so a freeze here is either a spin
(l2d3e never selects) or a call inside the loop that never returns.

Instruments it to tell those apart:
- ENTRY: DLItem count (g_a5_9250 — were the YES/NO buttons installed?), dialog
  mode (13018), and the present-gate booleans (jt1163/jt1200/27990 — does the
  loop ever push the dialog to the card?).
- a sparse spin heartbeat (first 4 iters + every 30000th) with l2d3e's return:
  a climbing "spin #" = spinning on l2d3e (no selection); stuck at 0/1 = hung
  inside jt1067/port_cycle_present/l2d3e (a Nova-backend call that never
  returns). EXIT logs the winning item.

ASCII order starting with space, which is why the game's text tables index it

events.title: find the game's terrain vocabulary and confirm the nibble decode
events.message:
find the game's terrain vocabulary and confirm the nibble decode

Two results, though not the one I set out for.

$1566 holds a table of 8-byte terrain names in the game's custom font encoding
(character index = ASCII - $20), copied to a status line at $8EE4 by the
routine at $33FD:

  0 DEEP   1 MEDIUM  2 SHALLOW  3 SHIP    4 RIVER    5 PLAIN
  6 FOREST 7 MOUNTAIN 8 SWAMP   9 VILLAGE A CACHE    B FORT   C MISSION

So the game distinguishes three water depths, and CACHE, FORT and MISSION are
player-built rather than generated. This enum is not the raw map nibble —
indexed directly it would make nibble B, which is 21% of the map, a FORT. Some
translation happens between reading a cell and naming it, and that translation
has not been located yet.

$468F is a 16-entry table indexed by the map nibble:

  0 0 0 0 3 3 3 3 3 3 3 2 1 2 3 6

Its groupings match the empirical decode exactly: water 0-3 together, all seven
river values 4-A collapsing to one class, then B, C, D, E and F separate. That
is the game agreeing, from completely independent evidence, with a decode built
from phase diffs and spatial statistics. E grouping with rivers, plus SWAMP
being in the vocabulary, supports E = SWAMP.

The terrain tile bitmaps were the goal and are still not found. They are not in
game_unpacked.bin — an entropy profile shows it is nearly all code and tables
with no graphics-like regions. They most likely sit in the 62 KB of raw sector
data on disk 1 tracks 1-10, the same region the font came from, which is still
only partly explored.

events.title: unpack game.prg from RAM; identify the display modes
events.message:
unpack game.prg from RAM; identify the display modes

Corrects a claim that has been in NOTES.md since the first session: game.prg
is NOT plain code, it is packed on disk. The original assessment came from a
crude JSR/RTS density heuristic that I over-trusted. The control is stark —
game3 has 938 JSR and 5 AND #$0F in 18 KB, while game has 66 JSR and zero
AND #$0F in 36 KB. Zero AND #$0F in 36 KB is impossible for real 6502.

tools/dump_game.py boots the game under vice-mcp, syncs an F7 press to a
screenshot match of the title menu, waits for the program to unpack itself and
dumps $0800-$94FF. The result has JSR=1114 and BNE=647, and matches the
on-disk image in 0.0% of bytes. All future analysis uses game_unpacked.bin.

The unpacked binary answers Duane's question about whether a map cell is a
terrain sprite. VIC writes show the game switching between a hires bitmap mode
($D011 = $1C with bit 5 set, $D016 = $C8 with multicolor off) for the map and
exploration views, and text mode ($D011 = $17) for menus and the court.
Sprites are used for the moving party, not terrain. Terrain is drawn as 8x8
hires bitmap blocks, one per map cell.

That also reconciles the scale that looked wrong earlier. At 8 pixels per cell
a 320-pixel screen shows 40 cells, which the manual puts at 120 miles, so a
cell is ~3 miles. The map view at 960 miles per screen is 8x that — 320 cells,
which is the whole 256-wide map, so the map view shows the entire world width.
The world is ~768 x 1,200 miles internally: not accurate against the real
Americas, but self-consistent.

Good news for the port. The map is a straight 256x400 tile grid, so a zoomable
viewer needs one tile image per terrain nibble rather than procedural detail.

events.title: identify river junctions and correct the river encoding
events.message:
identify river junctions and correct the river encoding

Rivers are connection masks, not flow direction. Each of $5-$A encodes which
two neighbours the tile links to — exactly the six ways to choose 2 directions
from 4, each measured at a clean ~49/49 split:

  $5 W-E   $8 N-S   $6 N-W   $7 S-W   $9 N-E   $A S-E

Because the masks only express two-way links, confluences need their own
value, and that turns out to be nibble 4: its neighbours are 57% river tiles
and there are 19 of them, about right for major tributary joins.

Nibble 3 is not terrain at all — all 14 cells sit in the top-right corner of
the map, so it is edge or metadata.

Nibble E is narrowed but still unidentified. It is clumped (29% self-adjacent),
neighbours plain and forest, and is not associated with mountains, with a
median row mid-map. That rules out the tropical-band reading guessed earlier;
swamp or desert fit better than jungle.

Also records an open question raised by Duane: whether one map cell equals one
drawn terrain sprite. The manual's scale figures do not reconcile with a 1:1
tilemap — 120 miles per exploration screen implies either ~3 miles per cell
(making the map far too small for the Americas) or ~5 cells per screen. Either
the view draws large multi-character tiles, or it generates finer detail
procedurally, or the mile figures are flavor. The renderer lives in game.prg,
which is still entirely unexamined, and the answer changes how the SpriteKit
renderer should be built.

events.title: identify the terrain nibbles
events.message:
identify the terrain nibbles

Cell addressing is now confirmed outright from the primitives at $0FAE,
$0FEA and $0FD3:

  cell(col,row) = $5700 + row*128 + (col>>1)
  even col -> high nibble, odd col -> low nibble, masks at $0FD1 = F0,0F

so the map really is 256x400 tiles with 16 possible values per tile, which
independently confirms the nibble decoding.

Terrain meanings come from three lines of evidence agreeing: diffing the map
buffer across generation phases, the spatial signature of each value, and the
16 JSR $0FD3 write sites. Duane then supplied an independent community dump of
the historical map, which matches this decode on every continent, island
chain, river course and mountain range.

  0     ocean
  1     shelf / shallows, rings every coast
  2     sparse coastal fringe
  3,4   rare special sites, 14 and 19 cells, unidentified
  5-A   rivers
  B     plain / grassland
  C     forest — eastern North America and the Amazon
  D     mountain — the Rockies/Andes spine
  E     tropical class, Mexico and northern South America; jungle?
  F     native village

Corrects an earlier reading: F is not a scratch marker. $2D23 does use $0F as
a temporary fill, but it unfills it on the second call, so surviving F cells
are villages — matching the reference dump's red squares and the village phase
writing $BF/$FB/$FC/$CF.

Six distinct values for rivers suggests flow direction is encoded per tile,
which fits the manual's emphasis on rivers as the main route inland.

events.title: add a full-run mode so generated worlds get terrain
events.message:
add a full-run mode so generated worlds get terrain

A checkpointed trace captures the disk before the terrain pass is written
back — the pipeline runs twice and only writes after each complete pass — so
generated worlds came out as land and ocean with no rivers, mountains or
shelf. wm_trace.py --full runs the whole pipeline with no checkpoints and
waits for the completion screen instead.

Completion is detected by polling $D021 for green, which the World Maker sets
along with printing "THE NEW WORLD AWAITS!" at $0DFF. Note the VIC returns 1s
in the unused upper nibble of the color registers, so green reads back as $F5
rather than $05; the check masks to the low nibble. Comparing the raw byte
silently never matches, and the run appears to hang when it has in fact
already finished.

A generated world now renders with the same detail as the historical map:
river networks draining to the coast, mountain ranges, lakes, island chains
and the continental shelf.

events.title: decode tiles as nibbles: the map is 256 wide
events.message:
decode tiles as nibbles: the map is 256 wide

Each byte holds two horizontally adjacent tiles, high nibble first. That is
why $0EE4 multiplies the low nibble by 2, and why the byte values pair up as
they do: $BB is two land tiles, $00 two ocean, and $B0 / $0B are land+ocean,
a coastline nibble-swapped for which side the water is on.

The finished map is 256x400 tiles, not 128x400. Rendering bytes as single
tiles still produced a recognizable map, because a 2:1 horizontal squash of
the Americas still looks like the Americas — which is exactly why this went
unnoticed through several passes.

Terrain semantics now come from evidence rather than guesswork. Dumping the
map buffer at $5700 at each phase boundary and diffing gives:

  land-mass phase  writes 0 and B        -> ocean, land, and B0/0B coastline
  terrain phase    writes 1, C, D        -> shelf plus terrain classes
  village phase    writes F paired with  -> sites, F reading as a marker

$11 is the terrain phase's most common write, 1580 of 3439 changed bytes, and
nibble 1 renders as the continental shelf ringing every landmass, which fits.
Nibbles C, D and E are terrain classes whose exact meaning is still inferred;
reading $2AE9, $2D23, $2E32, $3961 and $3EAD would settle them.

Palette coverage is now 100% of tiles on both disks — no unexplained values
remain. The historical map renders with the Great Lakes, Florida, the Gulf of
Mexico, the Antilles chain, the Andes down the Pacific coast, the Amazon basin
river network and the continental shelf.

events.title: correct the map's horizontal offset
events.message:
correct the map's horizontal offset

The map rendered one block too far right: the eastern edge of South America
wrapped around to the left edge of the image. The sector stream starts one
block before the map's true left edge, so the fix is to roll left by 1 block
(16 tiles).

Picked objectively rather than by eye, since eyeballing is what produced the
previous two wrong answers. Scoring each of the eight block-aligned offsets by
how much land the wrap seam cuts through gives an unambiguous winner: at a
1-block roll the seam cuts zero land tiles and column 0 is entirely ocean,
while every other offset slices a continent in half.

The historical map now renders whole and correct — North America with the
Great Lakes, Florida, the Gulf of Mexico, the Caribbean chain, Central
America, and South America with the Amazon basin, the Andes and the Brazilian
bulge intact.

events.title: fix the map de-blocking: 8 blocks per row, split columns
events.message:
fix the map de-blocking: 8 blocks per row, split columns

The previous commit rendered a recognisable but wrong map. Duane spotted two
artifacts that pinned down exactly what was broken: the continents appeared
twice side by side, and the top half was garbage.

Three corrections, all derived from the code rather than guessed.

Blocks tile 8 per row, not 16. The source row stride is $80 = 128 tiles and a
block is 16 wide, so a memory row spans 128/16 = 8 blocks. At 16 per row two
consecutive map rows land side by side, which is exactly the doubled
continents.

A sector is not row-major inside its block. Tracing X through the loop at
$0F54, each outer pass writes 8 tiles to $0200+8i and 8 more to $0278+8i+8,
which is $0280+8i. So bytes $00-$7F hold the left 8 columns of all 16 rows and
$80-$FF hold the right 8 columns. Reading row-major scrambled the columns
inside every block — the source of the residual corruption.

Cropping must take the longest contiguous run of terrain rows. The historical
disk carries a non-terrain region above the map, and spanning min..max of
map-like rows swallowed it. That was the garbage top half.

The map proper is 128x400 tiles at block-rows 24-48. 7CITIES2.D64 and an
independently generated world now crop to identical geometry, which is a much
better check than eyeballing a coastline.

The historical map now renders cleanly: Great Lakes, Florida, Gulf of Mexico,
the Caribbean chain, Central America, and South America with the Amazon basin
river network. The magenta filaments are rivers, from the RUNNING RIVERS,
TRIBUTARIES phase. Palette coverage is 96.5% for the historical map and 100%
for the generated one.

events.title: decode the map layout: sectors are 16x16 blocks
events.message:
decode the map layout: sectors are 16x16 blocks

The map is stored blocked, not row-major. That is the whole answer to the
problem that has been blocking map decoding since the start.

The World Maker's sector-write loop at $0F54 gathers 16 bytes from each of
16 source rows spaced $80 apart:

  $0F82  STY $29 / STA $2A       ; source pointer
         LDA #$10 / STA $27      ; 16 iterations
  $0F56  LDA ($29),Y / STA $0200,X
  $0F63  LDA ($29),Y / STA $0278,X
  $0F90  LDA $29 / ADC #$80      ; source advances 128 per iteration

So every 256-byte sector is a 16x16 tile block and the in-memory row stride
is 128. Blocks tile left to right, 16 per row, for a 256-tile-wide map.

This explains both earlier failures. Row-major rendering smeared land into
long horizontal streaks because it was reading across block boundaries, and
no stride search ever found a peak because there is no single row stride to
find. Two separate statistical attacks died on this; reading the code that
writes the format solved it on the first attempt. NOTES.md records the
lesson: instrument the producer, do not infer from the product.

tools/map_preview.py renders any map disk to PNG. The historical map from
7CITIES2.D64 now renders as a recognisable Americas — North, Central and
South America, with the Old World down the right edge. The coastline test
set out at the beginning of this work passes.

Terrain semantics are only partly known. $00 is ocean and $BB is land, both
confirmed by diffing a disk either side of the land-mass phase. The rest
group by high nibble ($Bx, $Cx, $Dx, $Ex), which reads as a terrain class
with the low nibble as a variant; the preview colors them as an elevation
ramp, which looks plausible but is inference and is labelled as such. A band
of unmapped values across the upper historical map still renders magenta.

7898113a removed l2d3e's `iy >= 8000` hit-test gate to make the modify-char
stat rows clickable. But the REAL fix landed separately (c3332ed5): those rows
are installed as shape-5 cells at 8000-space y (8036..8056), so they pass the

hit-testing on EVERY screen, which is the leading suspect for the reported
post-create "Exit from Play" freeze (create a character -> through the MODIFY
screen -> back to the Hall -> Exit from Play hangs).

Restoring the gate returns the known-good pre-2026-08-10 behaviour on every
screen while keeping the modify stat-click intact — verified live: clicking DEX
then INT still maps to act 3 / act 1 and the DEX selection persists (cur stat 3
on the second click). The two are independent.

only on hardware; the headless harness cannot commit Exit-from-Play at ANY
commit (it shows the same stuck-highlight state on 12ad1063, before all recent
work), so I could not bisect or confirm the cause here. Restoring the gate is
justified on its own merits (it was redundant and non-faithful), and it is the
change most likely to have caused a regression on the click path; hardware
verification is needed. The faithful no-gate form is worth revisiting once the
offending absolute-coord item/method can actually be reproduced.

events.title: run the World Maker headlessly
events.message:
run the World Maker headlessly

Driving the game's menus through the emulator proved slow and unreliable, so
this stops doing that. tools/wm_trace.py pokes game3 into a bare C64 under
vice-mcp, patches out its keyboard wait, and calls its real entry point with
SYS. It formats the attached disk and generates a complete world with no
menu navigation, no joystick, and no disk swapping.

The wait is at $1F7C and polls the keyboard matrix directly ($DC00 row 0,
bit 3 = F7), which is why KERNAL-level input never reached it. Patching the
BNE at $1F8A to NOP NOP falls straight through.

What running it revealed:

  - The pipeline $0E20 is called twice, from $0DB5 and $0DC3, each followed
    by a disk write. The world is generated in two passes.
  - The map is assembled on disk, not in RAM. 104 KB does not fit in 64 KB.
    RAM changes by only ~141 bytes across a whole phase boundary, which is
    what makes generation take 18 minutes — it streams sectors throughout.
  - Because writes only happen after a complete pipeline pass, snapshotting
    either RAM or the disk between phases shows nothing. That approach is a
    dead end and is recorded as such.
  - The land-mass phase writes mostly $00 and $BB. Rendering a generated map
    with $00 as ocean and $BB as land finally produces a recognisably
    map-like image, but land comes out as long thin horizontal streaks, so
    the row stride is still wrong.

A binarized stride sweep over land cells found no peak at any width from 64
to 6000, only monotonic decay. That is the second failed statistical attack
on the map layout; NOTES.md now says not to attempt a third. The next
instrument is a checkpoint on the sector-write routine $0F47, logging
(track, sector, payload) in write order, which gives the layout as ground
truth instead of inference.

Also fixes a race in the snapshot harness: after vice_execution_run the
emulator still reports "paused" briefly, so polling immediately returned at
once and silently produced several identical snapshots taken at the same
instant. It now confirms the machine resumed before waiting for a halt.
