Adds a compile-time branch so the FRUA_CBTSND fire path can run l709e(EV) in
the ALREADY-LOADED area instead of jt198(7)+l709e (which reloads GEO007 for
the old combat-sound harness). Lets a combat be fired in the fixture's own
area for the post-combat walk-return test.

Investigation result (the ogre-fight dead bar + teleport, reported on real
Mega STe hardware): CAUSE CONFIRMED BY INSPECTION. play_screen_relayout() —
the only function that rebuilds the walk command bar / DLItem pool after an
event resets it — has exactly ONE call site (boot.c:18320), and it is inside
the `if ((unsigned char)a_deep)` movement block (opened 18272). So after
combat returns to the walk loop, g_event_modal_shown is set but the relayout
that consumes it runs ONLY on the next ARROW key:
  - a bare A/E accelerator matches Phase-5 DLItems against the stale pool and
    claims nothing -> "dead";
  - Escape works because kc==27 is the direct key arm, not a DLItem;
  - the view cell (-12288..) is stale until the a_deep block snaps it to
    rec[46..], so the first render shows the wrong cell (~0,17) then snaps
    back -> the teleport. One bug, two symptoms.

Why headless accelerator tests all passed and the tavern event did not show
it: text/tavern events fire ON the entering step, so the relayout runs in that
step's a_deep block. Combat EXITS and re-enters the walk loop (jt948->jt240->
l63c0) on a fresh non-movement poll, stranding the pool. That is the whole
difference, and it is why the user only sees it after a fight.

Live repro reached the real ogre fight (slot H -> 3 steps -> roadwarden event
60 -> combat at 3,17) and confirmed it is long; FRUA_CBTPLAY stalls near the
end once the roadwarden NPC joins, so it does not cleanly finish headlessly —
next pass uses a lighter in-place combat via this flag.

Fix is identified but deliberately NOT applied here (hot-loop change; verify
against the working tavern/fixture cases first): run the pending relayout on
any event return, not only a movement step.

Eight dbg_file_str markers from main() entry through st_init, written to
DBG.LOG regardless of the console/file sink switch, plus a compile-time gate
that disables the Mega STe 16 MHz boost. Built for the real-hardware
black-screen hunt, and they earned their keep on the first outing: the diag
build moved the first file write BEFORE the display takeover, which turned an
invisible TOS timeout alert into a visible one and named the real culprit —
the SD card's writes time out on the UltraSatan (TOS "output device is not
receiving data"), leaving torn FAT updates (a directory loop on C:). Nothing
in the engine was hanging at all.

Boost A/B on emulated Mega STe at real speed, same binary otherwise:
boot-to-menu 50 s boosted vs 73 s not (-31%). Hatari 2.6.1 models the
$FFFF8E21 switch and the 16 KB cache (its status bar shows "16MHz(CE)").
On real hardware the walk loop feels similar either way, and that is
expected: the present-dominated phases are memory-bound against a bus that
still paces at 8 MHz, so the 16 MHz core + cache mostly accelerates the
compute between bus accesses — near-2x at boot, ~1.2-1.4x in blit-heavy play.

Verified on the real Mega STe today: boots, plays HEIRS through the caravan
event (the composite fix shows the merchant portrait on real silicon),
combat runs, event bigpics work.

events.title: ST: FIX the wrong event picture — the composite repainted a stale 3D scratch
events.message:
ST: FIX the wrong event picture — the composite repainted a stale 3D scratch

The "wrong picture" during the caravan event was never a wrong picture being
DRAWN: it was the last-rendered 3D corridor, repainted over the freshly-blitted
event bigpic by the viewport composite, and re-coloured through the event's
palette. The user called both halves of this from two phone screenshots
("scrambled the palette first, then never loaded the bigpic") after the
measurements had been read as "a different image". Settled with a palette-
independent edge-map test against frames from ONE run: the wrong frame shares
71.1% of its edge structure with the corridor and 42.9% with the merchant
portrait — the different-image floor is 43.6%, the same-image ceiling 100%.
A per-band colour test agrees (70.2% banded consistency vs a 36.3% control;
global mapping is the wrong test on a per-band quantiser).

Mechanism, in order:
  1. walk step: 3D view -> st_vp_scratch, commit sets s_vp_have and both
     pages' owes; the composite paints it and clears the owes — but
     s_vp_have stays set forever;
  2. event: the bigpic lands in chunky (and s_dt) via l2d4e/l309c;
  3. the event's palette install triggers a reband -> force-full, which
     rebuilds both pages from s_dt (the merchant IS there) — and then
     re-arms both owes because s_vp_have is still set (#61's fix: a page
     rebuilt from s_dt has a hole where composite content was, because the
     composite writes the PAGE, never s_dt);
  4. next present: the composite paints the STALE corridor scratch back
     over the merchant, through the new palette's remap. Deterministic, so
     byte-identical for eight days and untouched by every bridge flag —
     the composite is not a bridge.

The #61 re-arm is correct while the 3D view is the newest viewport content
and exactly wrong after a blit REPLACES that content. Fix: a superseding
screen blit now invalidates the committed scratch —
planar_viewport_overwrite(rect) in planar.c (no-op where no composite is
registered; only display_ste.c registers one), called from BOTH art writers:
l309c (the l2d4e path — where event bigpics actually land; a CopyBits-only
first attempt changed nothing, which is how that was learned) and the
CopyBits screen path. ANY overlap invalidates: compositing the whole scratch
would clobber the blit wherever they intersect, over-invalidation self-heals
on the next walk step's commit, and under-invalidation is this bug. Both
calls sit OUTSIDE the FRUA_DIAG_NO*BRIDGE guards — invalidation is about
what chunky holds, not about plane stamping, and the diag flags must not
resurrect the bug they exist to bisect.

Correction to 94f8e96b's claim: chunky never held a wrong picture. The
bridge eliminations only proved the bridges innocent; the composite writes
the PAGE directly, which is why every chunky-side probe looked clean.

Verified on the shipped ST planar config, same drive as every earlier arm:
the event viewport is now pixel-identical to the PLANAR=0 reference
(AE=0 vs the portrait, 28800 vs the old bad frame), the second text beat
keeps the portrait (matches the DOS oracle), the treasure screen's own
bigpic still shows, and the "thank you" epilogue returns to the portrait.
020 and Amiga builds clean (ECS/AGA register no composite and are
unaffected); 461 tests pass.

Known residual: fill/wipe writers (qd_pixmap_fill) do not yet invalidate.
A wipe that covers the viewport followed by NO re-render would composite
stale content back — no reachable screen does this today (the #140 wipes
are followed by a full recompose that re-commits), so it is left for the
day a screen proves otherwise.

events.title: diag: FRUA_DIAG_NOCOPYBRIDGE — the other half of the art-bridge bisect
events.message:
diag: FRUA_DIAG_NOCOPYBRIDGE — the other half of the art-bridge bisect

FRUA_DIAG_NOBRIDGE drops l309c's art-leaf plane stamp. That is NOT the path an
event picture takes: CopyBits carries "art/event pics" and stamps through
dc_plane_bridge_span, which NOBRIDGE leaves running. Testing the wrong-event-
picture bug with NOBRIDGE alone therefore proves nothing, and I read one result
that way before noticing. This flag drops just the CopyBits stamp so the two
can be used separately or together.

What the pair has established for the ST/STe planar wrong-picture bug:

  PLANAR=0                          -> correct portrait
  PLANAR=1 (shipped)                -> wrong picture
  + FRUA_PERPIXELBRIDGE             -> wrong, byte-identical
  + FRUA_DIAG_NOBRIDGE              -> wrong, byte-identical
  + FRUA_DIAG_NOCOPYBRIDGE          -> wrong, byte-identical
  + BOTH diag flags                 -> wrong, byte-identical

So the span encoder (#126b) and both art bridges are exonerated. With no art
plane-stamping at all those rows are rebuilt from chunky by st_dt_build_row, so
the CHUNKY SURFACE already holds the wrong picture — this is not a plane
conversion fault.

Also settled: it is not a palette permutation. Over the picture interior the
planar->chunky colour mapping scores 28.5-37.8% against a 28.6-31.7% noise
floor (chunky vs a 7px-shifted copy of itself); a slot permutation would sit
near 100%. The earlier greyscale-equalised comparison was suggestive but
assumed a monotonic colour error, which a permutation is not — the joint
histogram with a shifted-self control is the test that actually decides it.

That leaves an odd shape: nothing under FRUA_PLANAR in the engine or the shim
changes WHAT is written to chunky (every block is a parallel plane store), yet
chunky differs. The remaining hypothesis is layout sensitivity — the flag also
allocates ~160 KB of ST-RAM for s_dt/s_dt_cov/s_dt_idx/s_dt_rowcov and moves
every later allocation. docs say to settle that class with a RUNTIME switch in
ONE binary (see the #91 write-up: four compile-time probes changed the
incidence and some masked it entirely), which is the next step.

events.title: uainst: build frua.rsc from CKIT.EXE on the machine itself
events.message:
uainst: build frua.rsc from CKIT.EXE on the machine itself

frua.rsc was the one file you still needed a PC to produce. uainst now builds
it natively on the Atari and the Amiga, so a set of DOS floppies and the retro
machine are enough on their own — an ST reads DOS 720K/1.44M disks natively and
CrossDOS is standard on Workbench 2.1+, so the originals mount without help.

Drag CKIT.EXE onto UAINST.TTP, or `uainst CKIT.EXE .`. Dispatch is on the .EXE
extension so the existing ZIP flow, the GEM selector and the ASL requesters all
keep working untouched, and nothing in the fan corpus is a .EXE.

VERIFIED BYTE-IDENTICAL TO THE PC TOOL, THREE WAYS. The host build of the C and
tools/rsrc_from_dos.py agree over the real executable; then the SAME archive
came out of an emulated 8 MHz ST running UAINST.TTP (identical MD5, all three);
then the engine booted from that ST-built archive and drew correct menu text —
which is the functional check that matters, because STRS *is* the string pool,
so a wrong offset table would show up as garbage on screen rather than as a
load failure.

Memory was designed for the small machines: it never loads the 574 KB
executable. SHA-256 streams it in 4 KB chunks and the 2108 extractions are
seek+read, so peak use is the 29 KB pool — it runs on a 512 KB ST.

It refuses a build the map was not derived against, checking BOTH size and
SHA-256. A size-only gate would pass a same-length repack and emit a plausible
archive full of wrong strings; the test exercises both a truncated file and a
one-byte-flipped one and asserts no output file is created either time.

The 37 port-authored Mac-only strings are IMPORTED from tools/rsrc_from_dos.py
by the generator, never retyped — two hand-maintained copies would drift and
the drift would only surface as a wrong filename much later. The positions
table is generated into installer/strs_map_dos12.h at build time from the
committed JSON, the same way src/engine/a4_map.c is; positions only, no
extracted text, so the build stays redistributable.

Note the result is the DOS-sourced archive: 29 KB of STRS alone, against ~67 KB
from the Mac application which also carries FONT. Both play; with the DOS one
the engine draws its built-in 8x8 font, which is the only visible difference.

tests/test_installer.py had to learn the new source and -Iinstaller — its host
build of main.c now links the builder. 461 tests pass; all three engine builds
and both installers build; `make clean && make installer` regenerates the
header from a bare tree.

docs: the 68000 integrity check has to run on the objects, not the PRG

Asking "is this CPU68K=68000 build really free of 020 instructions?" by
grepping objdump over frua.prg gives ~6 false hits. A GEMDOS PRG's TEXT
segment carries the read-only data GCC parks in .text, and objdump
disassembles it as code — the 6 hits are one monotonic lookup table
(e9ba,61c6 / e9c2,61d4 / e9c6,61dc / ...) read as bfextu operands, with
operands like "@(623ce9fe)@(624e)" that no compiler emitted.

Summing --section=.text over every object file instead gives exactly 0.
Checked before writing a binary to a real Mega STe's UltraSatan, which is
where a phantom 020 instruction would have been an expensive thing to
wonder about later.

events.title: platform: ask a Mega STe for 16 MHz and its cache
events.message:
platform: ask a Mega STe for 16 MHz and its cache

A Mega STe boots at 8 MHz with its 16-byte cache OFF and stays there unless a
control panel or an AUTO-folder CPX says otherwise. Nothing in this engine had
ever looked — grep for _MCH / 8e21 / "mega" across src, compat and platform
returned nothing. The 68000 targets are exactly the ones that notice: the
ST/STe play loop is ~1.1 s per action at 8 MHz.

plat_cpu_boost() writes 0xFF (16 MHz + cache) to the byte at 0xFFFF8E21 and
plat_cpu_boost_restore() puts the user's value back at shutdown. The speed is
their setting, not ours.

Two details that decide whether this pokes the right machine at all:

  The register is at 8E21, not the 8E20 the Compendium's memory map prints.
  That table lists the region base with size "OB" (one byte), and ST-era
  byte-wide I/O lives at the ODD address of the word — the same convention as
  the rest of the 0xFF8xxx map.

  The gate is the WHOLE _MCH cookie == 0x00010010, not its high word. The
  Compendium's cookie table is ST 0/0, STe 1/0, ST Book 1/8, Mega STe 1/16,
  TT030 2/0 — so an "is the major 1?" test would write a nonexistent register
  on an ST Book. A plain ST has no cookie jar at all (TOS 1.04); that reads 0
  and is correctly not a Mega STe.

Verified in Hatari on all three machines, which is the specificity control that
matters for a flag like this: --machine megaste logs "Mega STe -> 16 MHz +
cache" and reaches the menu with blitter = 1; --machine ste and --machine st do
NOT log it and still reach the menu. The message lands on the CONSOLE, not
DBG.LOG — it fires before the backend takes the screen.

020 and Amiga builds unaffected (the Amiga backend does not define these and
the calls are #ifndef FRUA_AMIGA). 456 tests pass.

events.title: tools: a bisect harness for the ST/STe planar path
events.message:
tools: a bisect harness for the ST/STe planar path

Builds any SHA as the SHIPPED ST/STe planar build, drives it to the Skull Crag
caravan event, saves the frame and scores its viewport against two exact
references. Written to bisect the wrong-event-picture bug; kept because the
ST planar path has no other end-to-end regression handle.

Three traps are baked in, each of which cost a run to find:

  -DFRUA_PLANAR is passed EXPLICITLY. It only became the CPU68K=68000 default
  on 0be209c9 (26 Jul), but release-ste passed it by hand before that, so a
  bare `make CPU68K=68000` silently builds the CHUNKY path on the older half
  of the window — two different programs under one name. That produced one
  wrong conclusion before it was caught.

  It does NOT use driver.sh beginplay. That sequence assumes the Hall's letter
  accelerators ACTIVATE an item; on builds before ~27 Jul they only HIGHLIGHT
  it, so the party is never seated and the run ends in the Hall scoring as
  neither good nor bad. The extra Return here is harmless on newer builds.

  `shots` is called with gap=5, not the 0.4 s default. This screen loads a
  picture as it opens and one quiet interval mid-load reads as settled (#106) —
  that is what produced a black viewport once already.

Scoring is exact-match against both references rather than a threshold, and it
prints both distances so the caller can see "matched neither", which is what a
run that fell short of the event looks like. Do not read equal-ish distances as
a verdict; open the PNG.

capture_demo.sh had targets for falcon/tt/ste/aga/ecs but none for a plain ST,

arm of the ST/STe build had never actually been booted. Add the target, plus

It pins TOS 2.06 rather than the 1.04 the harness would pick, and the comment
says why at length: 2.06 is a real and widely fitted ST upgrade, but it is
also the ROM that dodges the Mxalloc bug fixed in the previous commit, and a
clean `st` capture must not be misread as evidence that a stock ST is fine.

docs/tos-compatibility.md records the GEMDOS-version table the bug turned on,
the five verified machine/ROM boots, the two ROM traps that each cost a run
(TOS 1.62 is STE-only and Hatari silently switches machines for it; TOS 1.04
does support GEMDOS HD emulation), the plain-ST DMA-sound gap, and the fact
that FRUA_MEM defaults to 14 MB — a size no real ST or STe can have.

events.title: platform: Mxalloc is TOS 2.01+, and its absence bus-errors the ST
events.message:
platform: Mxalloc is TOS 2.01+, and its absence bus-errors the ST

The Atari backends allocated every screen, shadow and DMA-sound buffer with
Mxalloc(size, 0). Mxalloc is GEMDOS 0x44, "available from GEMDOS version 0.19"
— and the Compendium's Sversion table pins 0.19 at TOS 2.01. So the call is
MISSING on every plain-ST ROM (1.00/1.02/1.04, GEMDOS 0.13/0.15) and on TOS
1.62 (0.17), the ROM most STes actually shipped with.

Missing is not safe. An unimplemented GEMDOS opcode returns EINVFN (-32), not
NULL, so the `== NULL` guard at each call site waved it through and st_init
then memset through 0xFFFFFFE0. Observed: frua on an emulated ST with TOS 1.04
takes a double bus error immediately after the backend logs its name, at 4 MB
and 14 MB alike.

Ruled the harness out before blaming the engine. The same TOS 1.04, same
emulated ST, same GEMDOS mount, no frua.prg: boots to the GEM desktop with a
HARD DISK icon and zero bus errors — so 1.04 does support GEMDOS emulation.
The same ST hardware with TOS 2.06 reaches the main menu. The ROM was the only
variable, which is why our whole ST/STe matrix never saw this: it has always
run TOS 2.06 (ste) and would have run 1.04 only through a target that had no
caller.

Route every site through a new plat_stram_alloc(), which picks Malloc below
GEMDOS 0.19 and collapses GEMDOS error codes to NULL so the existing NULL
checks become correct. Falling back loses nothing, provably rather than
hopefully: alternative RAM is reached through Maddalt, which is ALSO 0.19-only,
so a system without Mxalloc has no non-ST RAM for Mxalloc(size, 0) to have been
avoiding. TT and Falcon are 0.19 and 0.30 and keep the Mxalloc path.

Verified after: plain ST + TOS 1.04 reaches "menu: modal up" with
"ste: blitter = 0"; STe + TOS 1.62 reaches it with "blitter = 1"; the 020
Falcon build still smoke-boots to the menu. Sound still reports "init failed
(continuing silent)" on a plain ST — that is the absent DMA sound hardware,
tracked separately, not this.

jt312 RECT path, party seated, 60 Hz ticks on both.

  Atari STE 8 MHz (4 planes, 16 col): render 17 + present 18 = 35 ticks
  Amiga ECS 7 MHz (5 planes, 32 col): render 11 + present 22 = 34 ticks

split is what differs: ECS renders faster and presents slower.

Present is 51% (STE) / 65% (ECS) of a redraw, and both issue TWO redraws per
action, so that is where the next work belongs rather than in the renderer.

settle-detector never fires and reports its poll limit as the step time; and

events.title: Droid sprites are hires, not multicolour
events.message:
Droid sprites are hires, not multicolour

KC spotted it playing the real game in VICE: every droid is a single
colour plus transparency. The code agrees and is unambiguous:

  $190C  dMd0_droid, allocating a slot   LDA #0   / STA SpriteMC
  $187F  dMd1_bullet                     LDA #0   / STA SpriteMC
  $1BE8  ExplodeSprite                   LDA #$FF / STA SpriteMC

so only explosions are multicolour, and $190E-$1912 clear SpriteXExp and
SpriteYExp too, so there is no doubling in either direction.

A hires sprite is 3 bytes of 8 single-bit pixels - 24 pixels at the C64's
full 320-wide resolution. MODE 1 is also 320 wide, so it is a straight
1:1: 24 source pixels to 24 destination pixels, 4 per MODE 1 byte.

Worth recording WHY this survived a build, a run and a screenshot. Read
as multicolour, the same three bytes give 12 double-width pixels doubled
to 24 - the same WIDTH and the same BYTE COUNT. Nothing downstream could
catch it: the data fitted identically, every assert passed, the shifted
copy and the derived mask both still worked, and the result looked like a
droid. Only comparing against the actual game could find it.

The mask derivation is unaffected - a pixel is still transparent exactly
when both of its bits are clear - so no blitter change is needed and
drSprData stays 1743 bytes.

Colour is now DROID_COLOUR, one constant. It is logical 1: the C64 gives
enemy droids colour 0, black, but MODE 1's four logical colours belong to
the deck, and logical 1 is white on all sixteen decks whereas logical 2 is
black on fourteen and green on the other two. Per-type colour from
DColorTheme_t is a question for the combat layer.

events.title: perf: the step profiler was timing its own logger
events.message:
perf: the step profiler was timing its own logger

First measurement of the ST/STe PLAY LOOP (docs/TODO.md #4, open since the
"~47% of rows convert" figure was shown to be a BOOT number). It needed the
instrument fixed first.

`pdpf l67ca tk` sampled TickCount() at LOG time — after three dbg_log_num
calls, each an Fopen + Fseek + 3x Fwrite + Fclose through GEMDOS. It was
timing the logger. The giveaway was the value itself: 222 ticks on 40 of 43
samples (223 on the other three), because three open/write/close cycles are far
more deterministic than the work they stood in for. It also put one bracket at
3.7 s inside a step the wall clock timed at 2.4 s, which is what exposed it.
Now differenced from a stamp taken before the block, like every other bracket.

The deeper flaw was structural: J76_T/L67_T log INLINE, so any outer bracket
spanning them measures their logging too. The per-piece breakdown is now opt-in
behind -DFRUA_STEPPROF_DEEP; plain -DFRUA_STEPPROF gives clean outer totals.

With that, 24 clean samples from a 12-action walk on an 8 MHz STE (cycle-exact
Hatari, WALKTEST.DSN, ticks are 60 Hz: _hz_200 * 3/10):

    setup 0 | render 17 | present 18  = 35 ticks = 583 ms per redraw
    2 redraws per action              = ~1.2 s per walk action

Present is ~51% of a step even after the #63 work. The heavier full-recompose
path (entered via camp/menus) measured ~2.4 s per action by wall clock.

Two traps for whoever measures next: the play screen ANIMATES (torch/fire), so
"wait for two identical frames" never settles and silently reports the poll
limit as the step time; and fast-forward is safe for tick measurements (the
emulated 200 Hz timer tracks emulated time) but not for wall-clock ones.

Layer 5: two blitter optimisations, measured at 11%

Skip the always-transparent rows, and hoist the strip-wrap test out
of the row loop.

Rows 5, 14 and 20 are transparent for EVERY droid - the C64's
BuildDroidSprite and AnimateDroids simply never write them, so the
exporter points all three at the one blank row. A row that writes
nothing needs no background saved and none restored, so both passes
skip it: 14% of the rows for the price of one table lookup on the
other 18.

The wrap test was a JSR and ~27 cycles, 42 times a sprite, to answer a
question that depends only on where the sprite starts. The walk
advances at most 3 row-crossings, so if bufp + 3*ROW_BYTES + SPR_SPAN
clears SPR_WRAPLIM no row can straddle the end of the strip and every
row takes the fast path blind. True about 80% of the time; the rest
fall back to the per-row test.

Measured by A/B over 25 frames of full-speed diagonal with 7 sprites,
which is the worst case:

    before   22 px / 25 frames   3.98 frames/loop   ~19,850 cyc/sprite
    after    24 px / 25 frames   3.65 frames/loop   ~17,640 cyc/sprite

That is ~2,200 cycles a sprite, against ~1,900-2,400 predicted by the
cost model, so the model can be trusted for what is left.

Note this also corrects the figure in the previous session's notes.
14,500 came from a 10-frame sample whose +-1 px resolution is +-9%;
the 25-frame samples put the real baseline at ~19,850.

events.title: amiga: centre the AGA display window on PAL
events.message:
amiga: centre the AGA display window on PAL

First real-hardware report from the Amiga side (A1200 + Icedrake, AGA backend
on SAGA): "it also shifted the screen to the top of the monitor (might be the
fault of my monitor though)". It is not the monitor. DIWSTRT 0x2C81 /
DIWSTOP 0xF4C1 are the NTSC numbers — 200 lines from V=44 fills a 262-line
NTSC frame, but PAL has 312, so the picture sits against the top with a fat
border underneath. This file's own header already admitted it as a bring-up
simplification ("on PAL the 200 lines sit in a 256-line frame's top").

A PAL display is 256 lines from V=0x2C, so centre 200 inside it: +28 lines.
DIWSTOP's VSTOP is 8 bits with V8 implied as the complement of bit 7, so
244+28 = 272 encodes as 0x10. Safe to move — the palette is set in the copper
prologue and the list carries no line-locked WAITs, so nothing is pinned to a
scanline.

Detected at runtime from GfxBase->DisplayFlags, and logged, so a DBG.LOG says
which branch ran. Verified in amiberry (PAL by default): the log line appears
and the borders go from ~50 above / ~143 below to 102 / 91.

events.title: Layer 5 step 3a: generalise the blitter from one sprite to a pool
events.message:
Layer 5 step 3a: generalise the blitter from one sprite to a pool

sprite.asm now draws any of SPR_SLOTS sprites rather than just the
player. Slot 0 is the player; 1-6 are the droid pool, which is the
C64's arrangement too - one hardware sprite for the player and a pool
of six for everything else - so the same "no free slot" cases arise.

Per-slot state becomes arrays and the background save areas are a page
apart rather than packed into 147 bytes. A slot's save base then
differs only in its high byte, so retargeting the blit's seven
absolute addresses is seven pokes; packed bases would need a 16-bit
multiply per slot and a slower inner loop. That costs 763 bytes out of
the 5.8K step 1 released.

Restore walks the slots backwards and draw walks forwards, so where
two sprites overlap the one drawn last is restored first and the
background comes back in the order it was covered. All slots restore
before any slot draws, for the same reason.

CULLED, NOT CLIPPED for now: a sprite whose columns or scanlines do
not all fall inside the play area is skipped, so droids will pop in
and out a sprite's width from the edge. Clipping needs the slow path
taught a column and row range; deliberate for this step so the fast
path stays exactly as fast while the per-sprite cost is measured.

The cull limit also earns its keep elsewhere: with sprY <= 99 and
line <= 7 the last scanline is at most 126, one short of the strip, so
a sprite can never wrap the row 15/0 boundary and collide with the
scroll redraws.

The 2 px shifted artwork is no longer built into the gap below the
play buffer - at 1743 bytes for 24 types it does not fit. It is built
at startup directly into spare sideways RAM instead. Shipping it
pre-shifted was tried and reverted: PARADAT is staged in main RAM at
&3000 before being copied into the bank, and the extra 1743 bytes
pushed that staging area into the play buffer at &5800.

export_player.py is superseded by export_droids.py and is deleted, as
is its generated src/data/player.asm. Type 0's rows were verified
byte-identical to the old ones before removing them.

Verified in jsbeeb: the player renders and animates as before, moves
and scrolls without corruption on the shifted path, and the
runtime-built shift table at &A800 matches the Python reference byte
for byte (row 2: 00 03 F3 FF 0C 00 00 -> 00 00 3C FF CF 00 00).

events.title: Layer 5 step 2: export droid sprites, waypoints and type tables
events.message:
Layer 5 step 2: export droid sprites, waypoints and type tables

New tools/export_droids.py emits src/data/droids.asm. It supersedes
export_player.py: the player is droid type 0, so one table serves every
droid including him. Verified rather than assumed - type 0's rotor rows,
digit rows and blank row come out byte-identical to the existing
player.asm. The old files stay until sprite.asm is generalised in step 3.

Sprites: the rotor is identical for every droid and only the number
differs, so rows are shared - 5 rotor rows x 8 phases, 2 alternating end
rows x 8 phases, 8 digit rows x 24 types, one blank = 249 rows of 7
bytes. That needs two lookups, not one: a single table indexed by both
type and phase would be 24 x 8 x 21 entries. drOfs[] covers the rows
that depend on the phase, drDigit[type] the rows that depend on the type.

Waypoints: 239 records over 16 decks, 3 bytes each - char X, char Y and
a bitmask of permitted exits. Two asserts earn their place: every deck
has at least one waypoint, and each deck's records are sorted by Y,
which FindWaypoint relies on to bail out early.

Speeds are exported as both the raw C64 per-iteration value and an 8.8
per-frame conversion. Enemy droids use DSpeed_t directly - 1/2/4/8 px
per iteration, so 0.5/1/2/4 per frame - and only the player chains it
through PlayerSpeed_t.

Waypoint 0 is reserved for the player's per-deck spawn: InitDeckDroids
starts placing droids at waypoint 1 and never touches 0. Confirmed that
all 14 of deck 1's waypoints resolve through MapChar to floor, so
waypoint coordinates really are in our tile map's char space - worth
checking, since deckX/deckY in levels.asm are side-view positions
rather than map extents.

FillPanel moves out of SetupScreen to after PageDataIn: the staging area
for PARADAT now reaches past &4800 and would wipe the panel. Nothing is
displaying that early, since the IRQ is installed later.

Verified in jsbeeb: wpCount at &9FA6 and deck 0's records at &9FD6 match
the C64 byte for byte, and the deck still renders with its panel intact.

events.title: Layer 5 step 1: move PARADAT into sideways RAM
events.message:
Layer 5 step 1: move PARADAT into sideways RAM

Frees &3000-&4707 (5.8K), which Layer 5 needs for droid state and
per-slot background save buffers. Only 243 bytes were free below the
tile map.

PARADAT is assembled at &8000 so its labels resolve to their addresses
in the bank, but carries a catalogue load address of &3000 and is
copied up by PageDataIn. It cannot be *LOADed into the bank directly:
while the filing system is working the MOS has DFS paged in at &8000,
so the bytes would land in the ROM socket and be discarded.

The bank stays selected for the whole run, because MapChar reads
tiledefs and DrawHalf reads charRemap every frame. That displaces
BASIC, which we never return to, not DFS, which is in its own socket
and which the MOS pages in and back out around each of its own calls.

Banks 4 and 5 rather than 0 and 1: a Master 128's sideways RAM is
banks 4-7, so the same numbers work on both machines. A Model B SWRAM
board is jumpered to whatever you like, so nothing is lost. Probing at
boot is the eventual answer and is noted in the source.

ROMSEL and ROMSHAD are both written everywhere. The MOS restores
ROMSEL from its copy at &F4 after a service call, so writing one
without the other leaves them disagreeing and the next OS call pages
something unexpected back in.

Verified in jsbeeb rather than assumed: banks 0-7 are RAM in
B-DFS1.2; at runtime &F4 reads 4; tiledefs at &8800 is byte-identical
to the source; and changing deck still works, which exercises
BuildCharset, SetPalette and BuildLevel all reading from the bank.

events.title: Identify the source release: original/CE, not Redux
events.message:
Identify the source release: original/CE, not Redux

The listing this port is built from was documented as a disassembly of
Paradroid Redux. That was never verified, and it is wrong.

Unpacked all four C64 releases by running them under VICE and dumping RAM
at a checkpoint, then diffed them against the listing. It matches the 1985
original / 1986 Competition Edition lineage: 82.4% on the code image and
99.8% on core code at $1000-$3FFF, with "VERSION 1.0" present at $6E90.
Heavy Metal and Redux relocate everything and match at 1.2% and 2.9%.

So nothing extracted so far needs redoing, and the port is already faithful
to the original rather than to a community fork.

Original vs Competition Edition turns out to be very nearly a non-choice:
their staged code+data block differs by 8 bytes, core code is identical, and
PlayerSpeed_t/DSpeed_t are byte-for-byte the same. CE is faster because it
completes more GameLoop iterations per second, not because it moves droids
further per iteration - so on this port that dial is PLY_ITER_FRAMES.

Redux's bug list is adopted as a specification rather than as code; several
of its fixes are C64 platform bugs that cannot occur on the Beeb. Heavy Metal
is parked as a possible later tile set.

Adds tools/unpack_prg.ps1 so the unpacking is reproducible, documenting the
three runtime states a dump can land in and which regions are stable in each -
getting that wrong makes two near-identical releases look 99% different.

events.title: recreate_kit: Phase 6 — the seeded PSG read model
events.message:
recreate_kit: Phase 6 — the seeded PSG read model

The wall the Wonder Boy campaign's remaining work stands behind, built
on the registered finding: a write-ledger replay recreates the exact
false-green class it exists to fix (the RMW sites preserve bits the
game never writes), so THE CHIP'S CONTENTS ON ENTRY ARE AN INPUT —
supplied identically to both sides via psg_seed, or the run refuses.

The model: one 16-byte register file + known bitmask fed by the direct
path; select latched at $ff8800 (latch-known: a read before any
select REFUSES — the latch is an instruction, not a seed); data writes
store + append to an ordered EVENT ledger that now records READS too
(a candidate reading the wrong register is caught by the stream, not
trusted to the file); reads served only from seed or same-run writes;
unseeded reads refuse naming the remedy; final file + known part of
the differential surface. Always on; only the seed is opt-in —
nothing about the model is a claim about the game, so there is no
waiver to enforce. High-nibble selects refused (the real chip demands
a zero high nibble). Per-run reseed lives in enter_from_reset (the
CCR lesson, applied before the bench path could drift). Candidate API
include/psg.h + src/psg.c (psg_port_read/write), auto-linked.

Audio-capture mode re-based onto the shared file as a documented
relaxation; arm-from-off and audio_reset clear file AND latch (the
cross-worker leak, empirically reproduced then pinned); emu.run
refuses under an armed capture outside audio_capturing(); the
extraction re-run BYTE-IDENTICAL to the committed 43 assets.
Two-doors guard: psg_seed vs psg_regs() mis-aims refuse loudly.

Verification: kit 187 -> 247 (incl. a harness-level differential
smoke over a miniature candidate — the plumbing is exercised, not
claimed); 11/11 review mutants + 7/7 build mutants reddened;
buggyboy 292, joust 4369, wonderboy 2925 all green from clean
rebuilds; the kit's own make test now builds the oracle first (a
swept tree was silently skipping the smoke).

Docs, same commit: TRAP_MODEL Phase 6 (model/refusal tables, the
honest unpinned list); Joust STATUS's 0x152dc row (the PSG wall is
LIFTED — psg_seed={14:...}; Super is the sole remaining blocker);
BuggyBoy README's g_REFRESH latent-trap note; capture contract
docstrings aligned; the register file answers to ONE name.

events.title: Fix host pacing loop compounding usleep() overshoot into frame rate
events.message:
Fix host pacing loop compounding usleep() overshoot into frame rate

chq_sleep_handler re-anchored its "consumed" measurement from a fresh
stamp() every frame, so usleep()'s per-call overshoot (~4ms on this
host) never got clawed back and compounded frame after frame, giving a
steady ~42fps at speed=100% instead of 50fps. Switch to an absolute
wall-clock deadline that advances by the nominal duration each call, so
overshoot on one frame shortens the next frame's sleep instead of
repeating forever. A max-lag cap prevents a fast-forward burst after a
genuine stall (pause, breakpoint).

events.title: Park the Master shadow-RAM route to 2 px horizontal scrolling
events.message:
Park the Master shadow-RAM route to 2 px horizontal scrolling

Both buffers live at the same address, &5800-&7FFF, one in main RAM
and one in shadow: same 10K wrap, same R12/R13, same scroll
arithmetic, and the only difference between displaying one and the
other is ACCCON's D bit. So none of the addressing problems that
rule it out on a Model B apply - we are not fitting two circular
strips into one wrap region, we are using the same region twice.

Confirmed by KC rather than assumed: the Master's screen wrap is
driven the same way as the Model B's, via the System VIA addressable
latch, and writing ACCCON D takes effect instantly, even
mid-scanline.

Parked on cost, not feasibility. Either buffer might be displayed
next field so both must stay current, which doubles all drawing -
about +60-80% once B's edges are produced by shifting bytes out of A
instead of redrawing from the tile map, since the lookups are the
expensive half of a band. Roughly +12-16K cycles against ~5K spare.

Also corrects the Layer 3 note, which gave the Model B obstacle as
"no room for the second buffer". It is not room; it is that a
circular strip's period must equal the hardware wrap span and there
is only one such region - which is exactly why sharing one address
range across main and shadow works.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: Layer 4a: dead-zone camera and 2 px sprite positioning
events.message:
Layer 4a: dead-zone camera and 2 px sprite positioning

The CRTC's horizontal granularity is 1/80 of the display width in
every mode - it addresses in 8-byte units and a row is 80 of them -
so a scroll step is always ~4 MODE 1 pixels and at low speed the
whole world lurches. Two 10K circular strips would fix it and cannot
work on a Model B: a strip's period must equal the hardware wrap
span and there is exactly one wrap region, 10K at &5800.

So the camera moved instead. plyX is the player's own world
position at 1 px; posX only follows once the player leaves a +/-8 px
window, and then in whole 4 px units. Walking slowly the world holds
still and only the droid moves; at speed the window saturates and it
scrolls as before. Vertically nothing changed - the scroll is
already 1 scanline, so the player stays pinned.

The sprite is positioned every 2 px, which spills 24 px into seven
bytes, so rows are stored seven wide and there are two copies:
unshifted on disc, shifted built at startup into the spare space
above the panel. 2 px is not only thrift - a C64 multicolour pixel
is exactly two MODE 1 pixels, so the artwork holds no finer detail.

Masks are no longer stored. Every opaque pixel maps to logical 1, 2
or 3 and never 0, so a pixel is transparent exactly when both its
bits are clear and a 256-byte table recovers the mask. The sprite
data got smaller despite doubling.

Moving the collision reference from the view to the player changed
its offset from 159 to 11, and the C64's round-up snap then tips the
cell over - the one-pixel wall jitter, back by a different route.
Both snaps now stay inside the current cell.

Verified: 3.5 px/frame still holds on a full diagonal, and the play
buffer diffs byte-clean against RedrawAll at odd mapHX and non-zero
line with the sprite at a 2 px shift - 0 differences in 10240.

tools: the $bca2 diagnosis — Ghidra's 68000 sleigh is one deref too deep

HwPortabilityScan dropped TEN resolved `jsr (d16,An)` call edges image-
wide, $bca2 among them: 68000.sinc exports the (d16,An) operand as a
MEMORY varnode and spells the call `call [operand]`, so constant
propagation 'resolves' the site to the opcode STORED AT the target —
in no function — and the edge loop dropped it silently, while the
non-empty flow list kept it out of the I ledger. In neither ledger,
exactly as the batch-3 register entry recorded.

Fix: when a computed transfer's pcode reaches its target through a
LOAD, take the propagator's READ reference (the true EA) as the edge;
emit I whenever a computed transfer produced no row. Invariant kept:
every call/jump in exactly one ledger. 68000-specific by design.

Measured cost (Wonder Boy): +10 E rows, none removed, ten I rows
byte-identical; edges 233 -> 240. $bbca honestly -> $17b14 ->

drawer icon renders, the drawer OPENS on a double-click (which is what the
DrawerData fix buys), and the frua icon inside it draws "UA".

events.title: tools: hdr[2] is the pool's used-region length, and writing 0 was a real bug
events.message:
tools: hdr[2] is the pool's used-region length, and writing 0 was a real bug

Grounds the STRG fix in the engine instead of in statistics, and corrects the
TODO entry that sent it to the wrong layer.

l4e8a (add a string) and l501e (delete) both use header word 2 as the extent of
their jt406 move — `hdr[2] - slot` and `hdr[2] - (off+size)` — and adjust it by
+/- size. With the 0 we used to write, both go NEGATIVE for any slot past the
first, so adding or deleting a string in the in-game editor on a generated
module would move the wrong span over the packed data. That reclassifies this
from "fidelity gap, not a functional break" to a corruption bug on every module
mk_*_design.py has ever produced.

The same function settles the terminator without appeal to sampling: it takes
`len = jt423(text) + 1` and allocates `size = (len * 3 + 3) / 4`, which is
ceil(3*(strlen+1)/4) — our packing of strlen+1 codes exactly.

Adds two DATA-FREE tests for both rules, because the guards that drive the
encoder needed real areas and therefore skipped in CI: a dropped terminator was
invisible to CI even after the previous commit.

Verified end to end: a regenerated KOBOLD.DSN (hdr[2] = 163 where the old
encoder wrote 0) boots in Hatari and the engine renders its text at (3,3).

events.title: tools: geo.py STRG was not byte-faithful — the header word and the terminator
events.message:
tools: geo.py STRG was not byte-faithful — the header word and the terminator

Re-encoding a decoded SSI area rewrote 6628 of 7168 bytes. docs/TODO.md blamed
the 6-bit alphabet ("every character code comes out exactly ONE LESS than
SSI's"). That was wrong: re-packing all 1270 used strings in HEIRS reproduces
SSI's bytes EXACTLY. The alphabet and the 4-codes-per-3-bytes packing were
already right, and the accusation aimed the work at the wrong layer.

Two real defects, both outside the codec:

- STRG header word 2 is the USED BODY LENGTH (sum of the index). We wrote 0.
  Every one of the 26 HEIRS areas disagreed on exactly this field.
- SSI packs each string PLUS a NUL terminator, so the allocation is
  f(len+1), not f(len). 1218 of 1270 real strings carry it.

And one thing no encoder can derive, which is why the TODO's proposed oracle
("re-encode every SSI area and require byte equality") was unsatisfiable as
posed: SSI's allocation is EDITING HISTORY, not a function of the string.
GEO005 slot 4 and slot 67 are both 38 characters and carry different
allocations, 29 and 30 bytes, in the same file. The body tail is likewise full
of deleted-string residue (1740 nonzero bytes in GEO001).

So fidelity now comes from preserving provenance instead of deriving it:
strg_read() records each slot's index byte and raw bytes plus the tail, and
strg_write() reuses them for any string it did not change. Editing one string
perturbs that string and the offsets after it — not all 400 slots. Pass
preserve=False to force a fresh encode.

engine: a text event chaining into COMBAT froze the screen too — bound the hold

encounter on the southern edge of HEIRS. The dialogs run, combat starts — turn
sounds and all — and the display keeps the rider's bigpic. Everything after the
event is drawn into a frame nobody is allowed to show.

The step-context gate (6106cf5d) was right as far as it went, and the backstops
in l4d26 and l1806 covered a chained TEXT event and the Return prompt. A
step-triggered text event that CHAINS INTO COMBAT goes through neither: jt511's
loop runs to completion while the hold from l4d26's tail is still outstanding,
and only the walk loop's step render drops it — which cannot run until combat
returns.

event whose `chain` points at a combat event on the same square. Five Returns,
identical frame hashes throughout. The -DFRUA_NOEVHOLD control on the same drive

(AE = 0) to the control.

enumerated the exits and was wrong, which is evidence that enumeration is the
wrong shape for this. The hold now records the tick it was taken on, and

hold older than 30 ticks (0.5s) and shows the frame. The exact releases stay,
because they keep the common case flicker-free; what the bound adds is that
missing one costs a BLINK rather than a frozen game. The worst outcome now
available is the pre-#161 flash, which is where this started.

per-glyph typewriter present (6543b358) is independent and is what actually

events.title: Layer 4: the player droid - sprite, controls, wall collision
events.message:
Layer 4: the player droid - sprite, controls, wall collision

The player is pinned at the centre of the play area and the deck
scrolls underneath it, driven by the C64's own acceleration model.

The sprite does not exist in the C64 data: the dynamic sprite area
ships zeroed and BuildDroidSprite / AnimateDroids construct every
droid at runtime. tools/export_player.py replays both offline for
droid 001 and emits MODE 1 data - 8 rotor phases, 768 bytes.
PlayerSprite_dat puts the player at x=148, a multiple of 4, so it
lands on a CRTC unit boundary and needs no pre-shifted variants.

Scrolling is now a 16.8 pixel position rather than a fixed step, so
ScrollUp/Down/Left/Right and DrawScanline are gone, replaced by
ApplyMove and DrawBand. The addressing invariant that makes this
work is documented in scroll.asm.

The C64 speed constants are per GameLoop iteration and an iteration
is 2-3 frames, not 1 - DrawScreen alone is ~17,250 cycles against
~18,300 usable in a PAL frame. Converted to per-frame, top speed is
3.5 px rather than 7. That also halved the redraw work, so the frame
budget closes: 35 px per 10 frames on both axes of a full-speed
diagonal, frame-locked.

Collision is the 12-probe diamond from CheckPlyAdvance. The
reference cell must use the C64's ceiling-rounded origin, or the
snap moves the cell and the player jitters against walls.

Charset moved to &0400 - Layer 4 filled the space below &3000.

Verified: play buffer diffed byte-for-byte against RedrawAll at odd
mapHX and non-zero line after diagonal scrolling, 0 differences in
10240.

events.title: docs: a pgrep -f poll loop matches its own shell and never exits
events.message:
docs: a pgrep -f poll loop matches its own shell and never exits

Four background waiters were found still alive after 9, 6, 3 and 3 days, each
respawning a `sleep` forever and burning a few seconds of CPU per day. Three of
them were the same mistake:

    until ! pgrep -f "make release-all" >/dev/null; do sleep 10; done

That can never exit. The shell evaluating the pgrep has "make release-all" in
its OWN command line, so the pattern always matches something — itself — and the
loop polls until killed. The fourth waited for a marker string in a task output
file whose task had already died, which is the same shape of never.

This repo already warns "never pkill -f hatari — -f matches your own shell", in
CLAUDE.md and in the run-falcon-port skill. The warning was right and I wrote
the polling version of it anyway, three times. Generalised in the skill's
gotchas, with the fixes: wait on a marker the work itself writes, bracket the
pattern (`[m]ake release-all`), or run it in the foreground with a timeout.

Same family as de4455fc — a harness command that can wait forever eventually
does, and the cost is litter that outlives the session that made it.

events.title: harness: hatari_ui.sh could hang forever on the command FIFO
events.message:
harness: hatari_ui.sh could hang forever on the command FIFO

Two shells were found still alive after 7 days and 4 days respectively, each
holding Hatari's --cmd-fifo open and doing nothing — one blocked in `dbg`, one
in `quit` — long after the sessions that started them had ended. Zero CPU, no
output, no notification: exactly the kind of leftover nobody notices.

A write to a FIFO blocks until something opens it for reading. With Hatari dead
(or never started) `echo > "$STATE/cmd.fifo"` waits forever, and the
`2>/dev/null || true` on two of those call sites does not help at all, because
the block is in open(2) — there is no error and no exit status to ignore.

All six writers now go through fifo_send(), which refuses when hatari is not
running and bounds the write with `timeout` regardless, returning non-zero
instead of hanging. Callers decide whether that is fatal: `dbg` and `dump` die,
`quit` and the two start-time options carry on.

Also: `start` now checks DISPLAY itself. This script does NOT bootstrap an Xvfb
— driver.sh does — so calling it directly under `env -u DISPLAY` reached SDL and
produced "could not initialize the SDL library: x11 not available", which reads
like a broken X install on a machine where X is the only thing available. It
means DISPLAY is unset. That message is what the 7-day-old shell had logged
before it wedged, and it sent the diagnosis in the wrong direction.

Verified: `dbg` with nothing running exits 1 in under a second where it used to
hang; `quit` with nothing running exits 0; `start` with no DISPLAY names the
real cause. The live paths are unchanged — boot + stable screenshot + graceful
quit with --confirm-quit off completes in ~1s, which is the path that finalizes
an --avirecord AVI and the only reason `quit` exists.

events.title: engine: the #161 hold froze the Merchant chain — arm it only for a walk step
events.message:
engine: the #161 hold froze the Merchant chain — arm it only for a walk step

Shipped in v0.9.4-beta, reported from real hardware the same day: "the second
screen from the Merchant, when you hit enter, it seems the game freezes (I
think that is when it normally tries to load the treasure screen)."

It does, and it is the event-tail present hold from af8149bf. The repair half
of that hold lives in l63c0's per-step re-render, so it is only safe where that
re-render is guaranteed to follow. The area-ENTRY chain (jt948/jt953 -> l709e)
is not such a place: the HEIRS caravan pages run and hand off to the
give-treasure modal without ever reaching the step render, so a hold taken in
l4d26's tail was released by nobody, every later present was swallowed, and the
display stopped while the engine ran on behind it.

Reproduced in one drive (autoload.dat onto a HEIRS save): the caravan hand-over
page takes the Return — the button visibly highlights — and nothing advances;
ten seconds later the frame is byte-identical. The A/B settles the attribution
outright: the same drive on a -DFRUA_NOEVHOLD build goes straight to "EACH
CHARACTER RECEIVES 100 EXPERIENCE POINTS", and the fixed build now produces
that frame BYTE-IDENTICAL to that control.

Three changes:

  - g_event_step_ctx: the hold arms ONLY inside the walk step's event dispatch,
    the one context that provably reaches the release.
  - l4d26 drops any outstanding hold on entry, so a chained event cannot draw
    under the previous one's.
  - l1806 drops it too — that is the "Press RETURN to continue" wait, and the
    rule it encodes is the general one: NEVER WAIT FOR THE PLAYER BEHIND A HELD
    FRAME. That is exactly what "the game freezes" looks like from the chair.

Both behaviours verified on the Falcon. The Merchant chain now runs through to
the treasure pile with VIEW|TAKE|POOL|SHARE|EXIT; and the #161 case this hold
exists for is still fixed — a burst capture of a step onto an unprompted text
square goes typing -> settled with no blank-box, no-command-bar intermediate,
and the settled frame matches the known-good hash.

A hold whose release lives in a different function than its acquire is only as
safe as the narrowest path between them, and the cost of getting that wrong is
not a flicker — it is a frozen game.

446 host tests pass; ST/68000, Amiga AGA and Amiga ECS all link.

events.title: Fix diagonal scrolling corrupting the split row
events.message:
Fix diagonal scrolling corrupting the split row

DrawColumn writes all 8 scanlines of every row it touches, including
display row 0 - which is the split row, where scanlines 0..line-1
belong to map row mapYr+16 rather than mapYr. A column redraw
overwrote them. Those scanlines are invisible at the time, so the
damage only surfaced once `line` wrapped and that row rotated round
to the bottom of the window, which is why it read as mess being left
behind rather than a column drawn wrong.

DrawColumn now repairs its display-row-0 cell from mapYr+16 after
the main loop, via DrawHalfPart.

RedrawAll had the same blind spot, and that mattered beyond the bug:
it is the diff oracle, so every byte-clean result so far had been
blind to exactly the region where this class of bug lives. It now
applies the same repair across all 80 units, making a full redraw a
true repair at any scroll position and the oracle valid at any value
of line.

Verified at line = 3, where the split row is live: diagonal
right+down and diagonal left+up both 0 of 10240 bytes differing.

Note recorded in PLAN.md: the oracle must be allowed ~1,500,000
cycles to settle after releasing SPACE. RedrawAll plus its split
pass runs longer than that, and sampling it mid-redraw shows display
row 0 rewritten by the main loop but not yet repaired - which looks
exactly like the fix having failed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: kieranhj

events.title: Layer 3d: smooth vertical scrolling at 1-scanline granularity
events.message:
Layer 3d: smooth vertical scrolling at 1-scanline granularity

Vertical steps drop from 8 scanlines to 1, using R5 (vertical total
adjust) to give the playfield cycle `line` extra scanlines and take
them back from the cycle above it, so the frame total stays at 312.
Three CRTC cycles now, not two: with only two, the variable adjust
falls between VSync and the panel and the panel slides while
scrolling. A third tail cycle carries VSync so both adjusts sit
after the panel, where they cancel.

Buffer row 0 is a split row holding two map rows at once, in
disjoint scanline ranges, so a step costs one 80-byte scanline strip
rather than a 640-byte row. DrawRow is deleted along with the defect
it produced three times.

Hard-won details, all recorded in PLAN.md:

- R4/R5 belong to the cycle that samples them; R6, R7 and R12/R13
  must be written during the PREVIOUS cycle. Writing R7 at the row
  it should fire on means VSync never happens and the chip
  free-runs.
- Never write R5 near a cycle boundary. The vertical adjust compares
  a rising count against R5, so changing it after the count has
  passed runs the adjust on to its 5-bit wrap.
- The display window must fit inside ONE hardware wrap: the address
  translator subtracts once when MA12 goes high and does not
  iterate. 16 displayed rows is therefore the ceiling with the 10K
  wrap, so the play area is 15 visible rows - 320x120, not 320x128.
- Blank/unblank via CRTC R8 skew bits must land in horizontal
  blanking or it cuts a scanline part-way across. T1_PROBE measures
  the phase by cutting the solid panel box.

Verified by diffing the buffer against RedrawAll: 0 of 10240 bytes
differing across up, down, and mixed runs at odd mapHX with scrollS
wrapped mid-row. Frame confirmed at exactly 312 scanlines by
counting 1000 VSyncs in 39,936,000 cycles.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: kieranhj

events.title: Widen the scroll redraw window and fix diagonal CRTC ordering
events.message:
Widen the scroll redraw window and fix diagonal CRTC ordering

Release the main loop when the play area stops displaying rather than
at VSync. The play area is frame rows 8-23 and the panel draws from
&4800, so writing the play buffer while the panel shows is safe. That
makes the usable window rows 24 to 8 of the next frame - 24 rows,
against about 23 for a worst-case redraw. Releasing at VSync (row 34)
gave only 13 and was overrunning every step.

T1s three fires have to land in different windows and one period cannot
do it: cycle 1 setup needs rows 0-7, cycle 2 setup rows 8-15, and the
redraw release rows 24-26. The latch is therefore rewritten during fire
1; T1 reloads its counter at underflow, so the write takes effect one
reload later, keeping fire 2 at 8 rows while moving fire 3 out to 13.

SetCRTCStart is now called once, after all key handling and before any
drawing. Previously each Scroll routine parked the address itself, so
on a diagonal move the second ones park landed after the first ones
redraw - past frame row 3, where the IRQ latches R12/R13. The CRTC then
used an address missing one axis while the buffer held the combined
position, giving one frame of wrong graphics on the trailing edge. The
scroll routines now only set flags and DoRedraws does the drawing.

Redraws run in raster order: row 0 first since it displays at frame row
8, then the columns spanning rows 8-23, then row 15 which is not shown
until row 23. A diagonal does two redraws in one window, so the tightest
has to go first.

Adds a DEBUG_DRAW build flag that tints the background for the duration
of the redraw, making the scanlines it occupies visible. That is what
measured the window; the redraw is ~23 rows, not the ~14 previously
estimated. Off by default.

Corrects the record on the DrawRow defect. It was characterised as unit
39 onward after an odd offset; both halves are wrong. A diagonal diff
found it corrupting units 2-78 with mapHX even. Every column and every
other row matched a full redraw exactly, so DrawRow alone is at fault.
Diagonal movement calls it every step, so the artifact is now permanent
rather than occasional. PLAN.md recommends reverting DrawRow to the
pre-optimisation version, which diffed byte-clean twice.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: kieranhj

events.title: Layer 3c: vertical rupture - static panel above scrolled play area
events.message:
Layer 3c: vertical rupture - static panel above scrolled play area

Two CRTC cycles per TV frame. Reprogramming R4 mid-frame ends a cycle
early and the next reloads VMA from R12/R13, so each cycle has its own
screen start:

  cycle 1  static panel  R4=7   8 rows   R6=5   R7=255  &4800/8
  cycle 2  scrolled play R4=30  31 rows  R6=16  R7=26   (&5800+scrollS)/8
                                -------
                                39 rows = 312 scanlines

Cycle 1 shows 5 rows of panel then 3 blank - the title-plus-gap the C64
has above its play area. VSync lands at frame row 8+26 = 34, which is
MODE 1's default R7, so the TV sees an identically phased frame.

Three things were needed to make the split hold steady, and the first
two were wrong before KC spotted them:

Interlace off (R8=0). The OS leaves MODE 1 at R8=1, interlace sync,
which offsets VSync by half a scanline on alternate fields. Fixed
intervals measured from VSync then land the split in a different place
every other field.

System VIA T1 in continuous mode, not T2. T2 is one-shot only, so the
interval starts when the handler writes T2C-H and every interrupt's
service latency feeds into the next interval - jitter accumulates. T1
continuous auto-reloads from its latch at underflow, so the period is
exact however late we are serviced. VSync restarts it to keep the
stages phase locked.

IRQ1V taken over outright, nothing chained, so the MOS handler never
runs ahead of ours adding latency. Costs the MOS 100 Hz tick and with
it MOS sound. Keyboard is unaffected (OSBYTE &81 scans the matrix
directly) and the filing system is only needed before takeover, so
*LOAD now runs before InstallIrq. Both VIAs have every interrupt source
disabled except System VIA CA1 and T1; anything unserviced would hold
the IRQ line asserted. The MOS saves the interrupted A in &FC but not
X or Y, so the handler saves those itself.

Both stage interrupts deliberately land 3 rows inside their cycle
rather than on the boundary, leaving ~4 rows clear of the deadline
(C4 reaching the old R4).

SetCRTCStart no longer writes R12/R13 - the IRQ owns them - so it
computes the address and parks it, with SEI around the store.

Adds a DEBUG_RASTER build flag that tints the background at entry to
each interrupt, making the scanline each one lands on visible. That is
what diagnosed the margin problem; reasoning from the timing numbers
had led the wrong way. Off by default.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: Optimise vertical scrolling; fix two DrawHalf/DrawRow bugs
events.message:
Optimise vertical scrolling; fix two DrawHalf/DrawRow bugs

Vertical scrolling is now frame-locked, matching horizontal: 10 steps
in 10 frames, up from 4.

Two changes. Replacing the SetCell add-640 loop with lookup tables
moved vertical 4 -> 5, so that loop was not the dominant cost - that
diagnosis was wrong. The win came from rewriting DrawRow to hoist what
is constant across a row: cellY does not change, so the tile-map row
base and sub-row offset are computed once rather than 80 times, the
tile pointer only moves every 4 characters, and the character code is
fetched once per PAIR of units because a character is two 4-pixel
halves. DrawRow no longer calls DrawHalf/MapChar and reuses their zero
page.

Fixed: DrawHalf computed halfX >> 1 by shifting halfX+1 in place and
restoring it with ASL, which only works when the low bit was 0. Only
RedrawAll walks halfX incrementally, so the damage was written at deck
load and then persisted, because incremental scrolling only redraws
edges and never repairs the interior. Triggers when mapHX+79 crosses
256 - decks 2 and 14.

Fixed: on a row starting at an odd unit, DrawRow's right-half path read
chp before it had ever been set, drawing a stale character in the
leftmost column. chp is now primed by FetchChar before the loop.

KNOWN DEFECT, accepted for now: after scrolling to an odd unit then
scrolling vertically, the last row DrawRow drew is wrong from unit 39
onward - where its 6th tile begins. 41 cells, confirmed against both
RedrawAll and the tile map directly, so DrawRow is at fault. Root cause
not isolated. See PLAN.md for the revert option.

Adds a debug key (SPACE) that forces RedrawAll, so the incremental
buffer can be diffed against a full redraw at the same position. That
is what isolated both bugs. Note that two earlier runs of that harness
reported zero differences and were worthless: both used an even number
of horizontal steps, so the odd-column path never executed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: kieranhj

events.title: Go direct to hardware for palette and vsync
events.message:
Go direct to hardware for palette and vsync

Removes both OS calls from the main loop.

Palette: SetPalette writes the video ULA palette register &FE21
instead of going through VDU 19. The register takes
(logical << 4) | (physical EOR 7), and the logical field is a
content-addressable match - in a 4-colour mode only bits 7 and 5 are
compared, so bits 6 and 4 must be written in every combination or the
colour comes out split. All 16 entries are written, each mapped back
with logical = ((n AND 8) >> 2) OR ((n AND 2) >> 1), giving four
entries per logical colour and covering 0-15 exactly.

VSYNC: IrqHandler sits at the head of IRQ1V, counts fields and chains
on to the OS so its timers and keyboard scan keep working. Polling the
System VIA IFR bit 1 directly would race the MOS, whose own handler
services vsync and clears that flag before a poll is likely to see it.

Verified: palette output identical to the VDU 19 version, and
horizontal scrolling still measures exactly 10 steps in 10 frames.

keydown still uses OSBYTE &81. Replacing it means driving the keyboard
matrix directly, which contends with the MOS scan in its IRQ handler,
so it belongs with a full IRQ takeover rather than done piecemeal.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: kieranhj

events.title: Layer 3b: CRTC hardware scrolling with edge redraw
events.message:
Layer 3b: CRTC hardware scrolling with edge redraw

Play area verified against the C64: DrawScreen writes to $4940, which
is $140 past the $4800 screen base, so character row 8, and draws 17
rows by 39 columns. That includes the fine-scroll margin, so the
visible area is 38x16 chars = 304x128 px = 9.5x4 tiles.

Rounded up to 10x4 tiles = 320x128. 10240 bytes is exactly 16 rows of
640, and the BBC supports a 10K wrap natively - System VIA addressable
latch lines 4 and 5 both high select subtract $2800, restart $5800 - so
both axes wrap cleanly. Rounding up rather than down also avoids
narrowing the play area.

The buffer is a circular strip, not a flat grid: display cell (row,
unit) lives at BUF_BASE + ((scrollS + row*640 + unit*8) MOD 10240). The
CRTC gives a one-dimensional scroll through linear memory, so a
character leaving the left reappears one row up on the right. Drawn as
a flat grid that is corruption, and it scales with the offset - at 80px
the right quarter shows the wrong rows. Treated as a circular strip it
is just where the next column lives, and a step costs 16 cells
horizontally or 80 vertically instead of a ~640 character full redraw.

A MODE 1 CRTC unit is one byte per scanline = 4 pixels, and characters
are already stored as two 8-byte halves, so a 4-pixel column is exactly
one stored half-character. Sub-character horizontal scrolling needs no
pre-shifted data.

WaitVSync (OSBYTE 19) puts both R12/R13 writes and the edge redraw in
the blanking window. The two writes form a 14-bit value; a CRTC sample
landing between them would show a frame at a half-updated address.

Measured over 10 frames with the key held: horizontal 10 steps,
vertical 5. Replacing the SetCell add-640 loop with lookup tables took
vertical from 4 to 5, so that loop was not the dominant cost - that
diagnosis was wrong. OSBYTE 19 quantises to whole frames, so vertical
is sitting just above the one-frame boundary and crossing it jumps
straight to 10. MapChar is the likely remaining cost: it rebuilds the
tile-map row base per cell, which for DrawRow is constant across all 80.

Source split into screen.asm (buffer addressing, DrawHalf, MapChar,
RedrawAll), scroll.asm (scroll directions, SetCell, offset tables) and
level.asm (deck decode, charset build, palette, framing). Data moved to
&3000: the OS believes the screen is &3000-&7FFF but only &5800-&7FFF
is now fetched for display.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: Fix $D023, and confirm multicolour ALERT lettering is faithful
events.message:
Fix $D023, and confirm multicolour ALERT lettering is faithful

$D023 was set to 6 (blue) on a guess when I could not find where the
play area sets it. Tracing every write: the only character-mode writes
to $D022/$D023 are in DrawSideview ($308A/$308F), setting $F1/$F0, and
those persist into gameplay. The other hits in that area are +3/+4/+$C,
which are the sprite multicolour registers, not the character ones. So
$D023 is 0 (black). Having it wrong corrupted every multicolour cell on
every deck.

$D021 remains an assumption. It comes from bgColor, which
SetIntroColors loads from slot 3 of the deck record, but slot 3 does not
match the lavender floor in the reference screenshot - so gameplay sets
it somewhere not yet found. 14 is taken from the screenshot and is
marked [assumed] in export_bbc.py.

The joined ALERT letters are faithful, not a port bug. Row 0 of tile 22
is the lettering and sits on palette slot 7, which is multicolour under
8 of the 16 deck schemes - 4 pixels wide, so single-pixel letter gaps
cannot exist. The C64 renders it the same way. Keeping fidelity for now
rather than forcing those characters to hires.

New tools/compare_tile.py renders a tile side by side, C64 against port,
which is what settled this. analyse_alert.py was checking row 1 rather
than row 0, so it reported every deck as fine while eight of them drew
the letters in multicolour; it now checks the lettering itself and
distinguishes faithful joining from an actual port bug.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: kieranhj

events.title: Correct the tile format: hires and multicolour cells are mixed
events.message:
Correct the tile format: hires and multicolour cells are mixed

The tiles are neither 1bpp hires (first assumption) nor wholly
multicolour (second). $D016 bit 4 enables multicolour text mode
globally, but within that mode the choice is made PER CELL by bit 3 of
the colour RAM nibble: 0-7 renders hires, 8-15 renders multicolour. For
deck 1 the split is 930 hires cells to 190 multicolour.

That is why the ALERT lettering keeps single-pixel letter spacing while
the floor still carries four colours - a 4-pixel-wide multicolour
character could not produce the former. Much of the apparent richness is
per-cell colour rather than multicolour: adjacent hires cells with
different foregrounds read as a multi-coloured tile.

The mode is driven per character code by CharColor ($0800), whose upper
nibble is a palette slot. NewCharColors ($3577) rewrites the lower
nibble per deck from a 12-slot record at $6A44 selected by
deckColorScheme ($F160), and BuildLevel writes that byte to colour RAM.
Only slot 5 is multicolour in every scheme and only slot 11 is hires in
every scheme, so a character's mode genuinely changes between decks.
charset.asm is therefore built for deck 1 only; PLAN.md records
generating it at deck-load time as the way to cover all sixteen, which
needs less data than one converted charset.

export_bbc.py now selects the mode per character and assigns MODE 1
logical colours from measured usage across the tile set rather than by

rip_deck_mixed.py renders a deck as the C64 actually displays it, and

colour records at $6A44 number 8, not 16 - entries past that hold values

events.title: Layer 3a: map browser - scroll by character, switch decks
events.message:
Layer 3a: map browser - scroll by character, switch decks

Z/X/K/M scroll the viewport one character at a time; UP/DOWN switch
deck. Full-screen redraw per step, no hardware scroll yet. This proves
DrawScreen renders correctly from an arbitrary map origin, which is the
prerequisite for the CRTC scroll in 3b.

DrawScreen generalised to a (charX, charY) origin over the 256x64
character map. The row base is cheap because tilemap is page aligned
and 1K: lo = (tileRow AND 3) << 6, hi = HI(tilemap) + (tileRow >> 2).

Deck keys are edge triggered. A blocking wait-for-release deadlocks:
hold UP before releasing DOWN and it spins forever, swallowing the
press.

CentreOnDeck frames a deck on load, since decks sit at varying offsets
in the grid and a (0,0) origin lands in empty padding. Uses the
centroid of non-empty tiles rather than the bounding box - several
decks are two clusters far apart, and the midpoint of the extremes
falls in the gap between them. Division is by repeated subtraction; the
quotient cannot exceed 63 and this runs once per deck change.

Code moved to &1100 rather than DFS PAGE of &1900: &1100-&18FF is
random-access file buffer space that simple *LOAD never touches. 2K
reclaimed.

Measured: a full-screen redraw is ~466,000 cycles, about 11 frames, so
roughly 4 scroll steps per second. plot_char dominates at ~256 cycles
for its 16-byte copy. That is the number 3b has to beat by beating
redrawing only the leading column - 25 characters instead of 1000.

Confirmed INKEY codes: Z -98, X -67, K -71, M -102, UP -58, DOWN -42,
with *FX 4,1 to stop the cursor keys doing cursor editing.

events.title: Layer 2: static deck render
events.message:
Layer 2: static deck render

BuildLevel RLE-decodes a deck into a tile map; DrawScreen renders the
viewport from it.

Divergence from the C64: the original expands every tile into a 256x64
character map at $8000 (16K). We keep only the 64x16 tile map (1K) and
expand tiles to characters at draw time - two extra lookups per
character against a ~100 cycle 16-byte copy, for a 15K saving. Scrolling
redraws only the leading edge, so that overhead lands on a column of 25
characters rather than the whole screen.

Code and data now build as two disc files. VDU 22 makes the OS clear
what it still believes is its screen, &3000-&7FFF, so data loaded above
&3000 was wiped before BuildLevel could read it. PARADAT is *LOADed
after the mode change instead. The eventual fix is to program the video
ULA and CRTC directly rather than going through VDU 22.

verify_bbc.py --tilemap diffs a tile map dumped from the emulator
against a fresh Python RLE decode. Decks 1 and 3 both match all 1024
bytes, with non-empty counts agreeing with level_stats.txt. Deck 3 was
picked deliberately: its RLE lives above &3000 and so exercises the
clear-on-mode-change bug, where deck 1 sits below &3000 and rendered
identically either way.

events.title: Layer 1: graphics data pipeline
events.message:
Layer 1: graphics data pipeline

tools/export_bbc.py converts the C64 data to BeebASM sources in
src/data/: the $7800 charset to MODE 1, plus tile definitions, deck
maps and metadata carried over byte-identical.

The 1bpp -> MODE 1 conversion turns out to be a nibble split. MODE 1
holds pixel n low colour bit in bit 3-n, so storing the foreground as
logical colour 1 makes the left four pixels of a scanline (b >> 4) and
the right four (b & 0x0F). Two things fall out of that: per-deck
recolouring is a palette change rather than baked into the tiles,
mirroring the C64 CharColor table; and a character is 16 contiguous
bytes, so plotting one is a flat 16-byte copy with no shift or mask.

src/main.asm now renders all 32 tile definitions as an 8x4 sheet,
matching tools/output/tiles.png. tools/verify_bbc.py independently
round-trips the generated data back to C64 form and diffs it against
the listing - 5/5 checks pass.

src/data/ is gitignored: it is converted game artwork and level data,
so the same copyright position as tools/output/. Regenerate it with
tools/export_bbc.py.

events.title: engine: saved characters become <design>.DSN\SAVE\<NAME>.CCH
events.message:
engine: saved characters become <design>.DSN\SAVE\<NAME>.CCH

The last save-interop gap, and it was ours. Both original releases keep saved
characters as <NAME>.CCH in the design's SAVE folder — DOS demonstrably, and
the Mac through jt584, which builds design + "SAVE" + name + "cch" via jt431
and has been lifted in this tree the whole time. The slot-numbered
CHAR0000.CHR in the flat gamedata folder was this port's 8.3 workaround from
before that path existed, not a 1.0-vs-1.2 or Mac-vs-DOS difference.

The name goes through the faithful jt130 — strip the 17 filename-hostile
characters at A5 -31268, truncate to 8, uppercase — which is exactly DOS's 8.3
rule: LADY ILLIS -> LADYILLI.CCH, STRANILLA -> STRANILL.CCH. The list still
shows the full name; that comes from rec[96] inside the file.

The two formats turned out to be identical. A DOS BARBARUS.CCH and our
CHAR0000.CHR are both 506 bytes with the name at offset 96, so nothing had to
be converted — only named and filed correctly.

Verified in BOTH directions on the Falcon. A DOS-authored BARBARUS.CCH dropped
into HEIRS.DSN\SAVE\ appears in ADD A CHARACTER and joins the party at the
AC -3 / HP 62 the DOS release itself shows for it; and after our engine had
rewritten that file, DOS FRUA still lists it in its own Add screen.

Existing installs migrate on first boot: when the SAVE folder holds no .CCH the
loader falls back to the flat CHAR*.CHR and immediately writes the roster out
under the new names (all six HEIRS characters, verified). The old files are
left in place — a failed migration that also deleted the source would be
unrecoverable.

★ THERE IS DELIBERATELY NO SWEEP OF THE SAVE FOLDER. The old save_roster
deleted every CHAR*.CHR it had not just written, which was safe because it
owned that namespace. It does not own this one: DOS- and Mac-authored
characters live in the same folder, and "delete what we did not write" would
destroy them. Each pool slot now remembers the file it owns and drops only that
file when the character is renamed or deleted.

Two things this turned up on the way:

  - the Add-a-Character list is fed by l01be enumerating FILES, not by the
    in-memory pool. So a migrated roster looked EMPTY until something wrote the
    new files — the pool was full and the folder was not. Hence the immediate
    save after a migration read.
  - my own truncation bug cost a boot: l01be built its open path with a 19-char
    cap sized for a bare 8.3 name, so "HEIRS.DSN\SAVE\BARBARUS.CCH" was cut to
    "HEIRS.DSN\SAVE\BARB", FSOpen failed, and the list rendered as a blank box
    — indistinguishable from "no such file" until the pattern and the read were
    traced separately.

Also fixes cg_roster_merge_files, which required a 512-byte read of a file that
is ~506 bytes: the test could never pass, so that merge has been silently dead.
It now scans the SAVE folder and requires only enough bytes to hold the record.

446 host tests pass; ST/68000, Amiga AGA and Amiga ECS all link.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
